cases.title: When Something Your Partner's Family Said or Did Didn't Sit Right
cases.subtitle: Who is more likely to notice a family comment or behavior that needs a boundary?

questions.prompt: Who is more likely to notice a family comment or behavior that needs a boundary?

options.label: Me, no contest
Probably me
Probably them
Definitely them
Honestly, both of us about equally

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: What best explains that answer?

options.label: spots disrespect beneath polite wording
notices when the couple's privacy is crossed
tracks repeated family patterns
feels the impact of comments about identity or choices
wants the relationship protected without creating a family showdown
can separate the family member from the specific behavior

questions.interactionRule: Display as the answering player’s own voice.

questions.prompt: What boundary felt crossed?

options.label: Privacy
Respectful language
Time and access
Money or favors
Parenting or life choices
Loyalty to the couple's decisions

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: What response would feel proportionate?

options.label: A private couple check first
The partner addresses their own family
A brief in-the-moment redirect
Less access to one topic
A written boundary before the next visit
A follow-up only if the behavior repeats

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: Want to tell the court a bit more about what happened? (optional)
questions.interactionRule: Private context is used only to personalize the selected deterministic branch.

outcomes.verdict: [A] notices when a family comment or action crosses the couple's privacy, respect, or decision-making line. [B] sees the concern too, which means the relationship does not need a trial about whether the moment counted. The next move is proportionate support. [B] should address [B]'s own family when possible, using one specific behavior and one future boundary. [A] can request backing without asking [B] to reject the whole family system.
outcomes.actions_a: Name the specific behavior, impact, and future boundary without expanding it into a judgment of the family.
outcomes.actions_b: Address your family directly or agree on the exact in-the-moment response you will give next time.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Family Boundary Script with behavior, impact, boundary, speaker, repeat response, and post-visit check.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. The couple stands together around one clear boundary, not against an entire family.
outcomes.role_note: [A] = the partner both identified as more likely to notice a needed family boundary.

outcomes.verdict: [B] catches the family moment that unsettles privacy, respect, or the couple's shared decisions. [A] recognizes the issue, which gives you a chance to respond as a team before resentment attaches to the family relationship. [A] takes the lead with [A]'s own relatives when appropriate. [B] names the exact behavior and needed future line. The boundary stays focused enough to protect both the couple and workable family connection.
outcomes.actions_a: Take the lead with your family using the agreed behavior, impact, and future boundary.
outcomes.actions_b: Name the specific line you need and avoid asking [A] to defend you against unrelated family history.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Family Boundary Script with behavior, impact, boundary, speaker, repeat response, and post-visit check.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Support becomes visible without turning the family bond into collateral damage.
outcomes.role_note: [B] = the partner both identified as more likely to notice a needed family boundary.

outcomes.verdict: Both of you notice family boundary crossings, which means the couple has a strong shared instinct for privacy and respect. The risk is escalating each other's irritation until a focused issue becomes a family-wide story. Use a twenty-four-hour rule before major responses, unless safety or urgent harm is involved. Agree on the smallest boundary that protects the couple, and let the partner connected to that family deliver it.
outcomes.actions_a: Name the smallest boundary that would prevent a repeat and the outcome you want after it is delivered.
outcomes.actions_b: Draft the message to your own family and remove any extra history that does not change the request.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Smallest Effective Family Boundary with behavior, request, speaker, timing, repeat step, and desired relationship outcome.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Shared loyalty becomes precise protection instead of shared escalation.

outcomes.verdict: Each of you sees yourself as the family-boundary radar, which may mean you monitor different doors. [A] notices privacy or comments; [B] notices demands, access, or loyalty pressure. Keep both radars and assign lanes. The partner whose family is involved leads the response, while the other partner supplies impact and the boundary needed. Neither person has to police every door alone.
outcomes.actions_a: Choose the family-boundary lane you notice best and state the impact without scripting the entire response.
outcomes.actions_b: Choose your different lane and commit to leading with your own relatives when that door is crossed.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Family Boundary Radar Map with lanes, common triggers, family-side speaker, partner support, and repeat response.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Two radars protect different doors while the couple stays on the same side.

outcomes.verdict: Each of you thinks the other notices family issues first, which may reflect trust in the partner's read or hesitation to be the person who raises tension around family. Create a neutral check after visits: 'Anything we should clear before we move on?' Each partner names one moment at most. The family-connected partner does not have to agree with every interpretation before acknowledging the impact and considering a boundary.
outcomes.actions_a: Bring one specific moment to the check and state whether you need listening, reassurance, or action.
outcomes.actions_b: Acknowledge the impact first and choose whether the next step is no action, observation, or a boundary.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Post-Family Check with one moment each, impact, support mode, next step, speaker, and follow-up.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Family tension gets a small regular doorway instead of a delayed explosion.

outcomes.verdict: [A] sees one partner as the more frequent family-boundary detector. [B] sees the responsibility as shared. Both can be true. Use the frequent detector's observations as an early signal, then require the couple to agree on the boundary and let the family-connected partner deliver it. Detection does not become unilateral policy, and shared responsibility does not become silence. Early noticing and joint authority let the couple protect connection without creating unnecessary family drama.
outcomes.actions_a: Name the recurring behavior and impact, then invite a joint decision on the smallest protective boundary.
outcomes.actions_b: Take responsibility for the family-side delivery and report back without asking [A] to manage the response.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save an Observe, Agree, Address plan with signal, impact, boundary, family-side speaker, and repeat step.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Early noticing and shared authority become a coordinated team move.
outcomes.role_note: [A] = identified a specific frequent boundary detector; [B] = said both partners share the role.

cases.title: When You Felt Judged by Their Family and They Didn't Notice
cases.subtitle: Who is more likely to notice subtle judgment from family before their partner does?

questions.prompt: Who is more likely to notice subtle judgment from family before their partner does?

options.label: Me, no contest
Probably me
Probably them
Definitely them
Honestly, both of us about equally

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: What best explains that answer?

options.label: hears coded comments and comparisons
notices facial expressions or exclusion
feels the difference between family norms and couple norms
tracks repeated questions about identity or choices
needs private backing before any public response
can explain the impact without asking for a family confrontation

questions.interactionRule: Display as the answering player’s own voice.

questions.prompt: What made the judgment feel visible?

options.label: A repeated question
A comparison to an ex or relative
A comment about work, money, appearance, or culture
Being left out of a decision
A joke with a serious edge
Your partner's silence in the moment

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: What kind of backing would help?

options.label: Private acknowledgment afterward
A small in-the-moment redirect
Your partner answers the repeated question
A boundary before the next visit
A shorter visit or private exit signal
A follow-up only if the pattern continues

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: Want to tell the court a bit more about what happened? (optional)
questions.interactionRule: Private context is used only to personalize the selected deterministic branch.

outcomes.verdict: [A] notices subtle family judgment sooner because [A] is receiving the comparison, exclusion, or coded question from the outside position. [B] may be habituated to the family's style and miss the edge in real time, but both of you now recognize the pattern. [B] can offer specific private acknowledgment and one visible backing move next time. [A] can choose the smallest support that would feel meaningful without requiring a public confrontation.
outcomes.actions_a: Name the exact moment and choose whether you want private reassurance, a redirect, or a boundary next time.
outcomes.actions_b: Acknowledge the impact and practice the agreed backing line before the next family contact.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Family Backing Plan with trigger, private response, public line, exit signal, and repeat boundary.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. The partner inside the family system learns how to stand visibly beside the partner entering it.
outcomes.role_note: [A] = the partner both identified as more likely to notice subtle family judgment.

outcomes.verdict: [B] feels the judgment first because the person being assessed hears the undertone differently from the person raised around it. [A] may experience the comment as familiar family style and only recognize the impact later. Both of you see that difference now. [A] can become the translator and boundary carrier with [A]'s own family. [B] can request the level of backing that matches the moment.
outcomes.actions_a: Offer a private acknowledgment and use the agreed redirect with your family if the pattern returns.
outcomes.actions_b: Name the moment, the meaning you heard, and whether you need reassurance, intervention, or later action.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Family Backing Plan with trigger, private response, public line, exit signal, and repeat boundary.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Familiar family language gets translated before one partner has to stand alone inside it.
outcomes.role_note: [B] = the partner both identified as more likely to notice subtle family judgment.

outcomes.verdict: Both of you notice the judgment, which means the painful part may be less about recognition and more about response. You can see the same moment and still freeze, laugh politely, or wait for the other person to act. Choose roles before the next visit. The family-connected partner gives the first redirect. The other partner uses an exit signal if the comment continues. You leave with a team story, not two private disappointments.
outcomes.actions_a: Choose the exit signal and the level of response you want if the first redirect does not work.
outcomes.actions_b: Prepare the first redirect for your family and commit to using it without waiting for visible distress.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Family Visit Response Plan with trigger, first redirect, exit signal, repeat step, and post-visit check.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Shared awareness becomes visible teamwork in the moment.

outcomes.verdict: Each of you sees yourself as the faster detector, which may mean judgment lands in different domains. [A] notices comments about identity or belonging; [B] notices comparisons, money, work, or family-role expectations. Map both trigger categories and decide who responds when each appears. The family-connected partner still leads external communication, while the receiving partner controls how much support is needed.
outcomes.actions_a: Name the judgment category you catch fastest and the response that would feel proportionate.
outcomes.actions_b: Name your different category and draft the family-side line that can cover both without overexplaining.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Family Judgment Trigger Map with categories, signs, requested support, speaker, and escalation steps.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Two detectors build a wider safety net instead of competing over whose radar is sharper.

outcomes.verdict: Each of you thinks the other notices judgment first, which may be a sign that both people minimize their own discomfort to protect the visit. The result is polite endurance followed by uncertainty afterward. Add a private zero-to-five check during family time. A three means check in soon; a four means redirect; a five means leave. The number communicates impact without creating a scene.
outcomes.actions_a: Use the number when discomfort appears instead of waiting for your partner to infer it from mood.
outcomes.actions_b: Respond to the number with the agreed check, redirect, or exit, then discuss meaning privately later.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Family Visit Impact Scale with numbers, actions, discreet signal, exit plan, and post-visit conversation.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Quiet coordination replaces the hope that distress will become obvious enough on its own.

outcomes.verdict: [A] sees one partner as the quicker detector of family judgment. [B] sees noticing as shared or situational. Treat [A]'s identified pattern as an early weather alert, not the entire forecast. The detector names the specific signal; the family-connected partner checks impact and leads any response. Both retain the right to notice a different pattern later. That teamwork helps family contact feel more navigable without requiring constant vigilance.
outcomes.actions_a: Name the recurring signal and the smallest backing move that would change the experience.
outcomes.actions_b: Check the signal seriously, choose the response with [A], and deliver it to your family when needed.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save an Early Family Alert with recurring signal, impact question, backing move, family-side speaker, and repeat boundary.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Early noticing becomes coordinated protection without making every family moment a storm.
outcomes.role_note: [A] = identified a specific quicker detector; [B] = said noticing is shared or situational.

cases.title: When One of You Felt Caught in the Middle Between Partner and Family
cases.subtitle: How strongly do you feel pulled into carrying messages, emotions, or peace between your partner and family?

questions.prompt: How strongly do you feel pulled into carrying messages, emotions, or peace between your partner and family?

options.label: Hardly at all
A little in specific moments
Sometimes when expectations collide
Often, I feel responsible for both sides
Very strongly, I feel like the permanent bridge

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: How do you feel about the current middle-person role?

options.label: It works for me
Mostly okay, with a few hard moments
It regularly leaves me tense or disconnected
I need this pattern to change

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: What creates the pull?

options.label: Both sides vent to me
I am expected to translate intentions
A decision affects everyone
I fear disappointing either side
Boundaries are not spoken directly
Past tension makes every moment feel loaded

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: What would reduce the pressure?

options.label: Each side speaks for themselves
A shared couple position first
No private message-carrying
A clear family boundary
A pause before responding
Support without asking me to choose

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: Want to tell the court a bit more about what happened? (optional)
questions.interactionRule: Private context is used only to personalize the selected deterministic branch.

outcomes.verdict: You both recognize the middle-person pressure at a similar level and generally keep it from becoming one partner's permanent job. That means the couple can face family tension as a team instead of turning one person into the switchboard. Keep one rule clear: concerns about the relationship travel directly between partners, and family responses come from the partner connected to that family. Support stays shared while message-carrying stays limited.
outcomes.actions_a: Name one family situation where you can speak directly instead of routing the message through [B].
outcomes.actions_b: Name one response you will deliver to your own family so [A] does not have to manage both sides.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a No-Middle-Person Map with direct speakers, family-side lead, private support, no-carry messages, and review date.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. The bridge stays available without becoming someone's full-time address.

outcomes.verdict: [A] and [B] see similar pressure, but [A] is less okay with how it lands. [A] may be translating, calming, and absorbing reactions while [B] experiences the situation as managed. The hidden issue is not family closeness. It is unpaid emotional traffic control. [B] can take one communication lane back, and [A] can stop accepting private messages that belong in a direct conversation.
outcomes.actions_a: List the message-carrying task that drains you most and redirect it to the person who owns it.
outcomes.actions_b: Take over one family communication lane completely, including follow-up and emotional response.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Communication Lane Transfer with issue, direct speaker, family contact, redirect phrase, and next check.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. The person in the middle gets to return to being a partner.
outcomes.role_note: [A] = less content with the middle-person role; [B] = more content.

outcomes.verdict: You feel similarly trapped because both sides may be using the relationship as the safest route around direct discomfort. The more you translate, the less anyone has to build a clear boundary. Stop carrying interpretations. Share only concrete requests, and only with consent. Before responding to family, agree on the couple's position privately so the family-connected partner can speak without improvising under pressure.
outcomes.actions_a: Turn one complaint into a concrete request and decline to relay motives or emotional commentary.
outcomes.actions_b: Draft the couple's position and deliver it to your own family in your own voice.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Direct Request Protocol with concrete issue, couple position, speaker, no-relay boundary, and follow-up.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Direct requests replace the emotional relay race.

outcomes.verdict: [A] feels caught between partner and family much more strongly because [A] is the person whose relationships sit on both sides of the tension. [B] can stay clearer about the couple's need because [B] is not managing the same history. You are content because that difference is understood. Let [B] state the needed support privately, while [A] chooses the language and timing used with family within a firm shared boundary.
outcomes.actions_a: State the couple need without scripting how [A] must speak to family or demanding instant action.
outcomes.actions_b: Choose the family-facing language and date, then report back so the boundary does not disappear into delay.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Private Need, Family Voice plan with couple need, boundary, family-side wording, delivery date, and follow-up.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. The couple stays aligned while the family-connected partner keeps a human voice.
outcomes.role_note: [A] = feels more caught between partner and family; [B] = feels less caught.

outcomes.verdict: [A] feels heavily caught in the middle and is not okay with the current pressure. [B] feels less caught and may see direct couple loyalty as simple from outside the family history. The clarity belongs to [B], while the relational consequences land with [A]. [B] owes a narrower request. [A] owes a real boundary and date instead of absorbing tension indefinitely to keep everyone temporarily calm.
outcomes.actions_a: Ask for the smallest boundary that protects the relationship and leave [A] room to choose the delivery.
outcomes.actions_b: Set the boundary with your family by a specific date and stop privately translating each side afterward.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Minimum Protective Boundary with request, family wording, delivery date, no-relay rule, and repeat response.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Protection becomes specific enough to deliver without demanding a dramatic family split.
outcomes.role_note: [A] = feels more caught and is dissatisfied; [B] = feels less caught and is content.

outcomes.verdict: [A] is carrying partner pain in one hand and family reaction in the other, so every move feels like dropping someone. [B] feels exposed when family comfort repeatedly delays couple protection. Stop asking [A] to balance both in real time. Decide the couple boundary first, schedule the family conversation second, and arrange outside support for [A] afterward. The sequence separates partnership from emotional cleanup.
outcomes.actions_a: Name the boundary needed for relationship safety and avoid turning it into a demand for emotional rejection of family.
outcomes.actions_b: Deliver the boundary, then use a friend, counselor, or private decompression plan rather than asking [B] to comfort you for setting it.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Boundary Sequence with couple decision, family conversation, support person, repeat line, and recovery check.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. The order gets clear even when the feelings remain complicated.
outcomes.role_note: [A] = feels more caught between partner and family; [B] = feels more exposed by the delay.

cases.title: When Holiday Plans With Both Families Caused Tension
cases.subtitle: How strongly do family expectations shape the holiday plan you feel able to choose?

questions.prompt: How strongly do family expectations shape the holiday plan you feel able to choose?

options.label: Hardly at all
A little, but our plan leads
Somewhat, several expectations matter
A lot, changing tradition creates real pressure
Very strongly, family expectations feel nearly fixed

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: How do you feel about the fairness of your current holiday plan?

options.label: It works for me
Mostly okay, with a few hard moments
It regularly leaves me tense or disconnected
I need this pattern to change

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: What makes the plan hardest?

options.label: Travel time and cost
Both families want the same day
One tradition carries more emotional weight
Work, children, or health limits
One partner does more hosting labor
Saying no creates family fallout

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: What would help next holiday?

options.label: Alternate years
Split the season, not the day
Create one couple-only tradition
Set the plan earlier
Cap travel or hosting
Let impact, not equal hours, guide the split

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: Want to tell the court a bit more about what happened? (optional)
questions.interactionRule: Private context is used only to personalize the selected deterministic branch.

outcomes.verdict: You carry family expectations at a similar level and generally experience the holiday plan as fair. What holds this together is not equal hours. It is knowing the plan reflects both histories without exhausting the couple trying to satisfy every invitation. Keep one protected couple tradition and decide family time by capacity, travel, and meaning before invitations arrive. Early clarity lets warmth survive the logistics.
outcomes.actions_a: Choose the couple tradition you most want protected and place it on the calendar first.
outcomes.actions_b: Choose the family commitment with the highest meaning and the limit that keeps it sustainable.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Holiday Capacity Calendar with couple tradition, family visits, travel cap, hosting tasks, and announcement date.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. The holiday belongs to the relationship too, not only to the invitation list.

outcomes.verdict: [A] and [B] feel similar family pressure, but [A] is less satisfied because equal-looking plans can carry unequal labor. [A] may travel farther, host more, manage gifts, or absorb the family disappointment. [B] sees balanced dates; [A] experiences an unbalanced production schedule. Count preparation, recovery, money, and emotional labor alongside hours. Then move one entire task or visit decision to [B].
outcomes.actions_a: Name the invisible holiday labor making the current plan feel uneven.
outcomes.actions_b: Take full ownership of one visit, hosting lane, or family communication from planning through follow-up.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Holiday Labor Ledger with visits, travel, hosting, gifts, family messages, owners, and recovery time.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. The calendar stops looking equal while one partner runs the whole event.
outcomes.role_note: [A] = less content with holiday fairness; [B] = more content.

outcomes.verdict: You feel similar pressure and both dislike the plan because it is trying to solve fairness inside a single overloaded day. Stop dividing hours so finely that no one arrives emotionally present. Split the season instead: different days, alternating years, or one family gathering plus a couple ritual. A holiday can honor both families without physically visiting both in every window.
outcomes.actions_a: Propose one season-level option that reduces rushing and name what your family would still receive.
outcomes.actions_b: Propose a different option and draft the early message that sets expectations before plans harden.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Holiday Season Plan with dates, alternating rule, couple ritual, travel limit, and family announcement.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Fairness moves from the stopwatch to the whole season.

outcomes.verdict: [A] feels stronger obligation to family traditions, perhaps because of culture, aging relatives, children, or limited shared time. [B] has more freedom to reshape the holiday and wants the couple's capacity to lead. You are content because obligation and flexibility are both visible. Use a two-year rotation that protects [A]'s highest-value tradition while giving [B] a guaranteed couple-designed holiday window.
outcomes.actions_a: Choose the tradition that truly needs protection and release one lower-value obligation.
outcomes.actions_b: Design the couple-led window and accept the protected tradition without treating it as the permanent default.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Two-Year Holiday Rotation with protected tradition, couple window, released obligation, travel cap, and review month.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Family continuity and couple freedom take turns receiving the best time.
outcomes.role_note: [A] = feels stronger family obligation; [B] = feels more flexible.

outcomes.verdict: [A] feels stronger obligation and is not okay with the pressure to loosen family plans. [B] feels more flexible and sees the current arrangement as workable, perhaps because the costs of obligation land more on [A]. The issue may be less about attendance than support. [B] can take travel, hosting, or communication labor. [A] can identify which obligation is truly essential instead of protecting the full inherited schedule.
outcomes.actions_a: Select the one obligation that matters most and let one lesser expectation go.
outcomes.actions_b: Take ownership of a concrete support lane and stop asking [A] to prove why the essential tradition matters.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save an Essential Tradition Support Plan with must-keep event, released event, support owner, travel limit, and family message.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. The meaningful tradition stays while the burden around it gets redistributed.
outcomes.role_note: [A] = feels stronger obligation and is dissatisfied; [B] = feels more flexible and content.

outcomes.verdict: [A] fears losing belonging or hurting family by changing the holiday. [B] fears the couple will remain trapped in a schedule that drains time, money, and joy. Neither feeling needs a winner. Choose a holiday decision date six months early and compare three complete plans: family-heavy, couple-heavy, and rotating. Score energy, cost, meaning, and family impact, then commit to one for this year only.
outcomes.actions_a: Build the family-heavy plan honestly, including labor and recovery rather than only meaningful moments.
outcomes.actions_b: Build the couple-heavy plan and one rotation option, including what each family still receives.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Three-Plan Holiday Review with energy, cost, meaning, family impact, chosen year, and next decision date.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. One year gets a clear plan without pretending it must define every future holiday.
outcomes.role_note: [A] = feels stronger family obligation; [B] = wants more couple-led flexibility.

cases.title: When Your Partner Didn't Stand Up for You in Front of Their Family
cases.subtitle: Who is more likely to freeze or stay quiet when their family crosses a line with the partner?

questions.prompt: Who is more likely to freeze or stay quiet when their family crosses a line with the partner?

options.label: Me, no contest
Probably me
Probably them
Definitely them
Honestly, both of us about equally

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: What best explains that answer?

options.label: needs a moment to register the family dynamic
has learned to keep peace in that room
fears a public response will escalate things
plans to address it privately later
misses the impact until afterward
can respond when a line is prepared in advance

questions.interactionRule: Display as the answering player’s own voice.

questions.prompt: What support was missing?

options.label: A simple redirect
A clear correction
Changing the subject
Ending the visit
Private acknowledgment afterward
A later conversation with the family

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: What would help next time?

options.label: A prepared one-line response
A discreet partner signal
The family-connected partner speaks first
A public limit and private follow-up
An exit plan
A check-in before the next visit

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: Want to tell the court a bit more about what happened? (optional)
questions.interactionRule: Private context is used only to personalize the selected deterministic branch.

outcomes.verdict: [A] is more likely to freeze with [A]'s family because old peacekeeping habits activate before the partner role catches up. [B] already sees the pattern and needed visible evidence that the relationship was protected in the room. [A] can prepare one line and an exit response before the next contact. [B] can request the smallest action that would have changed the experience instead of asking for a dramatic family confrontation.
outcomes.actions_a: Practice the exact line and commit to using it at the first repeat, not only in a later private talk.
outcomes.actions_b: Name the smallest visible backing move that would help you feel accompanied in the moment.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Stand-Beside-Me Script with trigger, first line, discreet signal, exit step, and family follow-up.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Support becomes visible without requiring a public showdown.
outcomes.role_note: [A] = the partner both identified as more likely to freeze with their family.

outcomes.verdict: [B] tends to go quiet when [B]'s family crosses a line, often because family roles snap back into place faster than adult partnership can respond. [A] needed a small public sign that the two of you were still a team. [B] can rehearse a brief redirect and use it before explaining privately later. [A] can make the desired support specific and proportionate to the moment.
outcomes.actions_a: Name the visible support you needed and separate it from every later family consequence.
outcomes.actions_b: Rehearse the redirect, use it in the room, and handle the family follow-up without assigning it back to [A].
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Stand-Beside-Me Script with trigger, first line, discreet signal, exit step, and family follow-up.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. The family room gets one clear sign that the partnership is present too.
outcomes.role_note: [B] = the partner both identified as more likely to freeze with their family.

outcomes.verdict: Both of you can freeze around family because public response carries history, hierarchy, and consequences that a private couple conversation does not. That shared pattern calls for preparation, not courage contests. Choose three common triggers and one line for each. Either partner may use a discreet signal, while the family-connected partner speaks first whenever possible. The goal is prompt protection, not a perfect speech.
outcomes.actions_a: Choose one trigger and write the short line you can reliably say even when surprised.
outcomes.actions_b: Choose another trigger and define the exit signal if the first redirect does not hold.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Three-Trigger Family Response Card with lines, speaker, partner signal, exit step, and later follow-up.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Preparation lets partnership show up before old family reflexes take over.

outcomes.actions_b: Clarify the term with the giver and state the couple boundary rather than leaving [A] to enforce it alone.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Family Money Terms Check with amount, condition, repayment, access boundary, family-side speaker, and review.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. The couple responds to the actual condition, not only the helpful amount.
outcomes.role_note: [A] = less content with the current family-money boundary; [B] = more content.

outcomes.verdict: You share a caution level yet both feel uneasy because the money relationship changes by conversation. It is called a gift when accepted, a loan when conflict appears, or family help when access is requested. Freeze new funds until the current amount has one written status, repayment rule, and influence boundary. Ambiguity is not closeness when it can rewrite the couple's obligations later.
outcomes.actions_a: Draft the status and repayment terms you understand, including what was never agreed.
outcomes.actions_b: Contact the family giver with the shared clarification and record the confirmed answer.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Current Family Money Agreement with status, balance, repayment, influence limits, communication owner, and end date.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. One written meaning replaces a relationship-changing moving target.

outcomes.verdict: [A] is more cautious because family money can carry obligation, exposure, or future decision pressure. [B] is more comfortable because family support feels normal and relational. You are content because acceptance can follow the more protective threshold without rejecting the family bond. Use a low-exposure rule: smaller amounts, written status, both-partner approval, and no influence over couple decisions.
outcomes.actions_a: Define the maximum exposure and the conditions that would make an offer safe enough to consider.
outcomes.actions_b: Explain those terms to your family and accept that warmth does not require accepting every offer.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Low-Exposure Family Money Rule with amount cap, approval, terms, influence boundary, and decline script.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Family generosity stays welcome inside a boundary strong enough for both partners.
outcomes.role_note: [A] = more cautious about family money; [B] = more comfortable.

outcomes.verdict: [A] is more cautious and feels exposed by family money already treated as harmless. [B] is comfortable, perhaps because the support comes from [B]'s family and the relational cost feels familiar or unlikely. The benefit is shared, but the perceived obligation is not. [B] owes written clarification and responsibility for future family pressure. [A] owes a clear acceptance threshold rather than rejecting every form of support automatically.
outcomes.actions_a: State the terms and maximum exposure you could freely accept if family influence stays outside the couple's decisions.
outcomes.actions_b: Get written clarification and commit to handling any later pressure from your family directly.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Benefit and Obligation Split with amount, terms, acceptance threshold, pressure response, and repayment plan.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Support becomes acceptable only when the obligation has nowhere hidden to grow.
outcomes.role_note: [A] = more cautious and dissatisfied; [B] = more comfortable and content.

outcomes.verdict: [A] sees family money as a string that may tighten later. [B] sees it as a safety net the couple should not refuse. Both images can be true depending on the terms. Stop arguing about the family's character. Put the exact offer through a five-part test: label, repayment, influence, privacy, and exit. Accept only if every part is answerable and both partners can consent without pressure.
outcomes.actions_a: Score the offer on influence, privacy, and exit, then name the unanswered term that matters most.
outcomes.actions_b: Score label and repayment, obtain the missing answer, and accept no funds before both scores are reviewed.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Five-Part Family Money Test with label, repayment, influence, privacy, exit, and final decision.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. The offer gets evaluated by its terms, not by fear or family loyalty alone.
outcomes.role_note: [A] = more cautious about family money; [B] = more comfortable.

cases.title: When One of You Felt Their Family Wasn't Being Given Equal Time
cases.subtitle: How closely should time with both families balance over a season?

questions.prompt: How closely should time with both families balance over a season?

options.label: It does not need to balance if needs differ
Roughly fair over time
Similar effort even if hours differ
Quite closely balanced
As evenly as practical

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: How do you feel about the current balance of family time?

options.label: It works for me
Mostly okay, with a few hard moments
It regularly leaves me tense or disconnected
I need this pattern to change

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: What makes equal time complicated?

options.label: Distance and travel cost
One family needs more care
One family initiates more
Visits feel very different in energy
Work and holiday limits
Past imbalance still matters

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: What would feel fairer?

options.label: Track effort, not hours
Alternate priority weekends
Protect a minimum for each family
Count travel and hosting labor
Review quarterly
Separate emergency care from social visits

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: Want to tell the court a bit more about what happened? (optional)
questions.interactionRule: Private context is used only to personalize the selected deterministic branch.

outcomes.verdict: You define family-time fairness similarly and generally feel both sides receive meaningful connection. The strength is not perfect symmetry. It is shared confidence that neither family quietly becomes the default while the other survives on leftovers. Keep a seasonal view that counts travel, hosting, caregiving, and emotional effort alongside hours. Fairness remains flexible because it is visible.
outcomes.actions_a: Name the type of family contact that matters most on your side and the effort it requires.
outcomes.actions_b: Name a different fairness factor and add it to the seasonal review.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Family Time Balance Sheet with visits, calls, travel, hosting, caregiving, and quarterly review.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Both families stay visible without forcing unlike relationships into identical hours.

outcomes.verdict: [A] and [B] want similar balance, but [A] is less content because the current math may ignore distance, planning, or whose family repeatedly receives prime time. [B] sees comparable visit counts; [A] sees one family getting holidays and the other getting rushed leftovers. Compare quality and burden, not only frequency. Then reserve one high-value window for the underserved side.
outcomes.actions_a: Name the high-value time or type of connection your family has been missing.
outcomes.actions_b: Protect one equivalent-quality window and take ownership of the travel or planning required.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Quality of Family Time Review with prime dates, visit length, travel burden, planning owner, and next allocation.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Fairness starts measuring the experience, not only the number of entries.
outcomes.role_note: [A] = less content with family-time balance; [B] = more content.

outcomes.verdict: You agree on the fairness target, yet both feel behind because family time is allocated reactively. The loudest invitation or nearest relative keeps winning. Set minimum connection for each side before adding extras, then keep emergency care separate from social fairness. A baseline prevents every invitation from becoming a fresh referendum on whose family matters.
outcomes.actions_a: Choose the minimum seasonal connection your family needs and identify what can be flexible.
outcomes.actions_b: Choose the minimum for your side and propose the next two dates that protect both baselines.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Two-Family Baseline with minimum contact, prime dates, emergency exceptions, extra-visit rule, and review.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Both families receive a floor before urgency starts bidding for the rest.

outcomes.verdict: [A] wants a closer balance because equal visible effort signals that both family bonds belong in the shared life. [B] accepts more unevenness because distance, care needs, or relationship quality makes identical time impractical. You are content because fairness can be defined by minimum connection plus need-based extras. Protect a baseline for each family, then allocate additional time according to current needs without calling the baseline negotiable.
outcomes.actions_a: Set the baseline connection your family needs to remain meaningfully included.
outcomes.actions_b: Define the need-based exceptions and ensure they do not repeatedly consume the other family's baseline.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Baseline Plus Need plan with family minimums, extra-care criteria, protected dates, and quarterly review.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Equality protects belonging, and flexibility responds to real life.
outcomes.role_note: [A] wants closer balance; [B] accepts more need-based unevenness.

outcomes.verdict: [A] wants closer balance and is dissatisfied because one family appears to receive more time, convenience, or important dates. [B] accepts the imbalance and feels content, likely because the current pattern is familiar or justified by practical needs. [B] owes one visible correction: a protected date, travel effort, or planning lane for [A]'s family. [A] owes a fairness request based on meaningful connection, not exact hour matching.
outcomes.actions_a: Choose the one correction that would most improve belonging without requiring identical schedules.
outcomes.actions_b: Commit the date or effort, handle the planning, and protect it from routine invitations on your side.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Family Time Correction with underserved need, protected window, travel or hosting owner, exceptions, and review.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. One concrete shift makes fairness visible without turning family time into a stopwatch.
outcomes.role_note: [A] wants closer balance and is dissatisfied; [B] accepts more unevenness and is content.

outcomes.verdict: [A] sees imbalance as evidence that one family has become the relationship default. [B] sees strict balance as ignoring distance, need, or the real quality of each connection. Stop arguing from annual totals. Plan the next three months with one meaningful contact for each family, then allocate remaining capacity by need. Review after the quarter using energy, cost, and connection rather than resentment estimates.
outcomes.actions_a: Choose the meaningful contact your family needs this quarter and the flexibility you can offer afterward.
outcomes.actions_b: Choose the contact for your side and document the need behind any additional time.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Three-Month Family Time Plan with two protected contacts, need-based extras, cost, energy, and review date.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. A short planning horizon turns fairness into choices you can actually see.
outcomes.role_note: [A] wants closer balance; [B] accepts more need-based unevenness.

cases.title: When Their Parent's Opinion Seemed to Matter More Than Yours in a Decision
cases.subtitle: Who is more likely to give a parent's opinion extra weight in a shared decision?

questions.prompt: Who is more likely to give a parent's opinion extra weight in a shared decision?

options.label: Me, no contest
Probably me
Probably them
Definitely them
Honestly, both of us about equally

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: What best explains that answer?

options.label: trusts the parent's experience
seeks family approval under uncertainty
was taught to consult family on major choices
uses the opinion as reassurance
does not always notice when advice becomes influence
can reset once the couple's decision rights are named

questions.interactionRule: Display as the answering player’s own voice.

questions.prompt: Where did the parent's view enter?

options.label: Money
Housing
Career
Parenting
Health
Wedding, culture, or family plans

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: What would restore couple authority?

options.label: Decide the question before seeking advice
Ask for information, not permission
Share advice only after both partners speak
Keep one topic private
State who has final decision rights
Tell the parent the couple's decision together

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: Want to tell the court a bit more about what happened? (optional)
questions.interactionRule: Private context is used only to personalize the selected deterministic branch.

outcomes.verdict: [A] gives a parent's view extra weight because that voice carries history, expertise, or approval learned over many years. [B] sees the influence and needs evidence that the couple's decision is not merely waiting for outside confirmation. Put advice after the first couple round. [A] may seek information, but returns with it as one input. [B]'s lived stake remains equal inside the final decision.
outcomes.actions_a: State your view before outside advice enters and name the part of the decision you need equal authority over.
outcomes.actions_b: Ask family for information rather than permission and present it as input, not the closing answer.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Couple First Decision Order with partner views, advice question, decision rights, final choice, and family message.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Experience can advise the couple without outranking the person living the decision.
outcomes.role_note: [A] = the partner both identified as giving a parent's opinion extra weight.

outcomes.verdict: [B] leans more heavily on a parent's opinion because the advice feels experienced, familiar, or emotionally safe. [A] may hear that reliance as being demoted inside a decision that affects both partners directly. [B] can keep family wisdom while changing the sequence: couple views first, targeted advice second, couple decision last. [A] can identify the exact decision right that needs protection rather than rejecting all family input.
outcomes.actions_a: Name the decision right and the outside information you are still open to considering.
outcomes.actions_b: State your own view before consulting family and return the advice to the couple for a final decision.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Couple First Decision Order with partner views, advice question, decision rights, final choice, and family message.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Family wisdom becomes a resource, not a higher seat at the table.
outcomes.role_note: [B] = the partner both identified as giving a parent's opinion extra weight.

outcomes.verdict: Both of you sometimes elevate parental advice, which means family consultation is part of how safety and wisdom are built. The risk is inviting multiple family systems into a decision before the couple knows its own position. Hold a private first round and write each partner's priorities. Seek only the missing information, then return to decide without family members serving as votes.
outcomes.actions_a: Write your priorities and the one information gap an outside perspective could genuinely fill.
outcomes.actions_b: Choose the advice source based on relevant experience and keep the final discussion private to the couple.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save an Advice Without Votes sheet with partner priorities, information gaps, advisers, decision rights, and family response.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Family input gets a useful job without becoming a parallel decision board.

outcomes.verdict: Each of you sees yourself as more family-influenced, which may mean different topics activate different advisers. [A] may seek financial or career guidance; [B] may seek cultural, parenting, or health guidance. Map the domains and agree which decisions are consultable, private, or require mutual permission before details leave the relationship.
outcomes.actions_a: Name the advice domain you rely on and the information you want, not the approval you hope to receive.
outcomes.actions_b: Name your different domain and the privacy boundary that should apply before family is consulted.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save an Outside Advice Map with domains, approved advisers, privacy level, couple-first step, and final decision owner.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Advice becomes transparent and bounded instead of quietly entering through different doors.

outcomes.verdict: Each of you thinks the other gives parents more weight, which may reflect the moments when outside advice supported a view you did not share. Drop the family scorecard. Use one neutral test: would this advice still matter if it supported neither partner's preferred answer? If yes, keep the information. If not, return to the couple's priorities before seeking more voices.
outcomes.actions_a: Apply the neutral test to one piece of family advice and name the useful information inside it.
outcomes.actions_b: Apply the same test to advice from your side and remove any part functioning mainly as reinforcement.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Neutral Advice Test with advice, expertise, relevance, preferred outcome, usable fact, and final couple choice.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Useful wisdom survives while borrowed authority falls away.

outcomes.verdict: [A] sees one partner as more influenced by a parent. [B] sees the pattern as shared or topic-dependent. Treat the recurring domain as the marked lane. There, the couple writes its priorities before any call. Everywhere else, both partners use the same information-not-permission rule. The family voice stays audible without holding the steering wheel.
outcomes.actions_a: Name the recurring domain and write your priorities before the next outside conversation.
outcomes.actions_b: Use the information-not-permission question and bring the answer back without a family-endorsed conclusion.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Marked Advice Lane with domain, couple priorities, advice question, decision rights, and family message.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. The couple keeps the wheel while still asking experienced passengers for directions.
outcomes.role_note: [A] = identified a specific more family-influenced partner; [B] = said the pattern is shared or situational.

cases.title: When You Felt Like an Outsider Around Their Family
cases.subtitle: Who is more likely to feel outside the circle during family time?

questions.prompt: Who is more likely to feel outside the circle during family time?

options.label: Me, no contest
Probably me
Probably them
Definitely them
Honestly, both of us about equally

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: What best explains that answer?

options.label: misses shared history and inside references
is left out when language or routines shift
needs active introductions into conversation
does not know the unspoken family rules
feels the partner slip back into an old role
can connect when given one genuine way in

questions.interactionRule: Display as the answering player’s own voice.

questions.prompt: What created the outsider feeling?

options.label: Inside jokes or old stories
Language or cultural references
Seating, plans, or decisions
The partner disappearing into family roles
No one asked questions back
Being expected to adapt without guidance

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: What would create a real way in?

options.label: Context before the visit
An introduction tied to a shared interest
The partner checks in during the gathering
A role in one family activity
Language translation or recap
A planned exit and couple reconnect

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: Want to tell the court a bit more about what happened? (optional)
questions.interactionRule: Private context is used only to personalize the selected deterministic branch.

outcomes.verdict: [A] is more likely to feel outside because [A] enters a room full of shared history, shorthand, and roles already in motion. [B] sees the gap and can become a bridge without babysitting the entire visit. A quick context preview, two intentional introductions, and one mid-visit check can change the social map. [A] can choose one real point of participation instead of trying to win belonging everywhere at once.
outcomes.actions_a: Choose one person or activity you would genuinely like help connecting with.
outcomes.actions_b: Give context, make the introduction, and check in once before family momentum carries you away.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Family Way-In Plan with context, two introductions, activity role, check-in cue, and exit time.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Belonging begins with a few real doors, not instant access to the whole house.
outcomes.role_note: [A] = the partner both identified as more likely to feel outside the family circle.

outcomes.verdict: [B] feels outside more quickly because the family gathering has a script everyone else learned years ago. [A] recognizes the experience and can make the script less invisible. Share context before the visit, bring [B] into one conversation, and protect a mid-visit reconnect. [B] can ask for a specific way in rather than measuring belonging by every inside joke that remains outside.
outcomes.actions_a: Prepare the context and one introduction that connects [B] through a genuine shared interest.
outcomes.actions_b: Choose the way in you want and use the check-in cue before isolation hardens into the whole visit story.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Family Way-In Plan with context, two introductions, activity role, check-in cue, and exit time.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. The family script becomes readable enough for [B] to participate as a real person.
outcomes.role_note: [B] = the partner both identified as more likely to feel outside the family circle.

outcomes.verdict: Both of you can feel outside around the other's family, which means you share an experience that can become practical empathy. Create the same hosting standard for both sides: context before, introductions during, one check-in, and an agreed end time. The visiting partner also chooses one genuine point of engagement. Mutual outsider experience becomes a blueprint for better hosting.
outcomes.actions_a: Choose the hosting step you most need when visiting and promise to provide it with your family.
outcomes.actions_b: Choose a different step and name the activity you can join without performing instant closeness.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Mutual Family Hosting Standard with context, introductions, check-in, participation choice, and exit time.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Each outsider experience teaches the other partner how to host with care.

outcomes.verdict: Each of you sees yourself as the bigger outsider, likely because the barriers differ. [A] may face language, culture, or history. [B] may face emotional closeness, role expectations, or lack of curiosity. Comparing isolation will only make both people defend their family. Name the barrier, then design one bridge for each side. Different rooms need different entrances.
outcomes.actions_a: Name your primary barrier and the smallest bridge that would change the next visit.
outcomes.actions_b: Name your different barrier and take responsibility for building [A]'s bridge with your family.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Two-Family Way-In Map with barriers, bridges, host partner, check-in cue, and review after each visit.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Two different outsider experiences receive two custom entrances.

outcomes.verdict: Each of you thinks the other feels more outside, which may be an attempt to minimize your own discomfort or generosity toward the partner. Make the invisible visible without ranking it. After each visit, rate belonging, effort, and energy from one to five, then choose one hosting improvement. The numbers are not family grades; they reveal which bridge matters next.
outcomes.actions_a: Rate your experience honestly and request one hosting improvement without judging the whole family.
outcomes.actions_b: Choose the improvement to own before the next visit and state what support you also need as a host.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Post-Visit Belonging Check with three ratings, one bright spot, one barrier, and one hosting change.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Small data creates better hosting before quiet isolation becomes a family story.

outcomes.verdict: [A] sees one partner as the more frequent outsider. [B] sees the experience as shared or dependent on the family. Use the recurring barrier as the first design target while preserving the same hosting standard on both sides. The family-connected partner owns context and introductions; the visitor chooses participation and signals when a reconnect is needed.
outcomes.actions_a: Name the recurring barrier and the one host action that would make the biggest difference.
outcomes.actions_b: Deliver that host action and invite the visitor's chosen participation without forcing social performance.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Recurring Way-In Plan with barrier, host action, visitor choice, check-in cue, and exit option.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. One known barrier gets an intentional bridge inside a mutual hosting culture.
outcomes.role_note: [A] = identified a specific more frequent outsider; [B] = said the experience is shared or situational.

cases.title: When a Family Member Overstepped a Boundary in the Relationship
cases.subtitle: Who is more likely to notice the boundary crossing before the other partner does?

questions.prompt: Who is more likely to notice the boundary crossing before the other partner does?

options.label: Me, no contest
Probably me
Probably them
Definitely them
Honestly, both of us about equally

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: What best explains that answer?

options.label: spots when advice becomes control
notices private information being used
feels the cost of uninvited access
tracks repeated boundary testing
separates warmth from entitlement
can agree on a proportionate response once impact is named

questions.interactionRule: Display as the answering player’s own voice.

questions.prompt: Which boundary was crossed?

options.label: Privacy
Time or home access
Money
Parenting or life decisions
Relationship conflict details
Physical or emotional respect

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: What should happen next?

options.label: A clear private message
The family-connected partner speaks
Reduce access to one topic
Change visit or contact rules
Use one repeat-response line
Escalate distance only if it happens again

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: Want to tell the court a bit more about what happened? (optional)
questions.interactionRule: Private context is used only to personalize the selected deterministic branch.

outcomes.verdict: [A] notices the overstep faster because [A] feels the boundary's impact directly or is less accustomed to the family pattern. [B] sees the crossing too, which means the couple can move straight to response design. Let [B] address [B]'s family with one behavior, one boundary, and one consequence if repeated. [A] can define the protection needed without turning the response into a judgment of the relative's entire character.
outcomes.actions_a: Name the behavior, impact, and minimum protection you need next time.
outcomes.actions_b: Deliver the boundary to your family and own the repeat response instead of leaving enforcement to [A].
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Family Boundary Enforcement Card with behavior, line, speaker, access change, repeat consequence, and check-in.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. The couple protects one clear line without widening the conflict beyond it.
outcomes.role_note: [A] = the partner both identified as more likely to notice the overstep first.

outcomes.verdict: [B] detects the overstep first because the behavior touches privacy, access, or decision rights in a way [A] may experience as familiar family involvement. [A] now sees the impact and can take the external lead with [A]'s relatives. [B] names the smallest boundary that restores safety. [A] states it and follows through if the behavior repeats.
outcomes.actions_a: State the boundary to your family using the agreed behavior and consequence, then report back.
outcomes.actions_b: Name the minimum protection and avoid expanding the request into unrelated family grievances.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Family Boundary Enforcement Card with behavior, line, speaker, access change, repeat consequence, and check-in.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Familiar family involvement receives a clear relationship limit.
outcomes.role_note: [B] = the partner both identified as more likely to notice the overstep first.

outcomes.verdict: Both of you recognize family oversteps quickly, which gives the relationship strong perimeter awareness. The risk is designing consequences while still activated and making the response larger than the boundary requires. Use a three-step ladder: clarify, limit access to the affected topic or setting, then increase distance only after a repeat. The family-connected partner communicates each step.
outcomes.actions_a: Define the first clarification line and the exact behavior that triggers step two.
outcomes.actions_b: Define the access limit and the repeat condition that would justify step three.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Three-Step Family Boundary Ladder with behavior, clarification, access limit, repeat condition, and speaker.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. The boundary gets stronger through clear steps rather than sudden family-wide distance.

outcomes.verdict: Each of you sees yourself as the faster boundary detector because you notice different forms of access. [A] may catch privacy or commentary. [B] may catch time, money, or decision pressure. Combine the radars and assign the family-connected partner as communicator. The detecting partner supplies impact; the couple chooses the step together.
outcomes.actions_a: Name the boundary category you detect and the evidence that marks a real crossing.
outcomes.actions_b: Name your different category and prepare to communicate with your own family when either signal appears.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Boundary Radar and Response Map with categories, signals, impact, response step, and family-side speaker.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Two radars create earlier protection without creating two separate policies.

outcomes.verdict: Each of you thinks the other notices oversteps first, which may mean both people recognize the issue but hesitate to be the one who changes the family relationship. Set a neutral threshold: if a behavior affects privacy, money, home access, or couple decisions after a clear no, it enters the boundary ladder. The rule carries the decision so neither partner has to dramatize the moment.
outcomes.actions_a: Apply the threshold to the recent behavior and name the proportionate first step.
outcomes.actions_b: Take the family-side communication role and schedule the message instead of waiting for another incident.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save an Objective Overstep Test with protected areas, prior no, current behavior, response step, and delivery date.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. A clear threshold replaces the hope that the next crossing will somehow feel easier to address.

outcomes.verdict: [A] sees one partner as the more frequent boundary detector. [B] sees noticing as shared or situational. Use the recurring detector as an early alert, not a solo decision-maker. The couple verifies the protected area, chooses the smallest effective response, and the family-connected partner delivers it. Shared authority prevents both dismissal and overreaction.
outcomes.actions_a: Bring the early alert with the exact behavior and protected area rather than a conclusion about intent.
outcomes.actions_b: Help choose the response and deliver it to your family without asking [A] to prove the impact again.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save an Alert, Verify, Respond plan with behavior, protected area, joint decision, speaker, and repeat step.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Early detection gains shared authority and a clear route to action.
outcomes.role_note: [A] = identified a specific frequent detector; [B] = said noticing is shared or situational.

It regularly leaves me tense or disconnected
I need this pattern to change

Family remembers pain after we repair
Private details change how they see my partner
Safety or health support is needed
The same issue keeps returning
