questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: Want to tell the court a bit more about what happened? (optional)
questions.interactionRule: Private context is used only to personalize the selected deterministic branch.

outcomes.verdict: You draw the family privacy line in a similar place and generally trust each other not to turn a hard week into a permanent family narrative. That shared instinct protects both support and dignity. Make the rule explicit while things are calm: feelings can be shared, identifying details need consent, and safety exceptions stay open. After the issue resolves, update anyone who received the painful version so the family story does not freeze there.
outcomes.actions_a: Name the kind of emotional support you can seek without exposing [B]'s private details.
outcomes.actions_b: Name one topic that requires consent before sharing and one safety exception that remains available.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Family Privacy Guide with shareable feelings, protected details, consent topics, safety exceptions, and repair update.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Support stays available without making family the permanent archive of your hardest moments.

outcomes.verdict: [A] and [B] prefer similar privacy, but [A] is less content because the rule may be applied unevenly. [A]'s mistakes or vulnerabilities might reach family while [B]'s remain protected, or one family hears more detail than the other. Compare what was shared, not only the principle. The repair is symmetry, removal where possible, and a clear update to anyone holding an incomplete story.
outcomes.actions_a: Name the detail or audience that made privacy feel uneven and the correction you need.
outcomes.actions_b: Correct the family story, remove unnecessary detail from future sharing, and apply the same consent rule to yourself.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Privacy Symmetry Check with topics, audiences, consent status, correction message, and future rule.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. The same privacy standard begins protecting both partners in practice.
outcomes.role_note: [A] = less content with current family privacy; [B] = more content.

outcomes.verdict: You want similar privacy but keep crossing the line because support is sought while emotions are high and judgment is low. Create a three-tier system. Green topics can be shared generally. Yellow topics allow feelings but not identifying details. Red topics stay inside the couple or with a professional unless safety is involved. A simple label gives both partners a pause before disclosure.
outcomes.actions_a: Classify the recurring conflict topic and name the support you can seek inside that tier.
outcomes.actions_b: Classify a different sensitive topic and choose the alternative support person or professional route.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Green, Yellow, Red Privacy Map with topics, allowed detail, support routes, consent rule, and safety exception.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Privacy gets a usable system before the next upset starts talking.

outcomes.verdict: [A] wants more privacy because family memory and loyalty can outlast the conflict. [B] wants more sharing because family is a primary support network and carrying the issue alone feels isolating. You are content because support and privacy can be separated. Let [B] share personal feelings and practical needs, while details about [A], intimate information, and unresolved accusations require consent or a professional setting.
outcomes.actions_a: Define the details that belong to your privacy and the support request that remains okay to share.
outcomes.actions_b: Use feeling-centered language with family and move partner-specific detail to a consented or professional space.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Feelings Not Files rule with allowed support, protected details, consent process, safety exception, and update step.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. [B] keeps support without turning [A]'s private life into family material.
outcomes.role_note: [A] = wants more privacy; [B] = wants more family sharing.

outcomes.verdict: [A] wants more privacy and feels exposed by the current sharing. [B] wants more family support and feels the system works because disclosure reduces [B]'s emotional load. That relief is being funded with [A]'s reputation and privacy. [B] owes a new support habit: share the feeling, not identifying details, or choose a counselor or friend outside the family system. [A] owes clear boundaries rather than demanding total isolation.
outcomes.actions_a: List the details that need protection and the types of support seeking you can still accept.
outcomes.actions_b: Choose a non-family or low-detail support route and correct any family story that now feels incomplete.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Private Detail Firewall with protected facts, allowed feelings, support routes, correction message, and safety exception.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Support continues without making one partner the price of receiving it.
outcomes.role_note: [A] = wants more privacy and is dissatisfied; [B] = wants more family sharing and is content.

outcomes.verdict: [A] fears family will permanently hold temporary pain against the relationship. [B] fears privacy will become isolation and leave real distress unsupported. Build a support ladder instead of choosing secrecy or full disclosure. First use the couple check, then a neutral friend or professional, then family only for practical support or safety. If family is involved, share the repair update too.
outcomes.actions_a: Define the private first step and the conditions that move support to the next rung.
outcomes.actions_b: Identify the neutral support person and the practical or safety threshold for family involvement.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Relationship Support Ladder with couple check, neutral support, family threshold, protected details, and repair update.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Privacy and support become stages instead of opposing loyalties.
outcomes.role_note: [A] = wants more privacy; [B] = wants more family sharing.

cases.title: When Cultural or Family Expectations Clashed With What You Two Wanted
cases.subtitle: How much should cultural or family expectations shape the choice you make as a couple?

questions.prompt: How much should cultural or family expectations shape the choice you make as a couple?

options.label: Very little
Only when both genuinely choose them
Some influence with room to adapt
A lot because belonging and identity matter
Very strongly, departing would carry serious loss

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: How do you feel about the room your own shared version currently has?

options.label: It works for me
Mostly okay, with a few hard moments
It regularly leaves me tense or disconnected
I need this pattern to change

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: Where does the expectation show up?

options.label: Marriage or ceremony
Gender or family roles
Religion or holidays
Living arrangements
Money or caregiving
Children, names, or language

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: What would create room for both?

options.label: Protect one core cultural meaning
Adapt the format
Set a boundary with family
Create a private couple practice
Ask an elder or counselor to help translate
Choose a review point after trying the new version

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: Want to tell the court a bit more about what happened? (optional)
questions.interactionRule: Private context is used only to personalize the selected deterministic branch.

outcomes.verdict: You give cultural and family expectations similar weight and generally feel your shared version still belongs to both of you. That alignment is more than convenience. It means identity is being carried forward through consent instead of obedience. Keep naming the meaning behind each expectation and checking whether the format still serves it. A tradition can remain authentic even when the couple changes how it lives.
outcomes.actions_a: Name one expectation you actively choose and the meaning you want it to preserve.
outcomes.actions_b: Name one format you can adapt so participation stays genuine for both partners.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Meaning and Format Map with chosen expectation, core meaning, adapted practice, family message, and review.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Culture stays alive because the couple carries it intentionally.

outcomes.verdict: [A] and [B] give expectations similar weight, but [A] is less content because participation may cost [A] more identity, labor, or freedom. A shared yes can still hide unequal adaptation. Name what each person is asked to perform, give up, or explain. Then change the format where one partner is carrying the cultural translation alone.
outcomes.actions_a: Name the identity or labor cost that remains invisible inside the shared choice.
outcomes.actions_b: Take ownership of one family explanation or practical adaptation that reduces [A]'s load.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save an Expectation Impact Check with meaning, each partner's cost, adaptation, family-side speaker, and review date.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Shared values stop relying on one partner doing all the translating.
outcomes.role_note: [A] = less content with the current cultural balance; [B] = more content.

outcomes.verdict: You value cultural connection similarly yet both feel squeezed because the current choice is framed as keep everything or reject everything. Separate meaning from format. Preserve the value, story, language, or relationship that matters most, then redesign timing, roles, ceremony, or participation. The couple is not choosing between identity and autonomy; it is deciding how identity will be lived now.
outcomes.actions_a: Choose the cultural meaning you refuse to lose and the format you are willing to change.
outcomes.actions_b: Choose a different meaning and design one couple-led practice that carries it forward.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Keep the Meaning, Change the Form plan with values, adaptations, roles, family communication, and trial date.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Identity gets continuity without requiring the old script word for word.

outcomes.verdict: [A] gives cultural expectation more weight because it connects to belonging, family safety, faith, or identity. [B] wants more freedom to build a version that fits the couple. You are content because meaning and format can be assigned separate guardians. [A] protects the core meaning. [B] designs an adapted format that respects it. Try the version once before deciding whether it feels connecting or performative.
outcomes.actions_a: Define the core meaning in plain language and release control over one part of the format.
outcomes.actions_b: Design the adapted practice and show exactly where the protected meaning remains visible.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Meaning Guardian and Format Designer plan with core value, adapted practice, family message, trial, and review.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Belonging and authorship become different jobs on the same team.
outcomes.role_note: [A] gives cultural expectations more weight; [B] wants more couple-led freedom.

outcomes.verdict: [A] gives expectations more weight and feels a real belonging cost when they are loosened. [B] wants more freedom and is comfortable with the current shift. The freedom for [B] is arriving as cultural loneliness for [A]. [B] owes protection of one meaningful element. [A] owes an adaptation that does not require [B] to perform a role that feels inauthentic.
outcomes.actions_a: Name the one element whose loss would create the most disconnection and propose a flexible way to keep it.
outcomes.actions_b: Protect that element and name the role or expectation you cannot authentically perform.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Protected Meaning Agreement with core element, flexible format, role boundary, family message, and check-in.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. One partner keeps belonging without asking the other to disappear inside it.
outcomes.role_note: [A] gives expectations more weight and is dissatisfied; [B] wants more freedom and is content.

outcomes.verdict: [A] fears that choosing the couple's version will weaken family belonging or identity. [B] fears that inherited expectations will decide a life the couple is supposed to author. Do not resolve this through one high-pressure family event. Choose a six-month trial with one protected cultural practice, one redesigned role, and one private couple decision kept outside family influence. Review lived impact, not only family reaction.
outcomes.actions_a: Select the protected practice and the belonging need it serves.
outcomes.actions_b: Select the redesigned role and the private decision area the couple will keep fully its own.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Six-Month Culture and Couple Trial with keep, redesign, private lane, family message, and review criteria.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. The couple learns what preserves identity and what merely preserves pressure.
outcomes.role_note: [A] gives cultural expectations more weight; [B] wants more couple-led freedom.

cases.title: When One of You Felt They Had to Choose Between Their Partner and Their Parent
cases.subtitle: Who is more likely to feel trapped into choosing between partner and parent?

questions.prompt: Who is more likely to feel trapped into choosing between partner and parent?

options.label: Me, no contest
Probably me
Probably them
Definitely them
Honestly, both of us about equally

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: What best explains that answer?

options.label: feels responsible for both relationships
hears every boundary as a loyalty demand
fears hurting a parent who relies on them
fears losing the partner's trust
has not separated support from agreement
can move once the specific decision rights are clear

questions.interactionRule: Display as the answering player’s own voice.

questions.prompt: What created the choice feeling?

options.label: A parent needed care
A boundary was ignored
Both wanted the same time
A decision affected the couple
Private information was shared
Each side asked for proof of loyalty

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: What would remove the forced choice?

options.label: Separate the relationships from the decision
Name the couple boundary
Define caregiving responsibility
Stop message-carrying
Use an outside support person
Set different times for different needs

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: Want to tell the court a bit more about what happened? (optional)
questions.interactionRule: Private context is used only to personalize the selected deterministic branch.

outcomes.verdict: [A] feels the choice pressure more because both relationships may treat [A]'s response as evidence of loyalty. [B] sees the trap and can help by narrowing the request. Instead of asking [A] to choose a person, decide one behavior, time, or decision right. [A] can support a parent emotionally while still protecting the couple boundary in the specific situation.
outcomes.actions_a: State the narrow couple boundary without asking [A] to reject or downgrade the parent relationship.
outcomes.actions_b: Separate care for your parent from agreement with the behavior and deliver the boundary yourself.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a People Are Not the Decision note with parent care, couple boundary, behavior, speaker, and support plan.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. The relationship chooses a boundary, not a winner between two people.
outcomes.role_note: [A] = the partner both identified as more likely to feel trapped between partner and parent.

outcomes.verdict: [B] feels trapped because a parent's need and a partner's need are arriving as competing loyalty tests. [A] recognizes the pressure and can make the couple request more specific. [B] does not need to choose who matters more. [B] needs to choose what behavior, decision, or time commitment fits the relationship's boundary while arranging separate care for the parent.
outcomes.actions_a: Support the parent need separately, then state the couple boundary without making [A] enforce it.
outcomes.actions_b: Turn your concern into one specific request that leaves the parent relationship intact.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a People Are Not the Decision note with parent care, couple boundary, behavior, speaker, and support plan.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. A specific choice replaces the impossible demand to rank two relationships.
outcomes.role_note: [B] = the partner both identified as more likely to feel trapped between partner and parent.

outcomes.verdict: Both of you can feel caught between partner and parent, which gives you real empathy for how quickly a boundary can sound like a loyalty contest. Use one shared rule: no request may require emotional rejection of a parent, and no parent need automatically overrides couple decision rights. Translate every conflict into behavior, capacity, and timing. People remain loved while choices become discussable.
outcomes.actions_a: Translate one loyalty-sounding request into a behavior, amount of support, and time frame.
outcomes.actions_b: Do the same for your side and identify which couple decision right stays protected.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Loyalty-to-Logistics Translator with people, behavior, care need, couple right, timing, and speaker.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Love stays attached to people while boundaries attach to actions.

outcomes.verdict: Each of you sees yourself as the more trapped partner, likely because different parent relationships create different kinds of pressure. [A] may face caregiving dependence. [B] may face approval, tradition, or emotional obligation. Map the pressure source and the decision it is distorting. Then give each other one boundary and one support action rather than comparing whose parent dynamic is harder.
outcomes.actions_a: Name the parent pressure and the decision right you need help protecting.
outcomes.actions_b: Name your different pressure and offer one support action for [A] before asking for your own.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Two-Parent Pressure Map with needs, couple rights, boundaries, support actions, and review dates.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Two family pressures receive two tailored supports from one allied couple.

outcomes.verdict: Each of you thinks the other feels more trapped, which may mean both partners avoid naming parent pressure until a decision becomes urgent. Add a monthly family-capacity check covering time, money, care, and privacy. Early visibility turns a loyalty emergency into resource planning. Neither parent relationship needs to be placed on trial for the couple to set limits.
outcomes.actions_a: Bring one upcoming parent need to the check before it collides with a couple plan.
outcomes.actions_b: State the capacity you can offer and the couple commitment that must remain protected.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Monthly Family Capacity Check with upcoming needs, available support, protected couple plans, speaker, and follow-up.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Earlier planning keeps family care from arriving as a forced choice.

outcomes.verdict: [A] sees one partner as the more frequent receiver of parent-versus-partner pressure. [B] sees the experience as shared or situational. Use the recurring dynamic to plan earlier, while keeping the no-loyalty-test rule mutual. The pressured partner names the specific choice. The other partner helps separate parent care from couple boundaries and does not demand emotional proof.
outcomes.actions_a: Name the recurring choice and the care you want to preserve alongside the couple boundary.
outcomes.actions_b: Help design the separation and avoid using the pressure pattern as evidence about overall commitment.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Recurring Choice Separation with parent care, couple boundary, decision, timing, and support role.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. One known pressure point gets an earlier route that protects both relationships.
outcomes.role_note: [A] = identified a specific more frequently pressured partner; [B] = said the experience is shared or situational.

cases.title: When a Sibling or Family Member's Behavior Caused Friction Between You Two
cases.subtitle: Who is more likely to absorb or excuse a sibling or relative's disruptive behavior?

questions.prompt: Who is more likely to absorb or excuse a sibling or relative's disruptive behavior?

options.label: Me, no contest
Probably me
Probably them
Definitely them
Honestly, both of us about equally

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: What best explains that answer?

options.label: has known the pattern for years
expects the behavior and adapts automatically
fears setting a limit will create a larger family problem
separates family love from the behavior
does not always notice the cost to the partner
can act once the couple names a specific boundary

questions.interactionRule: Display as the answering player’s own voice.

questions.prompt: What behavior created friction?

options.label: Last-minute demands
Disrespectful comments
Money or favors
Uninvited involvement
Drama during family events
Repeated broken plans

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: What response fits the behavior?

options.label: Stop rescuing the consequence
Set a response window
Decline one category of favor
End the conversation when disrespect starts
Meet in a neutral setting
Increase distance only after a repeat

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: Want to tell the court a bit more about what happened? (optional)
questions.interactionRule: Private context is used only to personalize the selected deterministic branch.

outcomes.verdict: [A] is more likely to absorb the family member's behavior because years of adaptation made it feel like weather: inconvenient, familiar, and not fully changeable. [B] experiences the same pattern as a choice entering the relationship. [A] can stop rescuing one consequence and set one behavior-specific boundary. [B] can request protection without demanding that [A] stop loving the relative.
outcomes.actions_a: Choose one consequence you will no longer absorb and communicate the matching boundary.
outcomes.actions_b: Name the specific relationship cost and the minimum protection needed, without attacking the family bond.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Relative Behavior Boundary with behavior, consequence, new limit, speaker, repeat step, and couple check.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Family love remains while the disruptive behavior loses automatic access.
outcomes.role_note: [A] = the partner both identified as more likely to absorb or excuse the behavior.

outcomes.verdict: [B] has adapted to the relative's behavior so thoroughly that the cost may feel like normal family maintenance. [A] experiences the spillover without the same history or attachment. Both of you see the pattern now. [B] can reclaim one boundary lane and stop volunteering the couple to carry the consequence. [A] can focus the request on behavior, not the relative's entire place in [B]'s life.
outcomes.actions_a: Name the couple cost and request one behavior-specific limit.
outcomes.actions_b: Set the limit with your relative and stop repairing the consequence on the couple's time or money.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Relative Behavior Boundary with behavior, consequence, new limit, speaker, repeat step, and couple check.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Familiar chaos stops receiving an automatic household subsidy.
outcomes.role_note: [B] = the partner both identified as more likely to absorb or excuse the behavior.

outcomes.verdict: Both of you sometimes absorb family behavior, which means compassion is strong but boundaries become inconsistent. Choose categories, not personalities. Last-minute requests, disrespect, money, and uninvited involvement each get one default response regardless of whose relative is involved. A category rule feels fairer and is easier to use before emotion or family history takes over.
outcomes.actions_a: Choose one behavior category and write the default response you want applied to both families.
outcomes.actions_b: Choose a second category and the repeat step if the first response is ignored.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Two-Family Behavior Policy with categories, default responses, speakers, repeat steps, and emergency exceptions.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Compassion stays personal while boundaries become consistent.

outcomes.verdict: Each of you sees yourself as more likely to absorb family behavior, which may mean different categories trigger different rescue habits. [A] may step in around money or logistics. [B] may excuse comments, cancellations, or emotional drama. Trade categories and identify the couple cost. Then each partner sets the limit with their own family.
outcomes.actions_a: Name your rescue category and the cost it creates inside the relationship.
outcomes.actions_b: Name your different category and set the first boundary with your relative before the next request.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Rescue Habit Exchange with categories, couple costs, family-side speakers, boundaries, and review date.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Two rescue habits become two clear chances to protect the couple.

outcomes.verdict: Each of you thinks the other absorbs more family behavior, which often means both people can see the partner's exceptions more clearly than their own. Audit the last three family requests on both sides using the same questions: urgency, capacity, couple cost, and repeat pattern. The record reveals where compassion is becoming a default obligation.
outcomes.actions_a: Review one request from your side and name the couple cost honestly.
outcomes.actions_b: Review one from your side and choose the category rule that should apply next time.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Six-Request Family Audit with request, urgency, capacity, couple cost, response, and future rule.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. One shared test replaces selective memory about whose family gets more exceptions.

outcomes.verdict: [A] sees one partner as the frequent absorber. [B] sees family accommodation as shared or situational. Use the recurring category as the first boundary target and apply the same policy to both families. The frequent absorber gets a prepared decline line. The other partner supports the limit without taking over family communication.
outcomes.actions_a: Practice the decline line for the recurring request and use it before the couple absorbs the consequence.
outcomes.actions_b: Back the limit privately and avoid rescuing the family response for your partner.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Recurring Family Request Plan with trigger, decline line, speaker, partner support, and emergency exception.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. One repeated pattern loses its shortcut into the relationship.
outcomes.role_note: [A] = identified a specific frequent absorber; [B] = said accommodation is shared or situational.

cases.title: When Family Visits Left One of You Feeling Drained and Unheard
cases.subtitle: How draining do family visits tend to feel for you?

questions.prompt: How draining do family visits tend to feel for you?

options.label: Usually energizing
A little tiring but manageable
Mixed, depending on length and dynamics
Very draining without recovery time
Deeply draining, I struggle to stay present

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: How do you feel about the way your energy is handled during visits?

options.label: It works for me
Mostly okay, with a few hard moments
It regularly leaves me tense or disconnected
I need this pattern to change

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: What uses the most energy?

options.label: Constant social engagement
Translation or cultural effort
Hosting and practical work
Managing comments or tension
Lack of privacy
The visit lasts beyond my capacity

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: What would help next time?

options.label: A shorter visit
Private breaks
Shared hosting tasks
A check-in signal
An agreed exit time
Recovery time afterward

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: Want to tell the court a bit more about what happened? (optional)
questions.interactionRule: Private context is used only to personalize the selected deterministic branch.

outcomes.verdict: You leave family visits with a similar energy level and generally respect each other's limits. That shared pacing keeps family connection from consuming the couple's recovery time. Protect the strength by deciding the exit time before arrival and reserving one quiet window afterward. A good visit does not have to use every available hour to prove warmth.
outcomes.actions_a: Name the visit length that lets you remain present rather than merely endure the final stretch.
outcomes.actions_b: Name the recovery ritual that helps both of you return to the relationship afterward.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Family Visit Energy Plan with arrival, exit time, break, hosting split, signal, and recovery window.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Family time stays warmer because the visit ends before both batteries hit zero.

outcomes.verdict: [A] and [B] feel similar overall drain, but [A] is less content because [A] may be carrying more hosting, translation, or emotional scanning during the visit. [B] sees both people tired; [A] experiences being on duty. Separate social energy from visit labor. Transfer one full lane and give [A] a protected break that does not require an explanation to family.
outcomes.actions_a: Name the visit duty that keeps you from participating as a guest or partner.
outcomes.actions_b: Take that lane completely and explain [A]'s break to your family without making [A] justify it.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Visit Energy and Labor Split with duties, break times, family explanation, exit time, and recovery.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Tired stops meaning one partner worked while the other simply attended.
outcomes.role_note: [A] = less content with how visit energy is handled; [B] = more content.

outcomes.verdict: You become similarly drained and both keep agreeing to visits designed around family expectations rather than actual capacity. Build the visit backward from the energy you want left afterward. Set duration, one break, one shared responsibility, and a clean exit line. The family receives a more present version of both of you for less time, which is often better connection than a long depleted visit.
outcomes.actions_a: Choose the maximum duration and the break you need before your attention starts disappearing.
outcomes.actions_b: Choose the exit line and the hosting task you will own so the plan does not depend on improvisation.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Capacity-First Visit Plan with length, break, duties, exit line, and post-visit recovery.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. The visit gets smaller enough for the connection inside it to become real.

outcomes.verdict: [A] becomes more drained because family visits require greater social, cultural, sensory, or emotional effort. [B] has more capacity and may genuinely enjoy the extended time. You are content because attendance and duration do not need to match. [A] can leave earlier or take breaks while [B] stays longer. The couple reconnects afterward without treating different energy as rejection of the family.
outcomes.actions_a: Choose the visit portion you can attend warmly and the signal for your planned exit or break.
outcomes.actions_b: Explain the split plan to your family and enjoy the longer contact without pressuring [A] to match it.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Split-Duration Visit Plan with shared portion, separate time, break signal, transport, and reconnect ritual.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Family closeness expands without requiring equal social batteries.
outcomes.role_note: [A] is more drained by family visits; [B] has more capacity.

outcomes.verdict: [A] becomes more drained and feels unheard about visit limits. [B] has more capacity and finds the current length acceptable, so the visit is being designed by the fuller battery. [B] owes one concrete habit: agree on [A]'s exit time beforehand and defend it without apology. [A] owes honest participation during the chosen window rather than silently enduring until resentment takes over.
outcomes.actions_a: Choose the duration you can offer and use the exit signal at that time instead of extending from pressure.
outcomes.actions_b: Protect the exit plan with your family and arrange transport that does not trap [A] inside your preferred length.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Lower-Battery Visit Rule with shared window, exit time, transport, family message, and reconnect plan.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. The visit follows the capacity needed for genuine participation.
outcomes.role_note: [A] is more drained and dissatisfied; [B] has more capacity and is content.

outcomes.verdict: [A] enters family visits already budgeting every social minute. [B] enters expecting connection and feels hurt when [A] withdraws or wants to leave. The more [B] stretches the visit, the less presence [A] has to offer. Test three visits with a fixed shared window, optional extension for [B], and a no-questions break for [A]. Review connection quality, not endurance.
outcomes.actions_a: Attend the fixed window and use the break or exit without disappearing silently.
outcomes.actions_b: Keep extensions optional and reconnect with [A] later instead of making the visit length a measure of family care.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Three-Visit Energy Trial with shared window, optional extension, break, transport, connection rating, and review.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Presence becomes the goal, and duration stops impersonating devotion.
outcomes.role_note: [A] is more drained by visits; [B] wants more family time.

cases.title: When You Felt Your Partner's Loyalty to Family Came Before Loyalty to You
cases.subtitle: Who is more likely to feel the couple's needs get placed behind family expectations?

questions.prompt: Who is more likely to feel the couple's needs get placed behind family expectations?

options.label: Me, no contest
Probably me
Probably them
Definitely them
Honestly, both of us about equally

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: What best explains that answer?

[A] then handles the family answer. [B] names the exact protection needed without asking [A] to feel less attached to family.

outcomes.actions_a: Name the family door where you feel displaced and the consultation step you need.

Install a twenty-four-hour pause for nonurgent commitments involving shared time, money, home, or privacy. Neither person gives family an immediate answer. outcomes.actions_b: Respect the pause on your side and avoid making a tentative family response before consultation.

outcomes.closing: Case softened. The couple gets a real first turn before family momentum decides for you.

The family-connected partner pauses, consults, and owns the external answer.

outcomes.verdict: [A] is the partner who catches possible tension in small wording, timing, or punctuation. That sensitivity can spot real disconnection early, but text leaves enough blank space for the nervous system to write its own subtitle. [B] already sees this pattern, which gives you a shared starting point. Let [A] ask one direct meaning question, and let [B] answer the emotional tone before defending the sentence.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = the partner both identified as more likely to hear extra meaning in a text.

outcomes.verdict: [B] picks up possible subtext in short replies, delayed messages, or tiny wording shifts. That radar often comes from caring about connection, yet a screen removes voice, face, and the rest of the day. [A] recognizes the pattern and can help by answering the feeling behind the question before explaining intent. [B] can make the uncertainty visible without presenting the feared interpretation as a fact.
outcomes.actions_a: Respond to the tone concern directly and name whether you were rushed, stressed, playful, or upset.
outcomes.actions_b: Quote the line, ask what feeling was intended, and wait for the answer before building a larger story.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Text Tone Reset with the question, tone answer, voice-note option, sensitive-topic rule, and reply-time signal.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. The message gets its missing voice back.
outcomes.role_note: [B] = the partner both identified as more likely to hear extra meaning in a text.

outcomes.verdict: Both of you read beyond the literal words, so text can become a room full of echoes when either person is tired or already tender. The upside is strong emotional attention. The risk is two interpretations arriving before one clarification. Choose a shared signal such as 'tone check' that pauses the story and moves the topic to a voice note or live conversation. Your sensitivity becomes teamwork when it requests context instead of producing a verdict.
outcomes.actions_a: Use the shared signal the next time a message feels loaded and name the exact line needing context.
outcomes.actions_b: Reply with intended tone and choose text, voice note, or later conversation for the rest.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Tone Check protocol with signal phrase, response format, sensitive topics, delay message, and repair line.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Two active radars get one calm verification step.

outcomes.verdict: Each of you sees yourself as the one who notices hidden meaning because you track different clues. [A] may focus on wording and punctuation; [B] may focus on timing, recent tension, or what was left out. That means both readings can contain useful data without either interpretation being complete. Name the clue before naming the story. Then ask the sender which meaning was actually present.
outcomes.actions_a: Identify the specific clue you noticed and separate it from the conclusion you drew.
outcomes.actions_b: Identify your different clue, then let the sender answer both before either person responds further.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Clue Versus Story note with wording clue, timing clue, each interpretation, confirmed meaning, and repair message.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. The clues stay useful without pretending they are the whole message.

outcomes.verdict: Each of you thinks the other is more likely to misread text, which usually means both people remember being misunderstood more clearly than misunderstanding. That is normal memory, not a character problem. Skip the identity question and improve the channel. Sensitive subjects get a heads-up, rushed replies get labeled, and any message that requires three explanations moves to voice or live conversation.
outcomes.actions_a: Add a clear rushed, joking, or sensitive-topic label when the missing tone could change the message.
outcomes.actions_b: Ask for a channel switch after the first confusing exchange instead of proving how the text should have been read.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Text Channel Rule with tone labels, switch trigger, delay message, voice-note option, and reconnection line.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Better channel rules do what memory comparisons cannot.

outcomes.verdict: [A] sees one partner as the more frequent reader of subtext. [B] sees the habit as shared and wants both people responsible for clarity. Those views fit together. Use the identified pattern to target support, while keeping the same clarification right for either partner. The sender answers tone; the receiver names the exact phrase; both avoid using old examples to turn one confusing text into a personality case.
outcomes.actions_a: Name the recurring trigger and ask for one sender habit that would lower ambiguity.
outcomes.actions_b: Use the same clarification format when you are unsure and avoid treating [A]'s observation as a permanent label.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Shared Clarification Card with recurring trigger, sender habit, receiver question, channel switch, and reset line.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. A real pattern gets support without becoming anyone's identity.
outcomes.role_note: [A] = identified a specific partner; [B] = said both partners do this about equally.

cases.title: When Silence After a Disagreement Says Different Things to Each of You
cases.subtitle: How strongly does silence after a disagreement signal distance or danger to you?

A little, unless it lasts unexpectedly
It depends on whether reconnection was named

Very strongly, silence feels like the relationship is at risk

questions.prompt: What does silence usually mean from your side?

options.label: I am lowering my intensity
I need time to find words
I fear making things worse
I am waiting for them to approach
I feel hurt and disconnected
I think the conversation is finished

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: What signal would help most?

options.label: A clear return time
A short reassurance
Permission not to reply yet
A check-in by text
A boundary on how long the pause lasts
A simple way to restart

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: Want to tell the court a bit more about what happened? (optional)
questions.interactionRule: Private context is used only to personalize the selected deterministic branch.

outcomes.verdict: You give silence a similar meaning and the current rhythm generally lets both nervous systems settle without turning the pause into punishment. The useful part is the shared expectation of return. Protect it explicitly: name whether you are cooling down, thinking, or finished for tonight, plus when contact resumes. Silence remains spacious because neither partner has to guess whether the relationship is still in the room.
outcomes.actions_a: Use one sentence to name the purpose of your next pause and the time you expect to return.
outcomes.actions_b: Acknowledge the return time and use the pause for regulation rather than drafting a counterargument.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Quiet With Return rule with pause phrase, purpose, maximum length, reassurance, and restart line.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. The quiet keeps its calm without borrowing fear from uncertainty.

outcomes.verdict: [A] and [B] react to silence at similar intensity, but [A] is less okay with the current pattern. The difference may be follow-through. [A] hears a promised pause but still has to chase the restart, while [B] experiences space as successfully completed. Make the person requesting silence responsible for reopening the conversation. A pause becomes trustworthy when the return is an action, not a hopeful estimate.
outcomes.actions_a: Name the missed return or unclear ending that makes silence feel less safe for you.
outcomes.actions_b: Set the return time and initiate the restart yourself, even if the first message is only a readiness update.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Pause Ownership note with requester, reason, return time, restart owner, extension message, and next step.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Space gets a reliable door back in.
outcomes.role_note: [A] = less content with the current silence pattern; [B] = more content.

outcomes.verdict: You read silence similarly, yet neither person likes what happens inside it. The pause may lower volume while increasing private storytelling, so you return calmer but farther apart. Give the quiet one job: regulate, not decide the meaning of the relationship. Each person writes one feeling, one need, and one thing they can own. Bring those notes to a fixed restart instead of bringing a fully argued private trial.
outcomes.actions_a: During the pause, write one feeling and one need without explaining your partner's motive.
outcomes.actions_b: Write one part you can own and one curious question for the restart.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Pause Prep note with feeling, need, owned part, curious question, and scheduled restart.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. The quiet prepares connection instead of rehearsing distance.

outcomes.verdict: [A] experiences silence as possible disconnection and needs evidence that the bond is intact. [B] experiences silence as necessary regulation and needs freedom from immediate engagement. Your current rhythm works because reassurance and space can coexist. Keep the sequence clear: [B] sends a brief connection message and return time, then [A] protects the pause from repeated checking. Reconnection happens at the promised time even if the full issue needs longer.
outcomes.actions_a: Accept one reassurance and avoid adding new questions before the named return time.
outcomes.actions_b: Send the reassurance and reopen contact at the promised time without waiting to feel perfectly ready.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Reassure Then Pause script with connection line, return time, extension rule, restart opener, and maximum pause.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Reassurance protects the bond while space lowers the heat.
outcomes.role_note: [A] = feels more threatened by silence; [B] = experiences silence as useful space.

outcomes.verdict: [A] feels distance quickly and is not okay with a silence pattern that has no clear edges. [B] finds the current space comfortable because it reduces immediate pressure. The calm for [B] is being purchased with uncertainty for [A]. [B] owes one small habit: a return time and a connection sentence before going quiet. [A] owes the pause freedom from repeated messages once that habit is delivered.
outcomes.actions_a: Ask for the two specific signals you need, then stop seeking extra reassurance during the agreed pause.
outcomes.actions_b: Send the connection sentence, give a realistic return time, and initiate contact when it arrives.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Two-Signal Silence Agreement with reassurance, return time, no-chasing boundary, extension message, and restart owner.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Space stays available without making one partner wait in emotional fog.
outcomes.role_note: [A] = feels more threatened by silence and is dissatisfied; [B] = prefers silence and is content.

outcomes.verdict: [A] pursues contact because silence feels like the relationship is slipping away. [B] extends silence because each new message feels like the disagreement is still entering the room. The chase and retreat are feeding each other. Use a timed pause with one permitted logistics channel and one mandatory return. If either person cannot resume, they send a new time plus a short reassurance. Predictability lowers both urgency and avoidance.
outcomes.actions_a: Send no conflict messages during the timer and write your key need for the restart instead.
outcomes.actions_b: Choose a realistic timer, return when it ends, and request one bounded extension if regulation is still incomplete.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Timed Pause Protocol with duration, logistics channel, reassurance line, extension limit, and restart question.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. A clock replaces the chase, and a promised return replaces the disappearance.
outcomes.role_note: [A] = feels more threatened by silence; [B] = prefers silence for regulation.

cases.title: When One of You Wanted to Talk Right Away and the Other Needed Space

options.label: It works for me
Mostly okay, with a few rough moments
It regularly leaves me tense or disconnected
I need this pattern to change

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: What is your nervous system trying to protect?

options.label: Not saying something harsher
Getting my thoughts organized
Knowing the relationship is okay
Stopping the issue from growing
Being heard while the moment is fresh
Avoiding a conversation that feels endless

A pause phrase that does not sound rejecting

outcomes.verdict: You need roughly the same amount of time before talking, so conflict timing does not regularly force one nervous system to chase the other. The real asset is a shared sense of when conversation becomes useful. Keep a clear distinction between cooling down and avoiding. Name a return time, arrive with one topic, and stop when either person leaves the regulated zone. Your similar pace can support repair without making speed the goal.
outcomes.actions_a: Name the physical or emotional sign that tells you you are ready for a useful conversation.
outcomes.actions_b: Name the sign that tells you a pause is needed again before the talk becomes less kind.

outcomes.closing: Case softened. Matching timing becomes a skill, not just a lucky instinct.

outcomes.verdict: [A] and [B] want a similar delay, but [A] is less satisfied because the agreement may not survive the moment. The promised hour becomes three, or the quick talk begins before either person has settled. [B] remembers the intention; [A] experiences the broken timing. Pick a window you can actually keep and use one update if it changes. Reliable timing matters more than choosing the perfect number of minutes.
outcomes.actions_a: Name the part of the timing promise that keeps breaking and the window you could trust.
outcomes.actions_b: Choose a realistic return window and send the update before it expires rather than after.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Conflict Timing Promise with pause length, update deadline, restart owner, one-topic limit, and extension cap.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. A realistic promise does more for safety than an ambitious one that slips.

outcomes.verdict: You are close on timing, yet the talks still go badly because the pause is not changing how you reenter. You come back with the same opening line, the same evidence pile, and the same defensive posture. Use the break to prepare a softer first minute. Each person returns with one feeling, one impact, and one request. The issue can stay complex while the doorway becomes simpler.

outcomes.actions_b: Prepare one doable request and one sentence acknowledging what may have landed hard.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a First Minute Back note with feeling, impact, acknowledgment, request, and the one topic being discussed.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. The pause starts changing the conversation instead of only delaying it.

outcomes.verdict: [A] needs faster contact because uncertainty keeps the conflict active internally. [B] needs more space because immediate conversation overloads the ability to listen and speak carefully. You are content because the relationship has learned to build a small bridge before the longer crossing. Use a two-minute connection round now, then schedule the full talk. [A] receives evidence of return; [B] receives protected processing time.
outcomes.actions_a: Use the two-minute round only to name care, the topic, and the return time, not to start the argument.
outcomes.actions_b: Choose the return time and come back with your main point organized into one short paragraph.

outcomes.closing: Case softened. Immediate connection and slower processing stop competing for the same minute.
outcomes.role_note: [A] = needs faster contact; [B] = needs more space.

outcomes.verdict: [A] wants quicker conversation and feels stranded by the current delay. [B] needs more space and feels the arrangement works because pressure drops. That relief is landing unevenly. [B] owes a reliable bridge message and a return time. [A] owes a clean pause after receiving them. If the issue is urgent for safety, money, or logistics, use a separate short emergency lane rather than pulling the entire conflict into the pause.
outcomes.actions_a: Ask for one bridge message and one return time, then move your remaining thoughts into a note.
outcomes.actions_b: Send the bridge before stepping away and reopen the topic yourself at the agreed time.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Bridge and Return Agreement with message, time, emergency lane, no-pursuit boundary, and restart owner.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Space gets structure, and urgency gets a small safe lane.
outcomes.role_note: [A] = needs faster contact and is dissatisfied; [B] = needs more space and is content.

outcomes.verdict: [A] pushes for an immediate talk because delay feels like loss of connection. [B] asks for more space because immediate intensity makes careful conversation less possible. Each person's protection activates the other's fear. Stop negotiating timing while activated. Choose the standard rhythm when calm: brief reassurance now, a fixed processing block, and a twenty-minute first conversation. Extend only by mutual agreement after that first round.
outcomes.actions_a: Respect the processing block and prepare one priority instead of sending additional arguments.
outcomes.actions_b: Give the reassurance, honor the start time, and stay for the full first round before requesting more space.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Standard Conflict Rhythm with bridge message, processing block, first-round length, extension rule, and closing check.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. A prebuilt rhythm steps in before urgency and overload start directing each other.
outcomes.role_note: [A] = needs faster contact; [B] = needs more space.

cases.title: When Venting Got Met With Advice Instead of Just Listening

questions.prompt: Who is more likely to offer solutions when the other person mainly needs to vent?

options.label: Me, no contest
Probably me
Probably them
Definitely them
Honestly, both of us about equally

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: What best explains that answer?

options.label: shows care by looking for a fix
gets anxious when a problem stays open
spots practical next steps quickly
assumes sharing means asking for help
has trouble knowing what kind of support is wanted
can listen well once the support mode is named

options.label: My feelings were a problem to solve
The solution was obvious
I should move on faster

questions.interactionRule: Private context is used only to personalize the selected deterministic branch.

outcomes.verdict: [A] reaches for solutions because fixing feels like active love. [B] recognizes the intention but needed company inside the feeling before any exit route. Advice arrived one emotional beat early. Keep [A]'s practical strength, just move it later in the sequence: reflect, ask what support mode is wanted, then offer ideas only with consent. [B] can make the assignment visible before the story begins.

outcomes.verdict: [B] shows care by finding the next move, especially when seeing [A] upset creates urgency. [A] did not need the problem transferred into project mode yet. The missed connection happened before the advice, not inside the quality of the advice. Let [B] reflect the emotional center and ask permission before solving. Let [A] label whether this is venting, brainstorming, or a request for help.
outcomes.actions_a: Name the support mode at the start and signal clearly if you want it to change later.
outcomes.actions_b: Reflect what sounds hardest, ask permission, and hold every solution until the answer is yes.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Support Mode Menu with listening, comfort, ideas, mixed mode, switch question, and closing check.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Care lands once the support mode arrives before the suggestions.
outcomes.role_note: [B] = the partner both identified as more likely to offer solutions first.

outcomes.verdict: Both of you move toward solutions quickly, which makes sense when competence is one of the ways you care. The catch is that each person may enjoy giving advice more than receiving it while still emotional. Create a two-step rule: first summarize the feeling and ask whether anything is needed; only then brainstorm. You keep your shared problem-solving energy without skipping the moment that says, 'I get why this hit you.'
outcomes.actions_a: Practice a one-sentence reflection before offering any next step in the next venting moment.
outcomes.actions_b: Answer the support question directly and invite ideas only when your system is ready for them.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Feel First, Fix Second card with reflection line, support question, permission phrase, idea limit, and later check-in.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Your fixer energy becomes more connecting because it stops arriving first.

outcomes.verdict: Each of you sees yourself as the quick adviser, which may mean the pattern changes by topic. [A] may solve work or money; [B] may solve family or social stress. The useful discovery is not who does it more. It is which subjects activate the urge to rescue. Name those subjects and agree that high-trigger topics always begin with a support-mode question.
outcomes.actions_a: Identify the topic that makes you start solving and the discomfort you are trying to reduce.
outcomes.actions_b: Identify your different trigger topic and prepare the reflection you want to offer first.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Fixer Trigger Map with each topic, default support mode, reflection line, permission question, and later brainstorm option.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. The rescue reflex gets a map instead of another argument about who does it more.

outcomes.verdict: Each of you thinks the other is the adviser, which suggests the painful memory is receiving an unwanted fix, not noticing the moments you offer one. Drop the scorekeeping and use a universal rule. Every vent begins with the speaker naming the desired mode, and every listener reflects one sentence before adding anything. The structure works even when memory stays uneven.
outcomes.actions_a: Name listening, comfort, or ideas before the story and correct the mode early if needed.
outcomes.actions_b: Reflect one sentence and ask before changing modes, even when the solution feels obvious.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Universal Venting Opener with three support modes, reflection rule, switch phrase, idea cap, and check-in.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. A shared opener replaces the impossible job of proving who fixes more.

outcomes.verdict: [A] sees a clear default fixer. [B] sees solution mode as something both people enter depending on the subject. That combination points to a household habit, with one partner more likely to pull the lever first. Support the frequent fixer with a pause question, and give both partners the same responsibility to announce what they want. No one has to stop being practical; practicality just waits for an invitation.
outcomes.actions_a: Name the recurring situation where the fixer reflex appears and request the pause question there.
outcomes.actions_b: Use the support-mode label even when you believe the usual pattern already makes the need obvious.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Fixer Pause Agreement with recurring trigger, mode label, reflection step, invitation phrase, and later ideas window.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. The practical brain stays welcome after the emotional door opens.
outcomes.role_note: [A] = identified a specific frequent fixer; [B] = said both partners do this about equally.

cases.title: When a Joke Landed as Something More Serious Than It Was Meant To

The timing followed a hard moment
It sounded like a real belief
A similar joke has happened before
The reaction was laughed off instead of checked

Clarify intent without leading with it
Retire that joke topic
Check before teasing publicly
Offer reassurance tied to the insecurity
Ask what would make humor feel safe again

outcomes.verdict: [A] uses humor to create closeness or release tension, and [B] usually understands that style. This time the joke touched a live wire: an insecurity, audience, recent event, or repeated theme. Intent explains the route but impact shows where it arrived. [A] can name the specific sting before clarifying the joke. [B] can describe the tender spot without turning one miss into a full character description.
outcomes.actions_a: Acknowledge the exact impact, retire or adjust the topic, then clarify what you hoped the joke would do.
outcomes.actions_b: Name the tender spot and the future humor boundary without expanding the moment into unrelated examples.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Humor Boundary Note with sensitive topics, public limits, check-in cue, repair line, and safe teasing zones.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Humor stays part of closeness because tenderness gets a veto when it needs one.
outcomes.role_note: [A] = the partner both identified as more likely to joke around a tender topic.

outcomes.verdict: [B] reaches for humor to keep the relationship light, and [A] generally knows the affection underneath it. The joke landed on a tender place where playfulness could not carry the weight. [B] does not need to deny the loving intent, but impact has to be addressed before the explanation. [A] can make the boundary specific enough that humor still has plenty of room elsewhere.
outcomes.actions_a: Name the impact you now understand and change the topic, audience, or timing rule that allowed it.
outcomes.actions_b: Describe what made this joke different and identify the nearby forms of teasing that still feel safe.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Humor Boundary Note with sensitive topics, public limits, check-in cue, repair line, and safe teasing zones.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. The joke gets retired or resized without retiring the playfulness between you.
outcomes.role_note: [B] = the partner both identified as more likely to joke around a tender topic.

outcomes.verdict: Both of you use humor around vulnerable topics, which can create a private language and also make it harder to signal when a subject stops being fun. The strength is shared play. The missing tool is an easy opt-out that does not require proving why the joke hurt. Pick one phrase that ends the bit immediately, followed by a quick check and no debate about whether the reaction was proportional.
outcomes.actions_a: Use the opt-out phrase early when your body says the joke is no longer playful.
outcomes.actions_b: Stop the bit immediately, check the impact, and save intent for after the person feels understood.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Joke Off-Ramp with stop phrase, check question, public rule, sensitive topics, and repair step.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Shared humor gets a clean exit before it turns into distance.

outcomes.verdict: Each of you identifies as the one who jokes more, which probably means humor is woven into the whole relationship rather than owned by one person. The issue is not the amount. It is whether the person making the joke can notice the moment the audience stops playing. Agree that silence, forced laughter, or a flat 'okay' triggers a check rather than another punchline.
outcomes.actions_a: Name the reaction signal you tend to miss and practice asking whether the joke still feels fun.
outcomes.actions_b: Name the signal you show when hurt and use the shared stop phrase instead of hoping it gets noticed.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Humor Signal Guide with hurt cues, check question, stop phrase, public boundary, and reconnection move.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. The relationship keeps the comedy and gets better at reading the room.

outcomes.verdict: Each of you thinks the other is the one who turns tenderness into a joke. That may be because humor is easier to notice when you are the tender person than when you are the nervous comedian. Skip the tally. For one week, anyone joking about appearance, competence, family, intimacy, money, or a recent hurt checks first. The experiment will reveal which topics need consent more than a permanent label would.
outcomes.actions_a: Check before joking about one named sensitive category and record whether the moment still feels playful.
outcomes.actions_b: Use a clear yes, no, or not today response instead of agreeing out of social momentum.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Seven-Day Humor Check with sensitive categories, consent cue, reactions, repairs, and keep or retire decisions.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. A short experiment protects the tender zones without flattening your humor.

outcomes.verdict: [A] sees one partner as the frequent tender-topic joker. [B] sees humor as shared and situational. Both observations can be true: one person may initiate more while both participate once the bit starts. Give the initiator a check-before rule and give the other partner responsibility to exit honestly rather than laugh along. Shared play becomes safer when both the invitation and the answer are clear.
outcomes.actions_a: Use the check-before rule around the recurring topic or audience that tends to create impact.
outcomes.actions_b: Answer the check honestly and use the off-ramp as soon as the feeling changes.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Humor Consent Card with recurring topic, check phrase, honest response options, stop cue, and repair line.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. The joke becomes a real invitation instead of a momentum trap.
outcomes.role_note: [A] = identified a specific frequent joker; [B] = said both partners use humor this way.

has hinted at the need before

assumes familiar routines should make the need obvious

A familiar date or occasion
An unfinished task
A past conversation
A repeated relationship pattern
The seriousness of the situation

outcomes.verdict: [A] hoped the need would be noticed because being anticipated can feel like being deeply known. [B] saw the clues but did not assemble the same meaning, or missed them entirely. The hurt is real even when the signal was indirect. Keep the desire for attentiveness, but give it a second route: [A] makes the ask before disappointment hardens, and [B] builds one noticing habit around the recurring situation.
outcomes.actions_a: State the need in one sentence and name why being noticed mattered emotionally this time.
outcomes.actions_b: Choose one recurring cue you will actively check and respond to the direct ask without criticizing the timing.

outcomes.closing: Case softened. Being known gets help from being told.
outcomes.role_note: [A] = the partner both identified as more likely to hold an unspoken expectation.

outcomes.verdict: [B] wanted [A] to notice because the need felt familiar, meaningful, or visible through a change in mood. [A] did not receive a complete message, even if pieces were present. This gap does not cancel [B]'s wish to feel known. It shows where mind-reading has been standing in for a relationship system. [B] can ask before the hurt peaks, while [A] creates a reliable check around the recurring cue.
outcomes.actions_a: Build one noticing habit around the situation where the need tends to appear and ask before assuming everything is fine.
outcomes.actions_b: Say the need directly and separate the wish to be anticipated from the practical request that still needs an answer.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Notice and Ask plan with recurring cue, check question, direct request format, response, and follow-up.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. The need becomes easier to meet without becoming less meaningful.
outcomes.role_note: [B] = the partner both identified as more likely to hold an unspoken expectation.

outcomes.verdict: Both of you sometimes treat being known as being anticipated, which makes sense in a close relationship. The trouble starts when each person has a different invisible syllabus. Create a short list of recurring moments where proactive attention matters, such as hard workdays, anniversaries, illness, or arriving home overwhelmed. Everything outside that list gets a direct ask. Romance keeps a place, and daily care stops depending on a surprise test.
outcomes.actions_a: Add one recurring moment where proactive attention genuinely helps you feel cared for.
outcomes.actions_b: Add a different moment and practice one direct request for a need outside the shared list.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Known Moments List with recurring cues, expected check-ins, direct-ask rule, calendar support, and review date.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Attentiveness gets a map without turning love into an exam.

outcomes.verdict: Each of you sees yourself as the one with unspoken expectations, which means the relationship may contain two quiet bids waiting to be discovered at once. Neither partner has enough attention to decode both perfectly under stress. Trade one hidden expectation each and translate it into an observable cue plus a direct request. The surprise is that naming the need can create more intimacy than waiting for a perfect guess.
outcomes.actions_a: Reveal one hidden expectation and turn it into a cue plus a direct request you can actually use.
outcomes.actions_b: Reveal a different expectation and explain what emotional meaning sits underneath it.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Hidden Expectation Exchange with need, cue, direct ask, emotional meaning, and first practice date.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Two invisible bids become two reachable ways to show up.

outcomes.verdict: Each of you thinks the other expects mind-reading, which may mean direct requests are happening but arriving after frustration has already colored the tone. The receiver remembers demand; the speaker remembers having to ask at all. Move the ask earlier and make the response explicit. A yes, no, or alternative is kinder than vague agreement, and an early request carries less accumulated disappointment.
outcomes.actions_a: Make one recurring request at the first sign of need, before adding evidence that it should be obvious.
outcomes.actions_b: Answer with yes, no, or a concrete alternative so the need does not remain in interpretive limbo.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save an Early Ask and Clear Answer script with request, three response options, recurring cue, and follow-up time.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Earlier words prevent the need from arriving dressed as a case file.

outcomes.verdict: [A] sees one partner holding more unspoken expectations. [B] sees the pattern as shared because both people sometimes want effortless understanding. Use the specific pattern without making it permanent. The frequent situation gets a proactive check from the partner who can notice it; every other need gets a direct ask from whoever has it. That division rewards attentiveness while keeping communication mutual.
outcomes.actions_a: Name the recurring situation where a proactive check would prevent the most hurt.
outcomes.actions_b: Use the direct-ask rule outside that situation and avoid treating the pattern as proof about overall care.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Proactive Check Exception with recurring situation, check phrase, direct-ask default, response options, and reset date.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. One meaningful exception lives inside a clear shared rule.
outcomes.role_note: [A] = identified a specific partner; [B] = said both partners hold unspoken expectations.

still carries impact from an incomplete repair
uses examples to explain why the present feels bigger

Agree which issue needs action tonight

outcomes.verdict: [A] reaches backward because the present moment resembles an impact that never fully settled. [B] sees the connection but may feel the conversation suddenly expanded beyond what can be solved tonight. The old issue is information, not a second argument that must run simultaneously. Let [A] name the repeated feeling in one sentence, then park the earlier event with a real date for follow-up while both finish the current topic.

outcomes.actions_b: Acknowledge the connection briefly and help choose which present decision can be completed now.

outcomes.closing: Case softened. The past gets a real appointment without taking over the present.
outcomes.role_note: [A] = the partner both identified as more likely to bring in an older issue.

outcomes.verdict: [B] links today's disagreement to an older moment because the emotional pattern feels unfinished, even if the details differ. [A] can recognize the pattern while still needing a conversation with boundaries. [B] gets one sentence to name what repeated. Then both people resolve the current request and schedule the historical repair separately. This keeps the old impact visible without asking one discussion to carry two timelines.
outcomes.actions_a: Complete the current decision and reflect the repeated feeling you heard before the conversation closes.
outcomes.actions_b: Name the pattern in one sentence, place the old issue on the follow-up note, and return to today's request.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Present and Parked note with current issue, repeated feeling, today's decision, old issue, and follow-up date.

outcomes.role_note: [B] = the partner both identified as more likely to bring in an older issue.

outcomes.verdict: Both of you connect new tension to older moments, which means pattern recognition is strong but issue boundaries get porous under stress. Use a one-reference rule: either partner may name one earlier example to explain the emotional weight, but detailed history moves to a parking list. Finish one present request before opening the list. Your history becomes context rather than a stack of evidence.

outcomes.verdict: Each of you sees yourself as the pattern connector because you are tracking different archives. [A] may remember unmet promises; [B] may remember tone, withdrawal, or repeated timing. The useful discovery is that the archive categories differ. Name the category rather than opening every file. Then decide whether today's issue is another instance or only emotionally similar. The bright spot is that both of you are trying to stop repetition, and clearer categories can finally make that instinct useful.
outcomes.actions_a: Name the category your memory is tracking and the one fact that makes today's event relevant.
outcomes.actions_b: Name your different category and ask whether the present event needs a new response or an old repair.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Pattern Archive page with each category, current link, emotional similarity, action needed, and separate follow-up.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. The archives become clues instead of competing piles of proof.

outcomes.verdict: Each of you thinks the other brings up history, which usually means both people feel surprised when the conversation widens. Memory favors the moment when someone else's old example lands on you. Stop deciding who does it more. Use the same parking rule for either person and require a date before an old issue is set aside. The date matters because 'later' often sounds like dismissal.
outcomes.actions_a: Place any older issue on the note with one sentence about why it still matters.
outcomes.actions_b: Offer a real follow-up time and complete the present topic without adding your own historical counterexample.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Historical Issue Parking List with reason, urgency, owner, scheduled date, and current-topic outcome.

outcomes.actions_a: Use the one-sentence limit when the recurring older issue appears and state today's request next.
outcomes.actions_b: Help schedule the separate repair and avoid using shared responsibility to blur the frequent pattern.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Pattern Then Present script with pattern sentence, current request, parking note, follow-up date, and closing check.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. A recurring habit gets structure without becoming an identity.
outcomes.role_note: [A] = identified a specific frequent history-connector; [B] = said both partners do this.

A clear sign that the conversation is still safe

outcomes.verdict: You reach overload at a similar level and generally recognize the early signs before quiet becomes distance. That mutual literacy is protective. Keep naming the yellow-light cues, such as shorter answers, blankness, or repeating the same sentence, and pause before the system goes fully offline. A shutdown plan works best while both people can still use it, not after language has disappeared.
outcomes.actions_a: Name your earliest yellow-light cue and use the pause phrase before you lose access to clear words.
outcomes.actions_b: Name the cue you notice in your partner and ask one gentle capacity question instead of adding more points.

outcomes.closing: Case softened. You catch the quiet while it is still asking for help.

outcomes.verdict: [A] and [B] shut down at similar intensity, but [A] is less okay with the current recovery. The issue may be that one person's quiet receives patience while the other's is chased, interpreted, or forgotten. Apply the same pause and return rule to both partners. The person going quiet names capacity and a return time; the listener stops adding content and protects the restart.
outcomes.actions_a: Name where the recovery rule feels uneven and choose the signal you can use before going offline.
outcomes.actions_b: Apply the same response to [A]'s signal that you would want for your own, including a reliable restart.

outcomes.verdict: You shut down at similar levels, yet neither person knows how to restart without recreating the overload. Make the second conversation smaller than the first. Return with one topic, one question each, and a twenty-minute limit. Anything else goes on a later list. The restart should prove that reentry is survivable, not solve the entire relationship while both systems are still cautious.
outcomes.actions_a: Choose the single topic that must be discussed first and prepare one answer you can give clearly.
outcomes.actions_b: Choose one curious question and agree to move every second issue to the later list.
