outcomes.closing: Case softened. Reentry becomes a manageable doorway instead of another wall of intensity.

outcomes.verdict: [A] shuts down more easily because intensity reduces access to language and decision-making. [B] can remain verbal longer and may naturally keep explaining. You are content because the difference is recognized rather than interpreted as lack of care. Give [A] an early stop signal and written-response option. Give [B] a guaranteed return time and one question that will be answered then. Capacity and closure both receive a place.
outcomes.actions_a: Use the early signal and choose whether your first response back will be spoken or written.
outcomes.actions_b: Stop adding points when the signal appears and select the one question you need answered at reentry.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Capacity and Return plan with stop signal, response format, return time, one question, and extension rule.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Fewer words in the moment no longer means less commitment to return.
outcomes.role_note: [A] = shuts down more strongly; [B] = stays more verbally available.

outcomes.verdict: [A] shuts down more strongly and feels the current conversations exceed capacity. [B] stays verbal and feels the process works because [B] can continue organizing the issue aloud. That format privileges the partner who can keep speaking. [B] owes a slower habit: one point, one question, then silence. [A] owes a clear signal and a bounded return instead of disappearing from the topic.
outcomes.actions_a: Use the stop signal before full shutdown and state when and how you will respond.
outcomes.actions_b: Limit yourself to one point and one question, then protect the pause without further explanation.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a One Point, One Question rule with stop signal, response format, return window, and next-topic list.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. The conversation stops rewarding whichever nervous system can talk longest.
outcomes.role_note: [A] = shuts down more strongly and is dissatisfied; [B] = stays verbal and is content.

outcomes.verdict: [A] goes quiet when the conversation becomes too dense or intense. [B] talks more as quiet increases because silence feels like the issue is slipping away. Each reaction adds pressure to the other. Use short rounds: two minutes for [B], a written or spoken summary from [A], then a five-minute pause. Repeat only while both remain regulated. A paced exchange replaces the flood and the disappearance.
outcomes.actions_a: Prepare a short summary of what you heard and use the written option before blankness takes over.
outcomes.actions_b: Keep your round to one point and wait for the summary instead of filling the silence.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Short-Round Conversation format with speaker timer, summary option, pause length, regulation check, and stop rule.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. The conversation moves in breathable rounds instead of one long wave.
outcomes.role_note: [A] = shuts down more strongly; [B] = stays more verbally available.

outcomes.closing: Case softened. One extra phrase keeps privacy from sounding like emotional disappearance.

outcomes.verdict: [A] and [B] use 'fine' similarly, but [A] is less comfortable because the word may end the conversation only when [B] says it. [A]'s version gets investigated, while [B]'s version receives space, or the reverse burden of follow-up stays with [A]. Make the response symmetric. The speaker adds a modifier and owns any promised restart; the listener accepts the stated boundary.
outcomes.actions_a: Name the uneven response you experience and choose the modifier that states your actual boundary.
outcomes.actions_b: Give [A] the same space and follow-up structure you expect when you use the phrase.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Symmetric Fine Rule with modifiers, listener response, restart owner, maximum delay, and privacy limit.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. The same small truth and the same respect become available to both people.
outcomes.role_note: [A] = less content with the current signaling pattern; [B] = more content.

outcomes.verdict: You use 'fine' at similar levels and both dislike the guessing game it creates. The word is doing too many jobs: finished, overwhelmed, private, hurt, and please notice. Replace it with a five-option signal system that requires no long explanation. The goal is not instant disclosure. It is accurate routing, so the partner knows whether to offer comfort, space, a later check, or closure.
outcomes.actions_a: Choose the two signals you need most and write the exact low-effort phrases you can use.
outcomes.actions_b: Choose the listener response for each signal and avoid asking extra questions beyond the stated lane.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Five-Signal Feelings Menu with done, space, comfort, later, private, plus response and timing rules.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. The message becomes clearer without forcing a full emotional report.

outcomes.verdict: [A] is more likely to hide distress behind 'fine' because immediate disclosure feels unsafe, unclear, or exhausting. [B] is more direct and may notice the mismatch quickly. You are content because the pause does not erase the issue. Let [A] use a low-detail truth plus a return time. Let [B] ask once, accept the boundary, and trust the scheduled check rather than reading silence as a final answer.
outcomes.actions_a: Use a low-detail truth such as 'not okay, not ready' and choose the next check-in time.
outcomes.actions_b: Ask once, confirm the check-in, and offer one simple support option without reopening the topic.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Low-Detail Truth script with phrase, support choice, check-in time, privacy boundary, and restart owner.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Honesty stays possible even before the full words arrive.
outcomes.role_note: [A] = more likely to use 'fine' while upset; [B] = more direct.

outcomes.verdict: [A] hides more behind 'fine' and feels pressured or unseen in the current pattern. [B] is more direct and feels the approach is acceptable, perhaps because asking once seems sufficient. [A] needs a safer middle between full disclosure and a misleading close. [B] owes one consistent check phrase and respect for delayed disclosure. [A] owes an honest status marker and a time, not a promise, for return.
outcomes.actions_a: Replace 'fine' with one accurate status marker and name when you can revisit the topic.
outcomes.actions_b: Use the agreed check phrase, accept the status, and show up at the chosen time without demanding details early.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Status Not Story agreement with markers, check phrase, support options, return time, and extension message.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. The feeling gets acknowledged before it has to be fully explained.
outcomes.role_note: [A] = more likely to hide distress and is dissatisfied; [B] = more direct and is content.

outcomes.verdict: [A] says 'fine' because direct feeling language feels risky or unavailable. [B] presses because the mismatch between words and energy feels destabilizing. Pressure makes [A] hide more, and hiding makes [B] investigate harder. End the loop with a color code: green means settled, yellow means something is present but later, red means support or space is needed now. Each color has one fixed listener response.
outcomes.actions_a: Choose the honest color and add only the support or timing detail you can give.
outcomes.actions_b: Use the fixed listener response and stop investigating once the signal has been received.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Green, Yellow, Red Feelings Code with meanings, listener responses, support choices, and yellow follow-up time.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. A low-effort signal replaces both the mask and the interrogation.
outcomes.role_note: [A] = more likely to hide distress; [B] = more likely to seek immediate clarity.

cases.title: When You Each Remember the Same Argument Differently
cases.subtitle: Who is more likely to remember the exact words while the other remembers the emotional meaning?

questions.prompt: Who is more likely to remember the exact words while the other remembers the emotional meaning?

options.label: Me, no contest
Probably me
Probably them
Definitely them
Honestly, both of us about equally

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: What best explains that answer?

options.label: stores specific phrases clearly
replays the sequence afterward
tracks tone and body language
remembers the moment through how it felt
notices different details under stress
can accept two partial memories of the same event

questions.interactionRule: Display as the answering player’s own voice.

questions.prompt: Where do the versions diverge most?

options.label: Who spoke first
The exact wording
Tone or volume
What happened immediately before
Whether a repair was offered
What the conversation was really about

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: What would help without choosing a winner?

options.label: Agree on the impact
Separate known facts from uncertain details
Use texts or notes only for context
Name what each memory is protecting
Decide the next-time rule
Stop reconstructing once action is clear

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: Want to tell the court a bit more about what happened? (optional)
questions.interactionRule: Private context is used only to personalize the selected deterministic branch.

outcomes.verdict: [A] tends to retain the wording and sequence, while [B] may retain the emotional headline. Both of you recognize [A]'s detail strength, but memory under stress is still a recording with selective microphones. Use [A]'s timeline for concrete anchors without treating it as the complete meaning. Let [B] add the felt impact. Then stop reconstruction once you have a next-time rule that protects both.
outcomes.actions_a: Offer the sequence as your memory and mark any detail you cannot know with certainty.
outcomes.actions_b: Describe the emotional impact and the moment it began, without requiring every word to match your version.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Facts, Feelings, Future note with known facts, uncertain details, each impact, shared need, and next-time rule.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Detail and emotional memory become two sources, not rival recordings.
outcomes.role_note: [A] = the partner both identified as more likely to remember exact words and sequence.

outcomes.verdict: [B] remembers phrases and order more sharply, while [A] may remember the atmosphere and what the exchange came to mean. [A] already sees [B]'s detail advantage, but precision does not make the emotional experience disappear. Build a shared account with two columns: what seems concrete and what each person experienced. Then move to repair before the search for perfect reconstruction becomes the new conflict.
outcomes.actions_a: Name the impact and the part of the moment that changed your sense of safety or connection.
outcomes.actions_b: Offer the concrete sequence with uncertainty markers and avoid using detail recall to overrule impact.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Facts, Feelings, Future note with known facts, uncertain details, each impact, shared need, and next-time rule.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. The record gets context, and the feeling gets somewhere useful to go.
outcomes.role_note: [B] = the partner both identified as more likely to remember exact words and sequence.

outcomes.verdict: Both of you remember arguments in detail, which can make the disagreement feel researchable long after repair would be more useful. Two careful memories can still differ because attention narrows under stress. Cap reconstruction at ten minutes. Mark agreed facts, uncertain details, and each person's impact, then decide what behavior changes next time. Accuracy serves the relationship only until the repair path becomes clear.
outcomes.actions_a: Mark one fact you are confident about and one detail you are willing to leave uncertain.
outcomes.actions_b: Name the impact that matters regardless of the disputed detail and propose one future behavior.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Ten-Minute Reconstruction with agreed facts, open details, both impacts, action, and stop time.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Memory does enough work to guide repair, then gets to clock out.

outcomes.verdict: Each of you claims the stronger memory because each retained a different kind of evidence. [A] may hold sentences; [B] may hold timing, expression, or the point where the tone changed. Instead of comparing memory quality, label the evidence type. A phrase can be accurately recalled and still carry a different impact than expected. Put both forms into the shared account and choose a future safeguard.
outcomes.actions_a: Name the evidence type you remember and one uncertainty you can honestly admit.
outcomes.actions_b: Name your different evidence type and the impact it helps explain.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Memory Evidence Map with words, sequence, tone, context, uncertainties, impacts, and one future safeguard.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Different evidence types create a fuller picture without requiring identical recall.

outcomes.verdict: Each of you thinks the other is more focused on exact recall, which suggests both people may be tired of having feelings cross-examined by details. Stop debating who is the historian. Use a mutual sentence: 'My memory is partial, and this is what landed.' Each person gets one version without interruption. The only shared conclusion required is what you want to prevent or repeat next time.
outcomes.actions_a: Share your partial memory and impact in under two minutes without correcting the other version.
outcomes.actions_b: Listen, then state the future behavior you can agree to even if the timelines stay different.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Two Partial Memories note with each version, each impact, shared prevention goal, and next-time behavior.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Repair no longer waits for a perfect replay that neither nervous system recorded.

outcomes.verdict: [A] sees one partner as the detail keeper. [B] sees memory styles as mixed or shared. That likely means the role changes by topic, but one person took the historian seat in this argument. Let the historian supply anchors, not authority. The other partner supplies impact and missing context. Once a practical rule emerges, close the archive rather than asking memory to certify whose experience counts.
outcomes.actions_a: Offer the anchors and flag uncertain details without using them to dismiss the other experience.
outcomes.actions_b: Add the impact and context, then help translate both versions into one next-time rule.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save an Anchor and Impact page with timeline anchors, uncertainties, context, felt meaning, and future rule.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. The historian helps build the map without owning the entire territory.
outcomes.role_note: [A] = identified a specific detail keeper; [B] = said memory styles are shared or mixed.

cases.title: When Feedback Landed as Criticism Instead
cases.subtitle: Who is more likely to hear a request for change as a judgment about them?

questions.prompt: Who is more likely to hear a request for change as a judgment about them?

options.label: Me, no contest
Probably me
Probably them
Definitely them
Honestly, both of us about equally

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: What best explains that answer?

options.label: connects feedback with past criticism
notices tone before content
cares deeply about doing well in the relationship
hears broad words as character conclusions
needs reassurance before taking in a request
responds well when the request is specific and collaborative

questions.interactionRule: Display as the answering player’s own voice.

questions.prompt: What changed the feedback into criticism?

options.label: It used always or never
The timing was public or rushed
Several issues arrived together
No appreciation or context came first
The request was vague
The listener was already depleted

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: What format would land better?

options.label: One observation and one request
Ask whether now is a good time
Name the shared goal
Keep character out of it
Invite the listener's idea
Check what they heard before continuing

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: Want to tell the court a bit more about what happened? (optional)
questions.interactionRule: Private context is used only to personalize the selected deterministic branch.

outcomes.verdict: [A] hears evaluation quickly because feedback can sound like a verdict on effort, competence, or value before the request becomes clear. [B] already recognizes this sensitivity, which creates room to change delivery without avoiding honest needs. [B] can lead with the shared goal and one observable moment. [A] can repeat the request back before answering the emotional meaning that arrived with it.
outcomes.actions_a: Repeat the concrete request you heard and ask whether it is about one behavior or a broader concern.
outcomes.actions_b: Ask for timing, name one observation, connect it to a shared goal, and make one doable request.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Feedback Landing Script with timing question, observation, shared goal, request, and listener reflection.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. The request gets separated from the person's worth.
outcomes.role_note: [A] = the partner both identified as more likely to hear feedback as criticism.

outcomes.verdict: [B] can hear a small change request as a full performance review, especially when tone, timing, or broad language activates older experiences. [A] sees the pattern and can help by making the feedback narrow enough to hold. One moment, one impact, one request. [B] can check the scope before defending the whole self. The conversation gets smaller, which makes useful change easier to receive.
outcomes.actions_a: Deliver one observation and one request, then stop before adding a second issue or character explanation.
outcomes.actions_b: Ask whether the feedback concerns this moment or a pattern, then reflect the request before responding.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Feedback Landing Script with timing question, observation, shared goal, request, and listener reflection.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. A small request stays small enough to be heard.
outcomes.role_note: [B] = the partner both identified as more likely to hear feedback as criticism.

outcomes.verdict: Both of you are sensitive to feedback because the relationship matters and being disappointing can feel larger than the behavior being discussed. That care is the bright spot, but it needs a format. Ask permission, use one recent observation, and state the change you want to build together. The listener reflects the request before explaining. Feedback becomes a coordination tool rather than a surprise review.
outcomes.actions_a: Use the permission question and reflect the request before offering your context.
outcomes.actions_b: Keep the feedback to one recent example and one shared improvement, with no stack of supporting cases.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a One-Request Feedback Card with permission, observation, impact, shared goal, reflection, and follow-up.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Caring about the relationship stops turning every request into a grade.

outcomes.verdict: Each of you sees yourself as the more feedback-sensitive partner, which may mean different subjects touch different identities. [A] may feel exposed around reliability or care. [B] may feel exposed around competence, money, intimacy, or family. Map the tender domains and choose a gentler opening for each. Sensitivity becomes usable information when it guides delivery instead of deciding whether the request may exist.
outcomes.actions_a: Name the domain where feedback hits your identity hardest and the opening that keeps you receptive.
outcomes.actions_b: Name your different domain and the kind of specificity that helps you stay with the request.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Tender Feedback Map with each domain, safe opener, detail level, pause cue, and repair phrase.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Different tender spots receive different doorways into the same honest relationship.

outcomes.verdict: Each of you thinks the other hears criticism, which may be what happens when feedback is usually delivered after frustration has built. The speaker remembers a reasonable request; the listener receives the accumulated tone. Move feedback earlier and smaller. A weekly maintenance check gives ordinary adjustments a home before they arrive charged with ten missed moments. That regular rhythm protects honesty while keeping each adjustment small enough to receive with care.
outcomes.actions_a: Bring one small request to the scheduled check before it becomes a case about the relationship.
outcomes.actions_b: Receive one request, reflect it, and choose a doable response or alternative before adding your own topic.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Weekly Relationship Maintenance note with one appreciation, one adjustment, one response, owner, and check date.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Small feedback gets a regular home before it needs a dramatic entrance.

outcomes.verdict: [A] sees one partner as more likely to hear criticism. [B] sees sensitivity as shared or dependent on the subject. Use the recurring pattern without making one person the fragile one. The frequent trigger gets a tailored opening; both partners use the same one-observation, one-request structure everywhere else. Delivery improves, and each listener still owns the job of checking scope before reacting.
outcomes.actions_a: Name the recurring feedback trigger and the opening that helps it land as a request.
outcomes.actions_b: Use the shared structure and ask what scope was intended before responding to a character meaning.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Targeted Feedback Plan with recurring trigger, tailored opener, shared format, scope question, and follow-up.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. One pattern gets extra care without turning sensitivity into a permanent role.
outcomes.role_note: [A] = identified a specific feedback-sensitive partner; [B] = said sensitivity is shared or situational.

cases.title: When One of You Raised Their Voice and the Other Went Quiet
cases.subtitle: How strongly does a raised voice affect your ability to stay present and respond?

questions.prompt: How strongly does a raised voice affect your ability to stay present and respond?

options.label: Very little if the words stay respectful
Somewhat, but I can usually continue
A lot once the volume feels intense
Very strongly, I start to freeze or withdraw
Immediately, I cannot continue safely or clearly

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: How do you feel about the way volume and quiet are handled between you?

options.label: It works for me
Mostly okay, with a few rough moments
It regularly leaves me tense or disconnected
I need this pattern to change

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: What happens inside you when volume rises?

options.label: I focus on defending myself
I lose access to words
I feel urgency to end the topic
I become equally loud
I feel physically unsafe or flooded
I stop believing listening is possible

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: What should happen at the first volume shift?

options.label: Use a shared stop word
Lower voices and slow the pace
Take a timed pause
Move to written notes
End the conversation for the day
Check safety and reconnect later

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: Want to tell the court a bit more about what happened? (optional)
questions.interactionRule: Private context is used only to personalize the selected deterministic branch.

outcomes.verdict: You react to raised volume at a similar level and generally know how to bring the room back down before quiet becomes disconnection. Keep the threshold explicit. A shared stop word should mean voices lower immediately, the pace slows, and no one debates whether the volume was technically loud. The goal is preserving enough nervous-system safety for the actual issue to remain discussable.
outcomes.actions_a: Use the stop word at the first body signal instead of waiting until you have fully withdrawn.
outcomes.actions_b: Respond by lowering volume and reducing the conversation to one sentence or one question.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Volume Reset Card with stop word, immediate response, pause option, return time, and safety boundary.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. The room gets quieter before the connection has to disappear.

outcomes.verdict: [A] and [B] are similarly affected by volume, but [A] is less satisfied because one person's raised voice may receive context while the other's quiet is treated as refusal. Both are pressure signals. Apply one sequence every time: stop, lower volume, confirm whether conversation is still possible, and schedule a return if not. Neither signal gets to direct the next step alone.
outcomes.actions_a: Name the uneven interpretation you experience and use the stop word before silence becomes complete.
outcomes.actions_b: Treat quiet as a capacity signal, lower volume immediately, and ask whether a pause or slower conversation is possible.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Pressure Signal Sequence with stop word, volume response, capacity question, pause length, and restart owner.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Two stress signals enter one neutral protocol.
outcomes.role_note: [A] = less content with how volume and quiet are handled; [B] = more content.

outcomes.verdict: You are similarly affected, yet the same escalation keeps happening because the stop point arrives too late. Identify the first physical cue, not the first raised sentence: faster speech, tight chest, interruption, clipped answers, or blankness. That cue activates a ninety-second reset before either volume or withdrawal takes over. Early regulation is not avoidance; it protects the conversation you still want to have.
outcomes.actions_a: Choose your earliest physical cue and say it aloud as soon as it appears.
outcomes.actions_b: Choose a ninety-second reset action and return with one slower sentence about the issue.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save an Early Escalation Map with body cues, reset action, stop word, return sentence, and full-pause threshold.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. You interrupt the escalation before either partner has to shout or vanish.

outcomes.verdict: [A] is strongly affected by raised volume and may lose language or a sense of safety. [B] can stay present at higher intensity and may use volume to show urgency rather than threat. You are content because the difference is recognized. Set [A]'s threshold as the conversation limit. [B] can express urgency through clearer words, a written note, or a faster scheduled follow-up instead of greater volume.
outcomes.actions_a: Use the stop word at your threshold and state whether you need lower volume, writing, or a pause.
outcomes.actions_b: Honor the threshold immediately and translate urgency into one request plus a return time.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save an Urgency Without Volume plan with threshold, stop word, alternate channels, pause window, and restart request.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Urgency stays visible without asking either nervous system to absorb more intensity than it can use.
outcomes.role_note: [A] = more strongly affected by raised voices; [B] = can stay present at higher intensity.

outcomes.verdict: [A] is strongly affected by volume and feels the current pattern is too intense. [B] can stay verbal and feels the conversation still works, because [B]'s system remains online. The format is being measured by the person with the higher threshold. [B] owes a lower-volume habit at the first cue. [A] owes a clear stop word and a return plan rather than silent endurance followed by disappearance.
outcomes.actions_a: Use the stop word immediately and choose the alternate format or return time you can honor.
outcomes.actions_b: Lower volume on the first cue, stop explaining, and wait for the format [A] can use.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Lower Threshold Rule with first cue, stop word, alternate format, return time, and repeated-breach response.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. The usable threshold becomes the shared threshold.
outcomes.role_note: [A] = more strongly affected and dissatisfied; [B] = less affected and content.

outcomes.verdict: [A] goes quiet as volume rises because staying present becomes less possible. [B] raises volume as quiet grows because the lack of response feels like disappearing contact. The loop is mechanical even when the feelings are personal. At the first shift, end spoken debate for twenty minutes. Each person writes three lines: what happened, what they feel, what they need next. Reenter by reading, not improvising.
outcomes.actions_a: Leave the debate with the stop word and write your three lines before the return.
outcomes.actions_b: Stop speaking when the cue appears, lower your body intensity, and write the same three lines without adding a case history.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Twenty-Minute Written Reset with stop cue, three-line prompts, return time, reading order, and next action.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Written structure interrupts the volume-and-silence loop before it feeds itself.
outcomes.role_note: [A] = more strongly affected by volume; [B] = more likely to stay verbal as intensity rises.

cases.title: When an Apology Didn't Actually Feel Like It Landed
cases.subtitle: Who is more likely to need more than 'I'm sorry' before an apology feels complete?

questions.prompt: Who is more likely to need more than 'I'm sorry' before an apology feels complete?

options.label: Me, no contest
Probably me
Probably them
Definitely them
Honestly, both of us about equally

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: What best explains that answer?

options.label: needs the specific impact to be named
listens for real understanding before reassurance
needs a change plan, not only regret
has received apologies that did not change the pattern
needs time before warmth returns
can receive repair once the missing piece is clear

questions.interactionRule: Display as the answering player’s own voice.

questions.prompt: What was missing from the apology?

options.label: The exact impact
Responsibility without an explanation first
A sign the feeling made sense
A repair action
A plan for next time
Space to respond honestly

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: What would help it land now?

options.label: Try the apology again
Ask what still feels open
Complete one repair action
Name the pattern being changed
Allow more recovery time
Check back after the action, not immediately

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: Want to tell the court a bit more about what happened? (optional)
questions.interactionRule: Private context is used only to personalize the selected deterministic branch.

outcomes.verdict: [A] needs an apology to show that the impact was understood, not only that regret exists. [B] already sees this, which means the repair is not blocked by mystery. Use four parts: name the action, name the impact, acknowledge what should have happened, and state one change. [A] can then say which part landed and which part still needs time, without being pushed to perform instant warmth.
outcomes.actions_a: Name the missing piece in one sentence and say whether you need action, time, or another conversation.
outcomes.actions_b: Offer the four-part apology without leading with intent, then complete the promised change before asking if things are okay.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Repair Receipt with action, impact, acknowledgment, change promised, completion date, and later check-in.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. The apology becomes visible in both words and follow-through.
outcomes.role_note: [A] = the partner both identified as needing a fuller apology.

outcomes.verdict: [B] needs more than a regret statement because repair feels complete only when the specific impact and future change are visible. [A] recognizes the need and can make the apology easier to receive by keeping the explanation behind the acknowledgment. [B] can name the missing element without requiring the perfect emotional delivery. The follow-through gets to carry part of the meaning.
outcomes.actions_a: Give the apology in the order of action, impact, acknowledgment, and change, then follow through.
outcomes.actions_b: Name the missing element and the repair action that would matter most, while allowing recovery to take its own time.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Repair Receipt with action, impact, acknowledgment, change promised, completion date, and later check-in.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Repair stops depending on one sentence doing every job.
outcomes.role_note: [B] = the partner both identified as needing a fuller apology.

outcomes.verdict: Both of you need apologies with substance, which means 'sorry' is an opening rather than a complete repair. That shared standard can build trust if it stays practical. Each apology names the impact and includes one observable change, while the receiving partner does not require immediate emotional reset. Follow-up happens after the change has had a chance to exist. You already agree that repair matters; now the change itself can carry reassurance after the conversation ends.
outcomes.actions_a: When receiving the next apology, name the one repair action that would support trust without expanding the list.
outcomes.actions_b: When offering it, include the impact and one change with a time frame, then give recovery room.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Complete Apology Card with action, impact, acknowledgment, change, time frame, and no-instant-reset rule.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Your shared repair standard moves from words into behavior.

outcomes.verdict: Each of you sees yourself as the partner who needs more from an apology, which may mean your missing pieces differ. [A] may need emotional recognition; [B] may need action, detail, or time. Trade the exact ingredient rather than comparing who is harder to satisfy. A repair can be customized without becoming endless when each person names the single piece that matters most.
outcomes.actions_a: Choose your primary apology ingredient and explain how you know when it is present.
outcomes.actions_b: Choose a different ingredient if needed and state one bounded repair action that expresses it.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save an Apology Ingredient Exchange with each need, example language, repair action, timing, and follow-up.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Two repair languages become instructions instead of tests.

outcomes.verdict: Each of you thinks the other needs the fuller apology, which may mean both people experience their own apologies as complete and the other's as missing context. Stop grading length or emotion. Use the same six-line format for both partners and let the receiver circle the one part still open. Symmetry removes the debate about whose standards are harder. A shared format also makes generosity easier because neither partner has to guess which repair standard applies.
outcomes.actions_a: Use the shared format and ask which one part remains open instead of defending the apology as complete.
outcomes.actions_b: Circle one missing part and request a specific addition or action, not a total rewrite of the relationship history.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Six-Line Apology Template with action, impact, ownership, context later, change, and check-in date.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. One shared format replaces two competing standards.

outcomes.verdict: [A] sees one partner as needing fuller repair. [B] sees apology needs as shared or dependent on the event. Keep the recurring need visible without making one person impossible to satisfy. Use a baseline apology for both, then add the identified partner's key ingredient when the impact is larger. The receiver also names when enough information has been given and only time remains.
outcomes.actions_a: Name the recurring missing ingredient and the sentence or action that would supply it.
outcomes.actions_b: Use the shared baseline and ask whether the added ingredient or simply more time is needed.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Baseline Plus Repair plan with shared apology parts, added ingredient, action, recovery time, and check-in.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. A recurring need gets care without becoming a permanent label.
outcomes.role_note: [A] = identified a specific partner who needs fuller repair; [B] = said the need is shared or situational.

cases.title: When You Disagreed About Who Started It
cases.subtitle: Who is more likely to focus on the first visible action while the other focuses on what built up before it?

questions.prompt: Who is more likely to focus on the first visible action while the other focuses on what built up before it?

options.label: Me, no contest
Probably me
Probably them
Definitely them
Honestly, both of us about equally

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: What best explains that answer?

options.label: tracks the exact opening moment
notices the pressure that accumulated earlier
wants the sequence to feel fair
fears responsibility will be assigned from a partial timeline
uses the start point to explain the reaction
can move forward once both timelines are visible

questions.interactionRule: Display as the answering player’s own voice.

questions.prompt: What counts as the start from your view?

options.label: The first sharp sentence
The earlier mood or tension
A missed promise
The first defensive response
The moment the topic was raised
The point where listening stopped

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: What matters more than settling the start?

options.label: Stopping the repeating loop
Repairing the sharpest impact
Naming each person's first choice point
Agreeing on a restart cue
Separating buildup from escalation
Choosing one change for next time

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: Want to tell the court a bit more about what happened? (optional)
questions.interactionRule: Private context is used only to personalize the selected deterministic branch.

outcomes.verdict: [A] tends to mark the first visible move, while [B] may experience the start as a buildup that began earlier. Both of you see [A] as the clearer sequence tracker, but the first sentence is not always the first pressure. Build two timelines: buildup and escalation. Each person names the earliest point where a different choice was possible. Repair then focuses on those choice points instead of crowning one opening moment.
outcomes.actions_a: Lay out the visible sequence and mark the first place you could have slowed or clarified.
outcomes.actions_b: Lay out the buildup and mark your own earlier choice point without using it to excuse the later impact.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Buildup and Escalation Timeline with triggers, choice points, impacts, reset cue, and next-time action.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. The timeline finds exits instead of a single person to place at the entrance.
outcomes.role_note: [A] = the partner both identified as more likely to focus on the first visible action.

outcomes.verdict: [B] remembers the first visible action clearly, while [A] may locate the beginning in an earlier mood, missed bid, or unresolved pressure. [A] already recognizes [B]'s sequence focus, which can help if it is paired with the buildup. Draw both timelines and circle each person's first choice point. The useful question becomes where the loop could have changed, not which second officially began it.
outcomes.actions_a: Name the buildup and circle the first place you could have spoken more directly or paused.
outcomes.actions_b: Name the visible sequence and circle the point where your response could have changed course.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Buildup and Escalation Timeline with triggers, choice points, impacts, reset cue, and next-time action.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Two beginnings reveal more than one place to protect the relationship.
outcomes.role_note: [B] = the partner both identified as more likely to focus on the first visible action.

outcomes.verdict: Both of you track the opening move, so the argument about sequence can become extremely detailed while the repeating loop stays untouched. Cap the timeline at five minutes. Each person gets one sentence for what built up, one sentence for the visible escalation, and one sentence for their own first choice point. Then design the cue that would interrupt that point next time.
outcomes.actions_a: State your three sentences without correcting the other person's order or wording.
outcomes.actions_b: Listen for the choice point and help choose one interruption cue that works for both timelines.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Three-Sentence Timeline with buildup, escalation, personal choice point, shared cue, and future response.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Sequence serves prevention instead of becoming the whole dispute.

outcomes.verdict: Each of you claims the sequence lens because you are using different clocks. [A] starts at the first spoken edge; [B] may start at the missed bid, tense silence, or earlier broken expectation. Neither clock covers the whole interaction. Put the clocks side by side and identify the moment each person still had access to a calmer choice. That is the point worth practicing.
outcomes.actions_a: Name which clock you used and the earliest calmer choice available on your timeline.
outcomes.actions_b: Name your different clock and your own practice point without requiring the timelines to merge.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Two-Clock Conflict Map with each start point, buildup, escalation, choice point, and reset practice.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Different clocks reveal two usable exits from the same loop.

outcomes.verdict: Each of you thinks the other is more invested in who started it, which often means both people feel their buildup is missing from the other's version. Give each buildup equal space, then retire the start question for this event. The repair task is to name the first action each person wants to change in their own lane. Two self-owned changes reduce the need for one official beginning.
outcomes.actions_a: Name the buildup you want understood and one action you will change in your own lane.
outcomes.actions_b: Reflect the buildup before naming your separate change, with no comparison of which came first.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Two-Lane Repair note with each buildup, each choice point, each change, and a shared interruption cue.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. The repair gets two owners and no need for a starting-line trophy.

outcomes.verdict: [A] sees one partner focusing on the visible start. [B] sees start-point focus as shared or situational. Use the specific pattern to improve the next conversation without fixing a permanent role. The sequence-focused partner summarizes the buildup before naming the opening action. Both partners then identify their first choice point and one reset move. The relationship gains two prevention points instead of spending energy defending one official beginning.
outcomes.actions_a: Practice naming the buildup before the visible action so the timeline does not begin midstream.
outcomes.actions_b: Name your own first choice point and avoid using shared responsibility to blur the recurring sequence habit.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Full-Start Timeline with buildup summary, visible start, two choice points, reset move, and review.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. The timeline starts earlier and ends with a plan.
outcomes.role_note: [A] = identified a specific visible-start partner; [B] = said the focus is shared or situational.

cases.title: When a Text Went Unanswered Longer Than Expected

questions.prompt: How strongly does an unexpectedly late reply affect your sense of connection?

A little if the message seemed important
It depends on context and the usual rhythm
A lot, I start feeling dismissed or worried
Very strongly, the wait quickly feels like disconnection

options.label: It works for me
Mostly okay, with a few rough moments
It regularly leaves me tense or disconnected
I need this pattern to change

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: What does the wait make you wonder?

options.label: Whether something happened
Whether my message mattered
Whether they need space
Whether I am being avoided
Whether they are simply busy
Whether I should send another message

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: What signal would reduce the uncertainty?

options.label: A busy-now reply-later text
A rough response window
A rule for urgent messages
Permission to double text once
A status or calendar cue
A warm reconnect after the delay

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: Want to tell the court a bit more about what happened? (optional)
questions.interactionRule: Private context is used only to personalize the selected deterministic branch.

outcomes.verdict: You have similar expectations around reply time and generally interpret delays through real-life context rather than as a statement about care. That trust lets both people have full days without turning the phone into a relationship monitor. Keep one exception clear: messages involving safety, logistics, or emotional urgency need a label and a different response rule. Ordinary delay stays ordinary because urgent communication has its own lane.
outcomes.actions_a: Choose the messages that qualify as urgent and use the agreed label only for those.
outcomes.actions_b: Choose the response or acknowledgment window for urgent messages and protect ordinary no-pressure texting elsewhere.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Reply Timing Guide with ordinary rhythm, urgent label, acknowledgment window, double-text rule, and reconnect line.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Everyday silence stays light because true urgency has a clear signal.

outcomes.verdict: [A] and [B] react to delay at similar intensity, but [A] is less content because the expectation may be clear only after a miss. [A] might wait through a logistics deadline or tender message with no clue whether it was seen. [B] experiences flexible texting and assumes the bond is secure. Add a simple acknowledgment for messages that need later attention. The full reply can wait; the uncertainty does not have to.
outcomes.actions_a: Name the message category where an acknowledgment matters and the window you can reasonably expect.
outcomes.actions_b: Send a short seen-and-later response for that category, with a realistic time for the full answer.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save an Acknowledge Now, Reply Later rule with message types, short response, full-reply window, and extension cue.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. A tiny signal protects the waiting period without demanding constant availability.
outcomes.role_note: [A] = less content with current reply expectations; [B] = more content.

outcomes.verdict: You have similar sensitivity to delayed replies and both dislike the uncertainty, yet your phone habits still leave important messages floating. Build the rule around message type, not minutes. Casual sharing needs no deadline. Logistics needs acknowledgment before the decision point. Emotional messages need a warm receipt plus a chosen return time. The sender also labels the lane instead of expecting the content to announce its own urgency.
outcomes.actions_a: Label your next important message as casual, logistics, or emotional and include the actual deadline if there is one.
outcomes.actions_b: Use the matching response and avoid sending a rushed emotional answer when a warm receipt would be more honest.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Three-Lane Text Guide with message labels, response type, timing, urgency exception, and reconnect line.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Messages stop competing under one invisible deadline.

outcomes.verdict: [A] feels delay more strongly because an unanswered message leaves the connection in an open tab. [B] can close the phone and trust the relationship remains steady. You are content because neither rhythm is treated as the standard of care. [B] can send a low-effort receipt for meaningful messages. [A] can reserve urgency labels for real deadlines and let casual messages breathe.
outcomes.actions_a: Use an urgency or needs-reply label only when timing actually changes the outcome.
outcomes.actions_b: Send a brief receipt for meaningful messages and name when you can return if the answer needs thought.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save an Open Tab Text Plan with receipt phrase, urgency label, response windows, no-pressure lane, and reconnection habit.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. One partner gets closure without putting the other on permanent phone duty.
outcomes.role_note: [A] = more affected by delayed replies; [B] = less affected.

outcomes.verdict: [A] feels delayed replies strongly and is not okay with the current uncertainty. [B] is less affected and feels the rhythm is normal, so the absence of a signal costs [B] very little. [B] owes one small habit: acknowledge meaningful or time-sensitive messages. [A] owes a calmer habit: label urgency once and avoid turning response time into a full measure of affection.
outcomes.actions_a: Label urgency clearly, send one follow-up at most, and use another support source while waiting when the message is not time-sensitive.
outcomes.actions_b: Acknowledge meaningful messages within the agreed window and give a realistic return time instead of an automatic promise.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Meaningful Message Agreement with acknowledgment window, urgency label, one-follow-up rule, and return phrase.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. A small receipt carries more connection than a large argument about phone habits.
outcomes.role_note: [A] = more affected and dissatisfied; [B] = less affected and content.

outcomes.verdict: [A] interprets long waits through uncertainty and reaches again for contact. [B] feels pressure from repeated messages and avoids the phone longer. The second message and the longer delay are feeding each other. Use one labeled follow-up after a set interval, then switch urgent needs to a call and nonurgent needs to the agreed waiting window. [B] sends a receipt when returning, before explaining the delay.
outcomes.actions_a: Use the one-follow-up rule and move genuine urgency to the agreed call channel.
outcomes.actions_b: Send the receipt as soon as you return and answer the message before defending the delay.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Delay Loop Breaker with waiting window, one follow-up, urgent channel, return receipt, and later habit check.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. The phone stops amplifying both the pursuit and the avoidance.
outcomes.role_note: [A] = more affected by delayed replies; [B] = more likely to withdraw under message pressure.

cases.title: When One of You Needed to Be Right More Than to Resolve It
cases.subtitle: How strongly do you keep arguing your point once you feel misunderstood?

questions.prompt: How strongly do you keep arguing your point once you feel misunderstood?

options.label: Hardly at all
A little, then I can shift to repair
It depends on how important the fact feels
Strongly, I need my view clearly recognized
Very strongly, I struggle to stop before my point is accepted

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: How do you feel about the balance between being understood and resolving the issue?

options.label: It works for me
Mostly okay, with a few rough moments
It regularly leaves me tense or disconnected
I need this pattern to change

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: What are you protecting when you keep making the point?

options.label: Accuracy
Fairness
My intent
My credibility
The impact I experienced
Fear that moving on erases my version

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: What would make it easier to stop?

options.label: A clear summary of my view
Agreement on impact instead of facts
A written open question
A shared next step
Permission for two views to remain
A scheduled time for unresolved details

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: Want to tell the court a bit more about what happened? (optional)
questions.interactionRule: Private context is used only to personalize the selected deterministic branch.

outcomes.verdict: You have a similar need for your perspective to be understood and generally know when the point has been heard enough to shift toward repair. Keep one completion signal: each person summarizes the other's view to the speaker's satisfaction, then the fact debate closes unless the detail changes the next action. Understanding does not require identical conclusions, and resolution does not have to erase either version.
outcomes.actions_a: Summarize [B]'s view before restating yours and identify whether the disputed detail changes the next step.
outcomes.actions_b: Confirm the summary or correct it once, then help move the conversation toward the shared action.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Heard Enough rule with summaries, open fact, impact, action relevance, and resolution step.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Each view gets a clear landing without occupying the whole runway.

outcomes.verdict: [A] and [B] persist at similar levels, but [A] is less satisfied because one person's point may receive acknowledgment while the other's gets labeled as repetition. The issue is whether each person can hear their meaning accurately reflected. Use a two-minute turn, then require the listener to summarize before replying. The speaker gets one correction, not an unlimited closing argument.
outcomes.actions_a: Use your two minutes to state the point, impact, and why it matters without adding every supporting example.
outcomes.actions_b: Summarize before replying and allow one correction before moving to the practical next step.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Two-Minute Understanding Round with timer, summary, one correction, action question, and stop signal.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Equal understanding replaces the contest for the final word.
outcomes.role_note: [A] = less content with the current understanding-to-resolution balance; [B] = more content.

outcomes.verdict: You both keep arguing because neither person trusts that moving on will preserve their version. Create a written open column. Each unresolved fact or interpretation can stay there without being decided tonight. Then ask which action protects both people even if the column remains open. The relationship can resolve behavior before every memory and meaning reaches agreement. That is a mature kind of resolution: the open question stays visible, while care no longer waits behind it.
outcomes.actions_a: Write the unresolved point in one neutral sentence and state the protective action you still support.
outcomes.actions_b: Add your different view beside it and choose the same or another compatible action.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save an Open Question, Closed Action note with two views, shared impact, agreed behavior, and optional revisit date.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. The detail can remain open while the relationship closes the loop on what happens next.

outcomes.verdict: [A] needs stronger recognition of facts, intent, or fairness before shifting to repair. [B] can tolerate two versions and wants the conversation to move toward a workable outcome. You are content because persistence and flexibility already have roles. Give [A] a bounded evidence round and [B] the job of summarizing it. Then let [B] lead the move from what happened to what changes next.
outcomes.actions_a: Use one evidence round and state which practical decision the disputed point actually affects.
outcomes.actions_b: Summarize the point accurately, then lead the transition to impact, repair, and future behavior.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save an Evidence Then Repair format with disputed point, evidence cap, summary, action relevance, and next step.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Accuracy gets a hearing, and repair still gets the rest of the meeting.
outcomes.role_note: [A] = persists more strongly; [B] = shifts to resolution more easily.

outcomes.verdict: [A] persists more strongly and is not okay with feeling moved along before the point is understood. [B] prefers resolution and feels the current process is fine, perhaps because [B] decides when enough has been said. [B] owes a complete reflection before proposing closure. [A] owes a bounded point and an answer to one question: what action changes if this version is accepted?
outcomes.actions_a: State the point in under two minutes and connect it to one concrete repair or future action.
outcomes.actions_b: Reflect the point without dilution, then ask the action question before moving toward closure.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Point to Action Bridge with timed point, listener reflection, action relevance, repair, and remaining open detail.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Being heard becomes the bridge to resolution instead of the obstacle to it.
outcomes.role_note: [A] = persists more strongly and is dissatisfied; [B] = shifts to resolution more easily and is content.

outcomes.verdict: [A] keeps returning to the point because unresolved meaning feels like an unstable foundation. [B] pushes toward resolution because repeated argument feels like living in the construction zone. Both needs can fit in a checkpoint process. Spend ten minutes documenting the two views, then make the practical decision. Revisit the open point only if new information appears or the action fails.
outcomes.actions_a: Document your view and its action relevance within the ten-minute checkpoint.
outcomes.actions_b: Document the alternate view, help choose the protective action, and avoid demanding the disagreement disappear.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Ten-Minute Meaning Checkpoint with two views, evidence, impact, action, and revisit trigger.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. The foundation is documented, and the relationship can leave the construction zone.
outcomes.role_note: [A] = persists more strongly; [B] = shifts to resolution more easily.

cases.title: When Bringing Something Up Felt Like It Wasn't the Right Time, According to Them

questions.prompt: How much preparation or timing control do you need before discussing something difficult?

options.label: Very little, I prefer saying it when it appears
A quick check that there is enough time
Some notice and a calm setting
A scheduled conversation with mental space
A lot of notice and strong control over timing

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

options.label: It works for me
Mostly okay, with a few rough moments
It regularly leaves me tense or disconnected
I need this pattern to change

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: What makes a time feel unavailable?

options.label: Work, exhaustion, or hunger
Being in public or around family
Just before sleep or leaving
Another issue is already active
No clear time limit
Feeling ambushed by the topic

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: What would make timing fairer?

options.label: Ask 'now or later?'
Offer two concrete time options
Give a short topic preview
Set a length for the first talk
Protect genuine urgency
No repeated postponement without a date

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: Want to tell the court a bit more about what happened? (optional)
questions.interactionRule: Private context is used only to personalize the selected deterministic branch.

outcomes.verdict: You need similar preparation before hard conversations and generally respect each other's capacity. That shared timing sense keeps important topics from feeling like ambushes or indefinite delays. Preserve it with a simple invitation that includes the topic, estimated length, and two possible times. The speaker gets a real path in; the listener gets enough notice to arrive with attention. Your shared respect for capacity becomes a reliable way to keep difficult honesty welcome.
outcomes.actions_a: Use the topic, length, and two-times invitation for the next difficult conversation.
outcomes.actions_b: Choose a time or offer a specific alternative within the agreed scheduling window.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Hard Topic Invitation with preview, length, two time options, urgent exception, and no-delay limit.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Timing becomes a shared doorway instead of a test of perfect instinct.

outcomes.verdict: [A] and [B] need similar preparation, but [A] is less satisfied because 'not now' may be functioning as a trapdoor with no visible floor below it. [B] experiences timing protection; [A] experiences disappearance. Any postponement now requires a replacement time chosen before the conversation closes. If capacity changes again, the listener gives one new time and a short reassurance. The topic stays protected, and neither person has to create urgency just to keep it alive.
outcomes.actions_a: Ask for the replacement time before releasing the topic and avoid reopening it before then unless urgency changes.
outcomes.actions_b: Offer the replacement time yourself and initiate the conversation when it arrives.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Not Now Means When rule with topic preview, replacement time, restart owner, one reschedule, and urgent lane.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Timing protection no longer doubles as an exit from the subject.
outcomes.role_note: [A] = less content with current topic timing; [B] = more content.

outcomes.verdict: You agree that timing matters, yet every moment can still become unavailable because no conditions are specific enough. Define the red zones, such as driving, bedtime, work deadlines, or public settings, and create two recurring green zones each week. Difficult topics then have a predictable home. Spontaneous needs can be parked there with a short preview instead of being repeatedly introduced and rejected.
outcomes.actions_a: Choose the red zones that genuinely reduce your ability to listen and one weekly green zone.
outcomes.actions_b: Choose a second green zone and the preview format that lets a topic wait without disappearing.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Red Zone, Green Zone calendar with unavailable times, two weekly windows, topic preview, and urgent exception.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. The calendar creates available time instead of asking stress to produce it spontaneously.

outcomes.verdict: [A] needs more preparation so difficult topics do not arrive faster than the ability to process them. [B] prefers addressing things quickly so concern does not sit and grow. You are content because delay and urgency already receive respect. Use a brief heads-up now, then hold the full conversation within a fixed window. [B] gets confirmation that the topic is real; [A] gets time to gather thoughts.
outcomes.actions_a: Receive the preview and choose a full-talk time inside the agreed window rather than requesting open-ended delay.
outcomes.actions_b: Give a two-sentence preview without beginning the argument and hold the details until the chosen time.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Preview Then Talk rule with preview length, scheduling window, full-talk time, urgent exception, and restart owner.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. The topic enters the relationship now without demanding the full conversation now.
outcomes.role_note: [A] = needs more timing control; [B] = prefers earlier discussion.

outcomes.verdict: [A] needs more preparation and feels repeatedly approached at unusable moments. [B] prefers earlier discussion and feels the current timing is acceptable because speaking quickly reduces [B]'s internal pressure. The relief for [B] is arriving as overload for [A]. [B] owes the preview habit. [A] owes a concrete replacement time inside a reasonable window so preparation does not become indefinite shelving.
outcomes.actions_a: Choose the replacement time and initiate the talk then, with one reschedule maximum.
outcomes.actions_b: Use a brief preview, ask for timing, and stop adding detail once the topic has been scheduled.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Preview and Replacement Agreement with preview script, response window, chosen time, restart owner, and reschedule limit.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Urgency gets acknowledged, and capacity gets a real seat at the table.
outcomes.role_note: [A] = needs more preparation and is dissatisfied; [B] = prefers earlier discussion and is content.

outcomes.verdict: [A] keeps rejecting the moment because surprise or depleted capacity makes the talk feel unsafe. [B] keeps choosing immediate moments because carrying the concern alone feels worse. The loop makes every opening feel either like an ambush or avoidance. Create a standing twice-weekly check window and an urgency scale. Levels one and two wait; level three gets a ten-minute stabilization talk followed by a scheduled full conversation.
outcomes.actions_a: Protect the standing windows and use the urgency scale instead of a general 'not now.'
outcomes.actions_b: Rate the topic honestly and wait for the window unless the agreed level-three criteria are present.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Topic Timing System with standing windows, three urgency levels, stabilization format, full-talk rule, and review date.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Timing stops being improvised by whichever need is loudest.
outcomes.role_note: [A] = needs more timing control; [B] = prefers earlier discussion.

cases.title: When a Compliment or Joke About Someone Else Landed Differently Than Intended

Honestly, both of us about equally

notices comparisons even when they are indirect

wants impact recognized before intent is explained

Agree on public boundaries
Ask what context would make similar comments feel safe

outcomes.verdict: [A] hears possible comparison or relational meaning in comments about other people. [B] recognizes that sensitivity, but may still experience the original comment as casual. The important gap is not whether admiration was allowed. It is what the wording suggested about [A]'s place in the relationship. [B] can acknowledge the comparison that landed and offer specific reassurance. [A] can request a boundary tied to format, context, or audience.
outcomes.actions_a: Name the exact comparison you heard and ask for the future boundary that would reduce it.

outcomes.verdict: [B] is more likely to hear comparison or threat in a compliment or joke about someone else. [A] sees the pattern and may know the original intent was light. Intent can be true while the wording still brushes a tender part of trust or desirability. [A] can name what was meant, acknowledge what was heard, and give specific reassurance. [B] can make the requested boundary narrow enough that ordinary social warmth remains possible.
outcomes.actions_a: Offer specific reassurance and change the comment format, audience, or repeated joke that created the impact.
outcomes.actions_b: Name the exact relational meaning you heard and request a focused boundary rather than a total ban on outside compliments.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save an Outside-Person Comment Boundary with sensitive formats, public limits, reassurance style, and repair line.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. The relationship makes room for social ease and emotional security at the same time.
outcomes.role_note: [B] = the partner both identified as more likely to feel unsettled by the comment.

outcomes.verdict: Both of you can feel unsettled by comments about other people, which suggests comparison sensitivity is shared even if the triggers differ. That mutual understanding can create thoughtful boundaries. Trade the exact formats that sting, such as public teasing, body comparisons, repeated admiration, or comments about a known person. Keep the boundary about delivery and context, then pair it with the reassurance each person actually believes.

outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Comparison-Safe Comment Guide with triggers, allowed context, public limits, reassurance preferences, and repair cue.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Shared sensitivity becomes shared care instead of mutual monitoring.

outcomes.verdict: Each of you sees yourself as more affected, which likely means the triggers are different rather than the intensity being measurable. [A] may react to public comparison; [B] may react to a specific person, topic, or repeated joke. Map the trigger instead of comparing discomfort. Then choose one behavior change and one reassurance for each partner. Different tender spots do not need a single ranking.
outcomes.actions_a: Name the precise context that activates you and the behavior change that would address it.
outcomes.actions_b: Name your different context and the reassurance that would help without asking for constant proof.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Two-Trigger Trust Map with each context, heard meaning, behavior change, reassurance, and follow-up.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Two distinct tender spots receive two precise forms of care.

outcomes.verdict: Each of you thinks the other is more affected, which may be a generous attempt to appear secure or a sign that discomfort is only named after it grows. Make small discomfort easier to admit. Use a zero-to-five signal after a loaded comment, where two means 'please clarify' and four means 'pause and repair.' The signal prevents either person from having to build a dramatic case just to receive reassurance.
outcomes.actions_a: Use the number early and add one sentence about the meaning you heard.
outcomes.actions_b: Respond to the number with clarification or repair before debating whether the comment should have landed lightly.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Comment Impact Scale with numbers, meanings, response steps, public pause rule, and repair line.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Small discomfort gets a small, usable doorway into the relationship.

outcomes.verdict: [A] sees one partner as the more frequent receiver of loaded meaning. [B] sees sensitivity as shared or context-dependent. Treat the recurring trigger as a marked curve, not the entire road. Use extra care around that person, topic, or audience while keeping the same clarification right for both partners everywhere else. Focused caution preserves ease better than broad restriction. You preserve trust by giving one known tender area extra care while leaving the rest of connection breathable.
outcomes.actions_a: Name the recurring curve and the exact wording or context that needs extra care.
outcomes.actions_b: Use the shared clarification process outside that trigger and avoid making sensitivity a permanent role.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Marked-Curve Comment Plan with recurring trigger, wording boundary, clarification question, reassurance, and review date.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. One recurring risk gets attention without shrinking the whole social world.
outcomes.role_note: [A] = identified a specific more-affected partner; [B] = said sensitivity is shared or situational.

cases.title: When One of You Felt Talked Over During a Disagreement

I need this pattern to change

options.label: My point gets completed for me
The response starts before I finish
Volume or speed takes over
I forget what I was saying
My feeling is corrected mid-sentence
I stop believing the rest will be heard

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: What structure would help?

options.label: Two-minute turns
A visible hand signal
Notes for responses instead of interrupting
A summary before reply
One correction after the full point
A pause when speed increases

questions.interactionRule: Private context is used only to personalize the selected deterministic branch.

outcomes.verdict: You are affected by conversational overlap at a similar level and generally know how to leave enough room for the full thought. That creates a valuable kind of safety: neither person has to compete with speed to stay visible. Keep one habit that protects it under stress, such as summarizing before reply or writing down the response urge. Listening becomes easier when no one fears the point will disappear if it waits thirty seconds.
outcomes.actions_a: Practice finishing your point with one clear request rather than adding extra detail to hold the floor.
outcomes.actions_b: Write down your response urge and summarize what you heard before using it.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Full Thought Rule with turn length, note-taking cue, summary step, interruption signal, and pause trigger.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. The conversation keeps enough room for both thoughts to arrive whole.

outcomes.verdict: [A] and [B] are similarly affected, but [A] is less content because speaking space may be equal by minutes and unequal by interruption. [A] could be restarting, defending the right to finish, or losing the thread while [B] experiences lively exchange. Count clean turns, not total airtime. For one week, use a hand signal and require the listener to wait for 'done' before replying.
outcomes.actions_a: Use the agreed end word and hand signal instead of raising volume to reclaim the floor.
outcomes.actions_b: Wait for the end word, note your response, and summarize before presenting it.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Seven-Day Clean Turns Log with speaker, interruptions, recovery, summary, request, and final review.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Speaking space gets measured by completed thoughts, not just clock time.
outcomes.role_note: [A] = less content with current speaking space; [B] = more content.

outcomes.verdict: You are similarly sensitive to being interrupted and both keep doing it because the conversation speed rises faster than trust in memory. Each person jumps in to save a point. Put a note page between impulse and speech. During a five-minute round, the listener writes responses while the speaker finishes. Then switch. Your ideas stay safe without having to enter through each other's sentences.
outcomes.actions_a: Use your full round for one topic and finish with the response you want, not every supporting detail.
outcomes.actions_b: Write every interruption urge, choose the most important one, and lead with a summary when turns switch.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Write, Then Reply format with five-minute turns, note space, summary, one response, and stop time.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Thoughts stop fighting for survival inside the same sentence.

outcomes.verdict: [A] is strongly affected by being talked over and may lose language, confidence, or willingness to continue. [B] tolerates faster overlap and may experience it as engaged conversation. You are content because the difference is acknowledged. Use [A]'s threshold for conflict talks: complete turns, an end word, and summary before response. [B]'s energy still has a place in lower-stakes conversation where both people consent to overlap.
outcomes.actions_a: Use the end word clearly and request a pause if your thread is lost.
outcomes.actions_b: Hold responses in notes, wait for the end word, and summarize before adding your view.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Conflict Conversation Pace rule with end word, notes, summary, pause signal, and casual-overlap exception.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. The conflict pace follows the nervous system that needs more room.
outcomes.role_note: [A] = more strongly affected by being talked over; [B] = more comfortable with overlap.

outcomes.verdict: [A] is strongly affected and feels the current pace erases parts of the message. [B] is comfortable with overlap and experiences the conversation as active, not excluding. The format is being judged by the person who can still function inside it. [B] owes complete turns during conflict. [A] owes a concise endpoint so the protected floor does not become an endless monologue.
outcomes.actions_a: Keep your turn to one point, one impact, and one request, then say 'done.'
outcomes.actions_b: Wait for 'done,' summarize the point, and ask one question before presenting your response.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a One Point, One Impact, One Request card with end word, summary, question, and turn timer.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Full listening and concise speaking become a matched pair.
outcomes.role_note: [A] = more strongly affected and dissatisfied; [B] = more comfortable with overlap and content.

outcomes.verdict: [A] loses access to the conversation when interruptions stack up. [B] interrupts more as urgency grows, especially when fearing the point will be forgotten or misrepresented. The cycle makes [A] quieter and [B] faster. Use a speaker object or screen timer for the first ten minutes, then switch to ordinary conversation only if both people still feel heard. Structure lowers urgency by guaranteeing a turn.
outcomes.actions_a: Hold the speaker role for two minutes and stop when the timer ends, even if more remains.
outcomes.actions_b: Write your point while waiting, then use your guaranteed turn instead of entering early.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Ten-Minute Guaranteed Turns plan with timer, speaking order, notes, summary, and transition check.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Guaranteed turns remove the need to seize them.
outcomes.role_note: [A] = more strongly affected by being talked over; [B] = more likely to interrupt under urgency.
