[A] needs to name the exact words, state the real belief, and retire the phrase that crossed the line. [B] can describe what the words changed internally and what evidence would help safety return.

outcomes.verdict: [B] is more likely to speak from overload and regret the sentence once the intensity drops. [A] already sees the pattern, yet the words can still linger as a possible truth. [B] can repair by naming them directly, clarifying the settled belief, and choosing a replacement for future overload. [A] can state the impact without requiring endless reassurance after the concrete protection is in place.
outcomes.actions_a: State the impact and the one future protection that would make the repair believable.
outcomes.actions_b: Name the sentence, clarify your settled belief, retire the phrase, and practice the replacement aloud.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Heat-of-the-Moment Repair with exact words, settled belief, impact, retired phrase, replacement, and check-in.

Build a retired-phrases list for threats, insults, and sweeping statements, plus three replacement lines that communicate overload without attacking the bond. When either retired phrase appears, the conversation stops and repair begins before the topic resumes. Shared ownership gives you a real chance to make the next heated moment noticeably safer.
outcomes.actions_a: Add one phrase you will retire and one replacement that states your real state without targeting the relationship.
outcomes.actions_b: Add a different phrase and practice the shared stop-and-repair sequence.

outcomes.verdict: Each of you sees yourself as the more heat-driven speaker, which may mean you cross different language boundaries. [A] may threaten distance; [B] may use global judgments or personal edges. Do not compare severity. Retire the exact phrases and design replacements for the need underneath each one, such as space, reassurance, or a stop to the conversation. Each replacement keeps the underlying need speakable without making the bond absorb the impact.
outcomes.actions_a: Identify your phrase, the need underneath it, and a replacement that communicates that need directly.
outcomes.actions_b: Identify your different phrase and rehearse the replacement before the next tense conversation.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Two-Trigger Language Plan with each phrase, underlying need, replacement, stop cue, and repair step.

outcomes.verdict: Each of you thinks the other says the harsher thing, which is common because receiving a sharp sentence leaves a stronger trace than delivering one while flooded. Skip the ranking. Exchange one sentence each that still lingers, then each speaker repairs only their own words. The conversation does not move into comparison until both repairs are complete and both replacement phrases are recorded.
outcomes.actions_a: Name one received sentence and its impact, then listen to the repair without adding a second example.
outcomes.actions_b: Repair your own sentence fully, record the replacement, and give your partner equal uninterrupted space.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a One Sentence Each Repair with words, impacts, settled beliefs, replacements, and pause plan.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Each person cleans their own side before the pain gets compared.

outcomes.verdict: [A] sees one partner as the more frequent heat-driven speaker. [B] sees the behavior as shared or situational. Keep the frequent pattern visible while applying one safety rule to both. The identified partner gets an earlier pause trigger and a practiced replacement phrase. Either partner who crosses the line completes the same repair sequence. Focus stays on prevention and repair, not identity.
outcomes.actions_a: Use the earlier pause trigger and rehearse the replacement phrase tied to your recurring pattern.
outcomes.actions_b: Apply the same stop-and-repair rule to yourself and avoid using symmetry to minimize the frequent pattern.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save an Early Trigger and Shared Repair plan with cue, replacement, stop rule, repair steps, and review date.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. A recurring pattern gets extra support inside a rule that protects both people.
outcomes.role_note: [A] = identified a specific frequent heat-driven speaker; [B] = said the behavior is shared or situational.

cases.title: When You Each Interpreted a Plan Differently Without Realizing It

Both of you recognize the difference, which makes it easy to solve without questioning care or reliability. Give every plan a status: idea, hold, or confirmed. [A] waits for the label before building the day around it; [B] takes responsibility for updating the label when circumstances shift.

[A] recognizes the pattern but may not see the hidden cost of a plan that quietly dissolves. Use idea, hold, and confirmed labels. [B] checks the status before investing; [A] owns any update once a hold or confirmation exists. That small ritual protects [B]'s preparation and [A]'s flexibility at the same time.
outcomes.actions_a: Label the plan and send the update before changing a hold or confirmed arrangement.

outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Plan Status Key with idea, hold, confirmed, task owner, decision deadline, and change message.

outcomes.role_note: [B] = the partner both identified as more likely to hear a loose plan as a commitment.

The recap is not corporate; it protects the anticipation you already started building together.

outcomes.verdict: Each of you sees yourself as the person who treats plans seriously, which probably means the confusion lives in different details. [A] may lock in the date; [B] may lock in the guest list, duration, or responsibility. Compare the six fields rather than the overall plan. Any blank field remains undecided, and any change to a confirmed field gets a message.

outcomes.actions_b: Identify your different settled field and take ownership of confirming one open detail.

No one has to become the household project manager; confirmation becomes a two-tap ritual.

outcomes.actions_a: Name the one thing you need acknowledged before saying the issue is closed.

Let [A] identify one missing piece rather than requiring the whole conflict to be replayed.

outcomes.closing: Case softened. Reassurance moves into the conversation instead of hiding inside a search.
outcomes.role_note: [A] = the partner both identified as more likely to check the other's phone.

outcomes.verdict: [B] reaches for the phone when missing information starts feeling like danger. [A] recognizes this, which gives you a repair opening: respond to the real question without making device access the price of credibility. [B] can ask before acting. [A] can volunteer context tied to the concern. A consent-based agreement protects honesty and personal space at the same time.
outcomes.actions_a: Offer the relevant context and state which phone privacy boundary still matters to you.
outcomes.actions_b: Replace the next checking impulse with one direct question and accept the agreed answer process.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Phone Trust Agreement with private zones, shareable context, direct-question phrase, temporary exceptions, and review date.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. The phone stops doing the emotional work that belongs between you.
outcomes.role_note: [B] = the partner both identified as more likely to check the other's phone.

outcomes.verdict: Both of you may check when anxious, so the issue is not one suspicious partner. Your relationship has been using access as a shortcut around vulnerable questions. That shortcut creates information but rarely creates calm. Agree that concern gets named first, relevant context gets offered directly, and any temporary transparency has a purpose and an end date. Mutual privacy can coexist with mutual openness.
outcomes.actions_a: Write the question you tend to avoid and the context that would genuinely answer it.
outcomes.actions_b: Name one private phone zone and one situation where proactive context would help trust.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Question Before Screen rule with concern, response, private zones, temporary transparency, and end date.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. You trade mutual searching for mutual clarity.

outcomes.verdict: Each of you sees yourself as more likely to check, but your triggers may be different. [A] may react to silence or changed routines. [B] may react to specific people or past history. Treating both as generic jealousy hides the actual repair. Map each trigger, the question it creates, and the response that settles it without surprise access.
outcomes.actions_a: Name your trigger and ask for one concrete piece of context rather than open-ended phone access.
outcomes.actions_b: Name your different trigger and offer the reassurance that addresses [A]'s concern before requesting your own.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Two-Trigger Trust Map with trigger, feared meaning, direct question, useful response, and privacy line.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Two different alarms get two honest answers instead of one invasive habit.

outcomes.verdict: Each of you thinks the other is more likely to check, which can turn every phone moment into a silent courtroom. Stop trying to identify the more suspicious person and identify the missing protocol. When something feels off, ask within twenty-four hours, answer the relevant question, and do not conduct a surprise search. If trust is too damaged for that process, name that directly.
outcomes.actions_a: Own one moment when you relied on monitoring or hints instead of asking clearly.
outcomes.actions_b: Own one piece of context you could have offered sooner and commit to the twenty-four-hour question window.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Twenty-Four-Hour Trust Protocol with trigger, question, response standard, no-surprise-search rule, and escalation step.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Suspicion gets a door to knock on before it starts looking through windows.

outcomes.verdict: [A] identifies one partner as the more frequent checker while [B] sees the pattern as shared or situational. Frequency matters, and so does the relationship climate around it. The frequent checker needs a stop-and-ask routine. The other partner needs consistent, relevant disclosure rather than defensive vagueness. Neither job requires surrendering all privacy.
outcomes.actions_a: Use the stop-and-ask phrase at the next trigger and name only the information you actually need.
outcomes.actions_b: Respond to that need directly, then restate the privacy line without mocking the anxiety.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Check-to-Question Conversion with trigger, exact question, useful context, privacy boundary, and follow-up time.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. A recurring breach becomes a specific moment for honesty and restraint.
outcomes.role_note: [A] = identified a specific more frequent checker; [B] = said the pattern is shared or situational.

cases.title: When a Friendship With Someone Outside the Relationship Caused Tension
cases.subtitle: How much tension does an outside friendship create in the relationship?

questions.prompt: How much tension does an outside friendship create in the relationship?

options.label: Almost none
A little discomfort
Noticeable tension in certain situations
Frequent tension
Major strain on trust

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: How do you feel about the current boundaries around that friendship?

options.label: It works for me
Mostly okay, with a few hard moments
It regularly leaves me tense or disconnected
I need this pattern to change

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: What creates the tension?

options.label: Private or late-night contact
Emotional intimacy
Past romantic history
Being excluded
Flirty energy
Defensiveness when it is discussed

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: What would make the friendship easier to hold?

options.label: More context
A specific contact boundary
Inclusion sometimes
Protected couple time
Direct introductions
A review after trying the change

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: Want to tell the court a bit more about what happened? (optional)
questions.interactionRule: Private context is used only to personalize the selected deterministic branch.

outcomes.verdict: You read the friendship similarly and feel the current boundaries mostly work. The useful signal is not that neither person ever feels a flicker of discomfort. It is that discomfort can be named without automatically threatening the friendship or the relationship. Keep protecting couple time and sharing context before unusual plans. That habit makes outside connection feel integrated rather than hidden.
outcomes.actions_a: Name the friendship behavior that already helps you feel included and informed.
outcomes.actions_b: Keep offering context before plans that differ from the usual rhythm.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Friendship Confidence Note with helpful behaviors, protected couple time, unusual-plan check-in, and review cue.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Trust grows because outside connection is visible and the couple still has a clear center.

outcomes.verdict: [A] and [B] see roughly the same level of tension, but [A] is less content because a detail such as timing, tone, or exclusion keeps landing badly. [B] may see the friendship as ordinary and miss how that repeated detail changes the experience. Adjust the precise behavior instead of debating the friend's entire legitimacy. A small boundary can remove a large amount of static.
outcomes.actions_a: Identify the one repeated behavior that turns manageable discomfort into tension.
outcomes.actions_b: Change that behavior for a month and share context before the situations most likely to trigger it.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Friendship Friction Edit with specific behavior, replacement, couple-time protection, trial length, and review.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. The friendship stays intact while its sharpest edge gets filed down.
outcomes.role_note: [A] = less content with the current friendship boundaries; [B] = more content.

outcomes.verdict: You agree the friendship is creating some tension, yet the current conversation may keep circling whether anyone is overreacting. Move to observable behavior. Define what contact, disclosure, inclusion, and couple-time protection look like. The goal is not to make the friendship emotionally empty. It is to ensure closeness outside the relationship does not depend on secrecy or repeated displacement inside it.
outcomes.actions_a: Choose one behavior you need changed and explain the relationship impact without labeling the friendship itself.
outcomes.actions_b: Choose one boundary you can follow consistently and one form of context you can offer proactively.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save an Outside Friendship Boundary Card with behaviors, context, inclusion, protected couple time, and review date.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. A vague threat becomes a set of choices you can actually evaluate.

outcomes.verdict: [A] experiences more tension because the friendship touches a sensitive boundary, history, or exclusion point. [B] experiences it as safe and values the autonomy it represents. You are both content because difference does not automatically become control. [A] can ask for context tied to specific situations. [B] can provide visibility and protect couple time while keeping a meaningful friendship.
outcomes.actions_a: Name the situations that need context and release the demand to manage every interaction.
outcomes.actions_b: Offer that context before it is requested and visibly protect one recurring couple commitment.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save an Autonomy and Reassurance Plan with trigger situations, context, protected couple time, privacy line, and check-in.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. The friendship keeps room to breathe, and the relationship keeps something solid to stand on.
outcomes.role_note: [A] feels more tension about the friendship; [B] feels less tension.

outcomes.verdict: [A] feels substantial tension and is dissatisfied, while [B] feels little concern and likes the current arrangement. The comfort gap means [B] is currently setting the standard alone. [B] owes one concrete visibility or contact habit. [A] owes a behavior-based request that does not become blanket permission control. Review whether the new habit lowers tension before expanding the rules.
outcomes.actions_a: Request one observable change connected to the actual trigger, not total access or friendship removal.
outcomes.actions_b: Adopt one visibility or timing habit for thirty days and avoid dismissing the concern as insecurity.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Thirty-Day Friendship Trust Trial with trigger, new habit, protected autonomy, couple-time promise, and review score.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. The less-concerned partner contributes proof, and the more-concerned partner keeps the request proportionate.
outcomes.role_note: [A] feels more tension and is dissatisfied; [B] feels less tension and is content.

outcomes.verdict: [A] sees the friendship as a serious trust strain. [B] sees the relationship's reaction as a serious autonomy strain. Repeating the argument only deepens both fears. Set a review date after a short experiment: no secrecy, one clear contact boundary, protected couple time, and no surprise monitoring. Then assess behavior, not promises or worst-case stories.
outcomes.actions_a: Choose the contact behavior that most needs to change and the evidence that would help trust recover.
outcomes.actions_b: Choose the autonomy line that must remain and make the agreed behavior visible without being chased.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Four-Week Friendship Review with contact boundary, disclosure rule, autonomy line, couple time, evidence, and date.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. The disagreement becomes a testable plan instead of an endless referendum on trust.
outcomes.role_note: [A] feels more tension about the friendship; [B] feels less tension.

cases.title: When Liking or Commenting on Someone Else's Post Felt Like Too Much
cases.subtitle: How much does this kind of social media interaction cross a relationship boundary for you?

Only in certain contexts
It can feel too personal
It often crosses a line
It clearly violates an important boundary

questions.prompt: How do you feel about your current social media agreement?

options.label: It works for me
Mostly okay, with a few hard moments
It regularly leaves me tense or disconnected
I need this pattern to change

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: What changes the meaning most?

options.label: The person involved
The wording or emoji
Frequency
Public visibility
Past romantic context
Hiding or deleting the interaction

A rule for past partners

outcomes.verdict: You interpret likes and comments in a similar way and feel the current norm respects both freedom and public consideration. The strength is not a perfectly identical feed. It is shared context: you both know which people, wording, and patterns change a casual tap into a relationship signal. Preserve that nuance instead of turning the agreement into a giant list of forbidden clicks.
outcomes.actions_a: Name one context that changes an interaction's meaning for you.
outcomes.actions_b: Name one ordinary interaction you want to keep free from unnecessary suspicion.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Social Signal Guide with normal interactions, sensitive contexts, wording line, past-partner rule, and review cue.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Your online freedom works because both of you can read the same social context.

outcomes.verdict: [A] and [B] draw a similar line, but [A] is less content because the standard may become flexible when a specific person or type of comment is involved. [B] sees a small action. [A] sees a public signal with history attached. Use examples from the actual situation and agree on the feature that made it different, such as wording, frequency, or secrecy.
outcomes.actions_a: Point to the exact feature that changed the meaning and request a matching boundary.
outcomes.actions_b: Acknowledge that feature and change the repeat behavior without treating every online interaction as suspect.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Context Changes the Click note with person, wording, frequency, public meaning, boundary, and review.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. The rule becomes precise enough to protect trust without policing the whole feed.
outcomes.role_note: [A] = less content with the current social media agreement; [B] = more content.

outcomes.verdict: You are close on the boundary but dissatisfied because the agreement lives in assumptions. One person may mean harmless attention while the other reads suggestive public interest. Create examples for ordinary, sensitive, and clearly off-limits interaction. Include the person, wording, frequency, and whether anything was hidden. Shared examples prevent each new notification from reopening the entire relationship contract.
outcomes.actions_a: Write one ordinary example and one sensitive example from your perspective.
outcomes.actions_b: Write one off-limits example and the repair step if it happens.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Green, Yellow, Red Social Media Guide with examples, context factors, repair, and review date.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Ambiguous taps get a shared language before they collect extra meaning.

outcomes.verdict: [A] reads likes or comments as more relationally meaningful, especially when they are repeated, suggestive, or connected to history. [B] reads most of them as lightweight online behavior. You are content because you can use the stricter standard only in high-context situations. Ordinary interactions stay free. Sensitive people or wording get a quick check before posting.
outcomes.actions_a: Define the two or three context factors that move an interaction into sensitive territory.
outcomes.actions_b: Keep ordinary activity ordinary, but pause when those factors appear and ask before posting.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a High-Context Posting Rule with triggers, ordinary zone, check-in phrase, past-partner rule, and review.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Different online instincts share one filter exactly where the stakes change.
outcomes.role_note: [A] sees these interactions as more boundary-sensitive; [B] sees them as more casual.

outcomes.verdict: [A] sees the interaction as boundary-crossing and feels unprotected. [B] sees it as casual and feels the current freedom is fine. The same click has private intent but public impact. [B] owes a habit of checking the audience and history before suggestive engagement. [A] owes a narrow rule based on context, not a ban on ordinary online sociability.
outcomes.actions_a: Name the audience, history, or wording that created the impact and limit the request to those conditions.
outcomes.actions_b: Pause before that category of interaction and choose a neutral alternative when the context is loaded.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Public Impact Check with person, history, wording, audience, alternative action, and review date.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Intent matters, and so does what the interaction reasonably communicates.
outcomes.role_note: [A] is more boundary-sensitive and dissatisfied; [B] sees the interaction as casual and is content.

outcomes.verdict: [A] fears public interactions are quietly testing the edge of exclusivity. [B] fears the relationship will turn normal online behavior into constant surveillance. Set a one-month agreement around behavior, not passwords: no suggestive comments, a specific rule for past romantic connections, no secret deletion, and no monitoring hunts. Review the actual month instead of arguing from imaginary extremes.
outcomes.actions_a: Choose the behavior that most affects security and agree not to search for extra evidence outside the plan.
outcomes.actions_b: Choose the freedom you need protected and follow the high-context limits consistently for the month.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a One-Month Social Boundary Test with limits, freedoms, no-deletion rule, no-monitoring rule, and review date.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. The boundary gets real-world evidence without turning either phone into a probation office.
outcomes.role_note: [A] sees these interactions as more boundary-sensitive; [B] sees them as more casual.

cases.title: When One of You Kept Something Small From the Other
cases.subtitle: Who is more likely to keep a small thing quiet to avoid friction?

questions.prompt: Who is more likely to keep a small thing quiet to avoid friction?

options.label: Me, no contest
Probably me
Probably them
Definitely them
Honestly, both of us about equally

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: What best explains that answer?

options.label: expects a bigger reaction than the detail seems worth
needs time before talking
calls an omission privacy rather than secrecy
tries to manage the other person's feelings
underestimates how discovery changes the meaning
can improve with a clear timing rule

questions.interactionRule: Display as the answering player’s own voice.

questions.prompt: What kind of detail was kept back?

options.label: A purchase
A message or interaction
A changed plan
A mistake
A feeling
A family or work issue

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: What would make sharing easier?

options.label: A calm disclosure window
A no-interruption first minute
A twenty-four-hour timing rule
Clear privacy categories
A direct repair
Smaller consequences for honest early sharing

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: Want to tell the court a bit more about what happened? (optional)
questions.interactionRule: Private context is used only to personalize the selected deterministic branch.

outcomes.verdict: [A] is more likely to keep small things quiet because immediate peace can look cheaper than a difficult reaction. [B] sees the pattern and may experience discovery as proof the detail was not actually small. [A] needs an early-sharing window. [B] needs to make early honesty safer by hearing the fact before escalating to its possible meanings.
outcomes.actions_a: Share the next uncomfortable small fact within the agreed window and state why you hesitated.
outcomes.actions_b: Give the disclosure one uninterrupted minute, then respond to the fact before the fear around it.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Small-Thing Sharing Rule with categories, time window, first-minute response, privacy exceptions, and repair step.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Small facts stay small because they arrive before concealment adds weight.
outcomes.role_note: [A] = the partner both identified as more likely to keep small things quiet.

outcomes.verdict: [B] tends to delay small disclosures to avoid friction, but the delay changes the issue from the original detail to whether information is being managed. [A] recognizes the pattern and can help by separating honest early sharing from automatic punishment. [B] still owes the fact within a clear window, even when the conversation may be awkward.
outcomes.actions_a: Hear the early disclosure fully and keep the first response proportional to the actual detail.
outcomes.actions_b: Use the agreed window instead of deciding alone that silence is kinder.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Small-Thing Sharing Rule with categories, time window, first-minute response, privacy exceptions, and repair step.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Honesty gets an easier entrance before avoidance builds a second problem.
outcomes.role_note: [B] = the partner both identified as more likely to keep small things quiet.

outcomes.verdict: Both of you sometimes protect short-term calm by omitting small details. That means the relationship may be easy to disturb but also eager to preserve peace. Keep the care, change the method. Use a daily or twice-weekly low-stakes disclosure window where small purchases, plan changes, awkward interactions, and minor mistakes can be shared without turning each item into a summit meeting.
outcomes.actions_a: Bring one delayed small fact to the next window and keep the explanation simple.
outcomes.actions_b: Receive one fact with curiosity, then share a small detail you also postponed.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Small Stuff Check-In with schedule, shareable categories, first response, privacy line, and escalation threshold.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Peace comes from routine honesty instead of careful omission.

outcomes.verdict: Each of you sees yourself as the more frequent keeper of small things, but you may hide different categories for different reasons. [A] might avoid money or plan friction. [B] might delay feelings or outside interactions. One broad secrecy label will miss both mechanisms. Give each category its own timing rule and safer opening line.
outcomes.actions_a: Name the category you delay, the feared reaction, and the opening line that would help you share sooner.
outcomes.actions_b: Name your different category and commit to the response that would make [A]'s early honesty easier.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Two-Category Disclosure Map with topic, fear, time limit, opening line, and receiving response.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Two quiet habits become two specific routes back to openness.

outcomes.verdict: Each of you thinks the other is more likely to keep small things back, so memory may be organized around discoveries rather than your own delays. Review three recent examples without ranking them. Note the original fact, when it was shared, why it was delayed, and what the delay added. The pattern will show whether timing, reaction, or privacy definitions need the repair.
outcomes.actions_a: Add one example from your own behavior before adding an example about your partner.
outcomes.actions_b: Do the same, then choose the single timing rule that would have changed both moments.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Small Omission Audit with facts, timing, feared reaction, added impact, and future rule.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Shared evidence replaces the exhausting contest over who hides more.

outcomes.verdict: [A] identifies one partner as the more frequent keeper of small things while [B] sees the habit as shared or situational. Treat the recurring category first and keep the new rule mutual. The delaying partner owes disclosure within the window. The receiving partner owes a proportional first response. If either side breaks its part, name that part instead of reopening every past omission.
outcomes.actions_a: Use the disclosure window for the recurring category and include the reason for your hesitation.
outcomes.actions_b: Respond to the fact in proportion, then schedule any deeper conversation instead of stacking it immediately.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Recurring Omission Repair with category, time window, disclosure line, first response, and follow-up rule.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. One repeated silence gets a reliable exit instead of a growing history.
outcomes.role_note: [A] = identified a specific more frequent keeper; [B] = said the habit is shared or situational.

cases.title: When You Needed More Reassurance Than the Other Realized
cases.subtitle: How much reassurance do you need when the relationship feels uncertain?

questions.prompt: How much reassurance do you need when the relationship feels uncertain?

options.label: Very little
A brief check-in
Clear words and some follow-through
Frequent reassurance for a while
A lot of consistent reassurance before I settle

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: How do you feel about the reassurance you currently receive?

options.label: It works for me
Mostly okay, with a few hard moments
It regularly leaves me tense or disconnected
I need this pattern to change

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: What kind actually helps?

options.label: Direct words
Physical affection
Proactive updates
Kept plans
A specific repair action
Time together without distraction

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: What would make reassurance sustainable?

options.label: Ask for the exact form
Set a check-in time
Pair words with one action
Name when reassurance is enough
Avoid repeated cross-examination
Review after the stressful period

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: Want to tell the court a bit more about what happened? (optional)
questions.interactionRule: Private context is used only to personalize the selected deterministic branch.

outcomes.verdict: You need a similar amount of reassurance and generally recognize each other's signals. Your real strength is that comfort is not being treated as embarrassing or as an unlimited obligation. You can ask, receive, and return to ordinary life. Keep naming which form helps in the current moment because words, touch, updates, and follow-through are not interchangeable.
outcomes.actions_a: Name the reassurance form that works fastest when you are unsettled.
outcomes.actions_b: Name the sign that tells you reassurance has landed and the issue can rest.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Reassurance Menu with preferred forms, useful phrases, proof actions, enough signal, and check-in timing.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Comfort stays generous because both of you know what actually counts.

outcomes.verdict: [A] and [B] need similar reassurance, but [A] is less content because the offered form may miss the need. [B] might give words when [A] needs follow-through, or space when [A] needs a clear check-in. This is a delivery mismatch, not proof that care is absent. [A] should request the format. [B] should complete one matching action.
outcomes.actions_a: Ask for one specific form and say when it would feel complete.
outcomes.actions_b: Give that form without substituting your own preference, then confirm whether it landed.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Reassurance Translation Note with trigger, requested form, matching action, enough signal, and follow-up.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Care stops getting lost between the sender's intention and the receiver's nervous system.
outcomes.role_note: [A] = less content with current reassurance; [B] = more content.

outcomes.verdict: You need reassurance at a similar level but both feel underfed because requests may arrive as hints, repeated questions, or tests. Replace guessing with a compact sequence: name the trigger, request one form, give one honest answer plus one action, then name when the reassurance has landed. That final step matters because comfort cannot stay sustainable if there is no finish line.
outcomes.actions_a: Use the four-part sequence for one current worry and state what would be enough today.
outcomes.actions_b: Answer honestly, complete the matching action, and ask whether the reassurance can now rest.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Trigger, Ask, Answer, Enough script with preferred forms, action, finish line, and revisit condition.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Reassurance becomes a complete exchange instead of a question that keeps refreshing.

outcomes.verdict: [A] needs more reassurance because uncertainty stays active longer in [A]'s system. [B] settles with less and may assume one answer closes the issue. You are content because frequency can differ without becoming a character judgment. Schedule a temporary check-in rhythm during stressful periods, then taper it when [A] can name that safety has returned.
outcomes.actions_a: Choose the reassurance form and temporary frequency that help without requiring constant proof.
outcomes.actions_b: Provide the agreed check-ins reliably and avoid adding extra promises you cannot maintain.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Reassurance Taper Plan with trigger, form, frequency, enough signal, step-down date, and reset condition.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Different recovery speeds get a rhythm with both support and an exit.
outcomes.role_note: [A] needs more reassurance; [B] needs less.

outcomes.verdict: [A] needs more reassurance and feels alone with the uncertainty. [B] needs less and feels the current level is adequate. The mismatch means [B]'s calm has become the default measure of how much support should be necessary. [B] owes one scheduled reassurance habit. [A] owes a clear finish line and agrees not to turn the habit into repeated cross-examination.
outcomes.actions_a: Request one sustainable check-in and define the sign that will let the question rest.
outcomes.actions_b: Keep the check-in on schedule and pair your words with one visible follow-through action.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Sustainable Reassurance Contract with schedule, wording, proof action, finish line, and review date.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. One partner receives dependable comfort without making the other prove the relationship all day.
outcomes.role_note: [A] needs more reassurance and is dissatisfied; [B] needs less and is content.

outcomes.verdict: [A] fears that too little reassurance means distance is growing. [B] fears that no amount of reassurance will ever be allowed to count. Use a regular ritual rather than emergency negotiations: one weekly relationship check, one agreed response during triggers, and one explicit enough signal. If the same fear keeps returning unchanged, bring the pattern to a counselor rather than multiplying proof demands.
outcomes.actions_a: Bring the recurring fear to the weekly check and practice naming when the agreed response is enough.
outcomes.actions_b: Offer the agreed response consistently and name your limit before frustration turns into withdrawal.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Weekly Trust Ritual with check-in questions, trigger response, enough signal, limits, and outside-support threshold.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Comfort becomes a dependable practice instead of a test neither person can finish.
outcomes.role_note: [A] needs more reassurance; [B] needs less.

It regularly leaves me tense or disconnected
I need this pattern to change

Messages went unanswered
It was late
Safety conditions were unclear
The usual update did not happen
Past trust history amplified it

Share an expected return window
Use a safety emoji
