outcomes.verdict: You have similar tolerance for location uncertainty and your current updates mostly communicate care without turning into monitoring. The useful foundation is predictability: a changed plan, missed return window, or unusual silence means something because ordinary expectations are clear. Keep location sharing optional and reserve stronger measures for real safety conditions, not everyday reassurance.
outcomes.actions_a: Name the plan change that deserves an update and the delay that does not require concern.
outcomes.actions_b: Name the emergency threshold and the fastest low-effort safety signal you can send.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Whereabouts Safety Plan with update triggers, return windows, unavailable-phone note, emergency threshold, and consent rule.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Check-ins stay caring because they have clear limits and real purpose.

outcomes.verdict: [A] and [B] have similar worry levels, but [A] is less content because expected updates may be inconsistent. [B] experiences the silence as ordinary flexibility. [A] experiences a broken pattern and has to decide whether it means danger or disregard. Repair the pattern with two simple triggers: changed plan and missed return window. Everything else can remain spacious.
outcomes.actions_a: Name the two moments when an update matters most and stop requesting routine play-by-play outside them.
outcomes.actions_b: Send the update at those moments or warn when your phone will be unavailable.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Two-Trigger Check-In Rule with plan change, return window, unavailable-phone phrase, emergency step, and review.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. A tiny predictable signal prevents hours of unnecessary story-making.
outcomes.role_note: [A] = less content with current location check-ins; [B] = more content.

outcomes.verdict: You worry at a similar level but both dislike the current system because updates happen randomly or only after concern spikes. Build a safety protocol that is boring on purpose. Share the destination category and return window when plans matter, update meaningful changes, and define when a second contact or emergency step is appropriate. Routine information should not require repeated chasing.
outcomes.actions_a: Choose the information you can reliably send before plans and the delay that activates concern.
outcomes.actions_b: Choose the update method and the emergency step that avoids flooding the other person's phone.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Calm Safety Protocol with pre-plan info, change update, return window, contact ladder, and review date.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Worry gets a quiet procedure before it turns into panic or policing.

outcomes.verdict: [A] worries much sooner when whereabouts are unclear. [B] has a wider comfort window and values moving through the day without constant reporting. You are content because check-ins can be event-based instead of continuous. [B] sends updates for plan changes and missed windows. [A] does not request live tracking when those signals arrive reliably.
outcomes.actions_a: Define the event that needs an update and the emergency threshold that justifies another contact.
outcomes.actions_b: Send the event-based update and state in advance when you expect to be unreachable.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save an Event-Based Location Agreement with update events, return window, unreachable periods, emergency threshold, and tracking consent.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Safety gets dependable signals while ordinary movement keeps its freedom.
outcomes.role_note: [A] worries sooner about location uncertainty; [B] has a wider comfort window.

outcomes.verdict: [A] worries sooner and is dissatisfied with the current silence. [B] worries less and feels the existing freedom works. Because [B] controls the information, [B] owes one low-effort habit: update changed plans or missed return windows. [A] owes restraint after receiving the signal and does not turn care into requests for continuous proof.
outcomes.actions_a: Choose the minimum update that genuinely settles safety worry and respect the wider freedom outside it.
outcomes.actions_b: Send that update without waiting to be chased, especially when the agreed return window changes.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Minimum Viable Check-In with trigger, message, return window, no-tracking boundary, and emergency ladder.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. The informed partner contributes one habit, and the worried partner stops needing a live feed.
outcomes.role_note: [A] worries sooner and is dissatisfied; [B] has a wider comfort window and is content.

outcomes.verdict: [A] experiences silence as a possible safety emergency. [B] experiences frequent check-ins as being watched. Do not negotiate this while one person is missing and the other is panicking. Set a three-step contact ladder now: expected update, one follow-up after the agreed delay, then an emergency contact only at the named threshold. Continuous location sharing stays temporary and consent-based.
outcomes.actions_a: Follow the ladder and wait through the agreed interval before escalating to the next step.
outcomes.actions_b: Send the expected update and identify one emergency contact who can help if the threshold is reached.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Three-Step Safety Ladder with expected update, wait time, follow-up, emergency contact, and temporary-sharing consent.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Safety has an escalation path, and autonomy no longer has to fight panic in real time.
outcomes.role_note: [A] worries sooner about location uncertainty; [B] has a wider comfort window.

cases.title: When a Promise Didn't Get Followed Through On
cases.subtitle: Who is more likely to underestimate how much a missed promise affects trust?

questions.prompt: Who is more likely to underestimate how much a missed promise affects trust?

options.label: Me, no contest
Probably me
Probably them
Definitely them
Honestly, both of us about equally

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: What best explains that answer?

options.label: focuses on good intent
overcommits in the moment
forgets the promise once urgency passes
assumes an apology resets the impact
needs smaller commitments
can rebuild through visible follow-through

questions.interactionRule: Display as the answering player’s own voice.

questions.prompt: What happened to the promise?

options.label: It was forgotten
It kept getting delayed
Priorities changed
The promise was too vague
An obstacle was not shared
It was replaced with an apology

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: What repair would feel real?

options.label: Reset a smaller promise
Choose a deadline
Share obstacles early
Track completion
Repair the practical impact
Stop promising what cannot be delivered

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: Want to tell the court a bit more about what happened? (optional)
questions.interactionRule: Private context is used only to personalize the selected deterministic branch.

outcomes.verdict: [A] is more likely to underestimate a missed promise because intention remains vivid to [A] even after the action disappears. [B] lives with the practical gap and the uncertainty about whether future words will hold. [A] should replace the broad promise with one smaller dated action. [B] should name the specific impact rather than treating the miss as a verdict on every commitment.
outcomes.actions_a: Choose a smaller promise, put it on a date, and flag any obstacle before the deadline.
outcomes.actions_b: Name the concrete impact and what completion would repair, without expanding the case to every past miss.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Promise Reset Card with original impact, smaller commitment, owner, date, obstacle alert, and completion proof.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Trust gets rebuilt by a kept commitment small enough to become real.
outcomes.role_note: [A] = the partner both identified as more likely to underestimate the impact of a missed promise.

outcomes.verdict: [B] gives more weight to the intention behind a promise than to the gap left when it is missed. [A] recognizes that good intent matters but still needs something dependable. The repair is not a bigger apology or a more dramatic promise. [B] needs one realistic action with a date and an early obstacle update. [A] needs to evaluate that action on its own terms.
outcomes.actions_a: Describe the practical or emotional gap and request one finishable repair.
outcomes.actions_b: Set the finishable repair, schedule it, and communicate before the deadline if circumstances change.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Promise Reset Card with original impact, smaller commitment, owner, date, obstacle alert, and completion proof.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Credibility returns through one completed action instead of another hopeful sentence.
outcomes.role_note: [B] = the partner both identified as more likely to underestimate the impact of a missed promise.

outcomes.verdict: Both of you sometimes underestimate missed promises, which suggests enthusiasm or conflict relief may be creating commitments that daily life cannot support. Make fewer promises and give each one an owner, scope, and date. A request is not yet a promise, and an intention is not yet scheduled. That distinction protects affection from becoming a source of unreliable expectations.
outcomes.actions_a: Convert one current intention into a promise with scope and date, or clearly decline it.
outcomes.actions_b: Do the same for a different commitment and name the obstacle that could change the plan.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Promise Ledger with request, accepted promise, owner, date, obstacle update, and completion mark.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Your words become more trustworthy because fewer of them pretend to be commitments.

outcomes.verdict: Each of you sees yourself as more likely to minimize missed follow-through, but the patterns may live in different lanes. [A] may overpromise practical tasks. [B] may overpromise emotional or time commitments. Compare the cost, not the category. Each person chooses one active promise to shrink, schedule, and complete before taking on another.
outcomes.actions_a: Name your unreliable promise lane and reset one commitment to a finishable size.
outcomes.actions_b: Name your different lane and complete one dated action before offering a replacement promise.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Two-Lane Follow-Through Plan with promise types, impacts, smaller actions, dates, and completion evidence.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Two credibility gaps get two concrete repairs instead of one argument about who means well.

outcomes.verdict: Each of you thinks the other underestimates broken follow-through, so promises may be remembered mainly when the partner misses them. Audit the current commitments together. Mark each as accepted, still realistic, needs renegotiation, or was never actually agreed. Then close one overdue item apiece. Shared visibility can do what repeated reminders have not.
outcomes.actions_a: Own one overdue commitment and either complete it or renegotiate it with a real date.
outcomes.actions_b: Do the same before asking your partner to address another item.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Current Commitments Audit with promise, owner, status, new date, obstacle, and completion proof.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. The promise debate becomes a visible workload with honest statuses.

outcomes.verdict: [A] identifies one partner as the more frequent minimizer while [B] sees missed follow-through as shared or situational. Start with the recurring promise lane and use the rule for both people. The promiser must flag trouble before the deadline. The affected partner must state impact and repair without using reminders as punishment. Reliability grows through predictable updates as well as completion.
outcomes.actions_a: Reset the recurring promise with a smaller scope and alert [B] before any new delay.
outcomes.actions_b: State the repair that matters most and acknowledge an early obstacle update as part of trust-building.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Recurring Promise Repair with scope, owner, date, early-warning point, impact repair, and completion proof.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. One chronic letdown gets a structure that can finally interrupt it.
outcomes.role_note: [A] = identified a specific more frequent minimizer; [B] = said missed follow-through is shared or situational.

cases.title: When One of You Felt Suffocated by How Much Checking In Was Expected
cases.subtitle: How much checking in feels healthy during an ordinary day apart?

questions.prompt: How much checking in feels healthy during an ordinary day apart?

options.label: Only for important changes
One or two natural updates
A few regular check-ins
Frequent contact
Very frequent contact throughout the day

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: How do you feel about the current check-in rhythm?

options.label: It works for me
Mostly okay, with a few hard moments
It regularly leaves me tense or disconnected
I need this pattern to change

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: What makes checking in feel heavy?

options.label: Expected instant replies
Too many status questions
Work or focus gets interrupted
Silence is treated as rejection
Location details are expected
There is no clear enough point

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: What rhythm would feel connected and breathable?

options.label: Set two natural check-in windows
Use an urgent-only signal
Name focus hours
Share plan changes only
Remove reply-time assumptions
Review after one week

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: Want to tell the court a bit more about what happened? (optional)
questions.interactionRule: Private context is used only to personalize the selected deterministic branch.

outcomes.verdict: You want a similar amount of contact and the current rhythm mostly feels warm rather than compulsory. The real strength is that messages can be invitations, not attendance checks. Protect that feeling by naming focus hours and reserving a clear urgent signal for things that cannot wait. Connection stays sweeter when every delayed reply does not need an explanation.
outcomes.actions_a: Name the check-in moment you genuinely enjoy and the hours you want free for focus.
outcomes.actions_b: Name the urgent signal and agree not to use it for ordinary reassurance.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Connected and Breathable Rhythm with check-in windows, focus hours, urgent signal, reply expectations, and review.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Contact remains affectionate because it still has room for choice.

outcomes.verdict: [A] and [B] want roughly the same contact, but [A] is less content because the rhythm may carry hidden deadlines. A few messages can feel like many when each one expects an immediate response or location update. [B] may be seeking closeness, not control. Remove the timer from ordinary texts and keep one urgent channel for actual time-sensitive needs.
outcomes.actions_a: Name the reply expectation that creates pressure and the window that would feel reasonable.
outcomes.actions_b: Send ordinary messages without stacking follow-ups, and use the urgent signal only when timing truly matters.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a No-Hidden-Timer Agreement with reply window, focus hours, urgent signal, follow-up limit, and review.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. The number of messages stays familiar while the pressure inside them drops.
outcomes.role_note: [A] = less content with the current check-in rhythm; [B] = more content.

outcomes.verdict: You prefer a similar check-in level but both feel trapped by improvising it. Some days contact floods the schedule; other days silence creates concern. Set two natural windows, identify focus periods, and agree that plan changes deserve updates while ordinary gaps do not require repair. A rhythm should reduce interpretation, not create another task to manage.
outcomes.actions_a: Choose one natural check-in window and one focus period when delayed replies are expected.
outcomes.actions_b: Choose the second window and define which plan changes need an update.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Daily Check-In Rhythm with windows, focus periods, plan-change rule, urgent signal, and one-week review.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Connection gets a beat you can feel without counting every message.

outcomes.verdict: [A] wants more frequent contact because small updates create closeness and predictability. [B] needs longer stretches without interruption to feel focused and free. You are content because contact can be concentrated at dependable points. [A] gets two reliable windows. [B] gets protected space between them. Neither person has to copy the other's phone habits to show care.
outcomes.actions_a: Choose the two updates that matter most and release routine status questions between them.
outcomes.actions_b: Protect those two windows even on busy days and state focus periods in advance.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Reliable Windows Plan with check-in times, focus blocks, plan-change updates, urgent signal, and review.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. One partner receives consistency, and the other receives uninterrupted air.
outcomes.role_note: [A] wants more frequent check-ins; [B] wants fewer.

outcomes.verdict: [A] wants more checking in and feels disconnected without it. [B] wants fewer messages and feels the current distance is comfortable. The person needing less contact currently sets the rhythm by default. [B] owes two dependable check-ins. [A] owes no repeated prompts between them unless the agreed urgent condition applies. Reliability, not volume, is the bridge.
outcomes.actions_a: Choose the two moments that would create real connection and stop chasing updates between them.
outcomes.actions_b: Initiate those check-ins consistently and name in advance when a work block changes the timing.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Two-Check-In Contract with times, initiator, focus blocks, no-chasing rule, urgent exception, and review.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. More connection arrives on purpose without turning the whole day into a status report.
outcomes.role_note: [A] wants more check-ins and is dissatisfied; [B] wants fewer and is content.

outcomes.verdict: [A] experiences sparse contact as distance. [B] experiences frequent contact as surveillance or interruption. Stop renegotiating with every text. Try a weekly rhythm with set windows, declared focus blocks, plan-change updates, and one urgent signal. At the end of the week, rate connection and pressure separately. Adjust the schedule based on both numbers.
outcomes.actions_a: Follow the set windows and record whether connection improved without adding extra status requests.
outcomes.actions_b: Protect the windows and record whether pressure fell when focus blocks were respected.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a One-Week Contact Experiment with windows, focus blocks, urgent signal, connection score, pressure score, and review.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. The phone rhythm becomes shared data instead of a daily referendum on love.
outcomes.role_note: [A] wants more frequent check-ins; [B] wants fewer.

cases.title: When Something Was Downplayed Instead of Being Said Directly
cases.subtitle: Who is more likely to downplay an issue instead of saying it directly?

questions.prompt: Who is more likely to downplay an issue instead of saying it directly?

options.label: Me, no contest
Probably me
Probably them
Definitely them
Honestly, both of us about equally

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: What best explains that answer?

options.label: fears sounding dramatic
waits for the perfect moment
hopes the feeling will pass
uses jokes or hints
expects directness to start a bigger conflict
can speak sooner with a safer opening

questions.interactionRule: Display as the answering player’s own voice.

questions.prompt: How did the downplaying show up?

options.label: Saying it was fine
Making a joke
Using vague hints
Acting distant
Sharing only part of the issue
Bringing it up much later

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: What would support directness?

options.label: A simple opening phrase
A scheduled talk
No interruption for two minutes
Separate facts from fears
A response without instant defense
A time limit on postponing

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: Want to tell the court a bit more about what happened? (optional)
questions.interactionRule: Private context is used only to personalize the selected deterministic branch.

outcomes.verdict: [A] is more likely to downplay because directness may feel like creating conflict rather than preventing it. [B] sees the pattern but may only meet the issue after hints have turned into distance. [A] needs a low-drama opening phrase. [B] needs to reward early honesty with listening before defense. Speaking sooner keeps a concern closer to its actual size.
outcomes.actions_a: Use the phrase 'This is small, but I want to say it clearly' within twenty-four hours.
outcomes.actions_b: Give [A] two uninterrupted minutes, then reflect the issue before explaining your side.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Say It While It Is Small script with opening phrase, time limit, listening step, response, and follow-up.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Directness becomes the way you keep small things from growing in the dark.
outcomes.role_note: [A] = the partner both identified as more likely to downplay an issue.

outcomes.verdict: [B] tends to soften issues until the words no longer match the emotional weight. [A] then has to decode jokes, distance, or a late reveal. [A] can make directness safer by receiving the first version without immediate argument. [B] still needs to replace hints with a clear statement of fact, feeling, and request.
outcomes.actions_a: Listen to the first clear statement and confirm what you heard before offering context.
outcomes.actions_b: State the fact, feeling, and one request without testing whether [A] can guess the issue.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Say It While It Is Small script with opening phrase, time limit, listening step, response, and follow-up.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. The concern arrives through the front door instead of leaving clues around the room.
outcomes.role_note: [B] = the partner both identified as more likely to downplay an issue.

outcomes.verdict: Both of you downplay, so the relationship may look calm while each person waits for the other to notice a shift. Your care for peace is real, but hidden concern makes that peace fragile. Create a short weekly 'small but real' check where each person names one irritation, worry, or need before it becomes evidence in a larger case.
outcomes.actions_a: Bring one small issue in a fact, feeling, request format and keep it under two minutes.
outcomes.actions_b: Receive it, then bring your own without using the moment to countercharge.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Small but Real Check-In with schedule, fact-feeling-request prompts, response rule, and follow-up slot.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Quiet becomes honest calm rather than two people editing themselves.

outcomes.verdict: Each of you sees yourself as the bigger downplayer, but you may hide different signals. [A] may say 'fine' and withdraw. [B] may joke, hint, or reveal only half. Identify the signal each person uses and agree to translate it into direct words within a day. The listener responds to the translation, not to the imperfect lead-up.
outcomes.actions_a: Name your downplaying signal and the direct sentence it should become next time.
outcomes.actions_b: Name your different signal and practice receiving [A]'s direct sentence without focusing on the delay.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Hint-to-Direct Translation with signals, clear sentences, twenty-four-hour limit, and receiving response.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Your familiar disguises get a shared translation key.

outcomes.verdict: Each of you thinks the other downplays more, which may mean both people notice indirectness only when they are forced to decode it. For one week, do not evaluate motive. Log any 'fine,' joke, vague hint, or sudden distance and translate your own signal first. The goal is not catching the partner. It is reducing the amount of emotional detective work in the relationship.
outcomes.actions_a: Translate one of your own indirect signals into the direct issue and request.
outcomes.actions_b: Do the same before naming a signal from [A], then choose a shared opening phrase.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a One-Week Directness Log with signal, real issue, clear request, response, and outcome.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Both of you retire from guessing by practicing clearer first drafts.

outcomes.verdict: [A] identifies one partner as the more frequent downplayer while [B] sees the habit as shared or situational. Use the recurring signal as an agreed cue, not an accusation. When it appears, the speaker gets one chance to state the issue plainly. The listener offers attention rather than interrogation. Apply the same cue to either partner.
outcomes.actions_a: When the cue appears, replace it with one clear sentence and one request within the agreed time.
outcomes.actions_b: Respond with 'Tell me the direct version' and listen without turning the cue into evidence of dishonesty.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Direct-Version Cue with recurring signal, response phrase, time limit, request format, and follow-up.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. A familiar avoidance pattern becomes a gentle invitation to say the real thing.
outcomes.role_note: [A] = identified a specific more frequent downplayer; [B] = said the habit is shared or situational.

cases.title: When Flirting With Someone Else Crossed a Line for One of You
cases.subtitle: How strongly did the behavior cross your relationship's flirting boundary?

questions.prompt: How strongly did the behavior cross your relationship's flirting boundary?

options.label: It did not cross it
It felt ambiguous
It crossed a small but real line
It clearly crossed the line
It seriously damaged trust

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: How do you feel about the boundary and repair now?

options.label: It works for me
Mostly okay, with a few hard moments
It regularly leaves me tense or disconnected
I need this pattern to change

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: What made the behavior feel like flirting?

options.label: Sexual or suggestive words
Repeated attention
Touch
Private messaging
A past romantic connection
Hiding it afterward

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: What would clarify the line?

options.label: Name concrete examples
Include online and in-person behavior
Agree on context exceptions
Repair the public or private impact
Set a no-hiding rule
Review after consistent behavior

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: Want to tell the court a bit more about what happened? (optional)
questions.interactionRule: Private context is used only to personalize the selected deterministic branch.

outcomes.verdict: You read the behavior similarly and feel the boundary has been handled. The useful depth here is that you are not relying on the word flirting alone. You understand which combination of wording, repetition, touch, privacy, and history changes friendly energy into a relationship concern. Keep that behavioral clarity and update it when social contexts change.
outcomes.actions_a: Name one behavior that clearly stays friendly and one context that changes its meaning.
outcomes.actions_b: Name the repair behavior that helped this incident feel complete.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Flirting Boundary Guide with friendly zone, line-crossing examples, context factors, no-hiding rule, and repair.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Trust rests on examples you both understand, not a word that can mean anything.

outcomes.verdict: [A] and [B] place the line in a similar area, but [A] is less content because the impact may not have been repaired. [B] may have stopped the behavior and assumed that was enough. [A] may still need acknowledgment, changed context, or a direct correction. Finish the specific repair rather than reopening the whole definition of flirting.
outcomes.actions_a: Name the unfinished impact and the one action that would close it.
outcomes.actions_b: Complete that action and state the future boundary in behavior-based language.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Flirting Repair Receipt with behavior, impact, completed repair, future line, and review cue.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Agreement about the line finally reaches the part that was hurt.
outcomes.role_note: [A] = less content with the current flirting boundary or repair; [B] = more content.

outcomes.verdict: You are close on what crossed the line but dissatisfied because the boundary was vague before the moment and reactive afterward. Write examples for words, touch, repeated attention, private messaging, and concealment. Then choose the first repair for a future slip. Clear examples reduce the temptation to debate intent while one person is still absorbing impact.
outcomes.actions_a: Write two behaviors that cross your line and one that remains friendly.
outcomes.actions_b: Write two different examples and the first repair step you will take if the line is crossed.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Behavior-Based Flirting Agreement with examples, context, no-hiding rule, first repair, and review date.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. The boundary moves from vibes alone to choices both people can recognize.

outcomes.verdict: [A] defines flirting more broadly because repeated attention, suggestive tone, or private context carries relational meaning. [B] uses a narrower definition and sees more social play as harmless. You are content because you can use a high-context rule: when privacy, history, sexual tone, or repetition stack up, pause. Ordinary warmth stays free.
outcomes.actions_a: Choose the context factors that activate the stricter boundary and avoid extending it to every friendly interaction.
outcomes.actions_b: Pause when two or more factors appear and move the interaction back into the ordinary zone.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a High-Context Flirting Filter with factors, friendly examples, pause point, alternative behavior, and review.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Social freedom remains broad while the loaded combinations get extra care.
outcomes.role_note: [A] defines flirting more broadly; [B] defines it more narrowly.

outcomes.verdict: [A] sees the behavior as a clear line-crossing and is dissatisfied. [B] sees it as harmless and is comfortable with the current standard. Since the behavior involved another person, private intent cannot be the only measure. [B] owes one concrete limit around the loaded behavior. [A] owes a narrow definition that leaves ordinary sociability untouched.
outcomes.actions_a: Name the exact behavior and context that created the relationship impact, then release unrelated friendly behavior.
outcomes.actions_b: Stop or modify that behavior and avoid using harmless intent to erase the visible impact.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Narrow Flirting Boundary with exact behavior, context, friendly zone, changed action, repair, and review.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. The line becomes specific enough to protect trust without shrinking your whole social world.
outcomes.role_note: [A] defines flirting more broadly and is dissatisfied; [B] defines it more narrowly and is content.

outcomes.verdict: [A] fears a narrow definition leaves too much room for charged behavior. [B] fears a broad definition will make normal social confidence feel forbidden. Test a concrete agreement for six weeks: no sexual comments or touch, no hidden private messaging, context rules for past connections, and freedom for ordinary public friendliness. Review actual moments, not imagined extremes.
outcomes.actions_a: Track the moments that felt secure or concerning without searching for violations.
outcomes.actions_b: Follow the specific limits and track when ordinary friendliness remained fully available.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Six-Week Flirting Boundary Test with limits, freedoms, context rules, repair step, examples log, and review date.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. A loaded label becomes a lived agreement with evidence on both sides.
outcomes.role_note: [A] defines flirting more broadly; [B] defines it more narrowly.

cases.title: When One of You Found Out Something the Other Should Have Shared Sooner
cases.subtitle: Who is more likely to wait too long before sharing something relevant?

questions.prompt: Who is more likely to wait too long before sharing something relevant?

options.label: Me, no contest
Probably me
Probably them
Definitely them
Honestly, both of us about equally

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: What best explains that answer?

options.label: needs time to understand it first
fears the reaction
hopes the issue resolves itself
does not recognize when the information becomes shared
protects short-term calm
can improve with disclosure deadlines

questions.interactionRule: Display as the answering player’s own voice.

questions.prompt: What should have been shared sooner?

options.label: A message or contact
A money issue
A changed plan
A health or work issue
A family development
A feeling or decision that affected both

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: What would repair the timing breach?

options.label: Give the full timeline
Explain the delay without excusing it
Set category deadlines
Share partial facts early
Correct any practical impact
Create a proactive update habit

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: Want to tell the court a bit more about what happened? (optional)
questions.interactionRule: Private context is used only to personalize the selected deterministic branch.

outcomes.verdict: [A] is more likely to delay relevant information because waiting can feel like buying time to understand, solve, or soften it. [B] discovers not only the fact but that the relationship was operating with an information gap. [A] needs category-based deadlines and can share an incomplete update honestly. [B] needs the timeline and practical repair, not an endless interrogation.
outcomes.actions_a: Give the full timeline, name why you delayed, and set the deadline you will use for this category next time.
outcomes.actions_b: Identify the decision or safety impact created by the delay and request the matching repair.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Share-Sooner Protocol with categories, deadlines, partial-update phrase, timeline repair, and review.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Unfinished information can arrive early without pretending to be a finished answer.
outcomes.role_note: [A] = the partner both identified as more likely to share relevant information late.

outcomes.verdict: [B] tends to wait until information is settled, but [A] may need it while choices are still open. The delay removes [A]'s chance to prepare, decide, or support. [B] can share a partial fact with a clear update time instead of waiting for certainty. [A] can receive that first version without demanding answers [B] does not yet have.
outcomes.actions_a: Name the missed decision opportunity or impact and ask for a category deadline rather than constant updates.
outcomes.actions_b: Share the partial fact now, state what is unknown, and commit to the next update time.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Share-Sooner Protocol with categories, deadlines, partial-update phrase, timeline repair, and review.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Early uncertainty becomes more trustworthy than late certainty.
outcomes.role_note: [B] = the partner both identified as more likely to share relevant information late.

outcomes.verdict: Both of you sometimes share too late, which suggests the missing rule is when private information becomes relationship information. Define the threshold by impact: if it changes shared money, time, safety, plans, intimacy, or another person's involvement, it deserves an early heads-up. You can say 'I do not know everything yet' without withholding the fact that something is happening.
outcomes.actions_a: Choose one category and set the early heads-up threshold.
outcomes.actions_b: Choose another category and write the partial-update phrase you will use before details are complete.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Private-to-Shared Threshold Map with domains, triggers, deadlines, partial-update wording, and next-update time.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Relevance, not perfect certainty, decides when the couple gets included.

outcomes.verdict: Each of you sees yourself as the later sharer, but the delays may protect different things. [A] may hide uncertainty until there is a plan. [B] may hide likely conflict until it cannot be avoided. Those motives need different corrections: earlier incomplete updates for [A], earlier uncomfortable facts for [B]. Both restore the other person's chance to participate.
outcomes.actions_a: Name the information you delay while seeking certainty and practice giving an incomplete update.
outcomes.actions_b: Name the fact you delay to avoid conflict and practice sharing it before the consequence arrives.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Two-Delay Disclosure Map with motive, category, early phrase, deadline, and decision impact.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Two forms of waiting get two honest exits.

outcomes.verdict: Each of you thinks the other shares late, so the relationship may be running on dueling surprise files. Review the last four discoveries and mark which shared domain was affected and when disclosure should reasonably have happened. Build deadlines from those examples. Do not turn the audit into a hunt for unrelated private details.
outcomes.actions_a: Bring one example from your own delay and propose the deadline that would have preserved [B]'s choice.
outcomes.actions_b: Do the same, then agree on which domains trigger proactive updates.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Four-Discovery Timing Audit with fact, shared impact, reasonable deadline, repair, and future trigger.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Surprise loses power when relevance and timing become visible rules.

outcomes.verdict: [A] identifies one partner as the more frequent late sharer while [B] sees the issue as shared or situational. Start with the recurring information category and keep the deadline mutual. The delaying partner owes an early partial update. The receiving partner owes room for uncertainty without treating missing details as fresh concealment. Then schedule the next update.
outcomes.actions_a: Use the partial-update phrase for the recurring category before the information is fully settled.
outcomes.actions_b: Receive the update, ask only what is currently knowable, and agree on the next information time.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Recurring Late-Share Repair with category, early trigger, partial phrase, next update, impact repair, and review.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. One repeated surprise gets replaced by an honest work-in-progress.
outcomes.role_note: [A] = identified a specific more frequent late sharer; [B] = said delayed sharing is mutual or situational.

cases.title: When Talking to an Ex Became a Source of Tension
cases.subtitle: How much tension does contact with an ex create for you?

questions.prompt: How much tension does contact with an ex create for you?

options.label: Almost none
A little in certain contexts
Noticeable tension
A lot of trust strain
It feels incompatible with safety right now

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: How do you feel about the current boundaries around ex contact?

options.label: It works for me
Mostly okay, with a few hard moments
It regularly leaves me tense or disconnected
I need this pattern to change

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: What changes the meaning of the contact?

options.label: Why contact is happening
Frequency
Private or late-night messaging
Unresolved feelings
Shared responsibilities
Whether the contact was disclosed

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: What boundary would create clarity?

options.label: State the purpose
Share unusual contact proactively
Limit late-night private messages
Keep necessary logistics focused
Pause optional contact during repair
Review on a set date

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: Want to tell the court a bit more about what happened? (optional)
questions.interactionRule: Private context is used only to personalize the selected deterministic branch.

outcomes.verdict: You interpret ex contact similarly and feel the current boundary fits the actual context. The strength is not pretending the past never existed. It is keeping present-day purpose visible. Necessary logistics, old friendships, and unexpected messages each carry different meaning. Continue sharing unusual contact proactively and keep any required communication focused on its purpose.
outcomes.actions_a: Name the purpose that makes contact understandable and the context that would require a heads-up.
outcomes.actions_b: Name the boundary that keeps necessary contact from quietly becoming emotional fallback.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save an Ex Contact Purpose Plan with reasons, allowed channels, proactive updates, sensitive contexts, and review cue.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. The past stays legible instead of gaining power through mystery.

outcomes.verdict: [A] and [B] see similar tension, but [A] is less content because one detail such as late timing, hidden contact, or emotional tone has not been resolved. [B] may focus on the innocent purpose and overlook the way the contact was handled. Keep necessary communication, change the loaded feature, and complete the specific disclosure or repair.
outcomes.actions_a: Name the handling detail that created tension and the change that would settle it.
outcomes.actions_b: Change that detail, disclose unusual contact before discovery, and keep communication tied to its stated purpose.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save an Ex Contact Friction Edit with purpose, loaded detail, new boundary, disclosure step, and review.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. The contact keeps its legitimate function while losing the feature that made it feel unsafe.
outcomes.role_note: [A] = less content with current ex-contact boundaries; [B] = more content.

outcomes.verdict: You are close on how much ex contact matters but both dislike the ambiguity. Separate contact by purpose. Shared responsibilities need efficient logistics. Genuine established friendship needs visibility and present-day boundaries. Nostalgia, secret comfort-seeking, or romantic testing needs a pause. A purpose map is more useful than one rule pretending every ex relationship is identical.
outcomes.actions_a: Classify the current contact honestly and name the boundary that fits that purpose.
outcomes.actions_b: Choose the disclosure habit and the behavior that would move the contact into a pause category.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save an Ex Contact Purpose Map with categories, allowed behavior, disclosure, pause triggers, and review date.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Context gets room, and ambiguity loses its hiding place.

outcomes.verdict: [A] experiences ex contact as more threatening because history adds emotional weight to even ordinary messages. [B] sees the current contact as practical or settled. You are content because necessary contact can stay narrow and visible. [B] owns proactive context and purpose-focused replies. [A] receives that context without requesting a transcript of every exchange.
outcomes.actions_a: Name the situations that require a heads-up and release the need to inspect ordinary purpose-focused logistics.
outcomes.actions_b: Share unusual contact proactively and keep tone, timing, and channel consistent with the stated purpose.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Narrow and Visible Ex Contact Plan with purpose, channel, timing, update triggers, privacy line, and review.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Necessary contact stays contained without turning transparency into surveillance.
outcomes.role_note: [A] feels more tension about ex contact; [B] feels less.

outcomes.verdict: [A] feels substantial tension and is dissatisfied. [B] sees little concern and is comfortable with the current contact. Because [B] has the history and controls the communication, [B] owes one visible habit: state the purpose, disclose unusual contact, and remove loaded timing or tone. [A] owes a limited request that does not turn into monitoring every message.
outcomes.actions_a: Request the one change most connected to emotional safety and define what ordinary contact you will not monitor.
outcomes.actions_b: Adopt the visibility habit and move optional late-night or emotionally intimate contact out of the pattern.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Purpose and Visibility Contract with allowed contact, loaded behaviors, proactive update, privacy line, and review.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. The person with more context supplies clarity, and the person with more fear keeps the boundary focused.
outcomes.role_note: [A] feels more tension and is dissatisfied; [B] feels less tension and is content.

outcomes.verdict: [A] fears continued contact leaves an emotional door open. [B] fears the relationship is demanding erasure of a settled past or a necessary connection. Set a dated review instead of arguing forever. Until then, keep required logistics narrow, pause optional emotionally intimate contact, disclose unexpected messages, and avoid secret deletion. Review whether trust changed through behavior.
outcomes.actions_a: State which contact is necessary, which optional behavior needs a pause, and what evidence would lower concern.
outcomes.actions_b: Follow the temporary limits, share unexpected contact, and record whether the purpose remained consistent.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Dated Ex Contact Review with necessary contact, temporary pause, disclosure rule, no-deletion rule, evidence, and date.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. The boundary becomes a time-limited trust test instead of a permanent argument about the past.
outcomes.role_note: [A] feels more tension about ex contact; [B] feels less.

cases.title: When One of You Felt Their Privacy Was Crossed
cases.subtitle: Who is more likely to cross a privacy line while looking for clarity?

questions.prompt: Who is more likely to cross a privacy line while looking for clarity?

options.label: Me, no contest
Probably me
Probably them
Definitely them
Honestly, both equally

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: What makes that answer feel true?

options.label: Anxiety makes waiting difficult
The boundary was never stated
Access was mistaken for openness
A clue triggered fear
Past secrecy changed the stakes
The impact was noticed too late

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: Where did the line get crossed?

options.label: Phone or messages
Journal or notes
Conversation with a friend
Location or account access
Personal belongings
Information shared without consent

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: What would restore respect?

options.label: Name the exact private zone
Remove unneeded access
Ask before looking or sharing
Offer relevant context directly
Set a safety exception
Review the line after trust improves

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: Want to tell the court a bit more about what happened? (optional)
questions.interactionRule: Private context is used only to personalize the selected deterministic branch.

outcomes.verdict: [A] is more likely to cross the line because uncertainty can make access feel like the fastest route to safety. [B] experiences something different: a private zone stopped being theirs to open. [A] needs to ask for the missing context instead of taking it. [B] needs to define the boundary precisely, including any genuine safety exception, so privacy is not left to guesswork.
outcomes.actions_a: Name what you feared, return or delete what you accessed, and ask directly next time.
outcomes.actions_b: Define the protected zone and the specific context you can still share voluntarily.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Privacy Line Map with protected spaces, consent steps, shareable context, safety exceptions, and repair date.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Clarity gets a consent process, and privacy becomes something the relationship actively protects.
outcomes.role_note: [A] = the partner both identified as more likely to cross a privacy line.

outcomes.verdict: [B] tends to reach past privacy when a missing answer starts feeling more dangerous than the boundary. [A] understands the fear but still needs ownership of personal space. [B] can repair the exact intrusion and replace future searching with a direct request. [A] can answer the relationship-relevant question without making unlimited access the proof of honesty.
outcomes.actions_a: State which part of the intrusion affected you and what ownership needs to be restored.
outcomes.actions_b: Undo the access where possible, name the fear beneath it, and use a direct question next time.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Privacy Line Map with protected spaces, consent steps, shareable context, safety exceptions, and repair date.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. The needed answer can be requested without taking the route through someone else's private space.
outcomes.role_note: [B] = the partner both identified as more likely to cross a privacy line.

outcomes.verdict: Both of you may cross privacy lines when anxious, so the relationship has been treating closeness like an all-access pass. Real intimacy still needs doors that open by invitation. Decide which spaces are personal, which facts affect the couple, and what qualifies as a safety exception. Mutual privacy works when neither person has to hide the existence of the door.
outcomes.actions_a: Choose one private zone and explain why keeping it personal helps you stay emotionally honest.
outcomes.actions_b: Choose a different zone and define the couple-impact threshold that turns private information into shared information.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save an Intimacy With Doors agreement with private zones, shared-impact triggers, consent language, and safety exceptions.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Personal space stops looking suspicious because the boundaries around it are visible.

outcomes.verdict: Each of you sees yourself as the likelier boundary-crosser, but you may do it in different ways. [A] may seek devices or details. [B] may share private information with other people or use location access. Naming both forms prevents one visible incident from hiding the other. Each partner repairs the kind of privacy they personally disrupted.
outcomes.actions_a: Identify your form of crossing and make one concrete restoration without waiting for [B].
outcomes.actions_b: Identify your different form and state the consent question you will use before repeating it.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Two-Way Privacy Repair with each crossing type, affected space, restoration, consent phrase, and review.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Two different intrusions receive two direct repairs instead of competing for the bigger headline.

outcomes.verdict: Each of you thinks the other crosses more lines, which usually means privacy only becomes visible after it has been breached. Stop ranking incidents and inventory the zones: devices, conversations, belongings, location, accounts, and outside sharing. Mark the consent rule for each. A boundary written before the next trigger is easier to respect than one announced during panic.
outcomes.actions_a: Own one zone where you assumed permission and propose a clearer consent rule.
outcomes.actions_b: Own a different assumption and add the relevant safety or couple-impact exception.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Privacy Zone Inventory with access status, consent rule, shared-impact trigger, safety exception, and repair owner.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Invisible boundaries become usable instructions before either person has to defend them.

outcomes.verdict: [A] identifies one partner as the more frequent boundary-crosser while [B] sees the pattern as shared or situational. Start with the repeated zone, but make the rule mutual. The person reaching across the line owes restoration and a new consent habit. The other partner owes direct, relationship-relevant context without surrendering unrelated privacy.
outcomes.actions_a: Repair the recurring crossing and use the agreed permission question before approaching that zone again.
outcomes.actions_b: State the relevant answer or context clearly, then hold the boundary around information that is not part of the concern.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Recurring Privacy Trigger Plan with zone, feared meaning, consent question, relevant context, and restoration step.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. The repeat pattern gets interrupted without turning openness into unlimited access.
outcomes.role_note: [A] = identified a specific more frequent boundary-crosser; [B] = said the pattern is shared or situational.

cases.title: When a White Lie Got Found Out
cases.subtitle: Who is more likely to use a small lie to avoid an uncomfortable moment?

questions.prompt: Who is more likely to use a small lie to avoid an uncomfortable moment?

options.label: Me, no contest
Probably me
Probably them
Definitely them
Honestly, both equally

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: What makes that answer feel true?

options.label: They fear a reaction
They want to protect feelings
The truth feels embarrassing
They expect the issue to pass
They minimize the detail
They do not predict the discovery cost

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: What was the lie protecting?

options.label: A mistake
A purchase or plan
Someone else's interaction
A preference or feeling
An avoided responsibility
An image of being okay

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: What would repair the trust impact?

options.label: Tell the full version once
Explain the fear without excusing it
Correct the practical consequence
Set an honesty window
Use a gentler first response
Name which details are truly private

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: Want to tell the court a bit more about what happened? (optional)
questions.interactionRule: Private context is used only to personalize the selected deterministic branch.

outcomes.verdict: [A] is more likely to use a white lie because a smooth moment can feel worth protecting. [B] discovers that the comfort was purchased with an inaccurate version of reality. The repair is not dramatic confession forever. [A] needs to give the complete version and identify the feared reaction. [B] needs to make timely truth safer without pretending the lie had no impact.
outcomes.actions_a: Tell the whole version once, correct the consequence, and name what made honesty feel risky.
outcomes.actions_b: Respond to the fact first, then discuss the trust impact without turning honesty into a new punishment.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Truth Before Comfort rule with disclosure window, full-version prompt, first response, privacy line, and repair step.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Temporary comfort stops borrowing against tomorrow's trust.
outcomes.role_note: [A] = the partner both identified as more likely to use a white lie.

outcomes.verdict: [B] reaches for a small lie when the truth seems likely to create embarrassment, disappointment, or conflict. [A] may care less about the original detail than about being given a managed reality. [B] can restore trust by sharing the unedited version and repairing its practical effect. [A] can protect future honesty by keeping the first response proportional to what was actually revealed.
outcomes.actions_a: Hear the complete version, name the added impact of the lie, and keep the first response tied to this incident.
outcomes.actions_b: Give the unedited facts, repair the practical effect, and use the agreed honesty window next time.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Truth Before Comfort rule with disclosure window, full-version prompt, first response, privacy line, and repair step.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. A small truth gets a safer landing before it needs a disguise.
outcomes.role_note: [B] = the partner both identified as more likely to use a white lie.

outcomes.verdict: Both of you sometimes edit reality to keep the mood easy. That points to a couple culture that values harmony but may charge honesty an entry fee. Create a low-stakes reset phrase that allows either person to correct something within twenty-four hours. The correction still includes impact and repair, but it does not become evidence that every other statement is unreliable.
outcomes.actions_a: Use the reset phrase to correct one small omission and say what reaction you were trying to avoid.
outcomes.actions_b: Receive the correction, then name one truth you also softened instead of counterattacking.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Twenty-Four-Hour Truth Reset with phrase, eligible situations, full-fact step, response rule, and repair.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Honesty gets a return window before a tiny edit hardens into a trust problem.

outcomes.verdict: Each of you sees yourself as the more frequent white-liar, but the lies may serve different jobs. [A] may hide mistakes to preserve competence. [B] may soften feelings to preserve closeness. One honesty rule will miss that difference. [A] needs permission to be imperfect. [B] needs language for preferences that may disappoint without threatening the bond.
outcomes.actions_a: Name the image you protect and disclose one fact without polishing it.
outcomes.actions_b: Name the feeling you soften and state it as a preference rather than a rejection.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Two-Motive Honesty Map with protected image, hidden feeling, direct wording, receiving response, and repair.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Two kinds of self-protection get two routes into honest connection.

outcomes.verdict: Each of you thinks the other bends small truths more often, which can make ordinary inconsistencies feel like proof of a larger character issue. Review only recent, concrete examples. Separate privacy, incomplete information, forgotten details, and intentional misstatement. Then choose the one category that actually needs a new habit. Precision lowers the temperature while keeping accountability intact.
outcomes.actions_a: Bring one example from your own behavior and classify it honestly before naming your partner's.
outcomes.actions_b: Do the same, then choose one disclosure or response habit that addresses the shared category.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Small Truth Audit with examples, category, feared reaction, actual impact, new habit, and review.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Specific evidence replaces a global argument about who can be believed.

outcomes.verdict: [A] identifies one partner as the more frequent user of white lies while [B] sees the pattern as shared or situational. Treat the recurring topic as the pressure point and apply the reset rule to both. The person who edits the truth owes a prompt correction. The receiver owes a response that addresses the incident without making all future honesty feel dangerous.
outcomes.actions_a: Correct the recurring category within the reset window and repair any decision made from the inaccurate version.
outcomes.actions_b: Acknowledge the correction, state the trust impact, and keep the response proportional enough for future truth to arrive sooner.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Recurring Truth Pressure Plan with topic, reset phrase, deadline, decision repair, and receiving response.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. The familiar little lie loses the conditions that helped it keep returning.
outcomes.role_note: [A] = identified a specific more frequent white-liar; [B] = said the pattern is shared or situational.

cases.title: When One of You Needed Alone Time and It Got Read as Something Being Wrong
cases.subtitle: How much alone time do you need to feel like yourself?

questions.prompt: How much alone time do you need to feel like yourself?

options.label: Very little
A short reset now and then
Regular solo time
Long, protected stretches
A lot of independent space

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: How do you feel about the way alone time is handled now?

options.label: It works for me
Mostly okay, with a few hard moments
It regularly leaves me tense or disconnected
I need this pattern to change

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: What makes alone time easy to misread?

options.label: It is requested during tension
No return time is given
Affection drops at the same time
Past withdrawal lasted too long
The request sounds abrupt
The need was never explained

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: What would make space feel safer?

options.label: Name the purpose
Give a reconnect time
Offer one warm sentence first
Use a neutral signal
Protect recurring solo time
Check in after the reset

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: Want to tell the court a bit more about what happened? (optional)
questions.interactionRule: Private context is used only to personalize the selected deterministic branch.

outcomes.verdict: You need a similar amount of alone time and generally trust that space is a reset, not an exit. That shared reading protects both independence and closeness. Keep the meaning visible by naming when you are decompressing and when you will reconnect. Familiar solo time feels safe because it has a shape, not because either partner has stopped caring.
outcomes.actions_a: Name the solo activity that restores you and the signal you will use before stepping away.
outcomes.actions_b: Name the reconnect gesture that helps space end warmly rather than drift into distance.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save an Alone-Time Rhythm with purpose, signal, typical length, reconnect time, and warm return ritual.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Space works because both of you can see where it ends.

outcomes.verdict: [A] and [B] need similar space, but [A] is less content because alone time may arrive without a reassuring frame. [B] experiences a normal reset. [A] sees sudden distance and has to guess what it means. [B] can add one warm sentence and a return time. [A] can let the agreed window stay quiet without repeatedly checking it.
outcomes.actions_a: Name the reassurance and return time that would keep you from reading the pause as rejection.
outcomes.actions_b: Use that sentence before leaving and reconnect when promised, even if the conversation continues later.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Space Without Scare script with warm opener, purpose, return time, no-check window, and reconnect step.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. The same amount of space lands differently once it arrives with a clear return.
outcomes.role_note: [A] = less content with how alone time is currently handled; [B] = more content.

outcomes.verdict: You need roughly the same amount of solitude, yet both of you mishandle its timing. Space may be requested at the peak of conflict, sound like punishment, or continue without a return point. Create a neutral signal used before either person floods. Pair it with a set window and a scheduled return. A pause helps only when the issue is not abandoned inside it.
outcomes.actions_a: Choose the neutral signal and the maximum first pause that lets your body settle.
outcomes.actions_b: Choose the return question that restarts contact without relitigating the whole conflict immediately.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Pause and Return Protocol with signal, purpose, time window, contact limit, return question, and follow-up.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Alone time becomes a regulated pause instead of an unanswered disappearance.

outcomes.verdict: [A] needs more solo time because quiet is how [A] restores attention and emotional range. [B] needs less and feels connected through ongoing contact. You are content because amount does not have to match. Protect recurring solo blocks for [A] and dependable reconnect moments for [B]. The schedule keeps either need from looking like a verdict on the relationship.
outcomes.actions_a: Choose the recurring solo block that protects your energy and keep the reconnect promise attached to it.
outcomes.actions_b: Choose the reconnect moment that matters most and avoid filling the protected block with reassurance requests.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Solo and Reconnect Calendar with protected blocks, warm signal, return time, shared moment, and review.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Independence and contact receive separate appointments instead of competing for the same hour.
outcomes.role_note: [A] needs more alone time; [B] needs less.

outcomes.verdict: [A] needs more space and is dissatisfied because the current rhythm keeps requiring emotional availability past capacity. [B] needs less space and feels the contact level is fine, so [A]'s battery is being budgeted by the person who uses less solitude. [B] owes one protected block without pursuit. [A] owes a reliable return and visible affection afterward.
outcomes.actions_a: Request a defined block before depletion turns into coldness, and reconnect at the promised time.
outcomes.actions_b: Protect the block without follow-up messages and save the concern for the agreed return.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Lower-Battery Space Rule with early signal, protected length, contact exception, return time, and reconnect gesture.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. The partner who needs more quiet gets it before withdrawal becomes the only available boundary.
outcomes.role_note: [A] needs more alone time and is dissatisfied; [B] needs less and is content.

outcomes.verdict: [A] reads solitude as necessary maintenance. [B] reads extended quiet as a threat to connection. More spontaneous space increases [B]'s fear, while more pursuit makes [A] need even more distance. Break the loop with a two-week schedule: planned solo blocks, one warm departure line, no routine checking, and a fixed reconnect ritual. Review both restoration and security.
outcomes.actions_a: Use the planned blocks rather than disappearing only when overwhelmed, and record whether you returned more present.
outcomes.actions_b: Respect the no-check window and record whether the reliable reconnect reduced the fear of distance.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Two-Week Space Trial with blocks, departure line, exceptions, reconnect ritual, restoration score, and security score.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Space becomes predictable enough to restore one person without alarming the other.
outcomes.role_note: [A] needs more alone time; [B] needs less.

General feelings without specifics
Some context with one trusted friend
