Mostly okay, with a few hard moments
It regularly leaves me tense or disconnected
I need this pattern to change

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: What made the sharing feel exposed?

options.label: Intimate details
Screenshots or exact quotes
A one-sided conflict story
The friend knows both partners
The detail affected reputation
No consent was requested

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: What would create a fair line?

options.label: Share feelings, not private facts
Ask before exact details
Ban screenshots
Choose one neutral confidant
Update the friend after repair
Keep safety exceptions open

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: Want to tell the court a bit more about what happened? (optional)
questions.interactionRule: Private context is used only to personalize the selected deterministic branch.

outcomes.verdict: You draw the friend-sharing line in a similar place and generally trust each other to seek support without turning the relationship into group chat content. The shared strength is context control: friends can hear a feeling or support need without receiving intimate facts, screenshots, or a permanent one-sided portrait. Keep consent attached to details that belong to both people.
outcomes.actions_a: Name the kind of support you can seek without revealing [B]'s private information.
outcomes.actions_b: Name one detail category that always needs consent and one safety exception that remains available.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Friends and Privacy Guide with shareable feelings, protected details, consent topics, safety exceptions, and repair updates.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Support stays available without making the relationship public property.

outcomes.verdict: [A] and [B] prefer similar privacy, but [A] is less content because the rule may have been applied loosely in one real conversation. [B] may remember needing support. [A] remembers exact words, screenshots, or intimate facts leaving the relationship. Correct the specific disclosure, then separate emotional support from partner-owned details for future talks.
outcomes.actions_a: Name the detail that felt partner-owned and the correction you want made with the friend.
outcomes.actions_b: Give the correction, stop sharing that category, and use feeling-centered language when seeking support.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Disclosure Repair Note with exposed detail, audience, correction message, future support wording, and consent rule.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. The friend can support the feeling without keeping a file on the partner.
outcomes.role_note: [A] = less content with the current friend-sharing boundary; [B] = more content.

outcomes.verdict: You want similar privacy but both reach for friends while emotions are hot and judgment is narrow. Build three lanes. Green allows personal feelings and practical support. Yellow allows limited context without quotes or identifying detail. Red covers intimacy, trauma, health, screenshots, and information that could change a friend's view permanently. Safety remains outside the restriction.
outcomes.actions_a: Classify the topic you are most likely to overshare and choose the safer support language.
outcomes.actions_b: Classify a different sensitive topic and identify the neutral friend or professional route you can use.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Green, Yellow, Red Friend-Sharing Map with topics, allowed detail, audiences, consent, and safety exception.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Support gets lanes before an upset decides what leaves the relationship.

outcomes.verdict: [A] wants more privacy because friends often remember the painful version after the couple has repaired. [B] wants more room to talk because outside perspective prevents isolation. You are content because support and disclosure can be separated. [B] shares personal feelings and needs. Facts that expose [A], intimate material, screenshots, and unresolved accusations require consent or a professional setting.
outcomes.actions_a: Define which details belong partly to you and the kind of support language you can accept.
outcomes.actions_b: Keep friend conversations centered on your feelings and move partner-specific facts to a consented or professional space.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Support Without Exposure rule with allowed feelings, protected facts, trusted audiences, consent, and repair update.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. One partner keeps a support network without spending the other's privacy to access it.
outcomes.role_note: [A] wants more relationship privacy; [B] wants more freedom to seek friend support.

outcomes.verdict: [A] wants more privacy and feels exposed. [B] wants more sharing and feels the current support system works, so [B]'s relief is arriving with a reputational cost for [A]. [B] owes a new habit: share the emotion, not the evidence file. [A] owes a clear list of protected categories rather than demanding total silence outside the couple.
outcomes.actions_a: List the categories that need consent and the kinds of emotional support you can still welcome.
outcomes.actions_b: Choose a low-detail support format, correct the friend's incomplete picture, and stop forwarding exact private material.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Friend Support Firewall with protected categories, allowed feelings, chosen confidants, correction message, and safety exception.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Help remains reachable without turning private moments into social proof.
outcomes.role_note: [A] wants more privacy and is dissatisfied; [B] wants more sharing and is content.

outcomes.verdict: [A] fears friends will become a permanent jury for temporary relationship pain. [B] fears privacy will become isolation and remove needed perspective. Use a support ladder: first name the issue inside the couple, then use one neutral confidant or professional, and involve closer friends only for practical support or safety. Anyone who hears the rupture also receives the repair update.
outcomes.actions_a: Define the private first step and the details that stay protected at every rung.
outcomes.actions_b: Choose the neutral support person and commit to sharing the repair after the conflict changes.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Friend Support Ladder with couple check, neutral support, friend threshold, protected details, and repair update.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Privacy and support become stages instead of rival claims on the same story.
outcomes.role_note: [A] wants more relationship privacy; [B] wants more freedom to seek friend support.

cases.title: When One of You Felt Micromanaged Around Who They Spend Time With
cases.subtitle: How much say should a partner have over who the other spends time with?

questions.prompt: How much say should a partner have over who the other spends time with?

options.label: Very little beyond safety concerns
They can raise concerns, not decide
Some shared boundaries for loaded situations
A lot when trust is affected
Strong approval should matter for close or risky connections

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: How do you feel about the current balance between independence and input?

options.label: It works for me
Mostly okay, with a few hard moments
It regularly leaves me tense or disconnected
I need this pattern to change

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: What made the input feel like micromanaging?

options.label: Repeated questions
Pressure to cancel
Approval was expected
Every person became a concern
Plans required too much detail
A past issue was applied to everyone

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: What would protect both trust and choice?

options.label: Raise one behavior-based concern
Stop approval language
Share plans without seeking permission
Set a rule for loaded histories
Protect couple commitments
Review a specific friendship separately

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: Want to tell the court a bit more about what happened? (optional)
questions.interactionRule: Private context is used only to personalize the selected deterministic branch.

outcomes.verdict: You give partner input similar weight and generally preserve each person's social choices. The healthy part is that concern can be heard without becoming permission power. Keep feedback tied to observable behavior, loaded history, or broken couple commitments. Ordinary friendships should not have to pass a relationship interview every time plans are made.
outcomes.actions_a: Name the kind of concern you would want raised and the language that keeps your choice intact.
outcomes.actions_b: Name the plan information you can offer freely without turning it into an approval request.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Social Independence Agreement with concern threshold, plan context, loaded-history rule, protected couple time, and no-approval language.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Input remains caring because it never quietly becomes ownership.

outcomes.verdict: [A] and [B] give partner input similar weight, but [A] is less content because concern may arrive as repeated questioning, pressure, or an expectation to cancel. [B] may believe the final choice remains free while making every route except agreement exhausting. Replace repeated persuasion with one concern, one response, and a review only if new behavior appears.
outcomes.actions_a: Name the interaction that made choice feel costly and the boundary you want around repeated persuasion.
outcomes.actions_b: State one behavior-based concern once, hear the answer, and stop reopening it without new information.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a One-Concern Rule with behavior, concern statement, response, decision owner, new-information trigger, and review.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. A concern gets heard without wearing independence down through repetition.
outcomes.role_note: [A] = less content with the current balance of social independence and partner input; [B] = more content.

outcomes.verdict: You agree that neither partner should manage the other's social world, yet both of you slip into approval language when a person or plan creates anxiety. Separate notice, concern, and decision. Plans are shared as context. Concerns identify a behavior and impact. The person whose friendship it is makes the choice while remaining accountable for shared commitments and agreed high-risk boundaries.
outcomes.actions_a: Rewrite one approval-seeking plan message as clear context plus the couple commitment you will protect.
outcomes.actions_b: Rewrite one controlling concern as a behavior, impact, and request without deciding the friendship's future.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Notice, Concern, Decision guide with examples, decision owner, shared commitments, and high-risk exceptions.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Social choice stays personal while relationship impact remains discussable.

outcomes.verdict: [A] wants more partner input because certain friendships or settings feel connected to trust and shared safety. [B] wants more independence because social choice is part of identity and autonomy. You are content because the relationship can distinguish ordinary plans from loaded situations. Use stronger consultation only for romantic history, repeated disrespect, secrecy, or broken commitments.
outcomes.actions_a: Define the few conditions that make a social plan relationship-relevant and release ordinary choices from extra review.
outcomes.actions_b: Share context when those conditions appear and keep protecting the agreed couple commitments.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Loaded Situation Filter with triggers, ordinary freedom, consultation step, couple commitments, and review.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Most of the social world stays open, while the genuinely loaded corners receive more care.
outcomes.role_note: [A] wants more partner input; [B] wants more social independence.

outcomes.verdict: [A] wants more input and feels unprotected by the current freedom. [B] wants more independence and feels the balance is already fine, so [B] currently holds both the choice and the definition of acceptable impact. [B] owes proactive context in loaded situations. [A] owes a short, behavior-based concern instead of approval demands or repeated questioning.
outcomes.actions_a: State one observable concern, one requested protection, and then stop campaigning after the answer.
outcomes.actions_b: Offer context before loaded plans and protect the commitment most affected by your choice.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save an Independence With Accountability plan with loaded triggers, proactive context, one-concern limit, protected commitments, and review.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Freedom keeps its center while trust receives something more useful than a veto.
outcomes.role_note: [A] wants more input and is dissatisfied; [B] wants more independence and is content.

outcomes.verdict: [A] experiences unrestricted social choices as a recurring trust risk. [B] experiences partner input as shrinking an independent life. More control creates secrecy or resentment, while less context creates more alarm. Run a four-week trial with ordinary plans free, loaded plans disclosed early, one concern allowed, no forced cancellation, and protected couple time. Review trust and autonomy separately.
outcomes.actions_a: Use the single concern well and record whether proactive context lowered your need to manage the outcome.
outcomes.actions_b: Disclose loaded plans early and record whether freedom felt more secure when shared commitments stayed protected.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Four-Week Social Balance Trial with free zone, loaded triggers, context, concern limit, couple time, and two scores.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Independence and trust get tested as separate outcomes instead of being forced into one winner.
outcomes.role_note: [A] wants more partner input; [B] wants more social independence.

cases.title: When a Password, Location Share, or Account Access Became a Point of Tension
cases.subtitle: Who is more likely to treat digital access as proof of trust?

questions.prompt: Who is more likely to treat digital access as proof of trust?

options.label: Me, no contest
Probably me
Probably them
Definitely them
Honestly, both equally

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: What makes that answer feel true?

options.label: Access feels reassuring
A past breach raised the stakes
Convenience blurred consent
Removing access feels suspicious
The original reason expired
Privacy and secrecy got mixed together

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: Which access created tension?

options.label: Phone password
Live location
Social account
Email or cloud account
Banking or purchase account
Shared device login

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: What would make access consensual?

options.label: State the purpose
Limit the account or feature
Remove old access
Use a temporary end date
Create an emergency method
Review consent separately from trust

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: Want to tell the court a bit more about what happened? (optional)
questions.interactionRule: Private context is used only to personalize the selected deterministic branch.

outcomes.verdict: [A] is more likely to treat access as trust because a password or location dot offers immediate certainty. [B] may experience the same access as permanent observation or lost ownership. [A] needs reassurance that does not depend on open-ended visibility. [B] needs to offer a clear emergency or logistics route so removing access does not feel like withdrawing from the relationship.
outcomes.actions_a: Name the exact reassurance need and release any access that no longer serves that purpose.
outcomes.actions_b: Define the access you consent to, its purpose, and the emergency alternative for everything else.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Digital Access Register with feature, purpose, owner, consent status, end date, emergency route, and review.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Trust stops being measured by how many digital doors remain unlocked.
outcomes.role_note: [A] = the partner both identified as more likely to treat access as proof of trust.

outcomes.verdict: [B] reads shared passwords or location as visible commitment, while [A] may see ongoing access as more intimate than the original convenience required. Both of you recognize the tension. [B] can separate the real need from the access method. [A] can provide a limited logistics or safety option without agreeing to permanent observation.
outcomes.actions_a: State which access no longer feels consensual and offer the narrow alternative that still supports shared needs.
outcomes.actions_b: Accept the narrower route, remove unneeded access, and ask directly when reassurance is the actual need.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Digital Access Register with feature, purpose, owner, consent status, end date, emergency route, and review.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. A useful feature returns to being a tool instead of a relationship test.
outcomes.role_note: [B] = the partner both identified as more likely to treat access as proof of trust.

outcomes.verdict: Both of you may use digital access as shorthand for transparency, which can feel intimate until convenience becomes expectation. Audit every password, location share, and account connection. Keep only what has a current purpose and active consent. Emergency access can be secure without being routine access. Removing an expired permission should count as maintenance, not evidence of distance.
outcomes.actions_a: Review the access you hold and identify what you no longer need for its original purpose.
outcomes.actions_b: Review a different account or feature and design the emergency route that protects both privacy and practical safety.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Mutual Digital Access Audit with feature, purpose, current consent, removal task, emergency method, and quarterly review.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Your digital closeness gets cleaner because consent is allowed to stay current.

outcomes.verdict: Each of you sees yourself as more likely to equate access with trust, but the desired access may differ. [A] may care about location during plans. [B] may care about messages, accounts, or passwords. Those are not interchangeable. Evaluate purpose, intrusiveness, and duration separately. Each person releases one access that exceeds the need it was meant to serve.
outcomes.actions_a: Name your access request, the need behind it, and the less intrusive alternative you can accept.
outcomes.actions_b: Do the same for your different request and remove one permission whose purpose has expired.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Two-Need Access Review with feature, need, intrusiveness, alternative, duration, and removal date.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Two digital trust symbols get measured by the real jobs they are supposed to do.

outcomes.verdict: Each of you thinks the other relies more on access, which often happens when permissions accumulated without a clear agreement. Stop debating attitude and list the actual features. For each one, record who owns it, who can see what, why access exists, and when consent was last checked. The list will reveal whether the issue is safety, convenience, reassurance, or simple digital clutter.
outcomes.actions_a: Audit one feature you use and remove or narrow it if you cannot state a current purpose.
outcomes.actions_b: Audit a feature you provide and clarify the consent, emergency use, and review date.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Full Access Inventory with ownership, visibility, purpose, consent, emergency use, and expiration.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Vague suspicion turns into a finite set of permissions you can actually decide.

outcomes.verdict: [A] identifies one partner as more likely to use access as proof while [B] sees the behavior as shared or situation-specific. Start with the most intrusive recurring feature. The access-seeking partner states the underlying need and accepts a narrower method. The account owner gives a reliable alternative for genuine safety or logistics without surrendering unrelated digital space.
outcomes.actions_a: Replace the recurring access request with the least intrusive method that still meets the real need.
outcomes.actions_b: Set up that method reliably and revoke any broader permission that is no longer actively consented to.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Recurring Access Reset with feature, underlying need, narrower method, revoked permission, emergency route, and review.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. One familiar digital pressure point gets smaller, clearer, and consensual.
outcomes.role_note: [A] = identified a specific partner who relies more on digital access; [B] = said the pattern is shared or situational.

cases.title: When One of You Felt Their Word Wasn't Being Trusted
cases.subtitle: Who is more likely to feel their answer gets treated as incomplete?

questions.prompt: Who is more likely to feel their answer gets treated as incomplete?

options.label: Me, no contest
Probably me
Probably them
Definitely them
Honestly, both equally

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: What makes that answer feel true?

options.label: They are asked again in different ways
Past history follows current answers
They feel required to prove ordinary facts
Their tone is read as evidence
They have repaired but still feel on trial
The question has no clear finish line

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: What made the answer hard to trust?

options.label: A past inconsistency
Missing context
A change in behavior
The timing of disclosure
Different memories
Anxiety without new evidence

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: What would make trust fairer?

options.label: Ask one clear question
Name the evidence gap
Set a verification limit
Acknowledge kept commitments
Use a repair period
Stop reopening after the answer lands

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: Want to tell the court a bit more about what happened? (optional)
questions.interactionRule: Private context is used only to personalize the selected deterministic branch.

outcomes.verdict: [A] is more likely to feel disbelieved because one answer may be followed by new versions of the same question or demands for ordinary proof. [B] may be carrying a real history gap, but endless verification prevents any current answer from succeeding. [B] needs one clear question and a finish line. [A] needs consistent follow-through where past credibility was actually affected.
outcomes.actions_a: Answer the clear question once, provide the agreed relevant evidence, and keep the next commitment visible.
outcomes.actions_b: Name the exact evidence gap, stop changing the question after it is answered, and acknowledge kept follow-through.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Trust Question Protocol with concern, one clear question, relevant evidence, finish line, and follow-through review.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. A current answer finally gets a defined way to count.
outcomes.role_note: [A] = the partner both identified as more likely to feel their word is not trusted.

outcomes.verdict: [B] experiences repeated questioning as a message that ordinary words have lost all value. [A] may be trying to protect against an earlier inconsistency, but a trust repair cannot stay permanently unfinishable. [A] should identify the specific uncertainty and accept an agreed proof threshold. [B] should keep the commitments connected to that uncertainty rather than demanding trust detached from behavior.
outcomes.actions_a: Ask one precise question, state what would answer it, and acknowledge when that threshold is met.
outcomes.actions_b: Give the relevant answer and follow-through without treating every request for context as an attack.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Trust Question Protocol with concern, one clear question, relevant evidence, finish line, and follow-through review.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Trust becomes a path with markers instead of a test whose rules keep moving.
outcomes.role_note: [B] = the partner both identified as more likely to feel their word is not trusted.

outcomes.verdict: Both of you sometimes feel disbelieved, so the relationship may be using questions to regulate anxiety rather than gather missing facts. Before asking, name what new information is actually needed. After answering, summarize what is now settled and what remains uncertain. A question with no possible satisfying answer should be treated as an anxiety signal, not repeated as investigation.
outcomes.actions_a: Bring one recurring question and identify the exact new fact that would make it useful.
outcomes.actions_b: Bring a different question and define the sentence that marks it settled after a clear answer.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save an Answer Can Land agreement with useful-question test, evidence limit, settled statement, anxiety signal, and review.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Your words gain weight because questions are no longer allowed to multiply without new information.

outcomes.verdict: Each of you sees yourself as the more disbelieved partner, likely in different domains. [A] may feel questioned about plans or people. [B] may feel questioned about money, feelings, or follow-through. Map each domain to its history and current proof. Do not let one damaged lane remove credibility everywhere else. Trust can be specific while repair is still underway.
outcomes.actions_a: Name the domain where your word feels discounted and the behavior that already supports credibility there.
outcomes.actions_b: Name your different domain and the limited evidence standard you want both people to use.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Domain-by-Domain Trust Map with concern, history, current evidence, proof limit, and review date.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. One trust bruise stops spreading across every sentence in the relationship.

outcomes.verdict: Each of you thinks the other feels more disbelieved, which may mean distrust is communicated through tone, repeated checking, or quiet verification instead of direct words. Review three recent moments each. Record the question, answer, follow-up, and whether new evidence existed. The pattern will show where curiosity ended and reassurance-seeking took over.
outcomes.actions_a: Log one moment when you repeated a question without new evidence and name the fear driving it.
outcomes.actions_b: Log one moment when you withheld useful context and name what a complete first answer would have included.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Six-Moment Trust Log with question, answer, new evidence, repeated check, missing context, and future rule.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. The invisible trial becomes a visible pattern both of you can interrupt.

outcomes.verdict: [A] identifies one partner as more likely to feel disbelieved while [B] sees the experience as shared or situational. Focus on the recurring domain and keep the fair-question rule mutual. The questioned partner gives relevant context and dependable follow-through. The questioning partner asks once, accepts the agreed threshold, and stops reopening the issue without new evidence.
outcomes.actions_a: Give the complete answer for the recurring domain and follow through on the next visible commitment.
outcomes.actions_b: State the concern once, agree on the evidence threshold, and mark the answer settled when it is met.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Recurring Trust Lane Plan with domain, question, complete answer, evidence threshold, commitment, and settled marker.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. One repeated doubt gets a finish line without asking either person for blind faith.
outcomes.role_note: [A] = identified a specific partner who more often feels disbelieved; [B] = said the experience is shared or situational.

cases.title: When Being Vague About Plans Made the Other Feel Shut Out
cases.subtitle: How much plan detail should partners normally share?

questions.prompt: How much plan detail should partners normally share?

options.label: Only major changes
Basic who, what, and when
Enough detail to coordinate the day
Regular updates as plans develop
Most details so neither person feels out of the loop

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: How do you feel about the current level of plan sharing?

options.label: It works for me
Mostly okay, with a few hard moments
It regularly leaves me tense or disconnected
I need this pattern to change

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: What did the vagueness affect?

options.label: Shared scheduling
Safety or return time
An invitation or expectation
Trust around who was there
Ability to make separate plans
Feeling included in daily life

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: What update would be enough?

options.label: Share the basic plan
Give a return window
Update meaningful changes
Say when details are not settled
Add shared-impact plans to a calendar
Avoid making the other chase

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: Want to tell the court a bit more about what happened? (optional)
questions.interactionRule: Private context is used only to personalize the selected deterministic branch.

outcomes.verdict: You want a similar level of plan detail and generally feel included without needing a live itinerary. The working ingredient is shared-impact awareness: you know when a plan changes time, transport, safety, invitations, or the other's ability to organize the day. Keep sharing those facts early while allowing unsettled details to remain unsettled.
outcomes.actions_a: Name the plan detail that helps you coordinate without creating unnecessary reporting.
outcomes.actions_b: Name the kind of change that deserves a proactive update even when the rest of the plan stays private.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Plans That Affect Us guide with basic details, shared-impact triggers, update method, return window, and calendar rule.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Plan sharing stays light because both of you know which details actually belong to the couple.

outcomes.verdict: [A] and [B] want similar plan detail, but [A] is less content because basic information may arrive only after chasing. [B] sees the final plan as shared. [A] experiences the effort of extracting it. The repair is proactive timing, not more detail. [B] sends who, general place, time window, and meaningful changes before [A] has to ask.
outcomes.actions_a: Name the minimum four facts and when you need them to make your own plans.
outcomes.actions_b: Send those facts proactively and state clearly when a detail is still undecided.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a No-Chasing Plan Update with four facts, send time, unsettled-detail phrase, change trigger, and calendar step.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. The same information feels more inclusive when it arrives without an interview.
outcomes.role_note: [A] = less content with the current level or timing of plan sharing; [B] = more content.

outcomes.verdict: You agree on how much to share but both rely on vague phrases such as 'maybe later' or 'out for a bit,' leaving shared time impossible to plan. Use a compact update: activity, general location, time window, and whether the other person is included or free to plan separately. If details change, update only the shared-impact part.
outcomes.actions_a: Use the compact format for your next plan and explicitly release [B] to make separate plans when appropriate.
outcomes.actions_b: Do the same and add any shared-impact commitment to the calendar immediately.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Four-Part Plan Format with activity, location, time window, inclusion status, and change update.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Vagueness loses its grip because both people can organize real life from the information given.

outcomes.verdict: [A] wants more plan detail because context creates inclusion and makes shared logistics easier. [B] prefers looser updates because plans evolve and too much reporting feels restrictive. You are content because detail can follow impact. High-impact plans get the full compact update. Low-impact plans require only a return window or meaningful change.
outcomes.actions_a: Classify which plans need the full update and stop requesting extra detail for low-impact ones.
outcomes.actions_b: Share the full update for high-impact plans and send one line when low-impact timing changes.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save an Impact-Based Plan Guide with high-impact criteria, full update, low-impact update, change trigger, and review.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Information expands when the plan affects both people and stays light when it does not.
outcomes.role_note: [A] wants more plan detail; [B] wants less.

outcomes.verdict: [A] wants more detail and feels shut out. [B] wants less reporting and is comfortable with the current vagueness, so [B] controls both the plan and when it becomes visible. [B] owes proactive basics for shared-impact plans. [A] owes restraint after receiving them and does not turn coordination into a request for every social detail.
outcomes.actions_a: Request the minimum facts that affect your time, safety, or inclusion, then leave the rest alone.
outcomes.actions_b: Send those facts before being asked and update any change that alters [A]'s ability to plan.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Minimum Plan Visibility rule with shared-impact test, basic facts, send time, change trigger, and privacy line.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. One partner gains usable context without turning the other's plans into a live broadcast.
outcomes.role_note: [A] wants more detail and is dissatisfied; [B] wants less and is content.

outcomes.verdict: [A] reads vague plans as being kept outside the day's real story. [B] reads detailed questions as monitoring. More vagueness creates more pursuit, and more pursuit creates more vagueness. Try two weeks of impact-based updates: basics sent proactively, no follow-up for irrelevant detail, and a calendar entry for anything affecting shared time. Review inclusion and pressure separately.
outcomes.actions_a: Accept the compact update without expanding it into a full debrief, and record whether you felt more included.
outcomes.actions_b: Send the update before questions begin, and record whether proactive clarity reduced the sense of being monitored.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Two-Week Plan Clarity Trial with basic format, impact triggers, no-chasing rule, calendar entries, and two scores.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Clear basics interrupt the chase-and-retreat loop around everyday plans.

cases.title: When the Same Argument Keeps Coming Back in Different Forms

options.label: Me, no contest
Probably me
Probably them
Definitely them
Honestly, both equally

questions.prompt: What makes that answer feel true?

options.label: They recognize the emotional pattern
They remember the earlier version
They track the unmet request
They see the trigger beneath the topic
They name the cycle sooner
They want the root addressed before details

questions.prompt: What keeps changing on the surface?

options.label: Money
Time or attention

Family or friends
Tone and communication
Plans or priorities

Catch the opening trigger

outcomes.verdict: [A] is more likely to recognize the repeating argument because [A] hears the same unmet need beneath new topics. [B] may experience each incident as separate and focus on the current facts. The relationship needs both views: [A] names the root without dragging in every past example, and [B] chooses one present behavior that would test whether the root is finally being addressed.
outcomes.actions_a: Name the recurring need in one sentence and leave unrelated past scenes out of the next discussion.
outcomes.actions_b: Choose one visible behavior tied to that need and repeat it until the review date.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Repeat-Argument Root Card with surface topics, shared trigger, root need, one behavior, and review date.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. The next version of the fight meets a plan before it can put on a new outfit.
outcomes.role_note: [A] = the partner both identified as more likely to recognize the recurring argument.

outcomes.verdict: [B] more often spots the old argument hiding inside a new topic. [A] may keep litigating the current event because its details genuinely matter. [B] should name the shared pattern without flattening those details. [A] should agree to one root-level experiment instead of winning a single episode. A recurring fight changes when the repeated condition changes, not when one scene gets explained perfectly.
outcomes.actions_a: Acknowledge the recurring need and complete one behavior that addresses it in the current situation.
outcomes.actions_b: Describe the pattern without using it to dismiss the current facts, then set the review point.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Repeat-Argument Root Card with surface topics, shared trigger, root need, one behavior, and review date.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. The argument becomes one solvable pattern instead of a franchise with endless sequels.
outcomes.role_note: [B] = the partner both identified as more likely to recognize the recurring argument.

outcomes.verdict: Both of you know the fights are related, which means insight is no longer the missing piece. The gap is between naming the cycle and changing the conditions that feed it. Pick one early trigger and one tiny repeatable response. Track it for three weeks. A root issue becomes less powerful when daily behavior gives it fewer fresh examples.
outcomes.actions_a: Choose the first sign that the cycle is starting and the response you will use at that moment.
outcomes.actions_b: Choose the one recurring condition you will change and record every completed attempt.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Three-Week Cycle Interruption Log with trigger, root need, two responses, attempts, slips, and review.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Recognition finally graduates into a new pattern you can observe.

outcomes.verdict: Each of you sees yourself as the person who recognizes the repeat, but you may be naming different roots. [A] may hear lack of priority. [B] may hear lack of fairness, safety, or respect. Test each theory against the last three versions of the fight. The root that explains the most triggers and predicts a useful change deserves the first experiment.
outcomes.actions_a: List three versions of the argument and show how your proposed root connects to each one.
outcomes.actions_b: Test your different root against the same events and propose one behavior that would distinguish the two explanations.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Two-Root Test with past versions, proposed needs, predicted changes, trial behavior, and review.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Competing explanations become a real experiment instead of another version of the same fight.

outcomes.verdict: Each of you thinks the other notices the repeat first, which may mean both people can identify the cycle but hesitate to claim responsibility for interrupting it. Stop assigning the role of pattern expert. Each partner chooses one move they control at the earliest trigger. If both moves happen, the argument loses momentum before the familiar speeches begin.
outcomes.actions_a: Name the earliest trigger you personally can catch and the action you will take without prompting.
outcomes.actions_b: Choose a different interruption point and act there without waiting for [A] to name the cycle.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Two-Point Cycle Breaker with early trigger, each partner's move, reset phrase, and follow-up time.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. The pattern loses two automatic steps instead of gaining another analyst.

outcomes.verdict: [A] identifies one partner as the earlier pattern-spotter while [B] sees recognition as shared or situational. Use [A]'s early warning without making [A] the permanent relationship monitor. The other partner owns one concrete interruption. [A] states the root once, then steps back. The change is proven by repeated behavior, not by who names the cycle most accurately.
outcomes.actions_a: Use the agreed warning phrase once and avoid explaining the full history during the trigger.
outcomes.actions_b: Respond to the warning with the chosen behavior and record it before the cycle restarts.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Recurring Fight Early-Warning Plan with phrase, root need, interruption owner, behavior, and review.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. One partner can ring the alarm without being asked to fight the fire alone.
outcomes.role_note: [A] = identified a specific earlier pattern-spotter; [B] = said recognition is shared or situational.

[A] may hear another reset as empty because the earlier words already spent some credibility. [B] can rebuild through a smaller, observable action and early obstacle updates. [A] can leave room for honest renegotiation without treating any adjustment as abandonment.
outcomes.actions_a: Identify the concrete impact and the smallest completed action that would begin repairing it.
outcomes.actions_b: Choose that action, set the cue and date, and report trouble before the next missed attempt.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Promise-to-Practice Reset with original promise, smaller behavior, cue, first date, obstacle alert, and review.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Credibility returns in completed units instead of larger declarations.
outcomes.role_note: [B] = the partner both identified as more likely to promise change without a workable method.

Define the smallest repeatable behavior, the cue, and the weekly evidence. Pause every other improvement pledge until these two have real data.

outcomes.actions_b: Select a different promise and name the cue that will make it happen without reminders from [A].

outcomes.closing: Case softened. Fewer promises finally receive enough attention to become visible change.

Diagnose each promise separately before resetting it.
outcomes.actions_a: Name whether your promise lacks skill, cue, capacity, or honest willingness, then choose the matching reset.
outcomes.actions_b: Do the same for your promise and state clearly if the original commitment needs renegotiation instead of another deadline.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Two-Promise Diagnosis with barrier, chosen reset, first action, honest limit, and review date.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Two stalled changes stop receiving the same generic solution.

outcomes.verdict: Each of you thinks the other promises too easily, so the relationship may be full of half-accepted commitments. Audit what was actually requested, what was clearly agreed, and what was said only to end a tense moment. Remove false promises from the list. For the real commitments, assign one behavior, one owner, and one date.
outcomes.actions_a: Bring one promise you made and classify it honestly before listing anything your partner owes.
outcomes.actions_b: Do the same, then convert one genuine commitment into a scheduled behavior.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Promise Reality Audit with request, explicit agreement, owner, behavior, date, and renegotiation status.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. The relationship stops enforcing commitments that were never built clearly enough to hold.

outcomes.verdict: [A] identifies one partner as the more frequent unsupported promiser while [B] sees the habit as shared or situation-specific. Start with the longest-running promise and keep the reset rule mutual. The promiser chooses a small behavior and reports obstacles early. The affected partner requests evidence on a schedule instead of checking every day.
outcomes.actions_a: Complete the first small action and send the obstacle update before any missed date.
outcomes.actions_b: Choose the review schedule and stop turning unscheduled reminders into the main change system.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Longest-Promise Reset with behavior, cue, owner, first date, obstacle message, and review schedule.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. The oldest promise finally gets a method instead of another emotional renewal.
outcomes.role_note: [A] = identified a specific more frequent unsupported promiser; [B] = said the habit is shared or situational.

outcomes.verdict: You agree on what the silence has been protecting, but the emotional weight is now serious. The resentment is no longer only about the original issue. It also contains the loneliness of carrying it privately. Give the first conversation a narrow job: reveal the pattern, confirm the impact, and choose one repair. The full backlog can be paced across later talks.
outcomes.actions_a: Write the pattern in three sentences and choose the first repair request rather than unloading every example.
outcomes.actions_b: Reflect the impact without defending intent, then schedule the next conversation before ending this one.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Pacing the Backlog plan with pattern summary, first repair, listening rule, next topics, and two follow-up dates.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. The truth arrives in doses the relationship can actually use.

The resentment may look shared, but the protected fears need different responses. [A] needs safer disagreement. [B] needs evidence that honest impact will not be treated as cruelty.
outcomes.actions_a: Name the cost your silence was avoiding and make one direct request connected to it.
outcomes.actions_b: Name your different protected fear and state one truth without softening it into hints.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Two-Silence Resentment Map with protected fears, leak behaviors, direct truths, requests, and response needs.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Two quiet protections become two honest routes back into the relationship.
outcomes.role_note: [A] and [B] selected different reasons for keeping resentment quiet with manageable emotional weight.

outcomes.verdict: [A]'s resentment is guarding against one major threat, while [B]'s guards against another, and both now carry heavy weight. A single unstructured talk could turn two backlogs into mutual flooding. Use separate turns on separate days. Each speaker gets impact, need, and one repair. The listener summarizes before responding. If either conversation cannot stay regulated, use a counselor or mediator.
outcomes.actions_a: Prepare your one-page impact and request note for the first scheduled turn.
outcomes.actions_b: Prepare a separate note and practice summarizing [A]'s meaning before bringing your own case.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Two-Day Resentment Reset with speaking order, one-page notes, summary rule, repair requests, and support threshold.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Both backlogs receive real room without being forced through the same doorway at once.

cases.title: When an Issue Feels 'Resolved' but Keeps Resurfacing

options.label: Me, no contest
Probably me
Probably them
Definitely them
Honestly, both equally

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: What makes that answer feel true?

options.label: An apology feels like closure
Agreement gets mistaken for change
They want to move forward quickly
The remaining hurt is hard to see
A practical consequence still exists
No one defined what resolved meant

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: What keeps bringing it back?

options.label: The behavior repeated
The repair never happened
A trigger recreates the feeling
New information appeared
The agreement was vague
The hurt was acknowledged but not processed

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: What would make closure real?

options.label: Define the missing repair
Complete one practical step
Agree on a trigger response
Set a behavior review
Allow one paced follow-up
Name what will mark the issue closed

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: Want to tell the court a bit more about what happened? (optional)
questions.interactionRule: Private context is used only to personalize the selected deterministic branch.

outcomes.verdict: [A] is more likely to call the issue resolved because the conversation ended, an apology was accepted, or an agreement sounded clear. [B] keeps meeting the unfinished part in behavior, triggers, or practical consequences. [A] needs to ask what closure still requires. [B] needs to identify one missing repair rather than reopening every detail of the original event.
outcomes.actions_a: Name the closure assumption you made and complete the missing repair that [B] identifies.
outcomes.actions_b: Define the unfinished piece and the observable condition that would let this issue stay in the past.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Closure Checklist with acknowledged impact, missing repair, trigger response, behavior proof, and closed marker.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. The issue receives the part that the first ending skipped.
outcomes.role_note: [A] = the partner both identified as more likely to call the issue resolved too early.

outcomes.verdict: [B] moves toward closure when words have been exchanged, while [A] is still waiting for the practical or emotional evidence that those words changed anything. [A] does not need another full replay. [B] needs to finish the exact repair and respond differently at the known trigger. Closure becomes believable when the next similar moment has a different ending.
outcomes.actions_a: Name the missing evidence and the trigger where a new response would matter most.
outcomes.actions_b: Complete the repair and practice the new response before the next trigger arrives.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Closure Checklist with acknowledged impact, missing repair, trigger response, behavior proof, and closed marker.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. The next similar moment becomes the receipt for the original repair.
outcomes.role_note: [B] = the partner both identified as more likely to call the issue resolved too early.

outcomes.verdict: Both of you may declare resolution because the conversation was exhausting and ending it brought relief. Relief is not the same as completion. Define closure in three parts: the impact is understood, the practical repair is finished, and the recurring trigger has a new response. If one part is missing, name that part without reopening everything that is already settled.
outcomes.actions_a: Choose the closure part you tend to skip and state the action that completes it.
outcomes.actions_b: Choose a different part and define the behavior that will show it is holding.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Three-Part Closure Record with impact, repair, trigger response, evidence period, and final check date.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Resolution becomes a completed process instead of the moment both people run out of energy.

outcomes.verdict: Each of you sees yourself as the faster closer, which may mean different issues receive different premature endings. [A] may close practical matters before emotion catches up. [B] may process feelings but leave the changed behavior vague. Match the missing layer to the issue. One partner finishes the action. The other names the emotional marker that will make the action register as repair.
outcomes.actions_a: Identify the practical step you have left unfinished and schedule it.
outcomes.actions_b: Identify the emotional acknowledgment or trigger response you need and state it without adding unrelated history.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Practical and Emotional Closure Pair with missing action, acknowledgment, trigger, owner, and confirmation date.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Two incomplete kinds of closure finally meet in the same repair.

outcomes.verdict: Each of you thinks the other closes issues too quickly, so both may be carrying different files marked unfinished. List only the three issues that still affect current behavior. For each, name what is already complete and the one missing element. Close what can be closed, schedule what needs action, and retire items that no longer have a current impact.
outcomes.actions_a: Bring one issue and clearly separate the completed repair from the single missing piece.
outcomes.actions_b: Do the same before challenging [A]'s list, then agree which item gets handled first.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Three-Issue Closure Board with completed parts, missing part, current impact, owner, and close date.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. The backlog gets smaller because finished work is allowed to remain finished.

outcomes.verdict: [A] identifies one partner as the faster closer while [B] sees the tendency as shared or situational. Use the recurring issue as the test case and make the closure rule mutual. The faster closer asks what remains. The other partner identifies one specific missing repair and agrees to a final marker after it is completed.
outcomes.actions_a: Ask the closure question and finish the named repair without arguing that the first conversation should have been enough.
outcomes.actions_b: Limit the request to the actual missing piece and name the date or evidence that will mark completion.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Recurring Issue Closure Test with remaining piece, repair action, owner, evidence, and closed date.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = identified a specific faster closer; [B] = said the tendency is shared or situational.

outcomes.actions_b: Name a different contribution from [A] and the sign that would trigger a fairness check.

outcomes.verdict: [A] and [B] track fairness at a similar level, but [A] is less content because one category may be repeatedly excluded from the count. [B] sees overall balance. [A] sees planning, emotional labor, recovery time, or social compromise disappearing from the ledger. Add the missing lane, then reset one responsibility rather than debating the entire relationship total.
outcomes.actions_a: Name the invisible lane and the specific load that needs to move or be recognized.
outcomes.actions_b: Take one full task or protection in that lane and include it in the next fairness check.

outcomes.closing: Case softened. The score loosens once the work that created it becomes visible.

outcomes.verdict: You keep a similar mental tally and both dislike it because fairness is being checked only after depletion. Build a monthly review by lane: home, money, emotional support, social compromise, and rest. Do not force equal numbers. Ask whether each person has enough support and enough recovery. Unequal seasons can feel fair when they are visible, chosen, and time-limited.
outcomes.actions_a: Choose the lane where you are near capacity and request one specific transfer before resentment grows.
outcomes.actions_b: Choose a different lane and name the support or acknowledgment that would make its imbalance sustainable.

outcomes.closing: Case softened. Fairness becomes an early conversation instead of a secret arithmetic exercise.

outcomes.verdict: [A] tracks contributions more because uneven effort is easier for [A] to notice or has lasted longer. [B] tracks less and may trust the relationship's overall balance. You are content because [A]'s pattern awareness can inform one lane without turning every loving act into debt. Review the high-friction category monthly and leave ordinary generosity unpriced.
outcomes.actions_a: Bring one recurring imbalance with concrete examples and limit the review to that lane.
outcomes.actions_b: Take ownership of one measurable part of the lane and acknowledge the contributions you had not noticed.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a One-Lane Fairness Review with examples, load, new ownership, appreciation, and next check.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Useful pattern awareness gets a job without becoming the relationship's full accounting system.
outcomes.role_note: [A] keeps more score; [B] keeps less.

outcomes.verdict: [A] keeps more score and is dissatisfied because repeated imbalance has made memory serve as the unpaid accountant. [B] tracks less and feels the relationship is broadly fair, so the invisible benefit lands mostly on [B]. [B] owes one full ownership transfer. [A] owes a defined review period and agrees not to invoice unrelated acts of care.
outcomes.actions_a: Choose the lane with the strongest evidence, request a full transfer, and set the date when the tally can reset.

outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Fairness Debt Paydown with lane, full owner, trial length, success standard, excluded topics, and reset date.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. One concrete habit pays down the tally better than arguing about whether a tally should exist.
outcomes.role_note: [A] keeps more score and is dissatisfied; [B] keeps less and is content.

outcomes.verdict: [A] tracks nearly every imbalance because fairness no longer feels self-correcting. [B] resists counting because love measured transaction by transaction feels cold and impossible. Stop trying to merge those instincts. Use a recurring ritual: monthly lane review, one temporary rebalance, and explicit appreciation. Between reviews, neither person brings up unrelated historical credits during a new request.
outcomes.actions_a: Prepare the two lanes with the strongest current impact and retire old examples after the review records them.
outcomes.actions_b: Prepare the contributions you feel are missed and accept one concrete rebalance where the evidence is clear.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Monthly Score Reset with lanes, current impact, rebalance, appreciation, retired examples, and next date.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Fairness gets a regular home, so the tally does not need to follow every interaction.
outcomes.role_note: [A] keeps more score; [B] keeps less.

A current boundary
Confidence in our shared story

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: What would help now?

options.label: Hear the full impact
Correct the shared story
Answer one unanswered question
Make a present-day repair
Create a trigger response
Choose a closing ritual

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: Want to tell the court a bit more about what happened? (optional)
questions.interactionRule: Private context is used only to personalize the selected deterministic branch.

outcomes.verdict: You agree on why the old moment still matters, and its current weight is manageable enough for a focused repair. The goal is not to put the early relationship on trial with today's knowledge. It is to update the shared story with the impact that was missing then. One honest acknowledgment and one present-day action may give the memory a different ending.
outcomes.actions_a: Describe what the early event taught you to expect and the present evidence you need now.
outcomes.actions_b: Acknowledge that lesson without defending your younger self, then complete one current repair.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save an Early Chapter Update with event, learned meaning, missing acknowledgment, present repair, and closing ritual.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. The past stays part of the story without continuing to write every new chapter.

outcomes.verdict: You agree on the issue's meaning, but it still carries heavy emotional weight because time passed without the right repair. That delay can make the hurt feel woven into the relationship's origin story. Pace the conversation. First confirm impact, then answer one unanswered question, then choose one present behavior. Closure does not require reconstructing every detail from years ago.
outcomes.actions_a: Write the one meaning and one unanswered question that matter most now.
outcomes.actions_b: Answer what you can honestly, acknowledge what you cannot reconstruct, and choose the present behavior that addresses the lasting impact.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Three-Step Early Repair with meaning, question, honest answer, present behavior, and follow-up date.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. A late repair can still be real when it speaks directly to what lasted.

outcomes.verdict: [A] is bothered because the early moment affected safety or self-worth. [B] sees its continuing relevance through a different route, such as missing acknowledgment, new information, or a pattern that still appears. Those are not competing accounts. One concerns the wound. The other concerns why it stayed open. Address both in that order.
outcomes.actions_a: Name the lasting personal impact and the acknowledgment that would meet it.
outcomes.actions_b: Name the mechanism that kept the issue alive and the current behavior you will change.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Wound and Why-It-Stayed Map with impacts, missing acknowledgment, recurring mechanism, present repair, and review.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. The original pain and the reason it lingered finally receive separate answers.
outcomes.role_note: [A] and [B] chose different reasons the early issue still matters with manageable emotional weight.

outcomes.verdict: [A] carries one heavy meaning from the early relationship, while [B] carries another, and both influence current safety. A single debate over the definitive past will deepen the split. Use two witness statements: each person records what happened as remembered, what it meant, and what is needed now. Read for impact, not factual victory, then agree on present protections.
outcomes.actions_a: Write your one-page account with memory, meaning, current trigger, and requested protection.
outcomes.actions_b: Write a separate account and underline the part of [A]'s meaning you can validate even where memories differ.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Two-Account Early Story with memories, meanings, current triggers, mutual validations, and present protections.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Different memories stop blocking a shared decision about how you care for the impact now.
outcomes.role_note: [A] and [B] chose different reasons the early issue still matters with high emotional weight.

cases.title: When You Avoid a Topic Because It Always Turns Into a Fight
cases.subtitle: What makes this topic feel too risky to open?

Someone shuts down
Old examples take over
The topic threatens a major decision
Neither of us feels understood

options.label: It matters, but it is manageable
It carries real emotional weight
It affects how safe or close I feel
It needs attention before we can move on
