questions.prompt: What happens when it stays avoided?

options.label: Plans remain stuck
Resentment grows
Affection gets cautious
One person acts alone
Anxiety fills in the blanks
Smaller fights carry the topic indirectly

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: What would create a gentler entry?

options.label: Write the question first
Limit the first talk to twenty minutes
Use separate speaking turns
Ban historical pile-ons
Agree on a pause signal
Bring in a neutral third party

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: Want to tell the court a bit more about what happened? (optional)
questions.interactionRule: Private context is used only to personalize the selected deterministic branch.

outcomes.verdict: You agree on what makes the topic combustible, and the emotional weight is still manageable. That means you can redesign the doorway before the subject becomes more loaded. Give the first talk one narrow question, twenty minutes, and no decision requirement. Success means both positions are accurately understood, not that the issue is solved in one sitting.
outcomes.actions_a: Write the narrow question and the three points you need understood without arguing for the outcome.
outcomes.actions_b: Choose the listening summary and pause signal that will keep the first talk inside its limited job.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Gentle Entry Agenda with one question, time limit, speaking turns, pause signal, and next date.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. The topic gets a smaller doorway instead of waiting for a bigger explosion.

outcomes.verdict: You share the same fear about opening the topic, but it now carries enough weight that avoidance is making decisions by default. Use a staged conversation. Session one maps positions and stakes. Session two lists workable options. Session three chooses or seeks help. Separating understanding from deciding keeps urgency from forcing both jobs into one overheated hour.
outcomes.actions_a: Prepare your position, underlying need, and feared consequence for the mapping session.
outcomes.actions_b: Prepare the same three items and commit not to negotiate until both maps are accurate.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Three-Session Topic Plan with mapping date, needs, options date, decision date, pause rules, and support threshold.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. The hard topic gets stages, so neither person has to survive the whole climb at once.

outcomes.verdict: [A] avoids the topic because the interaction becomes emotionally unsafe or exhausting. [B] avoids it because the content threatens a major plan, identity, or decision. One needs a safer process. The other needs manageable stakes. Start with process rules, then discuss only the smallest decision connected to the topic. Do not demand total resolution as the price of beginning.
outcomes.actions_a: Name the interaction rule you need to stay present and the signal that should pause the talk.
outcomes.actions_b: Name the smallest decision that cannot remain avoided and remove every larger decision from the first agenda.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Safe Process, Small Decision plan with rules, pause signal, first decision, excluded issues, and follow-up.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Emotional safety and practical movement get separate jobs in the same careful start.
outcomes.role_note: [A] and [B] chose different reasons for avoiding the topic with manageable emotional weight.

outcomes.verdict: [A] fears the conversation process because escalation or shutdown has caused damage. [B] fears the topic's outcome because it could alter the future. Both risks are substantial. Do not attempt this as an unscheduled home conversation. Set a date, exchange written summaries beforehand, use timed turns, and preselect a counselor or mediator if the first meeting crosses the pause threshold.
outcomes.actions_a: Write your impact and process needs in one page and send it before the scheduled talk.
outcomes.actions_b: Write your stakes and non-final questions separately, then book the backup support before the meeting begins.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a High-Stakes Topic Packet with two summaries, meeting date, timed turns, pause threshold, and backup support.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. The topic receives enough structure that courage is not asked to do all the work.
outcomes.role_note: [A] and [B] chose different reasons for avoiding the topic with high emotional weight.

cases.title: When One of You Feels Like Nothing Actually Changes After You Talk
cases.subtitle: How much visible change usually follows your serious conversations?

questions.prompt: How much visible change usually follows your serious conversations?

options.label: A lot changes and holds
Some change usually sticks
Change starts but fades
Very little changes
The same pattern returns almost immediately

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: How do you feel about the way talk turns into action now?

options.label: It works for me
Mostly okay, with a few hard moments
It regularly leaves me tense or disconnected
I need this pattern to change

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: Where does the handoff fail?

options.label: No action was defined
No one owned the step
The step was too big
No reminder or cue existed
Progress was not noticed
The plan was never reviewed

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: What would make change visible?

options.label: Choose one behavior
Assign an owner
Set the first date
Track attempts, not perfection
Schedule a review
Renegotiate before abandoning

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: Want to tell the court a bit more about what happened? (optional)
questions.interactionRule: Private context is used only to personalize the selected deterministic branch.

outcomes.verdict: You see a similar amount of follow-through and generally trust that serious talks affect daily behavior. The reason this works is likely modest, visible change rather than perfect transformation. Protect it by ending each important conversation with one owner, one first action, and one review date. That keeps emotional insight connected to ordinary life after the intensity fades.
outcomes.actions_a: Name the behavior you changed most successfully and the cue that helped it stick.
outcomes.actions_b: Name the way you noticed or acknowledged [A]'s effort so progress did not become invisible.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Talk-to-Action Closeout with decision, owner, first step, cue, evidence, and review date.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Your conversations keep earning trust because they leave footprints afterward.

outcomes.verdict: [A] and [B] see similar follow-through, but [A] is less content because the change may not address the part that mattered most. [B] sees effort. [A] sees the original impact continuing. Translate the conversation into the exact behavior that would change [A]'s experience, then credit attempts without confusing motion with the right result.
outcomes.actions_a: Define the behavior that would make the original impact measurably different.
outcomes.actions_b: Redirect your effort toward that behavior and ask for feedback at the scheduled review, not every day.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save an Effort-to-Impact Check with original impact, target behavior, owner, attempts, evidence, and review.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Work starts landing where the hurt actually lives.
outcomes.role_note: [A] = less content with how conversation turns into change; [B] = more content.

outcomes.verdict: You agree that conversations create insight but not enough durable change. The missing bridge is operational: no behavior, owner, cue, or review survives the talk. Choose only one change per conversation. Put the first attempt on the calendar and review attempts after two weeks. If the step repeatedly fails, shrink or renegotiate it instead of restarting the same speech.
outcomes.actions_a: Choose one action you personally own and schedule the first attempt before the conversation ends.
outcomes.actions_b: Choose the cue and the evidence you will record without becoming [A]'s reminder system.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a One-Change Follow-Through Card with action, owner, cue, first date, attempt log, and review.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Insight gets a calendar entry before it evaporates into good intentions.

outcomes.verdict: [A] sees little change because the recurring impact remains visible. [B] sees more change because effort, intention, or partial improvement is visible from inside the attempt. You are content because both measures can share one dashboard. Track attempts and outcome separately. [B]'s effort deserves recognition, while [A]'s experience decides whether the chosen behavior is effective.
outcomes.actions_a: Define the outcome signal that would show the pattern is genuinely changing for you.
outcomes.actions_b: Track your attempts honestly and adjust the method if effort rises while the outcome stays flat.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save an Attempt and Outcome Tracker with behavior, effort count, impact signal, adjustment rule, and review date.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Effort can be honored without asking impact to pretend it has changed.
outcomes.role_note: [A] sees less change after talks; [B] sees more.

outcomes.verdict: [A] sees little change and is discouraged. [B] sees meaningful effort and feels the current process is acceptable. The person doing the effort is grading the outcome, while the person living with the impact has no final say. [B] owes one behavior measured by [A]'s experience. [A] owes a specific success signal and recognition of real attempts.
outcomes.actions_a: Choose one observable success signal and acknowledge attempts that genuinely move toward it.
outcomes.actions_b: Change the behavior tied to that signal and stop substituting unrelated effort for the requested impact.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save an Impact-Graded Change Plan with behavior, owner, success signal, attempt log, adjustment, and review.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. The person affected helps define whether the repair is working, without erasing the work behind it.
outcomes.role_note: [A] sees less change and is dissatisfied; [B] sees more change and is content.

outcomes.verdict: [A] believes talk has become a substitute for change. [B] believes change is happening but never receives credit or enough time to hold. Stop repeating the full conversation. Choose a thirty-day trial with one behavior, weekly evidence, a midmonth adjustment, and no new promises in that lane. At the end, review both completion and lived impact.
outcomes.actions_a: Define the behavior and impact measure, then pause new debate until the midmonth check unless harm is continuing.
outcomes.actions_b: Complete the weekly actions, record them without prompting, and propose an adjustment if the impact measure does not move.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Thirty-Day Change Trial with behavior, weekly evidence, impact measure, midpoint, adjustment, and final review.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. The relationship gets data from daily life instead of another beautifully explained intention.
outcomes.role_note: [A] sees less change after talks; [B] sees more.

cases.title: When a Habit One of You Asked to Change Hasn't Budged
cases.subtitle: Who is more likely to underestimate what it takes to change the habit?

questions.prompt: Who is more likely to underestimate what it takes to change the habit?

options.label: Me, no contest
Probably me
Probably them
Definitely them
Honestly, both equally

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: What makes that answer feel true?

options.label: The habit runs automatically
The request felt optional
The replacement behavior was unclear
The cue happens under stress
Progress was measured too broadly
The habit provides a hidden benefit

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: What keeps the habit in place?

options.label: Convenience
Stress relief
Environment or routine
A missing skill
Low personal buy-in
The request targets the symptom

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: What would make movement realistic?

options.label: Identify the cue
Choose a replacement behavior
Change the environment
Shrink the first goal
Track frequency
Set a renegotiation date

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: Want to tell the court a bit more about what happened? (optional)
questions.interactionRule: Private context is used only to personalize the selected deterministic branch.

outcomes.verdict: [A] is more likely to underestimate the habit because wanting it gone feels like the main requirement. [B] keeps experiencing the unchanged impact. [A] needs to map the cue, reward, and replacement instead of renewing motivation. [B] needs to request a measurable reduction or substitute behavior, not a personality transformation. A habit moves when its job is replaced.
outcomes.actions_a: Identify the cue and hidden payoff, then practice one replacement behavior at the next three occurrences.
outcomes.actions_b: Define the impact and the measurable change that would count as movement during the trial.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Habit Replacement Plan with cue, payoff, substitute, trial count, impact measure, and review.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. The habit finally meets a replacement instead of another request to disappear.
outcomes.role_note: [A] = the partner both identified as more likely to underestimate the work of changing the habit.

outcomes.verdict: [B] treats the habit as something intention should fix, while [A] lives with its repeated effect. The missing ingredient may be environment, skill, or personal buy-in rather than caring. [B] should identify the habit's cue and make the replacement easier than the old response. [A] should measure the agreed change without monitoring every imperfect attempt.
outcomes.actions_a: State the specific impact and the frequency reduction or replacement you need to see.
outcomes.actions_b: Change the cue environment, rehearse the substitute, and record attempts without waiting for reminders.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Habit Replacement Plan with cue, payoff, substitute, trial count, impact measure, and review.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Care becomes visible through design and repetition, not another promise to remember.
outcomes.role_note: [B] = the partner both identified as more likely to underestimate the work of changing the habit.

outcomes.verdict: Both of you underestimate habits, so requests may sound clear while the behavior remains supported by the same cues, convenience, and rewards. Pick one habit each. Remove one environmental trigger, add one replacement, and count attempts for two weeks. Do not use perfection as the measure. Look for fewer occurrences, faster recovery, or less impact.
outcomes.actions_a: Choose your habit, alter one cue, and record every use of the replacement.
outcomes.actions_b: Choose a different habit and define the recovery move for moments when the old response happens.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Two-Habit Experiment with cues, replacements, environment edits, attempt counts, recovery moves, and review.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. The habits lose part of the system that kept making them easy.

outcomes.verdict: Each of you sees yourself as the person underestimating change, but the habits may be held by different forces. [A]'s habit may be automatic and environmental. [B]'s may provide emotional relief or reflect weak buy-in. A reminder can help the first and annoy the second. Diagnose the job each habit performs before deciding how to change it.
outcomes.actions_a: Name what your habit gives you and choose a replacement that serves the same need with less relationship cost.
outcomes.actions_b: Name the different force holding your habit and make the matching environmental or commitment change.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Two-Habit Job Map with cue, benefit, relationship cost, replacement, support type, and review.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Two stubborn habits receive two explanations that can actually produce movement.

outcomes.verdict: Each of you thinks the other underestimates habits more, which can turn reminders into a second unwanted habit. Stop supervising each other for two weeks. Each person owns one target, chooses the cue and replacement, and records the attempts privately. At review, share data and impact. Ownership reveals whether the barrier is method, capacity, or willingness.
outcomes.actions_a: Choose your target and run the replacement without asking [B] to remind or manage you.
outcomes.actions_b: Choose a different target and track the impact on [A] as well as your attempt count.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a No-Reminder Habit Trial with targets, cues, replacements, private logs, impact notes, and review date.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Change ownership moves back to the person whose behavior can actually create it.

outcomes.verdict: [A] identifies one partner as the likelier underestimator while [B] sees the struggle as shared or situation-specific. Begin with the habit causing the clearest current impact and keep the method available to both. The habit owner runs the cue-and-replacement plan. The affected partner gives one scheduled impact update instead of constant correction.
outcomes.actions_a: Run the replacement at the next five triggers and record what made each attempt easier or harder.
outcomes.actions_b: Give one midpoint impact update and keep unscheduled reminders out unless the behavior creates immediate harm.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Five-Trigger Habit Reset with cue, substitute, attempts, midpoint impact, adjustment, and review.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. One stuck habit gets a real test without making either partner the other's full-time coach.
outcomes.role_note: [A] = identified a specific partner who underestimates the habit; [B] = said the struggle is shared or situational.

cases.title: When One of You Is Still Upset About Something the Other Thought Was Over
cases.subtitle: How much emotional charge does the old issue still carry?

questions.prompt: How much emotional charge does the old issue still carry?

options.label: Almost none
A little when reminded
It still affects certain moments
It regularly feels active
It feels as painful as when it happened

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: How do you feel about the repair and closure so far?

options.label: It works for me
Mostly okay, with a few hard moments
It regularly leaves me tense or disconnected
I need this pattern to change

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: What keeps the upset active?

options.label: The impact was minimized
The behavior repeated
The apology missed the point
A practical repair is unfinished
A trigger was never addressed
Pressure to move on came too soon

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: What would help it settle?

options.label: Name the remaining impact
Finish one repair
Respond differently to the trigger
Set a final follow-up
Acknowledge progress
Use outside support if it stays stuck

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: Want to tell the court a bit more about what happened? (optional)
questions.interactionRule: Private context is used only to personalize the selected deterministic branch.

outcomes.verdict: You read the remaining upset similarly and generally feel the issue is moving toward closure. The helpful part is that a trigger can still sting without erasing the repair already made. Keep distinguishing a memory response from a new offense. When it surfaces, name the trigger, use the agreed reassurance, and notice what is different now.
outcomes.actions_a: Name the trigger and the reassurance that helps you return to the present.
outcomes.actions_b: Offer that reassurance and point to one current behavior that shows the repair is holding.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Trigger-to-Present Note with trigger, remaining feeling, reassurance, current evidence, and close marker.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. The memory can echo without becoming the relationship's current reality again.

outcomes.verdict: [A] and [B] see a similar amount of lingering upset, but [A] is less content because the repair may have been recognized intellectually without landing emotionally. [B] sees an issue discussed and addressed. [A] still meets an unfinished impact at specific triggers. Complete the missing response there rather than replaying the entire original argument.
outcomes.actions_a: Name the trigger and the exact acknowledgment or behavior that is still missing.
outcomes.actions_b: Use that response at the next trigger and avoid insisting that the earlier conversation should have settled it.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Lingering Hurt Trigger Plan with trigger, missing response, repair owner, current evidence, and review date.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. One unfinished emotional step gets completed without reopening every settled detail.
outcomes.role_note: [A] = less content with the current repair; [B] = more content.

outcomes.verdict: You agree the issue still carries some charge and both dislike how easily it returns. The original event may be settled while the trigger response is not. Write a short protocol: name the old feeling, confirm whether anything new happened, offer one reassurance, and return to the present plan. If a new behavior did occur, treat that separately instead of folding it into old pain.
outcomes.actions_a: Practice naming 'old feeling, no new event' when that is accurate and request the chosen reassurance.
outcomes.actions_b: Give the reassurance without defensiveness, then ask whether any current behavior needs a separate conversation.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save an Old Hurt Check with trigger, new-event question, reassurance, current issue lane, and follow-up threshold.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Old pain gets care without automatically becoming new evidence.

outcomes.verdict: [A] still carries substantial hurt because the event changed safety, self-image, or trust. [B] experiences it as mostly complete and wants the repair to count. You are content because recovery speed can differ. [A] names specific trigger needs. [B] offers consistent present evidence. Neither person uses the difference to erase pain or declare repair meaningless.
outcomes.actions_a: Choose the two triggers that need support and state the response that helps without requiring a full replay.
outcomes.actions_b: Provide the response consistently and keep one visible repair behavior steady through the review period.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Different-Speed Healing Plan with triggers, responses, current evidence, review period, and closure signs.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. One partner's slower healing and the other's real repair can both remain true.
outcomes.role_note: [A] remains more upset; [B] experiences more closure.

outcomes.verdict: [A] remains deeply upset and feels pressure to be finished. [B] feels the issue is over and is comfortable with the current repair. [B]'s closure cannot set [A]'s emotional deadline, but [A]'s pain also needs a defined path rather than endless reopening. [B] owes one missing repair. [A] owes specific closure markers and a paced review.
outcomes.actions_a: Name the one repair still needed and the signs that would show healing is moving, even if not complete.
outcomes.actions_b: Complete that repair and stop using elapsed time as proof that the impact should be gone.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Healing Without Deadline plan with missing repair, trigger support, progress signs, review dates, and outside-help threshold.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Healing gets time, structure, and evidence instead of pressure or permanent limbo.
outcomes.role_note: [A] remains more upset and is dissatisfied; [B] experiences more closure and is content.

outcomes.verdict: [A] feels the hurt is still active. [B] feels trapped in an issue that never receives a final ending. Repeating spontaneous discussions reinforces both fears. Set three paced sessions: impact and acknowledgment, current repair evidence, then closure conditions. If the sessions cannot move beyond factual combat, use a neutral professional for the process rather than adding more home arguments.
outcomes.actions_a: Prepare the remaining impact and one present need for the first session without adding every historical example.
outcomes.actions_b: Prepare the repair evidence and one part you can acknowledge more fully before asking for closure.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Three-Session Hurt Completion Plan with agendas, dates, evidence, closure conditions, and support threshold.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. The hurt receives a route forward, and closure receives a route that does not require denial.
outcomes.role_note: [A] remains more upset; [B] experiences more closure.

cases.title: When You Keep Having Almost the Same Fight About Money, Time, or Space

Probably me
Probably them
Definitely them
Honestly, both equally

questions.prompt: What makes that answer feel true?

options.label: The urgent number takes over
The shared rule was never defined
Exceptions keep becoming defaults
Capacity changes without an update
The topic represents respect or freedom
Each fight starts after a decision is already made

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: Which resource keeps triggering the fight?

options.label: Shared money
Personal spending
Time together
Personal time
Home space
Time with family or friends

Protect recurring time

outcomes.verdict: [A] is more likely to debate the latest dollars, hours, or square feet because the immediate decision feels concrete. [B] sees a policy gap that keeps producing new incidents. [A] needs to help define the standing rule instead of negotiating every exception from zero. [B] needs a rule flexible enough for changing capacity, not a hidden preference presented as universal fairness.
outcomes.actions_a: Turn the current dispute into a threshold, notice period, or decision-right rule you can follow next time.
outcomes.actions_b: State the underlying fairness need and include one exception for real capacity changes.

outcomes.closing: Case softened. The next resource decision meets a rule before it becomes another familiar fight.
outcomes.role_note: [A] = the partner both identified as more likely to focus on the immediate amount.

outcomes.verdict: [B] keeps returning to the current amount while [A] experiences a repeated structure underneath it: unclear limits, missing notice, or unequal decision power. [B] can protect the current need by helping build a durable rule. [A] can make that rule measurable and allow a review when money, time, or space genuinely changes.
outcomes.actions_a: Name the recurring rule you need and the measurable threshold that would make it usable.
outcomes.actions_b: Apply the threshold to the current dispute and propose the exception process for unusual weeks or expenses.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Recurring Resource Rule with topic, threshold, decision owner, notice period, exceptions, and monthly review.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. One repeat fight becomes a policy the couple can improve instead of relive.
outcomes.role_note: [B] = the partner both identified as more likely to focus on the immediate amount.

outcomes.verdict: Both of you get pulled into the latest amount, which suggests money, time, or space is being allocated through emergencies rather than an agreed system. Choose the recurring category and define the normal rule, personal discretion zone, and exception process. The system should make most decisions boring. Save emotional energy for the few situations that truly fall outside it.
outcomes.actions_a: Define the normal threshold or protected block and the discretion you need inside it.
outcomes.actions_b: Define the exception request and how much notice keeps it from becoming a surprise transfer of resources.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Boring Resource System with baseline, personal zone, threshold, notice, exception process, and review.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. The recurring fight loses material because ordinary decisions stop requiring fresh negotiation.

outcomes.verdict: Each of you sees yourself as the person trapped in the immediate amount, but you may be fighting different hidden rules. [A] may defend autonomy. [B] may defend shared security, predictability, or equal access. Name the value behind each position, then build a two-part rule: a protected shared floor and a protected personal zone.
outcomes.actions_a: Define the shared floor you need and the evidence that tells you it is protected.
outcomes.actions_b: Define the personal zone you need and the limit that keeps it from consuming the shared floor.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Shared Floor, Personal Zone agreement with values, amounts or time, notice, exceptions, and review.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Security and autonomy stop fighting through the same weekly number.

outcomes.verdict: Each of you thinks the other gets lost in the latest number, so the relationship may be missing an agreed owner for the system itself. Review the last four fights and record what decision was made, who had notice, and which rule was absent. The recurring missing rule matters more than who argued the loudest in each episode.
outcomes.actions_a: Bring one example where your own last-minute choice added pressure and name the rule that would have prevented it.
outcomes.actions_b: Do the same, then draft the shared threshold or notice rule that appears most often.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Four-Fight Resource Audit with decisions, notice, impacts, missing rules, and first policy test.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. The repeated argument leaves behind a usable rule instead of another scorecard.

outcomes.verdict: [A] identifies one partner as more likely to focus on the current amount while [B] sees the pattern as shared or situational. Use the most repeated category to install one mutual rule. The detail-focused partner applies it to the current decision. The pattern-focused partner accepts a scheduled review rather than reopening the rule every time the outcome feels inconvenient.
outcomes.actions_a: Apply the new threshold or notice rule to the current decision and document any exception honestly.
outcomes.actions_b: State the root need behind the rule and wait until the review date to judge the full system unless harm is occurring.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a First Resource Policy Test with category, rule, current application, exception, impact, and review date.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. One familiar dispute becomes the first real test of a shared system.
outcomes.role_note: [A] = identified a specific partner who focuses more on the immediate amount; [B] = said the pattern is shared or situational.

cases.title: When Something Feels Unfair but Neither of You Has Said It Out Loud

options.label: The other person seems overloaded
I cannot prove it neatly
I fear sounding transactional
The arrangement used to make sense
I agreed before realizing the cost
I expect the talk to become defensive

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: What would make the conversation useful?

options.label: Compare load, not intent
Name the current cost
Ask for one transfer
Set a trial period
Include invisible work
Review after circumstances change

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: Want to tell the court a bit more about what happened? (optional)
questions.interactionRule: Private context is used only to personalize the selected deterministic branch.

outcomes.verdict: You identify the same fairness lane and the current weight is manageable. That means you can adjust before the imbalance becomes a story about who cares more. Describe the load, cost, and capacity without prosecuting motive. Then transfer one full responsibility, freedom block, or decision right for a short trial. Fairness becomes easier to discuss when it has a concrete shape.
outcomes.actions_a: Document your current load and request one specific transfer or protection.
outcomes.actions_b: Take ownership of the transfer and name what you need to complete it without hidden help.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Fairness Trial Card with lane, current load, cost, transfer, owner, duration, and review.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. An unspoken imbalance becomes a visible experiment before resentment writes the meaning.

outcomes.verdict: You agree on the unfair lane, but it now carries heavy emotional weight because silence has allowed the arrangement to feel normal. The first repair must include acknowledgment before redistribution. Name who benefited, who absorbed the cost, and how the arrangement started. Then redesign only the next month. A time-limited correction is safer than promising perfect equality forever.
outcomes.actions_a: State the cost you absorbed and the acknowledgment you need before discussing the new split.
outcomes.actions_b: Acknowledge the benefit without defending the origin, then take one complete lane for the trial month.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a One-Month Fairness Reset with acknowledgment, current cost, new ownership, support needs, and review date.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. The imbalance is named, and the next month stops repeating it automatically.

outcomes.verdict: [A] experiences unfairness in one currency, such as labor, money, or freedom. [B] experiences it in another, such as emotional support, family compromise, or decision influence. Comparing unlike currencies will make each person feel erased. Put both on the table, then choose one concrete correction in each lane instead of trying to calculate a single winner.
outcomes.actions_a: Name your fairness currency, its current cost, and one correction that would matter.
outcomes.actions_b: Name your different currency and choose a correction you can own without canceling [A]'s request.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Two-Currency Fairness Map with lanes, costs, benefits, corrections, owners, and review.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Two forms of unequal cost become visible without being forced into the same unit.
outcomes.role_note: [A] and [B] selected different fairness lanes with manageable emotional weight.

outcomes.verdict: [A] carries a heavy unfairness in one domain, while [B] carries a different heavy unfairness elsewhere. A simple trade can create fresh debt if one correction depends on the other person conceding first. Make parallel repairs. Each partner owns one transfer that addresses the other's lane. Review them on the same date without treating either repair as payment for the other.
outcomes.actions_a: Choose the transfer that directly reduces [B]'s burden and schedule its first full cycle.
outcomes.actions_b: Choose a separate transfer that reduces [A]'s burden and complete it without attaching conditions.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Parallel Fairness Repair with two lanes, two transfers, owners, first cycles, and shared review date.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Both imbalances receive movement without becoming bargaining chips.
outcomes.role_note: [A] and [B] selected different fairness lanes with high emotional weight.

cases.title: When an Apology Was Given but the Hurt Never Actually Went Away

A small ache
Noticeable hurt at certain triggers
A lot of unresolved pain
The apology barely changed the hurt

questions.prompt: How do you feel about the apology and repair now?

options.label: It works for me
Mostly okay, with a few hard moments
It regularly leaves me tense or disconnected
I need this pattern to change

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: What did the apology miss?

options.label: The specific impact
Full responsibility
A changed behavior
A practical repair
Space for the hurt response
Understanding why it happened

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: What would help the apology land?

options.label: Name the impact clearly
Add the missing responsibility
Complete one repair
Show consistent behavior
Create a trigger response
Set a final follow-up

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: Want to tell the court a bit more about what happened? (optional)
questions.interactionRule: Private context is used only to personalize the selected deterministic branch.

outcomes.verdict: You agree that only a small amount of hurt remains and generally feel the apology did meaningful work. The remaining ache does not automatically mean the apology failed. Some impacts fade through repeated safe experiences. Name the trigger when it appears, use one brief reassurance, and keep noticing the behavior that is now different.
outcomes.actions_a: Identify the trigger and the sentence that helps you recognize the present has changed.
outcomes.actions_b: Offer that sentence and continue the one behavior that makes the apology credible over time.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save an Apology Landing Note with impact, trigger, reassurance, changed behavior, and closure sign.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. The apology is allowed to keep working through the life that follows it.

outcomes.verdict: [A] and [B] see similar remaining hurt, but [A] is less content because the apology may have addressed intention while skipping impact, or offered words without the practical repair. [B] believes the apology was sincere. Keep that sincerity and add the missing layer. One precise acknowledgment or action can help the apology reach the place it missed.
outcomes.actions_a: Name the exact missing layer and the single addition that would make the apology feel complete.
outcomes.actions_b: Add that acknowledgment or repair without repeating the original defense.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save an Apology Addendum with original words, missed impact, added responsibility, repair action, and check-in.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. A sincere apology gets the missing sentence or action it still needs.
outcomes.role_note: [A] = less content with the apology and repair; [B] = more content.

outcomes.verdict: You agree some hurt remains and neither person feels the apology fully landed. Stop repeating broader versions of 'sorry.' Build the apology from five parts: the act, the impact, responsibility, repair, and changed behavior. The hurt partner chooses which missing part matters most. The apologizing partner completes that part before asking whether the issue can close.
outcomes.actions_a: Identify the missing part and explain why it matters more than another general apology.
outcomes.actions_b: Deliver that part plainly and complete the repair before requesting closure.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Five-Part Apology Repair with act, impact, responsibility, repair, changed behavior, and follow-up.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. The apology stops getting louder and starts getting more accurate.

outcomes.verdict: [A] carries much more remaining hurt because the event affected safety or identity beyond what words could quickly repair. [B] feels the apology was sincere and the current behavior is different. You are content because both realities have room. [A] names trigger support. [B] keeps the changed behavior steady without demanding that visible pain disappear on schedule.
outcomes.actions_a: Choose the two situations where support is still needed and state the response that helps.
outcomes.actions_b: Keep the repair behavior visible and use the chosen response without treating the trigger as rejection of your apology.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Long-Tail Apology Plan with triggers, support responses, changed behavior, evidence period, and closure signs.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Sincere repair and slower healing stop competing for the same truth.
outcomes.role_note: [A] carries more remaining hurt; [B] feels more repaired.

outcomes.verdict: [A] still hurts deeply and is dissatisfied. [B] feels the apology should have closed the matter and is content with the repair. The apology has become a receipt [B] wants accepted, while [A] is still waiting for the service it was meant to prove. [B] owes one missing repair. [A] owes clear healing markers instead of an undefined sentence.
outcomes.actions_a: Name the missing repair and the observable signs that would show the hurt is moving.
outcomes.actions_b: Complete that repair and maintain the changed behavior without using the apology as a deadline.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save an Apology-to-Repair Contract with missing action, owner, behavior proof, healing markers, and review dates.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. The apology gains value through what happens after it, not through repeated presentation.
outcomes.role_note: [A] carries more hurt and is dissatisfied; [B] feels more repaired and is content.

outcomes.verdict: [A] experiences the apology as too small for the impact. [B] experiences ongoing hurt as proof that nothing offered will ever count. Do not repeat the old argument while negotiating repair. Set two sessions: first identify the missing apology component, then review a concrete behavior period. If agreement on basic impact remains impossible, use neutral support before seeking final closure.
outcomes.actions_a: Prepare the impact and one missing component for the first session, without expanding into unrelated history.
outcomes.actions_b: Prepare the responsibility you can own and the behavior you will sustain through the review period.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Two-Session Apology Completion plan with impact, missing component, behavior period, evidence, and support threshold.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Hurt receives a specific repair path, and effort receives a fair way to become visible.
outcomes.role_note: [A] carries more remaining hurt; [B] feels more repaired.

options.label: It matters, but it is manageable

It affects how safe or close I feel

options.label: Short replies
Reduced effort
Irritation at small things

options.label: Name one current example

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: Want to tell the court a bit more about what happened? (optional)
questions.interactionRule: Private context is used only to personalize the selected deterministic branch.

outcomes.verdict: You recognize the same unmet need and the frustration is still manageable. That is good timing for a clean request before irritation recruits unrelated evidence. Name one current example, the need underneath it, and one behavior that would help this week. The listener should respond to the request, not investigate every sign that appeared before it was spoken.
outcomes.actions_a: Turn the frustration into one direct request with a clear time frame.
outcomes.actions_b: Respond to the request and complete one visible action without demanding a perfect explanation of the delay.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Quiet-to-Clear Request with example, need, behavior, owner, time frame, and follow-up.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Frustration gets a voice before it needs to keep borrowing attitude.

outcomes.verdict: You agree on the need, but the frustration now carries real weight because silence has also created distance. The repair has two parts: address the unmet need and acknowledge how the quiet leak affected the atmosphere. Choose one immediate relief action and one sustained habit. A single kind gesture cannot replace a pattern, but it can make room to build one.
outcomes.actions_a: Name the accumulated cost and the immediate relief action that would help you reenter connection.
outcomes.actions_b: Complete that action, then own a repeatable habit with a date for reviewing whether it changed the pattern.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save an Immediate and Ongoing Frustration Repair with impact, relief action, habit, cue, and review.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. The relationship receives help for today and evidence for the weeks after it.

outcomes.verdict: [A]'s quiet frustration is asking for more support, follow-through, or attention. [B]'s is asking for more space, initiative, respect, or another distinct need. These requests may look like opposites, but each points to a different depleted lane. Make one change for each lane and avoid trading them as conditions. Neither need has to lose for the other to become visible.
outcomes.actions_a: State your need as one behavior [B] can complete without guessing.
outcomes.actions_b: State your different need and choose one action you can take for [A] before the review.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Two-Lane Frustration Reset with needs, behaviors, owners, start dates, and shared review.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Two quiet frustrations become two clear chances to show up.
outcomes.role_note: [A] and [B] selected different unmet needs with manageable emotional weight.

outcomes.verdict: [A] and [B] carry different frustrations, and both have grown heavy enough to affect warmth or effort. Solving only the louder one will teach the quieter partner to store more. Use parallel first aid: one immediate action for each need, followed by separate habit plans. Review progress together, but do not make either repair contingent on gratitude for the other.
outcomes.actions_a: Choose the immediate action that would reduce [B]'s current strain and schedule it now.
outcomes.actions_b: Choose a separate action for [A], then build the longer habit attached to your own responsibility.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Parallel Frustration First-Aid plan with two actions, two habits, cues, owners, and review date.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Both warning lights receive attention before either becomes the whole dashboard.
outcomes.role_note: [A] and [B] selected different unmet needs with high emotional weight.

cases.title: When You Both Agreed to Something but Never Actually Followed Through
cases.subtitle: Who is more likely to leave a shared agreement in the conversation instead of putting it into motion?

questions.prompt: Who is more likely to leave a shared agreement in the conversation instead of putting it into motion?

options.label: Me, no contest
Probably me
Probably them
Definitely them
Honestly, both equally

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: What makes that answer feel true?

options.label: They assume the other person will start
The first step was never named
The agreement was polite, not committed
Daily life displaced it
No date or owner existed
The plan needed resources that were never arranged

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: What kind of agreement stalled?

options.label: A household change
A money plan
Quality time
A boundary
A health or lifestyle goal
A future decision

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: What would restart it honestly?

options.label: Confirm it is still wanted
Name the first step
Assign owners
Put it on the calendar
Arrange the missing resource
Allow a clear no or redesign

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: Want to tell the court a bit more about what happened? (optional)
questions.interactionRule: Private context is used only to personalize the selected deterministic branch.

outcomes.verdict: [A] is more likely to leave the agreement in conversation because shared enthusiasm can feel like shared execution. [B] may wait for the promised movement and read silence as low priority. [A] needs to own the first visible step or state that commitment has changed. [B] needs to confirm the plan is still mutually chosen before enforcing an old yes.
outcomes.actions_a: Confirm whether you still choose the agreement, then own and schedule the first step.
outcomes.actions_b: State the impact of the stall and ask for a fresh yes, redesign, or honest no.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save an Agreement Restart Sheet with current yes, first step, owners, resources, date, and redesign option.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. An old agreement gets a current decision instead of indefinite imaginary progress.
outcomes.role_note: [A] = the partner both identified as more likely to leave the agreement unstarted.

outcomes.verdict: [B] treats agreement as enough to create momentum, while [A] experiences a plan that never leaves the meeting. [B] should either schedule the first action or withdraw the commitment honestly. [A] should not keep carrying a plan that may only have received a conflict-ending yes. A fresh agreement needs owners and resources before it deserves another deadline.
outcomes.actions_a: Ask whether the plan is still genuinely chosen and identify the consequence of continued delay.
outcomes.actions_b: Give a current answer, then schedule the first action or clearly propose a redesign.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save an Agreement Restart Sheet with current yes, first step, owners, resources, date, and redesign option.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. The plan receives a real start or an honest release from pretending.
outcomes.role_note: [B] = the partner both identified as more likely to leave the agreement unstarted.

outcomes.verdict: Both of you agree easily and start slowly, which suggests the relationship is good at shared intention but vague about execution. Before making another plan, close the old loop. Confirm desire, assign the first action to one person, set the date, and identify the resource. If no one wants the first step, the agreement needs redesign rather than motivation.
outcomes.actions_a: Choose one stalled agreement and either claim the first step or say which part you no longer choose.
outcomes.actions_b: Choose the next dependent step and arrange the resource it needs before the start date.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Stalled Agreement Triage with keep, redesign, release, first step, owner, resource, and date.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Shared intention becomes action only where both people still choose the plan.

outcomes.verdict: Each of you sees yourself as the one who fails to start, but different agreements may be waiting on different owners. Map the dependency chain. [A]'s action may need to happen before [B] can move, or both may be waiting for a joint resource. Identify the true first domino instead of dividing vague responsibility equally.
outcomes.actions_a: Name the earliest action you control and complete it before requesting the next step from [B].
outcomes.actions_b: Name the action that depends on [A]'s step and prepare everything you can in advance.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a First-Domino Plan with dependency order, owners, resources, dates, and completion marks.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. The stalled plan discovers which action actually has to move first.

outcomes.verdict: Each of you thinks the other usually leaves agreements untouched, which means shared ownership may be functioning as ownerless work. Audit the three active agreements. Give every first step one name, not both names. Remove anything neither person currently chooses. A smaller list with clear owners will reveal more than another argument about initiative.
outcomes.actions_a: Claim one first step and release one agreement you no longer genuinely support.
outcomes.actions_b: Claim a different step and state the date by which you will report completion or an obstacle.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Three-Agreement Ownership Board with keep or release status, first steps, single owners, dates, and obstacles.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Shared plans stop disappearing into the space between two responsible people.

outcomes.verdict: [A] identifies one partner as the more frequent nonstarter while [B] sees the pattern as shared or situational. Start with the longest-stalled agreement and make ownership explicit. The nonstarter takes the first action. The other partner prepares the next dependency and does not rescue the first step. Review only after the agreed date.
outcomes.actions_a: Complete the first action without waiting for reminders and report any real obstacle before the date.
outcomes.actions_b: Prepare the dependent action and let the first owner carry their step fully.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Longest-Stalled Restart with current commitment, first owner, next dependency, dates, obstacle rule, and review.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. One old plan gets movement without hiding responsibility inside the word 'we.'
outcomes.role_note: [A] = identified a specific more frequent nonstarter; [B] = said the pattern is shared or situational.

cases.title: When a Compromise Made Early On No Longer Feels Fair to One of You

Mostly works with small updates
The fit is noticeably uneven
It costs one person much more now
It no longer works as a fair agreement

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: How do you feel about the compromise as it currently operates?

options.label: It works for me
Mostly okay, with a few hard moments
It regularly leaves me tense or disconnected
I need this pattern to change

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: What changed since you made it?

options.label: Income or work
Health or energy
Family responsibilities
Location or schedule
Relationship priorities
The true cost became clearer

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

options.label: Recheck the original purpose
Measure today's costs
Shift one responsibility

Review after the new arrangement runs

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: Want to tell the court a bit more about what happened? (optional)
questions.interactionRule: Private context is used only to personalize the selected deterministic branch.

outcomes.verdict: You see the old compromise similarly and it still fits well enough because its purpose remains relevant and its costs remain visible. That is not permission to leave it untouched forever. Name what has changed and schedule a future review. A fair compromise stays fair partly because both people are allowed to update the data without threatening the original goodwill.
outcomes.actions_a: Name the current benefit you still receive and the change that should trigger an earlier review.
outcomes.actions_b: Name the cost you still accept and the limit that would make the arrangement need revision.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Living Compromise Record with original purpose, current benefits, current costs, trigger points, and review date.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. The agreement stays strong because it is allowed to remain current.

outcomes.verdict: [A] and [B] see a similar fit, but [A] is less content because a small update has become overdue. [B] sees the original exchange still functioning. [A] feels a changed schedule, energy level, or responsibility making one side more expensive. Preserve the purpose and adjust the part whose real cost changed.
outcomes.actions_a: Identify the updated cost and request one proportional shift rather than discarding the whole compromise.
outcomes.actions_b: Accept the cost update and take or fund the adjustment for a defined trial period.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Compromise Tune-Up with original purpose, changed cost, specific shift, trial dates, and review.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. A small update protects the bargain from becoming quietly outdated.
outcomes.role_note: [A] = less content with the current compromise; [B] = more content.

outcomes.verdict: You agree the compromise no longer fits comfortably, but may be preserving it because changing it feels like undoing earlier generosity. The original agreement solved an older life. Honor that purpose, then retire the obsolete mechanics. Recalculate today's time, money, energy, and alternatives. Choose a three-month version with an automatic review instead of another permanent promise.
outcomes.actions_a: List the cost you carry now and the part of the old arrangement you are ready to release.
outcomes.actions_b: List your current cost and design the three-month shift you can sustain without hidden dependence.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Three-Month Compromise Update with old purpose, current costs, new split, start date, and automatic review.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. The earlier compromise can be appreciated without being forced to govern a different life.

outcomes.verdict: [A] experiences the compromise as much less fair because circumstances changed the cost on [A]'s side. [B] still experiences it as workable and may value the stability it provides. You are content because stability can remain while the unequal cost is offset. Keep the original structure temporarily, but transfer one responsibility, resource, or freedom block to rebalance it.
outcomes.actions_a: Quantify the changed cost and choose the offset that would make the next month sustainable.
outcomes.actions_b: Provide that offset fully and help collect the data for the scheduled redesign review.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Stability With Offset plan with current structure, changed cost, offset, owner, trial month, and redesign date.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Continuity stays, but it no longer asks one partner to absorb the whole update in circumstances.
outcomes.role_note: [A] experiences the compromise as less fair; [B] sees more remaining fit.

outcomes.verdict: [A] experiences the old compromise as deeply unfair and is dissatisfied. [B] still benefits from or trusts the arrangement and feels content. The agreement's history cannot make today's unequal cost automatic. [B] owes one immediate offset and a redesign date. [A] owes a concrete cost account and a bridge proposal rather than withdrawing without transition.
outcomes.actions_a: Document the current cost and propose the shortest bridge that protects essential commitments.
outcomes.actions_b: Take the immediate offset, agree to the redesign date, and stop treating the original consent as permanent consent.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Compromise Exit Bridge with current cost, immediate offset, protected commitments, bridge length, and redesign date.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. The old agreement receives an orderly update instead of permanent authority.
outcomes.role_note: [A] experiences the compromise as less fair and is dissatisfied; [B] sees more fit and is content.

outcomes.verdict: [A] sees an arrangement that now extracts too much. [B] sees the risk of losing stability if it changes quickly. Do not choose between continued unfairness and sudden collapse. Set an end date for the current terms, create a temporary bridge, and design the next arrangement from current capacity. A dated transition makes change safer than indefinite resentment.
outcomes.actions_a: Name the nonnegotiable end date and the essential commitments the bridge must protect.
outcomes.actions_b: Name the stability need and take responsibility for one transition task before the old terms expire.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Dated Compromise Transition with end date, bridge terms, protected needs, transition owners, and new-plan meeting.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Fairness gets a date, and stability gets a bridge instead of a veto.
outcomes.role_note: [A] experiences the compromise as less fair; [B] sees more remaining fit.

cases.title: When Trust Was Affected by Something and It's Never Fully Been Talked Through
cases.subtitle: What has kept the trust issue from being fully discussed?

questions.prompt: What has kept the trust issue from being fully discussed?

options.label: The facts are painful
One person fears the reaction
Memories or accounts differ
The issue touches privacy
The timing never felt safe
Talking could force a major decision

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: How much weight does the unfinished trust issue carry now?

options.label: It matters, but it is manageable
It carries real emotional weight
It affects how safe or close I feel
It needs attention before we can move on

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

outcomes.verdict: You agree on what blocked the trust conversation and its current weight is manageable enough for a paced start. Do not attempt the whole history at once. Exchange short timelines, identify one fact question, and separate it from the impact discussion. Trust repairs better when clarity and emotion each receive a turn instead of competing inside every sentence.
outcomes.actions_a: Write the timeline as you remember it and mark the one question whose answer matters most now.
outcomes.actions_b: Write a separate timeline, identify any uncertainty honestly, and prepare to reflect the impact before explaining intent.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Trust Talk Starter with two timelines, one fact question, impact turn, pause rule, and next date.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. The unfinished issue gets a first chapter small enough to tell accurately.

outcomes.verdict: You share the reason the topic stayed unfinished, but it now carries heavy weight and shapes checking, intimacy, or belief. This needs more than an improvised late-night conversation. Schedule two sessions and preselect support. The first establishes facts and unknowns. The second addresses impact, responsibility, and repair. Either person can call the agreed pause without canceling the process.
outcomes.actions_a: Prepare your timeline, known facts, unknowns, and the impact you need acknowledged.
outcomes.actions_b: Prepare the same structure and identify the responsibility you can discuss without waiting for perfect agreement on every detail.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Two-Session Trust Process with agendas, dates, pause rule, knowns, unknowns, repair question, and support contact.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. The issue receives enough structure that honesty does not have to survive chaos to be heard.

outcomes.verdict: [A] avoided the trust talk because the facts or reaction felt dangerous. [B] avoided it because privacy, uncertainty, or a major decision was at stake. One barrier needs emotional safety. The other needs scope control. Begin with written boundaries around what the first session will cover, what remains private, and which decision is explicitly not being made yet.
outcomes.actions_a: Name the safety condition and first question you need in order to stay present.
outcomes.actions_b: Name the privacy or decision boundary and the information you can still share inside it.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Safe-Scope Trust Agenda with first question, safety rules, privacy line, deferred decisions, and next step.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. Two different barriers become instructions for a conversation that can actually begin.
outcomes.role_note: [A] and [B] chose different barriers to the trust conversation with manageable emotional weight.

outcomes.verdict: [A] and [B] carry different heavy barriers, and the unfinished trust issue already affects daily closeness. Trying to solve facts, impact, privacy, and future decisions in one talk will overwhelm the process. Use a counselor or mediator and divide the work into four meetings: scope, facts, impact, and repair choices. Safety exceptions remain active throughout.
outcomes.actions_a: Prepare a one-page scope note with what you can discuss, what support you need, and the first factual question.
outcomes.actions_b: Prepare a separate note with privacy limits, known information, and the repair outcome you hope the process can reach.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Four-Meeting Trust Roadmap with scope, facts, impact, repair sessions, facilitator, and safety exceptions.
outcomes.closing: Case softened. The relationship gets a route through the issue without asking either person to carry the whole route alone.
outcomes.role_note: [A] and [B] chose different barriers to the trust conversation with high emotional weight.

Name the issue in one sentence, choose the first decision or repair, and put the talk on the calendar. A continuation note keeps the subject from disappearing when the mood improves.
outcomes.actions_a: Write the one-sentence issue and the first outcome you need from the scheduled talk.
outcomes.actions_b: Choose the date and prepare the information or reflection needed for that first outcome.

The first repair is reliability: schedule the conversation, keep it, and finish one defined task. Do not promise to solve everything. Proving that the issue can stay on the table long enough for one outcome matters more than an ambitious agenda.

outcomes.actions_b: Book the meeting, own the preparation task, and protect the time from lower-priority interruptions.

One partner needs commitment to return. The other needs a smaller scope. Set the date first, then narrow the meeting to one question that can actually be completed.
outcomes.actions_a: Name the cost of postponement and the date by which the first talk needs to happen.
outcomes.actions_b: Turn the broad issue into one answerable question and list what is outside the first meeting.

outcomes.role_note: [A] and [B] selected different reasons the issue is postponed with manageable emotional weight.

outcomes.verdict: [A] experiences repeated postponement as evidence the issue will never matter enough. [B] experiences the topic as too large or destabilizing to approach safely. Both concerns now carry heavy weight. Use a firm date, written summaries, timed turns, and a preselected support option. If the first meeting stalls, the support appointment activates rather than the issue disappearing again.
outcomes.actions_a: Write the impact of postponement and the one outcome you need from the first meeting.
outcomes.actions_b: Write the scope and safety rules you need, then arrange the backup support before the meeting date.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save an Anti-Avoidance Escalation Plan with summaries, firm date, timed turns, first outcome, and automatic support step.

questions.prompt: What feels most important to protect?

options.label: Financial independence
Private time and personal space
The relationship from avoidable pressure
Commute, work, or study needs
Existing family or pet responsibilities
The ability to leave safely if needed

questions.prompt: Anything the court should know about the lease, timing, distance, or fear underneath this decision? (optional)
questions.interactionRule: Private context is used only to personalize the selected deterministic branch.

outcomes.verdict: You are arriving at this decision at a similar pace, which means neither person has to drag the future forward or quietly hold it back. Your readiness shows up in the way you can treat moving in as a system change, not a romantic graduation. Keep the warmth, but test the ordinary details that decide whether a home feels safe: money, solitude, mess, guests, sleep, work, and exits. Matching excitement becomes durable when daily life has somewhere to land.
outcomes.actions_a: Choose one routine you need preserved in a shared home and explain what support would make it realistic.
outcomes.actions_b: Choose a different daily pressure point and propose one household rule that would protect both people.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Shared Home Readiness Board with budget, routines, private space, guest rules, trial dates, and exit plan.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. The feeling is mutual, and the practical foundation gets equal attention.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = less satisfied with the current move-in process; [B] = more content.
outcomes.verdict: [A] and [B] report similar readiness, but [A] does not feel equally protected by the process. [A] may be carrying the lease risk, losing more privacy, moving farther, or doing the planning while [B] experiences shared momentum. The readiness gap is small; the exposure gap may not be. Name who gives up what and build one protection around the larger sacrifice. A shared address should not require one person to act fearless so the timeline stays cute.
outcomes.actions_a: Name the specific sacrifice or uncertainty that makes the current process feel uneven.
outcomes.actions_b: Take ownership of one protection, cost, or planning task that directly reduces [A]'s exposure.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Move-In Exposure List with each sacrifice, matching protection, task owner, deadline, and go or wait date.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Similar readiness now comes with a fairer share of the risk.

outcomes.verdict: You are close in readiness, yet the decision still feels bad because it has become one giant yes or no. Break it into proof points. Test a normal workweek together, build the real budget, divide recurring chores, and tour neighborhoods with both commutes in mind. Each test should answer a named concern, not perform commitment. You do not need more pressure to feel certain. You need smaller experiences that turn imagined home life into usable information.
outcomes.actions_a: Choose the practical uncertainty you want the first trial to answer and define what success would look like.
outcomes.actions_b: Design a different trial around routine, money, or space and schedule it on the shared calendar.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Four-Test Move-In Plan with question, trial, dates, success signs, notes, and final decision appointment.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. The big decision becomes a series of honest, low-drama proofs.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = less ready to move in; [B] = more ready.
outcomes.verdict: [A] is checking whether shared housing can protect independence, money, and the parts of the relationship that currently work. [B] is ready to turn closeness into everyday partnership and may already see separate homes as unnecessary friction. You are content because readiness is not being treated as a love score. Use a readiness checklist with no forced average. [B] can prepare concrete options while [A] owns the timing of the unresolved conditions, followed by a real review date.
outcomes.actions_a: List the two conditions that must become true before your answer can move, with evidence for each.
outcomes.actions_b: Prepare one housing option that respects those conditions without repeatedly campaigning for an earlier yes.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Move-In Conditions Sheet with ready items, unresolved conditions, evidence needed, housing option, and review date.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Commitment stays visible without making caution pay a loyalty tax.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = less ready and dissatisfied; [B] = more ready and content.
outcomes.verdict: [A] feels pressure inside a process that currently favors [B]'s preferred future. [B] may hear the general relationship commitment and assume housing is the natural next step, so the waiting seems procedural rather than emotional. [A]'s hesitation needs a protected voice, and [B]'s need for direction deserves more than an endless maybe. Set a decision date, but make it a date to choose among move now, run a defined trial, or wait for named conditions. The calendar creates clarity without predetermining the answer.
outcomes.actions_a: Translate hesitation into named conditions and stop using open-ended uncertainty as the whole answer.
outcomes.actions_b: Pause persuasion until the decision date and gather options for all three legitimate outcomes.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Move-In Decision Appointment with conditions, three outcome options, evidence tasks, no-pressure period, and calendar date.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. The timeline becomes clear without forcing the destination.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = less ready to move in; [B] = more ready.
outcomes.verdict: [A] may protect the current relationship by keeping housing risk separate until trust, money, or daily compatibility feels proven. [B] may experience separate homes as a ceiling on intimacy, convenience, or shared future planning. Repeating the question makes [A] feel cornered and [B] feel rejected. Stop voting on the move for one month. Instead, assign [A] the safety design and [B] the shared-life design. Compare both plans at a scheduled checkpoint and identify whether one home can honestly hold both.
outcomes.actions_a: Design the financial, privacy, and exit protections required for a safe shared home.
outcomes.actions_b: Design the routines, location, and shared benefits that would make moving worthwhile rather than merely symbolic.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save two Move-In Blueprints with safety needs, shared-life benefits, costs, nonnegotiables, overlaps, and checkpoint date.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. The next conversation compares livable plans, not competing levels of love.

options.label: My own career momentum
Family or caregiving support

Affordable housing or lifestyle
Healthcare, school, or legal stability
