questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: What would make a relocation offer more mutual?

options.label: A job plan for the relocating partner
A fixed trial period
Moving and setup costs covered
Regular travel back home
A future turn for the other career
A clear exit if the new city does not work

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: Anything the court should know about the city, career opportunity, or sacrifice behind your answer? (optional)
questions.interactionRule: Private context is used only to personalize the selected deterministic branch.

outcomes.verdict: You have a shared definition of how far love should stretch for a career without erasing the person who moves. That alignment matters because relocation costs arrive in different currencies: income, community, identity, caregiving, and momentum. Your strength is not equal willingness alone. It is the chance to recognize sacrifice before it becomes invisible. Keep a record of what the move gives the couple and what it asks from each person, then fund the losses as seriously as the moving truck.
outcomes.actions_a: Name the part of your life that would need active rebuilding, not just emotional reassurance, after a move.
outcomes.actions_b: Name one concrete resource you would commit to protecting that rebuilding process.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Relocation Cost Ledger with gains, losses, career impact, support budget, return travel, and exit date.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. The opportunity belongs to both of you only when the sacrifice stays visible too.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = feels less understood or satisfied with relocation expectations; [B] = more content.
outcomes.verdict: [A] and [B] show similar willingness, but [A] may already sense that [A]'s career, family ties, or rebuilding work would count as background detail. [B] sees shared flexibility and assumes the sacrifice is balanced because both say they would consider moving. Willingness is not the same as equal cost. Price the move from each person's starting point, then assign resources to the partner losing more continuity. Appreciation becomes convincing when it changes the plan.
outcomes.actions_a: List the three hardest-to-replace parts of your current life and what practical support each would require.
outcomes.actions_b: Turn one of those needs into a funded line item or protected weekly commitment in the relocation plan.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Relocation Impact Table with each person's losses, replacements, cost, owner, timing, and deal-breakers.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Equal willingness no longer hides unequal disruption.

outcomes.verdict: You are similarly willing, but the idea still feels unfair because no one knows how a future sacrifice gets repaid. A move can quietly crown one career as the permanent priority while the other becomes flexible by default. Before any offer exists, agree on reciprocity that is more specific than someday. It might be a two-year review, funded retraining, or first consideration for the next location choice. The promise should create an actual claim on future decisions, not a sentimental thank-you.
outcomes.actions_a: Propose one concrete form of career or location reciprocity with a time horizon.
outcomes.actions_b: Propose a different protection that keeps the relocating partner's own momentum from going dormant.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Relocation Reciprocity Pact with sacrifice, protections, career rebuild, future priority, and dated review.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Flexibility earns a visible place in the couple's future ledger.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = less willing to relocate; [B] = more willing.
outcomes.verdict: [A] has more location-bound value to protect, perhaps career licensing, family care, community, or a life that took years to build. [B] is more portable and sees relocation as a workable way to back the relationship. You are content because flexibility is not being mistaken for greater devotion. Treat [B]'s mobility as an option, not an unlimited promise, and treat [A]'s roots as real assets. Evaluate each offer against both careers and the support system, not against who can pack faster.
outcomes.actions_a: Document the location-bound commitments and the rare conditions that could justify leaving them.
outcomes.actions_b: Define the limits of your flexibility and what you would need to build a life in a new place.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Location Flexibility Profile with portable assets, rooted commitments, move conditions, support needs, and reevaluation date.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Roots and mobility become planning facts, not measures of love.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = less willing and dissatisfied; [B] = more willing and content.
outcomes.verdict: [A] may feel that [B]'s willingness has become the moral standard, making [A]'s roots look selfish instead of costly to move. [B] feels generous and may assume the relationship is secure because at least one person is flexible. The current story flatters [B] while isolating [A]. Stop comparing willingness in the abstract. Choose one realistic city and model the actual impact on income, care, community, and daily life for both partners. Specifics can replace the loyalty contest.
outcomes.actions_a: Build the realistic cost of leaving your current base, including losses that money alone cannot replace.
outcomes.actions_b: Build the realistic cost of staying or moving for your own career, without presenting flexibility as emotional proof.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a One-City Relocation Model with income, career path, support network, housing, travel, losses, and decision date.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. A real city gets evaluated, and devotion leaves the witness stand.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = less willing to relocate; [B] = more willing.
outcomes.verdict: [A] experiences relocation as uprooting a whole ecosystem. [B] experiences it as taking a difficult but survivable leap for shared growth. Each person is arguing from a different unit of change, so repeating how willing you are will not create agreement. Give any future offer a two-checkpoint process. First decide whether the opportunity is strong enough to justify serious planning. Only then build protections and decide whether this specific move is livable. No partner owes a blank check before an actual offer exists.
outcomes.actions_a: Define the minimum opportunity quality required before you will enter full relocation planning.
outcomes.actions_b: Define the protections that would make your willingness sustainable rather than heroic for six months.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Two-Checkpoint Relocation Rule with opportunity threshold, planning protections, sacrifice cap, final decision date, and exit option.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. You evaluate the opportunity first and the move second.

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: What most shapes your answer?

options.label: The kind of life I genuinely want
Health, fertility, or timing realities
Money, housing, or childcare
Career and freedom
Family history or caregiving experience
Confidence in sharing the work fairly

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: What must stay true during this conversation?

options.label: No one treats uncertainty as a promise
No one waits for the other to change
Biological and medical realities stay visible
Alternatives are discussed honestly
The relationship is not used as leverage
A serious mismatch is faced directly

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: Anything the court should know about the hope, fear, health factor, or pressure behind your answer? (optional)
questions.interactionRule: Private context is used only to personalize the selected deterministic branch.

outcomes.verdict: You are close in what you want and, just as importantly, you can say it without performing certainty for each other. That emotional safety is the real foundation here. It lets you discuss health, timing, money, identity, and workload before those realities become a referendum on commitment. Keep separating the desire for children from the conditions required to parent well. Alignment becomes more honest when both the dream and the labor are allowed into the same conversation.
outcomes.actions_a: Name one part of the future you genuinely want and one parenting condition you would need protected.
outcomes.actions_b: Name one hope and one concern that you want treated as information rather than persuasion material.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Kids Conversation Snapshot with current position, hopes, conditions, workload expectations, health facts, and revisit date.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Your shared direction gets stronger because honesty is safe inside it.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = feels less safe or satisfied in the kids conversation; [B] = more content.
outcomes.verdict: [A] and [B] appear close on the answer, but [A] does not feel equally free to change, qualify, or admit fear. [B] sees alignment and may hear uncertainty as a temporary wobble inside an agreed future. [A] may hear the same conversation as a contract already being drafted. Pause future planning long enough to record both positions in each person's own words. Safety returns when agreement is not allowed to erase the conditions and doubts living inside it.
outcomes.actions_a: Write your current position with every important condition and name what response would make honesty feel safer.
outcomes.actions_b: Reflect [A]'s position without translating it toward your preferred outcome or asking for reassurance immediately.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save two separate Kids Position Notes plus a shared page of overlap, differences, unknowns, and next conversation date.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Similar answers no longer require identical certainty.

outcomes.verdict: You are near each other on wanting kids, but the conversation has become emotionally unsafe. That means the danger is not only a future mismatch. It is the way every hesitation gets interpreted as rejection, delay, or a hidden promise. Hold one conversation where no decision is allowed. Each person describes the life each of you imagines with children and the life each of you imagines without children, including grief and relief in both versions. Complexity is not disloyalty. It is the information a real decision requires.
outcomes.actions_a: Describe both possible lives without arguing for one, including what you would gain and mourn in each.
outcomes.actions_b: Listen for the values underneath both visions and ask one curious question without seeking a final answer.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Two-Futures Reflection with gains, losses, fears, conditions, unanswered facts, and a separate decision date.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. The conversation makes room for truth before it asks for certainty.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = less interested in having children; [B] = more interested.
outcomes.verdict: [A] is protecting a life that feels authentic without parenting or is naming conditions that currently make parenting feel unlivable. [B] is protecting a future relationship to family, meaning, and care that feels central rather than optional. You are handling the difference honestly, which is a major act of respect. Do not convert that safety into indefinite waiting for someone to change. Set a serious review date and identify which facts may evolve, while acknowledging that desire itself may remain a real boundary.
outcomes.actions_a: State which parts of your position are values, which are conditions, and which are genuinely unknown.
outcomes.actions_b: State your timeline needs and the point at which continued uncertainty would no longer be fair to you.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Kids Alignment Record with present positions, fixed values, changeable conditions, timelines, outside information needed, and review date.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Care for each other includes refusing to hide the size of this difference.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = less interested in having children and feels less safe or satisfied; [B] = more interested and feels content with the conversation.
outcomes.verdict: [A] may feel that the relationship is quietly waiting for a future yes, so every honest no or maybe risks disappointment. [B] feels hopeful and may interpret continued conversation as evidence that the gap is temporary. That hope is currently making the process easier for [B] than for [A]. [B] owes a period with no persuasion and no future-casting that assumes children. [A] owes a clear account of whether the position is a boundary, a condition, or an unknown.
outcomes.actions_a: Name your position category clearly and identify any information you genuinely still need.
outcomes.actions_b: Stop treating continued love as evidence of future agreement and write your own timeline without using it as pressure.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a No-Persuasion Agreement with current positions, prohibited pressure moves, information tasks, personal timelines, and review date.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Hope stays human, but it no longer gets to rewrite the other person's answer.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = less interested in having children; [B] = more interested.
outcomes.verdict: [A] may fear losing the relationship by telling the full truth. [B] may fear losing the chance to parent if the truth arrives too late. Softening the difference protects tonight while putting both futures at risk. This is not a problem to solve through a clever compromise, because a child cannot be halfway wanted. Set a near-term, protected conversation and consider a qualified couples counselor. The goal is clarity, not conversion, followed by an honest decision about compatibility.
outcomes.actions_a: Prepare a direct statement of your current answer, its stability, and what you cannot promise.
outcomes.actions_b: Prepare your real parenting desire and timeline without bargaining against [A]'s autonomy.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a High-Stakes Conversation Plan with separate statements, counselor option, date, ground rules, decision window, and support contacts.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. The most loving move here is clear truth with care around both futures.

cases.title: Who's More Ready to Talk About Marriage?

The silence or pressure is hurting the relationship

questions.prompt: What does the word marriage bring up first?

options.label: Commitment and being chosen
Legal and financial protection
Family or cultural expectations
Fear from past relationships or divorce
A timeline for shared life plans
Concern about losing freedom or identity

questions.prompt: What should the first serious talk accomplish?

options.label: Define what marriage means to each of us
Separate desire from timing
Discuss legal and money realities
Name fears without fixing them
Identify conditions for readiness
Set a date for the next conversation

questions.prompt: Anything the court should know about the pressure, hope, history, or timeline behind this topic? (optional)

outcomes.verdict: You are ready for this conversation at a similar depth, which means marriage can be discussed as a shared-life design instead of a surprise test. Neither person needs a proposal, joke, or family comment to smuggle the topic into the room. Use the openness to separate meaning, legal structure, and timing. Couples can want the same commitment while picturing very different ceremonies, finances, names, or family roles. Alignment grows when the word stops carrying every decision at once.
outcomes.actions_a: Describe what marriage would change emotionally and practically for you, including one thing it would not change.
outcomes.actions_b: Describe your preferred timing conditions and one assumption you want checked before planning begins.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Marriage Meaning Map with commitment, legal changes, finances, family expectations, timing conditions, and next talk date.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. The topic is safe enough to become specific.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = less satisfied with the current marriage conversation; [B] = more content.
outcomes.verdict: [A] and [B] are similarly ready to talk, yet [A] is getting less clarity from the current version. [A] may hear warm statements with no timing, or practical questions with no emotional reassurance. [B] feels the subject is open because it is not forbidden. Openness is not the same as progress. Give the next conversation one job, such as defining meaning or naming timing conditions, and leave with a written next step rather than another cloud of good intentions.
outcomes.actions_a: Choose the single unanswered question that would reduce the most uncertainty for you.
outcomes.actions_b: Answer that question directly or name the information and date required before you can answer it.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a One-Job Marriage Talk note with the question, each answer, unknowns, next step, owner, and follow-up date.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. The conversation stops circling and produces one honest piece of clarity.

outcomes.verdict: You are close in readiness, but each conversation seems to trigger a different fear before the useful part begins. One person may hear pressure; the other hears evasion. The topic then becomes a test of tone instead of a discussion of the future. Use two rounds. First, each person says what marriage represents and what it threatens. On another date, discuss timing and conditions. Emotional meaning gets heard before logistics try to solve it, and logistics get a clean space afterward.
outcomes.actions_a: Prepare your meaning and fear statements without adding a deadline or proposed solution.
outcomes.actions_b: Prepare your own statements and schedule the separate practical conversation before the first talk ends.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Two-Round Marriage Conversation with meaning notes, fear notes, practical questions, two dates, and pause phrase.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Meaning and timing each get their own room.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = less ready to discuss marriage; [B] = more ready.
outcomes.verdict: [A] needs the topic to stay exploratory so discussion does not feel like an obligation to produce a timeline. [B] needs enough directness to know the relationship is not using vagueness as a permanent holding pattern. You are content because both needs currently fit inside honest conversation. Keep a boundary between talking and deciding, then schedule the next checkpoint. [A] gets space from immediate pressure; [B] gets evidence that the topic will not vanish after one reassuring evening.
outcomes.actions_a: Name what you can discuss now and the condition that must change before timing becomes answerable.
outcomes.actions_b: Ask for clarity within that scope and avoid treating the conversation itself as a commitment to marry.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Talk Versus Decide agreement with current scope, off-limit decisions, readiness conditions, questions, and checkpoint date.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Conversation stays open without becoming a hidden deadline.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = less ready and dissatisfied; [B] = more ready and content.
outcomes.verdict: [A] may feel that every mention of marriage is a pop quiz where hesitation will be graded as weak commitment. [B] feels secure because the subject is active and may not see how much pressure sits inside the questions. The current setup gives [B] hope while making [A] manage the emotional consequences of uncertainty. Establish a pressure-free information phase with a clear end date. [A] explores meaning and fears; [B] receives updates without lobbying for the preferred answer.
outcomes.actions_a: Use the information phase to name the real barriers and the facts that could change your readiness.
outcomes.actions_b: Stop proposal hints and repeated timeline checks until the agreed date, while clarifying your own needs privately.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Marriage Information Phase with no-pressure rules, reflection questions, outside facts, end date, and next-step options.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Curiosity gets a deadline, and pressure loses its disguise.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = less ready to discuss marriage; [B] = more ready.
outcomes.verdict: [A] retreats because the conversation feels like a request for certainty that is not available. [B] pushes because silence feels like being asked to invest indefinitely without knowing the direction. That loop makes both people less safe and less informed. Replace spontaneous check-ins with a monthly marriage conversation for three months, each with one topic: meaning, fears, then conditions and timing. At the end, decide whether you have a shared path, more information to gather, or a core mismatch to face.
outcomes.actions_a: Show up to each scheduled topic with direct answers and stop using delay to avoid naming hard limits.
outcomes.actions_b: Keep marriage questions inside the scheduled talks and stop seeking reassurance between them.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Three-Conversation Marriage Series with monthly dates, topics, individual notes, unresolved items, and final direction decision.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. A steady process replaces the chase and retreat.

It means you have a shared compass, which is most useful when the actual map gets messy. Turn the priority into a measurable filter: minimum income, maximum housing cost, travel time, support access, or daily quality standard. A value becomes a decision tool only when it can eliminate an attractive city that fails real life.

outcomes.actions_b: Choose a second factor that should challenge the leader if a city looks good on paper but weak in practice.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Long-Term Location Scorecard with lead factor, thresholds, deal-breakers, secondary checks, and three candidate places.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Your shared compass gets numbers strong enough to guide an actual move.

outcomes.verdict: You agree on the leading factor, but it carries more emotional or practical weight than the simple label reveals. Family support may mean childcare to one person and belonging to the other. Affordability may mean freedom for one and protection from past instability for the other. Before ranking cities, define what the priority is supposed to provide. Then compare places by that outcome, not by reputation. The same word can hide two different needs, and a city must serve both if it is going to feel mutual.
outcomes.actions_a: Describe the lived outcome you expect the leading factor to create in an ordinary week.
outcomes.actions_b: Describe your own outcome and identify where it differs from [A]'s even though the category matches.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Priority Meaning Sheet with each person's desired outcome, proof points, hidden risks, candidate cities, and visit questions.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. The shared priority gets defined deeply enough to protect both lives.

outcomes.role_note: [A] and [B] chose different leading factors with relatively light emotional weight.
outcomes.verdict: [A] is optimizing the engine of the future, perhaps income, career, or practical stability. [B] is optimizing the place where that future has to feel worth living, perhaps community, lifestyle, or support. Because the stakes are not emotionally overheated, you can test both facts instead of debating which value sounds more adult. Build a shortlist only from cities that clear a minimum in both categories, then let the remaining factors break the tie.
outcomes.actions_a: Set a realistic minimum for your factor and bring evidence for three possible locations.
outcomes.actions_b: Set a separate minimum for your factor and remove any location that fails it, including your favorite.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Two-Minimum City Shortlist with each threshold, evidence links, eliminated options, finalists, and decision weekend.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. The future needs an engine and a place you both want to wake up.

outcomes.role_note: [A] and [B] chose different leading factors with high emotional weight.
outcomes.verdict: [A]'s location priority protects something foundational, such as career identity, financial safety, or access to care. [B]'s different priority protects belonging, family connection, daily wellbeing, or a life that does not feel borrowed. Averaging scores may hide a painful trade where one person wins on paper and the other loses every Tuesday. Give each partner one nonnegotiable floor, then compare only places that pass both. If none do, set a dated temporary location with an exit condition instead of pretending the compromise is permanent.
outcomes.actions_a: Name the minimum your life genuinely requires and distinguish it from preferences that can flex.
outcomes.actions_b: Name your own floor and propose what a fair temporary solution would need to protect.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Two-Floors Location Plan with nonnegotiables, flexible wants, viable places, temporary option, exit condition, and review date.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Neither partner has to disappear inside the winning city.

Mostly good, with a few unresolved details

The process is creating major strain

Location or long-term plans
Repair and maintenance responsibility
What happens if the relationship or housing need changes

A shared emergency and repair reserve

A rent-versus-buy comparison
A neighborhood trial
A clear exit and buyout process

outcomes.verdict: You are moving toward or away from homeownership at a similar pace, which protects the relationship from one person becoming the dreamer and the other the permanent brake. Caution can be discussed as design work rather than doubt about the couple. Use this window to define what a home must not cost you: emergency security, career flexibility, rest, or the ability to leave fairly. A house is supportive only when the ownership plan supports both people too.
outcomes.actions_a: Name one financial condition that must stay healthy after closing, not just on closing day.
outcomes.actions_b: Name one legal or lifestyle protection that would make shared ownership feel durable.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Home Readiness Standard with monthly cap, reserves, ownership shares, repair duties, location needs, and exit terms.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Similar readiness becomes a shared definition of safe ownership.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = less satisfied with the home-buying process; [B] = more content.
outcomes.verdict: [A] and [B] have similar readiness, but [A] may be carrying the less visible risk: a smaller emergency cushion, weaker credit, more cash in the down payment, or less protection in the title structure. [B] sees a sensible shared pace because the process looks balanced from the outside. Readiness should be measured after the deal, not only before it. Model what each person owns, owes, and can still access once the keys arrive.
outcomes.actions_a: Identify the specific post-closing vulnerability that makes the current plan feel unsafe.
outcomes.actions_b: Adjust one contribution, reserve, or ownership term so [A] is not asked to absorb that vulnerability silently.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save an After-Closing Snapshot with each person's cash left, monthly duty, ownership share, repair reserve, and exit access.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. The keys do not arrive by emptying one partner's safety net.

outcomes.verdict: You are close in readiness, yet the process feels overwhelming because home buying has bundled six decisions into one emotional headline. Separate affordability, ownership, location, maintenance, timing, and exit. Give each topic a pass, not yet, or needs expert input. You may discover that the relationship is ready while the market is not, or that the money works while the legal setup does not. Precision gives hesitation somewhere useful to go.
outcomes.actions_a: Own the affordability and reserve review using real monthly numbers instead of listing prices.
outcomes.actions_b: Own the ownership and exit questions and identify where legal or professional advice is needed.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Six-Part Home Buying Gate with topic status, evidence, expert questions, task owner, and next review date.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. One giant fear becomes six answerable decisions.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = more hesitant about buying; [B] = more ready.
outcomes.verdict: [A] is inspecting the foundation before letting the relationship pour money into concrete. [B] is ready to build equity, stability, or a place that finally feels like yours. You are content because the inspection is not being treated as sabotage and the vision is not being treated as recklessness. Let [B] lead market exploration while [A] owns the readiness gate. No offer happens until the written financial, legal, and location conditions pass.
outcomes.actions_a: Define the readiness gate with measurable conditions and avoid adding new requirements after they are met.
outcomes.actions_b: Research homes within those conditions and treat browsing as information, not a countdown to an offer.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Browse Versus Buy rule with readiness gate, search range, viewing purpose, offer authority, and reevaluation date.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. The dream can browse while the foundation still gets tested.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = more hesitant and dissatisfied; [B] = more ready and content.
outcomes.verdict: [A] experiences the process as momentum toward a debt and ownership structure that does not yet feel safe. [B] experiences progress, perhaps because current rent feels wasteful or the market feels urgent. The pressure of rates or listings is landing more heavily on [A]'s nervous system and finances. Set a no-offer period with a fixed end date. During it, [B] gathers market facts and [A] completes the protection plan. The pause has work inside it, so it is neither delay nor surrender.
outcomes.actions_a: Complete the financial, ownership, and exit conditions you need by the end of the no-offer period.
outcomes.actions_b: Gather comparable costs and viable options without requesting offers, deposits, or emotional promises during the pause.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a No-Offer Preparation Month with tasks, market facts, protection plan, expert appointments, end date, and decision options.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. The process pauses commitment while continuing to build real information.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = more hesitant about buying; [B] = more ready.
outcomes.verdict: [A] may fear that buying will lock in financial exposure, location, and a difficult exit. [B] may fear that waiting will keep the couple paying rent and postponing stability forever. Arguing about whether buying is good cannot answer whether this purchase is good. Choose one realistic property profile and run it through three futures: stay together, one income interruption, and a sale or buyout. If the plan survives all three, readiness becomes less personal and more factual.
outcomes.actions_a: Build the income-interruption and exit scenarios with the protections you would need.
outcomes.actions_b: Build the ordinary ownership scenario with true monthly costs, repairs, and time horizon.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Three-Futures Home Model with normal costs, income shock, sale or buyout, reserves, ownership, and decision date.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. The home earns trust by surviving more than the best-case future.

cases.title: How Should a Job Offer in Another City Actually Get Decided?

Whether the move remains reversible

options.label: It should decide unless there is a deal-breaker
It should lead but not decide alone
It should be equal with two or three other factors
It matters, but the whole picture should stay open

questions.prompt: Anything the court should know about the offer, city, deadline, or person who would be giving more up? (optional)

outcomes.verdict: You agree on the factor that should lead and neither person is currently treating the offer as a relationship emergency. That calm gives you room to test whether the headline survives the first-year math. A salary can look bigger while housing, travel, lost income, and setup erase the gain. A career leap can still be worth it, but the decision should name who benefits now and who is investing for later. Shared excitement becomes fairer when the investment has terms.
outcomes.actions_a: Translate the leading factor into one measurable success target for the first year.
outcomes.actions_b: Identify the largest hidden cost and the protection or negotiation that should cover it.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save an Offer Decision Brief with lead factor, first-year math, hidden costs, success target, negotiation asks, and answer date.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. The offer gets judged by the life it creates, not the title alone.

outcomes.verdict: You agree on the decision lens, but it carries serious weight because the offer could reorder both lives. The same priority may still point to different answers. Career upside can mean title growth to one person and long-term family security to the other. Reversibility can mean a trial year to one and a guaranteed path home to the other. Define the evidence that would make each of you say yes, not yet, or no before the deadline compresses the conversation.
outcomes.actions_a: Write the evidence you need for each of the three answers and identify one question only the employer can resolve.
outcomes.actions_b: Write your own thresholds and identify the personal cost that must receive a concrete protection.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Yes, Not Yet, No offer matrix with thresholds, employer questions, personal costs, protections, and response deadline.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Shared values become clear decision thresholds before urgency takes over.

outcomes.role_note: [A] and [B] chose different leading factors with relatively light emotional weight.
outcomes.verdict: [A] is evaluating what the offer builds, such as income, expertise, or future options. [B] is evaluating what the move consumes, such as community, career continuity, or daily quality. Those are not rival opinions. They are the two sides of the return. Calculate a first-year return that includes both partners' gains and losses, then decide what must be negotiated before acceptance. A good offer should be strong enough to fund the transition it asks the couple to make.
outcomes.actions_a: Quantify the career and financial upside, including when it is likely to become real.
outcomes.actions_b: Quantify the relocation and life costs, then turn the largest ones into specific negotiation requests.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Couple Return on Offer sheet with gains, losses, timing, negotiation asks, walk-away line, and answer date.

outcomes.role_note: [A] and [B] chose different leading factors with high emotional weight.
outcomes.verdict: [A]'s priority protects a rare opening that may not return. [B]'s priority protects a life, career, or support system that cannot be packed into boxes. A scorecard alone may turn the larger sacrifice into a low number on someone else's opportunity. Use a consent gate and a compensation plan. The move proceeds only if both partners can freely agree, and the person giving up more receives named money, time, career support, and an exit route. Consent needs resources behind it.
outcomes.actions_a: Name the minimum value the offer must create and the support you can commit to the relocating partner.
outcomes.actions_b: Name the losses you cannot accept and the concrete protections that could make consent possible.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save an Offer Consent Package with opportunity value, sacrifice list, protections, employer asks, exit route, and final answer appointment.

cases.title: Who's More Willing to Compromise Their Career for the Relationship?

options.label: It feels mutual and respected

options.label: Turning down a role or promotion

Changing fields or pausing work
Relocating or accepting a worse commute
Taking on more home or caregiving work
Giving up income, benefits, or retirement growth

questions.prompt: What should make a compromise fair?

options.label: A clear end date
Financial recognition and protection
A future turn for my career
Active support rebuilding momentum
The choice stays genuinely voluntary
The relationship benefit is specific and shared

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: Anything the court should know about the opportunity, sacrifice, or repeated pattern behind your answer? (optional)
questions.interactionRule: Private context is used only to personalize the selected deterministic branch.

outcomes.verdict: You share a similar willingness to let career serve the relationship without letting it disappear inside the relationship. That balance suggests compromise is being treated as a strategic choice, not proof that one ambition matters less. Reciprocity protects this balance over time because equal sacrifice rarely happens in the same year. Keep a visible record of whose work bent, what the couple gained, and when the next major decision should restore room to that person's career.
outcomes.actions_a: Name one compromise you could make freely and the limit that would keep it from becoming identity loss.
outcomes.actions_b: Name how you would protect [A]'s momentum during that compromise and what future priority you would honor.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Career Flex Ledger with past compromises, shared gains, time limits, protections, rebuild steps, and next-priority partner.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Flexibility stays loving because it does not become invisible.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = less satisfied with the balance of career compromise; [B] = more content.
outcomes.verdict: [A] and [B] sound similarly willing, but [A] may have already spent more of that willingness. A commute change, missed promotion, reduced hours, or extra home load can become the relationship's normal operating system while [B] still experiences mutual flexibility in theory. Stop measuring attitude and audit history. If one career has bent more, the next available resource should restore that person's time, training, networking, or decision priority.
outcomes.actions_a: List the compromises you have already made and identify the one career resource that would repair the greatest loss.
outcomes.actions_b: Acknowledge the history without comparing intentions, then fund or protect that resource on a calendar.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Career Compromise Audit with past changes, lost value, shared benefit, repair resource, owner, and delivery date.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Willingness is measured by what each career has actually carried.

outcomes.verdict: You are similarly willing, yet both careers feel underfed. That usually means the relationship keeps solving short-term pressure by taking small pieces from work, while no one owns the long-term repair. Choose a protected season for each career. During one defined period, [A]'s growth goal gets priority and [B]'s minimum protections stay intact. Then switch or reassess. Sequencing is not permanent hierarchy. It is a way to stop both people from compromising at the same time until neither recognizes the plan.
outcomes.actions_a: Define one six-month career goal and the specific household support it requires.
outcomes.actions_b: Define your minimum protection during [A]'s season and the goal you want considered in the following season.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Career Seasons Plan with first-priority goal, support duties, protected minimums, checkpoint, and next-season decision.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Careers take turns receiving real oxygen instead of sharing a permanent shortage.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = less willing to compromise career; [B] = more willing.
outcomes.verdict: [A] treats career continuity as a core source of identity, security, or future freedom. [B] has more flexibility and sees work as one part of a life that can be reshaped around the relationship. You are content because those differences are not being moralized. Protect [A]'s hard boundary while making sure [B]'s flexibility earns concrete support, not automatic assignment to every move, caregiving gap, or domestic need. Voluntary compromise must remain a choice each time.
outcomes.actions_a: State the career boundary you need and name the resource you will contribute when [B] flexes instead.
outcomes.actions_b: Define which compromises you can offer freely and which would require a time limit, repayment, or future priority.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Career Boundary and Flexibility Map with hard limits, voluntary options, support exchange, end dates, and future priority.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. One career keeps continuity, and the more flexible career keeps its full value.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = less willing to compromise and is content; [B] = more willing and dissatisfied.
outcomes.verdict: [A] has successfully protected career continuity. [B] has repeatedly made room, but that generosity may now feel like an unpaid relationship job. [A] experiences stability; [B] experiences accumulated opportunity cost. The next repair should not be another abstract promise of appreciation. [A] owes one new habit or resource that rebuilds [B]'s career, such as protected hours, funded training, networking travel, or priority on the next location decision.
outcomes.actions_a: Choose one career-rebuilding commitment for [B], fund it, and place it on the calendar.
outcomes.actions_b: Name the specific momentum you want restored and stop offering new compromises during the repair period.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Career Rebuild Contract with lost momentum, chosen resource, protected time, cost, start date, and progress check.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Flexibility receives a real repayment instead of another thank-you.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = less willing to compromise career; [B] = more willing.
outcomes.verdict: [A] fears that bending career will create lasting dependence or regret. [B] fears that refusing to bend means the relationship will always organize around [A]'s work. The debate keeps asking who should sacrifice, which makes every solution feel like a loss. Divide the problem by function. Protect [A]'s career continuity, then give [B] control over another high-impact variable such as location, household outsourcing, schedule design, or the next major career turn. Fairness can be distributed across decisions instead of forced into one identical sacrifice.
outcomes.actions_a: Name the continuity you cannot give up and offer two other decision areas where [B] can hold real priority.

outcomes.verdict: You are close on timing, yet both of you feel stuck because the start date is carrying every prerequisite at once. Perfect savings, housing, career stability, health, and confidence may never line up on the same Tuesday. Sort conditions into must have, actively building, and nice to have. Then choose a date to review readiness using those categories. The date is not an order to proceed. It is a promise that preparation will produce a decision instead of expanding forever.
outcomes.actions_a: Sort your conditions into the three levels and explain why each must-have truly belongs there.
outcomes.actions_b: Do the same, then take ownership of one actively-building condition with a deadline.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Must Have, Building, Nice to Have board with owners, evidence, review date, and proceed or wait options.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Preparation gains a finish line without pretending certainty can be perfect.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = prefers a later timeline; [B] = prefers an earlier timeline.
outcomes.verdict: [A] wants more runway for money, identity, career, relationship stability, or simple readiness. [B] feels time more urgently, whether because of health, age, life vision, or the emotional cost of waiting. You are content because both realities can be spoken without turning them into selfishness. Set a midpoint information date, not a forced start date. Before then, gather medical or process facts, price the plan, and test the parenting-work assumptions. Then decide with better information and full respect for bodily autonomy.
outcomes.actions_a: Name what the additional time would concretely build and begin one step now rather than relying on delay alone.
outcomes.actions_b: Name the source of urgency and gather the facts that distinguish a real constraint from generalized fear.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Family Timing Information Plan with later-goal needs, urgency facts, appointments, budget work, workload questions, and decision date.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Time becomes information and preparation, not leverage.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = prefers a later timeline and is content; [B] = prefers an earlier timeline and is dissatisfied.
outcomes.verdict: [A] benefits from the current delay because it creates more time to prepare or remain unchanged. [B] absorbs the cost of waiting and may feel asked to stay hopeful without an endpoint. The relationship cannot promise a specific reproductive outcome, but it can stop making uncertainty one-sided. [A] owes a dated decision process with active preparation. [B] owes honest boundaries about how long waiting remains emotionally and practically possible, without using them as threats.
outcomes.actions_a: Commit to concrete preparation tasks and a decision date that you will not move without a serious new fact.
outcomes.actions_b: State your personal timeline boundary and the support you need while the process runs.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Waiting Has Terms agreement with preparation tasks, health or adoption facts, personal limits, decision date, and outcome options.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Waiting stops being free for one person and indefinite for the other.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = prefers a later timeline; [B] = prefers an earlier timeline.
outcomes.verdict: [A] fears entering parenthood before enough stability or desire is present. [B] fears that the chance, energy, or life plan may disappear while the relationship keeps preparing. A compromise date can still be coercive if either person is not freely ready. Treat this as a high-stakes compatibility and information process. Gather medical or adoption facts, complete a real workload and budget plan, and consider a qualified couples counselor. Then face the remaining difference directly rather than promising that love will erase it.
outcomes.actions_a: State the earliest timeline you could freely choose and what must become true before then.
outcomes.actions_b: State the latest timeline you can genuinely accept and which constraints make it meaningful.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Family Timing Decision Plan with earliest and latest windows, facts needed, counselor option, preparation tasks, and final conversation date.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Clarity protects both futures better than a pressured calendar compromise.

cases.title: Who's More Willing to Live Far From Their Own Family?
cases.subtitle: How willing are you to live far from your own family for the life you are building together?

questions.prompt: How willing are you to live far from your own family for the life you are building together?

options.label: Very unwilling, staying close is a core need
Only with strong support and frequent visits
Open to it for the right location or season
Quite willing if the shared life works better
Very willing, distance from family is manageable for me

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: How do you feel about the way family distance is weighed in your shared plans?

options.label: Both families and both needs are respected
Mostly fair, with a few future concerns
One person's family ties carry more weight
The imbalance feels lonely or unsustainable

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: What would distance change most?

options.label: Everyday emotional support
Caregiving for parents or relatives
Help with children or emergencies
Cultural, language, or holiday connection
Travel cost and available time off
My sense of identity and belonging

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: What would make distance more workable?

options.label: A protected travel budget
Scheduled extended visits
A plan for family emergencies
Living near another support network
Remote-work flexibility
A date to reconsider the location

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: Anything the court should know about caregiving, family closeness, distance, or whose side is currently nearer? (optional)
questions.interactionRule: Private context is used only to personalize the selected deterministic branch.

outcomes.verdict: You have a similar relationship to distance from family, so location decisions are less likely to cast one person as independent and the other as overly attached. You can plan connection as a shared responsibility. Distance works because of budgets, calendars, emergency routes, and local support, not because everyone promises to call more. Build those structures while things are calm, especially if aging parents, children, or limited time off could change the equation quickly.
outcomes.actions_a: Name the family connection that needs a protected rhythm and the realistic cost of maintaining it.
outcomes.actions_b: Name one emergency or caregiving change that should automatically reopen the location plan.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Family Distance Plan with visit rhythm, travel budget, call routine, emergency triggers, local support, and review date.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Family closeness gets infrastructure instead of relying on good intentions.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = less satisfied with how family distance is handled; [B] = more content.
outcomes.verdict: [A] and [B] are similarly willing to live far away, but [A] may be paying more of the distance bill in loneliness, travel planning, caregiving worry, or missed cultural moments. [B] sees the arrangement as broadly workable because the connection cost is less visible or lands elsewhere. Audit not only flights, but who remembers, schedules, hosts, and recovers after visits. Shared geography should come with shared maintenance of the family ties it stretches.
outcomes.actions_a: List the practical and emotional work you carry to keep family connection alive from a distance.
outcomes.actions_b: Take ownership of one recurring planning task and one travel or hosting responsibility.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Family Connection Worklist with calls, visits, hosting, travel costs, task owners, and next six dates.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. The miles stop creating a second job for one partner.

outcomes.verdict: You are close in willingness, yet the current distance still feels bad because willingness cannot replace a support system. Holidays, emergencies, childcare, cultural life, and ordinary companionship may all be asking the relationship to cover roles a wider network once held. Decide whether the repair belongs in travel, a stronger local circle, extended stays, or a location change. Then fund one lane seriously for six months. Missing family is not a failure to adapt; it is information about what your shared life needs around it.
outcomes.actions_a: Choose the missing form of support that hurts most and propose one realistic replacement or reconnection step.
outcomes.actions_b: Choose the resource, time, or social effort you can commit to making that step sustainable.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Six-Month Support Rebuild with missing support, chosen lane, budget, recurring actions, owner, and review date.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Distance gets answered with a support plan, not a demand to miss people more quietly.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = less willing to live far from family; [B] = more willing.
outcomes.verdict: [A] experiences family proximity as part of daily wellbeing, caregiving duty, culture, or future support. [B] can carry connection across distance and may value the career, affordability, or freedom available elsewhere. You are content because roots and mobility are both treated as legitimate. Keep the arrangement fair by pricing the distance: travel money, time off, longer visits, and emergency access. If those supports cannot be funded, the location decision needs to reopen rather than asking [A] to absorb the gap emotionally.
outcomes.actions_a: Define the minimum contact and emergency access that makes distance livable rather than merely tolerable.
outcomes.actions_b: Help fund and protect that minimum, while naming the location benefits the arrangement is meant to preserve.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Livable Distance Agreement with contact minimums, travel budget, extended visits, emergency plan, location benefits, and review trigger.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Mobility stays valuable because connection is not expected to survive on leftovers.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = less willing and dissatisfied; [B] = more willing and content.
outcomes.verdict: [A] may feel that [B]'s easier relationship with distance has become the couple's default, while [A] carries homesickness, care anxiety, or the fear of missing irreplaceable time. [B] feels the current location works and may see visits as an adequate solution. The benefit of staying currently lands more with [B], while the family loss lands more with [A]. [B] owes a recurring connection budget and one habit of sharing the logistics. [A] owes clarity about the minimum that would genuinely help.
outcomes.actions_a: Name the visit rhythm, emergency access, and contact pattern that would materially reduce the loss.
outcomes.actions_b: Fund and schedule one recurring part of that plan, including taking ownership of bookings or hosting work.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Distance Repair Calendar with visit dates, budget, booking owner, family calls, emergency travel rule, and three-month check.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. The location keeps its benefits while distance stops being one person's private bill.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = less willing to live far from family; [B] = more willing.
outcomes.verdict: [A] may experience distance as disconnection from care, identity, and people whose time cannot be postponed. [B] may experience moving closer as losing career options, affordability, autonomy, or the life the couple built. Neither loss becomes smaller through another abstract debate. Set a location review date and compare three real models: stay with stronger connection support, move closer, or choose a middle location. Price each model in money, time, career, care, and daily wellbeing before deciding.
outcomes.actions_a: Build the move-closer model with real housing, work, care, and support outcomes.
outcomes.actions_b: Build the stay model with a funded connection plan, then help research one middle-location option.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Three-Location Family Distance Review with costs, careers, support, caregiving, visits, wellbeing, and decision date.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. The next choice compares livable lives, not who should care less.

cases.title: How Should You Actually Handle a Major Health Decision That Affects You Both?
cases.subtitle: Which principle should lead a major health decision that changes both of your lives?

questions.prompt: Which principle should lead a major health decision that changes both of your lives?

options.label: The patient's bodily autonomy and informed choice
The medical outcome and urgency
The effect on caregiving, work, and shared life
The option that preserves the most future flexibility
A decision process supported by qualified medical guidance

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: How much weight should that principle carry?

options.label: It should decide unless safety changes
It should lead while the other impacts stay visible
It should be balanced with two or three other factors
No single principle should dominate

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: What must not get lost in the decision?

options.label: The patient's consent
Clear medical facts and alternatives
The caregiver's real capacity
Money, leave, and daily logistics
Mental health and quality of life
A plan if the first option does not work

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: What would make the process feel safer?

options.label: A second medical opinion
Separate questions from each partner
A written care and work plan
A defined decision deadline
Support from a counselor or patient advocate
Clear roles during appointments

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: Anything the court should know about the health issue, urgency, autonomy, or caregiving impact? (optional)
questions.interactionRule: Private context is used only to personalize the selected deterministic branch.

outcomes.verdict: You agree on the principle that should lead, and the decision is not currently splitting the relationship into patient versus partner. That gives you a strong base: medical authority can stay with the person whose body is involved while shared-life consequences stay discussable. Write down which choice belongs to the patient, which facts both people need, and which caregiving commitments require an honest capacity check. Support becomes more trustworthy when consent and logistics are never confused.
outcomes.actions_a: Name the decision that belongs to your body or your support role, and list the information you still need.
outcomes.actions_b: Name the practical impact you can carry and the limit you need to state before care begins.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Health Decision Roles page with patient authority, shared facts, care capacity, appointment questions, and backup plan.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Care stays close without crossing the line into control.

outcomes.verdict: You share the leading principle, but the health decision carries more weight than that agreement can absorb by itself. The patient may hear urgency as pressure; the partner may hear uncertainty as a threat to the future you share. Give the medical choice and the relationship impact separate conversations. One establishes informed consent. The other plans caregiving, money, work, and emotional support around the choice that is actually made.
outcomes.actions_a: Prepare the medical questions and name what kind of support helps you think clearly.
outcomes.actions_b: Prepare an honest capacity statement covering time, money, care tasks, and emotional limits.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save two linked notes titled Medical Choice and Shared-Life Plan, with owners, facts, support limits, and dates.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. The body gets autonomy, and the relationship gets a realistic care plan.

outcomes.verdict: [A] is protecting the steering wheel, making sure the person receiving care keeps informed control. [B] is watching the dashboard, where work, money, caregiving, and future plans show the effects on both people. These are different facts, not competing rights. Let the patient make the medical choice after qualified guidance, then let both partners design the support plan and state what help is realistically available.
outcomes.actions_a: Identify the choice that must remain voluntary and the medical fact needed before making it.
outcomes.actions_b: Identify the shared consequence that needs planning and one resource that can reduce it.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Choice and Consequence map with patient decision, medical facts, shared impacts, support resources, and review date.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. One person owns the medical choice, and both people prepare for its real-life effects.
outcomes.role_note: [A] and [B] chose different leading principles with relatively manageable emotional weight.

outcomes.verdict: [A]'s principle protects consent, safety, or the best medical chance. [B]'s principle protects the caregiver's capacity, financial stability, or a future that may be reshaped by the outcome. High stakes can make either person feel erased. Use a supported decision process: collect medical guidance, let the patient state the choice without bargaining, then build a care plan the partner can freely commit to. If care needs exceed that capacity, add professional or community support instead of turning love into an unlimited obligation.
outcomes.actions_a: State your decision rights, fears, and the support you can accept without feeling managed.
outcomes.actions_b: State your care capacity, nonnegotiable limits, and the outside help needed beyond that line.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Supported Health Decision plan with medical options, patient choice, care limits, outside resources, and emergency contacts.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Autonomy and dependable care both get protected in plain language.
outcomes.role_note: [A] and [B] chose different leading principles with high emotional weight.

cases.title: Who's More Ready for the Relationship to Look Different in the Next Chapter?
cases.subtitle: How ready are you for the relationship's routines, roles, or priorities to change in the next chapter?

questions.prompt: How ready are you for the relationship's routines, roles, or priorities to change in the next chapter?

options.label: I want to preserve life mostly as it is
I can accept limited changes with strong continuity
I am open to a planned transition
I am ready for meaningful changes
I actively want the next chapter to look different

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: How do you feel about the way change is being discussed and paced?

options.label: It works for me
Mostly okay, with a few rough moments
It regularly leaves me tense or disconnected
I need this pattern to change

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: Which change feels most real?

options.label: Where or how you live
Career or school demands
Family or caregiving roles
Money and shared responsibilities
Time, intimacy, or social life
Health, identity, or personal growth

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: What would help the transition?

options.label: A part of the old routine that stays
A short trial before permanence
Clear new roles
A date for the change
More individual space
A regular check on how both people are doing

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: Anything the court should know about the next chapter, the change you want, or what you fear losing? (optional)
questions.interactionRule: Private context is used only to personalize the selected deterministic branch.

outcomes.verdict: You are meeting the next chapter with a similar level of openness. That does more than reduce resistance. It lets you decide what deserves reinvention and what should remain recognizably yours. Choose one anchor from the current relationship, one role that needs updating, and one experiment for the future. Change feels intimate when both people can recognize the relationship inside it, not when every old routine is treated as baggage.
outcomes.actions_a: Choose the relationship anchor you most want to preserve and explain the need it serves.
outcomes.actions_b: Choose one outdated routine or role and propose a realistic replacement.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Keep, Change, Try page with one anchor, one role update, one experiment, and a thirty-day check.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. The next chapter grows without erasing the parts that already feel like home.

outcomes.verdict: [A] and [B] show similar readiness, but [A] is not experiencing the process as equally secure. [A] may be losing more routine, identity, or decision power while [B] sees a shared transition. The gap is not enthusiasm. It is whose version of normal gets edited. List what changes for each partner in an ordinary week, then give the person absorbing more disruption one protected anchor and one real choice over implementation.
outcomes.actions_a: Name the weekly routine, role, or identity marker you fear losing in the transition.
outcomes.actions_b: Give [A] ownership of one implementation decision and help protect the named anchor.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Next-Chapter Impact Grid with each change, who absorbs it, protected anchors, decision owners, and check-in date.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Similar readiness now comes with a fairer share of authorship.
outcomes.role_note: [A] = less content with the current transition process; [B] = more content.

outcomes.verdict: You are close in readiness, yet the future still feels unsettled because next chapter is too vague to plan. One of you may picture new priorities while the other pictures a new location, household, or pace. Describe a normal Tuesday one year from now before discussing the big label again. Daily details will expose the choices hiding inside the phrase and show where your visions already overlap.
outcomes.actions_a: Write a one-year Tuesday from waking up through bedtime, including work, home, and time together.
outcomes.actions_b: Write your own version independently and mark the three details you care about most.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save two Future Tuesday notes plus a shared list of overlaps, conflicts, experiments, and a decision date.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. The next chapter becomes a life you can compare instead of a mood you keep debating.

outcomes.verdict: [A] wants more continuity because stability, identity, or a hard-won routine still matters. [B] is ready for a larger shift and may see change as the path to growth rather than a threat to closeness. You are content because neither pace is being graded as more committed. Sequence the transition. Keep a protected anchor first, test one meaningful change second, and expand only after a scheduled check shows both people still feel like themselves.
outcomes.actions_a: Choose the anchor that must stay intact during the first stage and the signal that shows you feel secure.
outcomes.actions_b: Choose one change small enough to test but meaningful enough to teach you something.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Three-Stage Chapter Plan with anchor, first experiment, success signals, expansion choice, and checkpoint dates.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Change earns trust one stage at a time.
outcomes.role_note: [A] = wants more continuity; [B] = wants more change.

outcomes.verdict: [A] wants more continuity and feels the current plan is already leaving the station. [B] wants larger change and feels fine because movement matches [B]'s preferred future. The ticket cost is landing unevenly. Freeze any irreversible step until [A] names the actual loss and [B] names the actual gain. Then choose a reversible pilot with a return route. A trial can create evidence without making hesitation fight permanence.
outcomes.actions_a: Define the loss you need the pilot to protect against and the condition for ending it.
outcomes.actions_b: Define the benefit the pilot should produce and stop treating participation as a promise of permanent change.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Reversible Chapter Pilot with change, protected anchor, expected gain, return route, start date, and review.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. The relationship tests a new direction without locking the door behind it.
outcomes.role_note: [A] = wants more continuity and is dissatisfied; [B] = wants more change and is content.

outcomes.verdict: [A] is protecting continuity because too much change at once feels like losing the relationship while still being in it. [B] is pushing for reinvention because staying the same feels like giving up on growth. More persuasion will only make stability feel like stagnation and change feel like abandonment. Hold a monthly chapter meeting for three months, each focused on one domain: daily life, roles, then future direction. Decide after the pattern is visible, not during the loudest moment.
outcomes.actions_a: Prepare the continuity needs and the changes you can test without resentment.
outcomes.actions_b: Prepare the growth needs and the current routines you are willing to preserve.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Three-Meeting Chapter Series with monthly topics, each partner's needs, experiments, findings, and final direction date.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. The future gets built through evidence, not a contest between comfort and growth.
outcomes.role_note: [A] = wants more continuity; [B] = wants more change.

cases.title: How Should You Actually Decide to End a Lease or Buy Property Together?
cases.subtitle: Which factor should lead the decision to end a lease or buy property together?

questions.prompt: Which factor should lead the decision to end a lease or buy property together?

options.label: True monthly affordability
Readiness for a longer commitment
The quality and stability of the location
Ownership fairness and legal protection
Whether buying improves your actual life versus renting
The cost and flexibility of each exit route

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: How much weight should that factor carry?

options.label: It should decide unless a deal-breaker appears
It should lead while other protections stay firm
It should be equal with several other factors
No factor should lead until the full plan is tested

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: What could make the exciting option a bad fit?

options.label: Draining savings for the upfront cost
Unequal ownership after unequal contributions
A location that limits one partner
Repairs and fees changing the real payment
A difficult sale, buyout, or lease exit
Buying mainly because it feels like progress

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: What should happen before notice or an offer?

options.label: Compare total rent and ownership costs
Get financing and credit facts
Write contribution and ownership terms
Test the location and commute
Price repairs and reserves
Agree on sale, buyout, or break-lease steps

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: Anything the court should know about the lease date, property, contribution gap, or pressure to decide? (optional)
questions.interactionRule: Private context is used only to personalize the selected deterministic branch.

outcomes.verdict: You agree on the factor that should lead and the choice is not currently carrying a heavy emotional split. Use that calm to test whether the next home improves your real life instead of merely looking like progress. Compare the full cost, time horizon, location, ownership, and exit. A shared address is a good decision when it protects ordinary Tuesdays and difficult endings, not only the day you sign.
outcomes.actions_a: Turn the shared priority into one measurable threshold that a property or lease plan must pass.
outcomes.actions_b: Choose the strongest secondary filter and collect the evidence needed to challenge an exciting option.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Rent, Exit, or Buy scorecard with thresholds, total costs, ownership terms, location test, and decision date.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. The next address has to work after the milestone feeling wears off.

outcomes.verdict: You share the leading rule, but the decision carries serious weight because one move can bind money, location, and exit rights for years. Agreement on affordability may hide different definitions of safe. Agreement on commitment may hide different expectations about ownership. Translate the shared rule into numbers and documents, then stress-test it against one income loss and one early exit. The plan should still look fair when life stops cooperating.
outcomes.actions_a: Define the safe threshold from your income, reserves, and likely responsibilities after signing.
outcomes.actions_b: Define the ownership or exit protection that must survive an income shock or relationship change.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Housing Stress Test with full cost, reserves, ownership, one-income scenario, early exit, and go or wait date.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Shared readiness gets measured in the scenarios that put it under pressure.

outcomes.verdict: [A] is protecting one part of the housing decision, such as flexibility, affordability, or location. [B] is protecting another, such as equity, commitment, or legal fairness. Because the emotional weight is manageable, you can make both priorities earn their place. Build a shortlist only from options that clear each partner's minimum, then compare the remaining choices by total five-year cost and daily-life fit.
outcomes.actions_a: Set a minimum for your priority and remove any option that fails it, even if you like the rest.
outcomes.actions_b: Set a different minimum and gather the evidence required to apply it consistently.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Two-Minimum Housing Shortlist with thresholds, eliminated options, five-year cost, daily-life score, and deadline.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Two housing truths become filters instead of competing speeches.
outcomes.role_note: [A] and [B] chose different leading factors with relatively light emotional weight.

outcomes.verdict: [A]'s rule protects the foundation, perhaps cash safety, legal ownership, or freedom to exit. [B]'s rule protects the life built on top, perhaps stability, location, or a future that feels shared. High emotional weight means a simple average could conceal a major sacrifice. Require both floors to pass. If no option clears them before the lease deadline, choose a time-limited rental bridge rather than forcing property ownership to solve the relationship's urgency.
outcomes.actions_a: Name the nonnegotiable floor your financial or personal safety requires.
outcomes.actions_b: Name your own floor and design the shortest rental bridge that would preserve momentum without forcing the purchase.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Housing Floors and Bridge plan with two minimums, viable options, temporary lease terms, search tasks, and review date.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. The deadline gets a bridge, not permission to skip either partner's safety floor.
outcomes.role_note: [A] and [B] chose different leading factors with high emotional weight.

Moving or housing
Travel or personal goals
Family planning
Money or major purchases
Health, recovery, or personal growth
