questions.prompt: Anything the court should know about the personal timeline, shared goal, or sacrifice already made? (optional)
questions.interactionRule: Private context is used only to personalize the selected deterministic branch.

outcomes.verdict: You share a similar willingness to adjust personal timing, which means the shared future is not being built from one person's permanent waiting room. The strength is not equal delay in every season. It is confidence that a pause will be seen, bounded, and returned. Record which plan is slowing, what progress the pause buys, and when that plan regains priority. Generosity lasts longer when it has an end condition.
outcomes.actions_a: Name one personal plan you could slow freely and the limit that keeps the choice from becoming resentment.
outcomes.actions_b: Name the shared progress you would produce during that pause and how you would help restore momentum later.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Personal Plan Pause card with paused goal, shared purpose, end condition, support, and restoration date.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Flexibility stays loving because waiting has terms.

outcomes.verdict: [A] and [B] sound similarly willing, but [A] is less satisfied because willingness may already have become a job. [A] might be delaying applications, travel, education, or family goals while [B] experiences a shared pace. Audit what has actually moved. If one timeline has absorbed more delay, the next resource, decision window, or protected season should restore that person's plan before another sacrifice is requested.
outcomes.actions_a: List the plans you have already delayed and identify the one that most needs movement now.
outcomes.actions_b: Acknowledge the history and assign time, money, or decision priority to restart that plan.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Timeline Delay Audit with paused plans, dates, shared benefit, restoration resource, owner, and restart date.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Similar intentions now answer the actual history of who waited.
outcomes.role_note: [A] = less satisfied with the balance of delay; [B] = more content.

outcomes.verdict: You are similarly willing to slow down, yet both of you feel stalled because the shared future has no visible construction site. Waiting only feels meaningful when something is being built. Name the shared goal, assign two monthly progress markers, and decide which personal plan restarts if the markers are missed. A pause should create movement elsewhere, not become the relationship's default speed.
outcomes.actions_a: Define one measurable sign that the shared future is genuinely advancing this month.
outcomes.actions_b: Define a second marker and the personal plan that automatically restarts if progress stops.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Shared Future Progress Board with goal, monthly markers, task owners, pause limit, and restart trigger.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Waiting becomes an investment with visible returns.

outcomes.verdict: [A] protects personal momentum and knows some opportunities do not wait politely. [B] is more willing to slow down because synchronizing the relationship feels worth a temporary detour. You are content because flexibility is offered, not extracted. Keep [B]'s pause specific and give [A] a role in protecting the paused plan from disappearing. The faster-moving partner can keep moving without treating the other's patience as free infrastructure.
outcomes.actions_a: State the personal deadline you cannot move and the support you can give the plan that pauses.
outcomes.actions_b: State the exact pause, its end condition, and the minimum action that keeps your own goal alive.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Momentum and Pause agreement with protected deadline, paused plan, maintenance action, support, and return date.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. One timeline keeps moving while the other remains alive and respected.
outcomes.role_note: [A] = less willing to slow down; [B] = more willing.

outcomes.verdict: [A] protects personal timing and feels the current balance is fine. [B] has been more willing to slow down and is no longer okay with the cost. [A]'s momentum is partly supported by [B]'s deferred plans. The repair is not asking [A] to feel guilt. It is assigning one concrete new habit: protected time, funding, childcare, relocation priority, or a future decision window that restarts [B]'s path now.
outcomes.actions_a: Choose a resource you will transfer to [B]'s plan and put the commitment on the calendar.
outcomes.actions_b: Name the next milestone you want restored and pause any new sacrifices until it receives support.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Timeline Restoration Contract with delayed goal, support resource, protected hours, milestone, start date, and check-in.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. The shared future begins paying back the timeline that carried more of it.
outcomes.role_note: [A] = less willing and content; [B] = more willing and dissatisfied.

outcomes.verdict: [A] fears losing opportunities or identity by slowing down. [B] fears the relationship has no shared future if personal plans always move first. Pushing for equal sacrifice will only create two stalled lives. Divide the calendar into seasons. Protect [A]'s urgent deadline now, assign [B]'s goal the next protected window, and define what the couple builds in both seasons. Sequencing turns rivalry into a time-bound exchange.
outcomes.actions_a: Define the urgent deadline and the exact date when priority changes hands.
outcomes.actions_b: Define the goal for your protected season and the support that must already be prepared before it begins.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Two-Season Timeline with current priority, shared tasks, handoff date, next goal, support duties, and review.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Neither future disappears; they stop demanding the same month.
outcomes.role_note: [A] = less willing to slow down; [B] = more willing.

cases.title: How Ready Is Each of You to Support the Other Through a Major Life Change?
cases.subtitle: How much capacity do you currently have to support your partner through a major life change?

questions.prompt: How much capacity do you currently have to support your partner through a major life change?

options.label: Very little beyond basic care
Limited capacity with firm boundaries
Enough for defined support tasks
Strong capacity for a demanding season
A great deal, I can reorganize life around the transition for a while

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: How do you feel about the support expectations between you?

options.label: It works for me
Mostly okay, with a few rough moments
It regularly leaves me tense or disconnected
I need this pattern to change

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: What would use the most capacity?

options.label: Emotional reassurance
Extra household or caregiving work
Money or reduced income
Appointments, paperwork, or logistics
Giving up time and plans
Staying steady through uncertainty

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: What would make support sustainable?

options.label: A clear list of needed tasks
Outside professional or family help
A weekly capacity check
Protected rest for the supporter
A defined transition period
Permission to say what I cannot carry

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: Anything the court should know about the life change, current capacity, or support already being provided? (optional)
questions.interactionRule: Private context is used only to personalize the selected deterministic branch.

outcomes.verdict: You have a similar read on the support available, which means neither person is writing checks the household cannot cash. That honesty is a form of closeness. It allows care to be dependable instead of dramatic for one week and depleted the next. Match each need to a source: partner, family, friend, professional, workplace, or paid help. Your relationship stays central without pretending it must become the entire support system.
outcomes.actions_a: Name the support task you can carry consistently and the limit that protects your capacity.
outcomes.actions_b: Name a different need and identify an outside source before it becomes the partner's default assignment.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Support Network Map with needs, partner tasks, outside helpers, limits, emergency backup, and weekly check.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Honest capacity turns care into something both of you can trust.

outcomes.verdict: [A] and [B] estimate similar capacity, but [A] feels less secure because the support may be promised in broad language and delivered through invisible labor. [A] could be coordinating appointments, meals, emotions, and updates while [B] counts good intentions as participation. Replace supportive with named tasks. Assign owners, frequency, and a backup. The gap closes when care can be seen on the calendar and in the household.
outcomes.actions_a: List the invisible support work you expect or already carry and choose what needs reassignment.
outcomes.actions_b: Take full ownership of one recurring task, including planning and follow-through, not only helping when asked.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Major Change Support Roster with tasks, owners, frequency, backup, capacity limits, and review date.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Care becomes visible enough to share fairly.
outcomes.role_note: [A] = less content with current support expectations; [B] = more content.

outcomes.verdict: You are close in capacity, yet both of you feel unsupported because the same limited relationship battery is being asked to power the crisis and the connection. Separate transition work from couple care. Build a task plan for the change, then protect one tiny routine where neither person manages the problem. Ten quiet minutes, a walk, or one normal meal can remind you that the relationship is more than the emergency department.
outcomes.actions_a: Choose the transition task you can own without needing repeated reminders.
outcomes.actions_b: Choose the small relationship routine you will protect even during the hardest week.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Support and Us plan with transition tasks, outside help, capacity limits, protected ritual, and check-in day.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. The change gets managed without consuming every place you usually meet each other.

outcomes.verdict: [A] has less capacity, perhaps because work, health, money, or caregiving is already using the available margin. [B] can give more and is willing to reorganize for the transition. You are content because capacity is being treated as a current fact, not a love ranking. Assign [B] the high-load tasks for a defined season while [A] owns one complete, dependable lane. Add outside help before [B]'s generosity becomes exhaustion.
outcomes.actions_a: Choose one support lane you can fully own and state what remains outside your capacity.
outcomes.actions_b: Choose the higher-load tasks you can carry, plus the warning sign that triggers outside help or redistribution.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Capacity-Based Support Plan with lane owners, heavy tasks, limits, outside resources, warning signs, and end date.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Unequal capacity still creates a dependable team when the limits stay visible.
outcomes.role_note: [A] = has less current support capacity; [B] = has more.

outcomes.verdict: [A] has less capacity and feels strained by what is expected. [B] has more capacity and feels the arrangement is acceptable, perhaps because [B] assumes love should stretch until the change is over. [A] is already beyond the safe line. Reduce the partner workload before asking for more reassurance. [B] can recruit outside help, simplify the plan, or postpone nonessential demands. [A] can then offer one smaller promise that is reliable.
outcomes.actions_a: State the task or emotional demand you can no longer carry and replace it with one sustainable promise.
outcomes.actions_b: Remove, outsource, or simplify one demand before requesting additional support from [A].
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Support Load Reduction list with stop items, outside help, sustainable promise, emergency exceptions, and review date.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Care gets smaller and steadier before either partner burns out.
outcomes.role_note: [A] = has less capacity and is dissatisfied; [B] = has more capacity and is content.

outcomes.verdict: [A] is protecting a nearly empty reserve. [B] sees available strength and keeps stepping in, then feels alone when support is not returned in the same form. Capacity has become both workload and evidence of love. Stop comparing totals. Give each partner a different job: one handles practical transition tasks, the other protects communication, records decisions, or maintains the one stable routine they can manage. Review weekly because capacity can change quickly.
outcomes.actions_a: Choose the lower-energy role you can perform reliably and report honestly when capacity changes.
outcomes.actions_b: Choose the high-load role you can carry for one week and name the support you need around it.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Weekly Capacity Roster with different roles, energy rating, outside backup, protected routine, and reassignment day.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Support becomes a changing division of labor, not a test of who loves harder.
outcomes.role_note: [A] = has less current support capacity; [B] = has more.

cases.title: Who's More Anxious About the Idea of Combining Finances Long Term?
cases.subtitle: How anxious do you feel about combining any part of your finances long term?

questions.prompt: How anxious do you feel about combining any part of your finances long term?

options.label: Hardly anxious at all
A little cautious but open
Mixed, depending on the account or obligation
Very anxious without strong protections
Deeply uncomfortable with long-term financial merging

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: How do you feel about the way this anxiety is handled between you?

options.label: It works for me
Mostly okay, with a few rough moments
It regularly leaves me tense or disconnected
I need this pattern to change

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: What does financial merging make you fear most?

options.label: Losing independence
Being exposed to debt or poor decisions
Unequal income becoming unequal power
Carrying family or past obligations
A difficult exit if life changes
Being judged for everyday spending

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: What would lower the anxiety?

options.label: A yours, mine, and ours structure
Full debt and credit disclosure
Personal money with no commentary
Contribution rules based on capacity
Written exit and emergency terms
A small trial before larger merging

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: Anything the court should know about the debt, past experience, control concern, or account structure behind this anxiety? (optional)
questions.interactionRule: Private context is used only to personalize the selected deterministic branch.

outcomes.verdict: You carry a similar level of caution, so neither person has to argue that financial independence and financial partnership can coexist. That shared setting gives you room to design the structure account by account. Combine only what serves a shared job, keep personal lanes that preserve adult freedom, and write rules for contributions, visibility, debt, and exits. Trust grows from choosing the boundary together, not from proving closeness by merging everything.
outcomes.actions_a: Choose one financial lane that would benefit from shared management and define its exact job.
outcomes.actions_b: Choose one personal lane that should remain separate and name the boundary that keeps it fair.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Yours, Mine, and Ours Map with account jobs, contributions, visibility, debt rules, and exit steps.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Financial closeness becomes intentional instead of total.

outcomes.verdict: [A] and [B] report similar anxiety, but [A] feels less protected by the current conversation. [A] may be revealing more debt, income, or spending detail while [B] keeps greater privacy, or [A]'s money may be more exposed to shared obligations. [B] sees mutual caution and assumes the border is even. Compare disclosure, access, and liability on both sides. A shared lock only works if both people know which doors it opens.
outcomes.actions_a: Name the disclosure or protection that feels uneven and the reciprocal rule you need.
outcomes.actions_b: Match that disclosure, correct the access gap, or explain the legal fact that changes the risk.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Financial Boundary Symmetry Check with disclosures, access, liabilities, personal lanes, and correction date.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Similar caution receives equally strong protection on both sides.
outcomes.role_note: [A] = less content with the current financial-merging process; [B] = more content.

outcomes.verdict: You are close in anxiety, yet the topic still feels unsafe because combine finances has no agreed size. One person may imagine a bill account while the other imagines shared savings, credit, and spending review. Build an account ladder from lowest to highest exposure. Start with one purpose-built shared lane, run it for three months, and move up only if contributions, access, and communication remain clean.
outcomes.actions_a: Choose the lowest-exposure shared account or process that would solve a real problem now.
outcomes.actions_b: Define the trial rules, including contributions, allowed uses, alerts, and the condition for stopping.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Financial Combining Ladder with exposure levels, first trial, account rules, stop trigger, and review date.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Trust grows through a controlled first step instead of one giant merge.

outcomes.verdict: [A] feels more anxious because merging money threatens independence, safety, or a boundary learned through hard experience. [B] feels more comfortable and sees shared finance as useful coordination rather than surrender. You are content because anxiety is informing the design instead of blocking all partnership. Let [A] set the exposure ceiling and let [B] optimize inside it. Combine shared bills or goals while keeping personal accounts and individual emergency access intact.
outcomes.actions_a: Set the maximum shared exposure you can freely accept and identify the personal safety lane that stays separate.
outcomes.actions_b: Design the shared lane inside that ceiling and avoid treating more merging as the default next step.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save an Exposure Ceiling plan with shared purpose, maximum balance or liability, personal safety funds, access, and review date.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Partnership gets coordination without demanding financial surrender.
outcomes.role_note: [A] = more anxious about combining finances; [B] = more comfortable.

outcomes.verdict: [A] is more anxious and feels the current direction exposes money, autonomy, or exit options too quickly. [B] is comfortable and may experience the proposed merge as ordinary commitment. The ease belongs to [B], while the perceived downside sits with [A]. [B] owes a slower habit: no new account, debt, or access until the current layer has a clean track record. [A] owes clear conditions rather than an endlessly moving finish line.
outcomes.actions_a: Write the protections and three-month evidence that would make the next layer discussable.
outcomes.actions_b: Pause expansion, follow the current rules cleanly, and gather the records that answer [A]'s conditions.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a No Expansion Until Proven agreement with current layer, protections, evidence period, prohibited steps, and review date.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Financial trust earns the next level instead of assuming it.
outcomes.role_note: [A] = more anxious and dissatisfied; [B] = more comfortable and content.

outcomes.verdict: [A] hears combining finances as potential control or exposure. [B] hears continued separation as a sign that shared goals may never become fully real. Repeating the symbolism will not solve the design. Assign money to purposes, not relationship status. Create one shared operating account, one shared goal account, and protected personal accounts. Review behavior and usefulness quarterly. The structure can become more or less connected as evidence changes.
outcomes.actions_a: Define the personal account protections and the actions that would count as financial control.
outcomes.actions_b: Define the shared goals that genuinely need pooled money and the contribution rule that feels sustainable.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Purpose-Based Money Structure with operating account, goal account, personal accounts, contribution rules, and quarterly review.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. The accounts answer practical needs while trust stays free to grow at its own pace.
outcomes.role_note: [A] = more anxious about combining finances; [B] = more comfortable.

cases.title: Who Actually Does More Around the House?
cases.subtitle: On a day-to-day basis, who's actually carrying more of the household load?

questions.prompt: On a day-to-day basis, who's actually carrying more of the household load?

options.label: Almost entirely me
Mostly me
Pretty even
Mostly them
Almost entirely them

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: Which kind of work feels most lopsided?

options.label: The hands-on stuff (cooking, cleaning, chores)
The behind-the-scenes stuff (planning, remembering, scheduling)
Both, across the board
Honestly, it's more of a vibe than a task list

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: Does the current split actually bother you?

options.label: Not really, it works
A little, but I've never said anything
Yes, and I've brought it up before
Yes, but I've never said it out loud

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: Anything the court should know about your schedules right now? (optional)
questions.interactionRule: Private context is used only to personalize the selected deterministic branch.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = the partner reported as carrying more load.
outcomes.verdict: This isn't [B] being lazy, it's that the work [A]'s doing is the kind that doesn't leave a visible trail, remembering the dentist, noticing the fridge is empty, tracking what needs to happen before it becomes a problem. [B]'s not blind to effort, [B] just can't see effort that never announces itself. Once that invisible work is visible, it stops being a solo job and starts being something you can actually divide on purpose.
outcomes.actions_a: say the invisible task out loud once this week, right when you're doing it, not after.
outcomes.actions_b: pick up one task [A] usually handles quietly, without being asked first.
outcomes.try_together: Sit down for five minutes and write out every single household task either of you can think of, no matter how small. Keep the list. You'll both be surprised by what's on it.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Now go look at that list again next month.

outcomes.role_note: [B] = the partner reported as carrying more load.
outcomes.verdict: This isn't [A] being lazy, it's that the work [B]'s doing is the kind that doesn't leave a visible trail, remembering the dentist, noticing the fridge is empty, tracking what needs to happen before it becomes a problem. [A]'s not blind to effort, [A] just can't see effort that never announces itself. Once that invisible work is visible, it stops being a solo job and starts being something you can actually divide on purpose.
outcomes.actions_a: pick up one task [B] usually handles quietly, without being asked first.
outcomes.actions_b: say the invisible task out loud once this week, right when you're doing it, not after.
outcomes.try_together: Sit down for five minutes and write out every single household task either of you can think of, no matter how small. Keep the list. You'll both be surprised by what's on it.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Now go look at that list again next month.

outcomes.verdict: This isn't luck, it's rarer than that: your instincts for 'this needs doing now' happen to fire in the same order, so neither of you is ever the one stuck waiting for the other to notice. Most couples negotiate their way into balance. You just happened to get assigned compatible alarms.
outcomes.actions_a: keep doing exactly what you're doing.
outcomes.actions_b: same. Don't overthink it.
outcomes.try_together: Write down, right now, the last three household things either of you did without being asked. Compare timestamps, bet they're closer together than you'd think. Keep the list as proof this works.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Alarms stay synced.

outcomes.verdict: Here's the twist nobody saw coming: you both think you're the one holding this together. Which means somewhere along the way, you both quietly started keeping score, and neither of you ever compared notes. Comparing lists usually turns two exhausted martyrs into a team that finally sees the full picture together.
outcomes.actions_a: name one thing you assumed [B] wasn't noticing. Ask if they actually noticed it.
outcomes.actions_b: same, in reverse.
outcomes.try_together: Each write down, separately, the three things you do most that you think go unnoticed. Swap lists. See how many overlap with what the other actually saw.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Turns out you were both keeping the same secret ledger.

outcomes.verdict: This was never really about workload, it's that neither of you wants to be the one who admits they're carrying more, because that feels like keeping score. Somebody's doing more here, and you're both too polite to claim it. Once someone claims it, out loud, you both get to actually redistribute the load instead of quietly resenting an imbalance nobody's named.
outcomes.actions_a: accept, out loud, one specific thing you actually do more of.
outcomes.actions_b: same, no 'no it's fine' allowed.
outcomes.try_together: Trade one honest sentence: 'I think I actually do more of ___.' No deflecting it back. Just let it sit there.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Somebody's finally allowed to say it.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = the partner who reported the imbalance and is bothered by it; [B] = the other partner.
outcomes.verdict: [A], you're not overreacting, you're the only one running the Mental Load Department, and departments nobody funds tend to feel invisible until they quietly shut down. [B], this isn't about not caring, it's that you've never had to build the department that already runs fine. Once that department's staffed, the load actually gets shared instead of quietly carried by one of you.
outcomes.actions_a: name the exact task you want handed over this week, specifically, not 'help more.'
outcomes.actions_b: take that one task fully, start to finish, no reminders needed.
outcomes.try_together: Pick one recurring task and formally 'transfer ownership' tonight, out loud, like a handoff ceremony. Put a reminder in both your phones so it actually sticks.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Department successfully staffed.

cases.title: How Should Cooking Actually Get Split?
cases.subtitle: How much of the cooking do you currently handle in your household?

questions.prompt: How much of the cooking do you currently handle in your household?

options.label: Almost none
A smaller share
About half
Most of it
Nearly all of it

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: How do you feel about the current cooking setup?

options.label: It genuinely works for me
Mostly okay, but it could be easier
It regularly drains or frustrates me
I really need the setup to change

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: Which part of cooking eats the most bandwidth?

options.label: Deciding what to make
Shopping and keeping ingredients stocked
Prepping and cooking
Cleaning up afterward
Making sure meals happen on busy days

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: What would make the split feel most sustainable?

options.label: Fixed cooking nights
One cooks, one handles cleanup
Rotating full meal ownership
More easy meals and planned takeout
Dividing planning, shopping, cooking, and cleanup separately

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: Anything the court should know about your schedules, diets, or cooking setup? (optional)
questions.interactionRule: Private context is used only to personalize the selected deterministic branch.

outcomes.verdict: Your kitchen already has good mise en place,not matching cooking styles, but a shared understanding of who steps in and what counts as a completed meal. Neither of you is spending extra energy decoding whether dinner is covered. That predictability is the deeper win: the food gets made without turning care into a nightly negotiation. Protect the system by documenting the backup plan that currently lives only in your instincts.
outcomes.actions_a: Name one meal you can reliably take over when the normal routine gets disrupted.
outcomes.actions_b: Name one different meal you can reliably take over when the normal routine gets disrupted.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you create a saved ‘Kitchen Backup Menu’ with four emergency meals, the ingredients each requires, and who can own each one without discussion.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Dinner already knows where it’s going.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = dissatisfied with the current setup; [B] = content with it.
outcomes.verdict: [A] is reading the full restaurant ticket,planning, checking ingredients, cooking, and cleanup,while [B] may be counting only the plate that reaches the table. That is how two people can carry similar visible shares and still experience the job differently. The good news is that the missing labor has identifiable stages. Move one stage instead of vaguely redistributing ‘cooking,’ and relief becomes measurable rather than theoretical.
outcomes.actions_a: Identify the one pre-meal or post-meal stage that makes your share feel heavier than it looks.
outcomes.actions_b: Take complete ownership of that stage for the next two weeks without waiting for instructions.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a ‘Full Dinner Receipt’ listing Decide, Stock, Prep, Cook, and Clean, then put one owner beside every stage for three upcoming meals.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. The whole ticket is now visible.

outcomes.verdict: The split is not the main failure if you’re contributing at similar levels and both still dread the system. Your kitchen is charging a nightly decision tax: every meal begins from zero, so even fair labor feels exhausting. The fix is not asking both people to try harder. Build defaults for different energy levels and stop treating every Tuesday dinner like a fresh creative brief.
outcomes.actions_a: Choose one low-effort meal you are willing to make on autopilot.
outcomes.actions_b: Choose a different low-effort meal you are willing to make on autopilot.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you create a saved three-level menu,‘We Have Energy,’ ‘Bare Minimum,’ and ‘Absolutely Not Cooking’,with three options and one default owner in each level.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Tuesday has lost creative-director privileges.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = handles more cooking; [B] = handles less.
outcomes.verdict: [A] is the kitchen lead, not automatically the kitchen victim: cooking may offer control, creativity, competence, or simply a better fit with [A]’s schedule. [B] is the support lane, and the arrangement works because [B] is not treating food as magic that appears without labor. This is healthy specialization. Its only vulnerability is that too much household knowledge can remain trapped in one person, so the system needs a backup without dismantling the split you both like.
outcomes.actions_a: Choose one repeatable meal whose full process you can comfortably hand over.
outcomes.actions_b: Learn and own that meal from ingredient check through cleanup, without using [A] as live tech support.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a one-page ‘Kitchen Coverage Plan’ recording the lead cook, support responsibilities, one backup meal, and what happens during the lead cook’s busiest week.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Specialization stays; fragility goes.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = handles more cooking and wants change; [B] = handles less and is currently content.
outcomes.verdict: [A] is not necessarily asking [B] to stand beside the stove more often; [A] is asking to stop being the person who guarantees that eating happens. [B] experiences the current system after the hardest uncertainty has already been removed, so the amount of coordination behind each meal can disappear from view. The root need is dependable ownership, not occasional assistance. Give [B] complete meals with dates, and [A] gets real off-duty time instead of supervised help.
outcomes.actions_a: Choose two weekly meal slots you are genuinely willing to release, including the decisions attached to them.
outcomes.actions_b: Own those two meals end to end,plan, check ingredients, cook or order, and close the kitchen.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you place the next eight dinners on a shared calendar with one owner and one fallback beside every date, then save the schedule before leaving the conversation.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Help has been promoted to ownership.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = handles more cooking; [B] = handles less.
outcomes.verdict: [A] has become the kitchen’s permanent lead, carrying both production and the pressure of making sure meals exist. [B] is contributing less but is not enjoying the arrangement either,often because entering someone else’s established kitchen can feel like joining a show in season six with no recap. You do not need a philosophical debate about fairness. You need a short transfer period: [B] receives two complete episodes, and [A] stops directing from off-camera.
outcomes.actions_a: Hand over two meals with the required dietary facts, then stay fully off duty while [B] runs them.
outcomes.actions_b: Plan and deliver those two meals completely, asking necessary questions before cooking rather than during every step.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you create a two-week ‘Kitchen Transfer’ plan with two [B]-owned meals per week, a shared shopping list, and a dated review after the fourth meal.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. The new season has a second lead.

outcomes.verdict: [A] cleans like a restoration specialist. [A] can see the finished room hiding underneath the buildup and knows which sequence will uncover it without creating extra work. [B] is not incapable. [B] simply has less practiced vision for what regular tidying leaves behind. This gives you a real skill advantage to use, but expertise should set the method. It should not become a permanent sentence to clean every difficult zone alone.

outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Expertise documented, sentence commuted.

outcomes.role_note: [B] = the partner both identified as better at deep cleaning.
outcomes.verdict: [B] cleans like a restoration specialist. [B] can see the finished room hiding underneath the buildup and knows which sequence will uncover it without creating extra work. [A] is not incapable. [A] simply has less practiced vision for what regular tidying leaves behind. This gives you a real skill advantage to use, but expertise should set the method. It should not become a permanent sentence to clean every difficult zone alone.

outcomes.actions_b: Choose that zone and reduce your method to the three steps that create the biggest visible difference.

outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Expertise documented, sentence commuted.

outcomes.verdict: You both have the patience to tolerate the ugly middle of a deep clean because you trust the final transformation. That is more specific than being equally tidy. You can pull everything out, treat what normal cleaning misses, and rebuild the room correctly. Your risk is not quality. It is diffusion. When either person could lead, the reset can wait for an obvious volunteer. Assign territories and turn two capable cleaners into parallel progress.
outcomes.actions_a: Claim the deep-cleaning zone you can finish with the least friction.
outcomes.actions_b: Claim a different deep-cleaning zone you can finish with the least friction.

outcomes.verdict: You are probably winning two different competitions under the same title. One of you may score skill by microscopic thoroughness. The other may score it by speed, organization, or how long the result survives. That is why both claims can feel evidence-based without producing the same winner. The useful verdict is not one all-purpose champion. Define the scorecard, then assign each person to the zones where that version of ‘better’ actually matters.
outcomes.actions_a: Name the result you use to judge your own deep-cleaning skill and one zone where it clearly shows.
outcomes.actions_b: Name your different judging result and one zone where it clearly shows.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a four-part scorecard for Thoroughness, Speed, Organization, and Lasting Result, then rate one recently cleaned zone separately and record the zone leader for each metric.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Same title, four actual events.

outcomes.verdict: This is a cross-certified praise gap. Each of you has noticed a cleaning strength in the other but left your own competence unofficial. That mutual credit feels generous, yet it can create a strange system where both people wait for the expert they believe they live with. The evidence suggests you are not missing skill. You have split skill without naming the split. Claiming your own specialty lets admiration become a usable division of labor.
outcomes.actions_a: Claim one deep-cleaning technique or zone you handle better than [B], without returning the compliment.
outcomes.actions_b: Claim one different technique or zone you handle better than [A], without returning the compliment.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you teach each other one signature deep-cleaning move, save the two tips in a shared note, and assign each teacher a different lead zone.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Compliments converted into credentials.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = named a specific partner; [B] = said both are equally good.
outcomes.verdict: [A] sees a clear lead cleaner because one person’s method, endurance, or results stand out enough to organize around. [B] sees interchangeable competence and remembers the times either person could deliver a strong reset. The disagreement is not whether both of you can clean. It is whether one person’s edge deserves permanent ownership. Treat the edge as a lead role with a trained backup, not as proof that the lead should carry every reset.
outcomes.actions_a: Name the observable result that makes the lead cleaner stand out, not just the impression that they are better.
outcomes.actions_b: Choose one zone where your equal-skill claim is strongest and own its next full reset.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you run a two-zone trial with separate owners, save before-and-after photos plus completion times, and record whether you need a lead cleaner or simply different territories.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. The edge gets evidence, not a life sentence.

outcomes.actions_b: Claim a different admin domain you already understand well enough to own without [A] supervising.

Once [A] spots the mess, it can feel like a task has already landed in [A]’s head. [B] sees the same room as still manageable and assumes there is time. Things may not have clear homes, the storage may be inconvenient, or your routine creates clutter faster than either person can reset it. By the time [B] thinks cleanup is becoming necessary, [A] may have spent hours looking at unfinished work and wondering whether speaking up will sound controlling. [B] is not necessarily ignoring the mess. [B] simply does not receive the same internal alert. The useful discovery is that [B] cannot rely on personal discomfort as the cue. A shared time or visible standard can protect [A]’s ability to relax without making [B] live under constant correction.

outcomes.actions_b: Check that space at the agreed time instead of waiting until the mess personally bothers you.

outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Comfort no longer depends on matching internal alarms.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = lower mess tolerance; [B] = higher mess tolerance.
outcomes.verdict: [A]’s cleanup alarm goes off early, while [B]’s goes off much later. Right now, [A] feels forced to act before getting overwhelmed, and [B] feels like cleanup starts before it seems necessary. Both of you end up resenting the same room for opposite reasons. You do not need identical alarms. You need a checkpoint between them. A short scheduled reset gives [A] predictability and gives [B] freedom from surprise requests throughout the day.
outcomes.actions_a: At the checkpoint, name only the mess that has crossed the shared standard instead of everything you personally notice.
outcomes.actions_b: Treat the checkpoint as your cue to act, even when your own tolerance has not been reached.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you schedule a recurring fifteen-minute reset, save a four-item priority list, and set one review date after three weeks to adjust the checkpoint.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Two alarms, one agreed checkpoint.

A smaller share

Nearly all of it

questions.prompt: How do you feel about the current outdoor-task setup?

Mostly okay, but it could be easier
It regularly drains or frustrates me
I really need the setup to change

questions.prompt: Which part creates the biggest imbalance?

options.label: Mowing, trimming, raking, or snow removal
Watering and plant care
Seasonal cleanup and preparation
Outdoor trash, bins, sidewalks, or shared areas
Tools, supplies, and equipment maintenance
Scheduling contractors or checking property rules

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: What makes these tasks harder to divide?

options.label: Weather decides when they need to happen
One person has more physical ability or experience
One person notices seasonal needs earlier
Your standards for done are different
Tools and supplies are not organized
The tasks happen too irregularly to form a habit

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: Anything the court should know about your outdoor space, weather, physical limits, or seasonal responsibilities? (optional)
questions.interactionRule: Private context is used only to personalize the selected deterministic branch.

outcomes.verdict: You have a shared seasonal rhythm. Both of you understand that outdoor work changes with weather, daylight, and the time of year, and neither person is constantly discovering that the other expected something different. The deeper relationship strength is adaptability. You can respond to what the home needs without turning every weather window into a negotiation. Writing down the rhythm will protect it when life gets busier or the season changes.
outcomes.actions_a: Claim one recurring outdoor task you naturally handle at the right time.
outcomes.actions_b: Claim a different recurring task you naturally handle at the right time.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you create a saved seasonal outdoor calendar with recurring tasks, weather-dependent tasks, supply checks, and one owner for each.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. The seasons already make sense to both of you.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = dissatisfied with the current setup; [B] = content with it.
outcomes.verdict: [A] and [B] may complete similar amounts of outdoor work, but [A] is probably carrying more timing pressure. These tasks cannot always wait until a convenient evening. Rain, heat, snow, daylight, watering needs, or pickup rules create narrow windows. [B] sees comparable physical effort. [A] feels the responsibility of watching for the moment when the work has to happen. Sharing that monitoring can make an already similar workload finally feel similar too.
outcomes.actions_a: Identify the seasonal or weather trigger you are tired of monitoring alone.
outcomes.actions_b: Take responsibility for tracking that trigger and initiating the next task it controls.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a weather-trigger list with the task, the condition that activates it, the owner, and the next date to check supplies.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. The forecast is no longer one person’s job.

outcomes.verdict: You are both doing a similar amount and both still dislike the setup. The work may be arriving as a series of avoidable emergencies. Tools are missing, supplies run out, seasonal tasks are remembered late, and every job takes longer because preparation begins after the task is already due. The issue is not effort. Your outdoor work lacks a reliable lead time. A basic seasonal plan can turn stressful weekends into shorter, predictable resets.
outcomes.actions_a: Choose one upcoming seasonal task and list everything needed before the workday arrives.
outcomes.actions_b: Choose a different upcoming task and prepare its tools or supplies in advance.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you build a saved ninety-day outdoor plan with task dates, preparation dates, required supplies, and a clear owner for each step.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. The work gets a head start this season.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = handles more outdoor work; [B] = handles less.
outcomes.verdict: [A] is the outdoor lead because the work fits [A]’s skills, preferences, physical capacity, or schedule better. [B] is the support crew, and both of you are comfortable because the role difference feels intentional rather than assumed. That can be a genuinely good division. It only becomes fragile when [A] is unavailable or a task exceeds [A]’s capacity. Give [B] one independent lane and agree on the point where either person calls for outside help.
outcomes.actions_a: Choose one outdoor task you can fully release and name the jobs that should never be handled alone.
outcomes.actions_b: Own the released task and learn where the tools, supplies, and service contacts are kept.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save an outdoor responsibility sheet with Lead Tasks, Support Tasks, Independent Backup Tasks, and Call-for-Help Tasks.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. The outdoor lead now has real coverage.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = handles more outdoor work and wants change; [B] = handles less and is currently content.
outcomes.verdict: [A] is carrying both the physical work and the loss of flexibility that comes with it. The lawn, plants, snow, bins, or shared outdoor area may need attention on a specific day regardless of [A]’s energy. [B] sees the finished space but does not feel the same deadline pressure. [A] needs guaranteed relief, not help offered after the window has already arrived. One fixed outdoor responsibility owned by [B] gives both of you a plan you can trust.
outcomes.actions_a: Choose one recurring outdoor responsibility you need to stop scheduling and protecting.
outcomes.actions_b: Take full ownership of that responsibility, including weather checks, supplies, and completion timing.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you put the next four outdoor work windows on a shared calendar with one owner, one rain-date rule, and one completion standard for each.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Relief now has a date and an owner.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = handles more outdoor work; [B] = handles less.
outcomes.verdict: [A] is overloaded, while [B] may be unsure where to enter a system built around [A]’s experience or standards. That leaves [A] doing too much and [B] feeling criticized, disconnected, or assigned only the leftover jobs. The useful split is based on task type. [A] can keep the work that genuinely requires existing skill. [B] can fully own planning, supplies, cleanup, contractor contact, or a recurring physical task that does not depend on [A]’s method.
outcomes.actions_a: Keep only the tasks where your skill or physical ability makes a meaningful difference, and release one complete support lane.
outcomes.actions_b: Own that support lane from planning through completion without waiting for [A] to direct each step.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you create a monthly outdoor checklist divided into Skilled Work, Recurring Work, Preparation, Cleanup, and Professional Help, then schedule a fifteen-minute review each month.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. The work is divided by reality, not habit.

cases.title: Who’s More Likely to Let Chores Pile Up?
cases.subtitle: How often do you let chores pile up before you start dealing with them?

options.label: Almost never. I handle things early
Occasionally
About half the time
Pretty often
Constantly. I need the pressure first

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: How do you feel about the current difference or similarity between your habits?

options.label: It genuinely works for me
Mostly okay, but it causes small annoyances
The backlog regularly stresses me out
It creates real tension between us

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: Which kind of chore is most likely to pile up?

options.label: Dishes and kitchen cleanup
Laundry
Clutter and putting things away
Cleaning bathrooms or floors
Mail, forms, and household admin
Small repairs and unfinished projects

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: What usually causes the delay?

options.label: I am too tired when I first notice it
I need enough tasks to justify starting
The first step feels weirdly hard
I am not sure whose job it is
I forget once the task is out of sight
I want to do it properly, so I keep waiting for more time

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: Anything the court should know about the chore backlog that keeps coming back? (optional)
questions.interactionRule: Private context is used only to personalize the selected deterministic branch.

outcomes.verdict: You both let chores build at roughly the same pace, and neither of you feels abandoned by that rhythm. You may both prefer early resets, or you may both prefer waiting until there is enough work to make the effort worthwhile. The important match is expectation. Neither person is watching the same pile and privately wondering why the other is still relaxed. That gives you room to choose a routine based on real energy instead of performing tidiness for each other.
outcomes.actions_a: Name the chore you prefer handling early and the one you prefer batching.
outcomes.actions_b: Name a different early chore and a different batch chore.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a two-column list called ‘Do Early’ and ‘Worth Batching,’ place your recurring chores once, and add a reset date for the batch column.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Your timing already feels fair to both of you.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = dissatisfied with the current setup; [B] = content with it.
outcomes.verdict: [A] and [B] allow a similar amount of buildup, but [A] experiences the waiting period differently. [A] sees a backlog with no guaranteed ending, while [B] sees tasks being saved for a later batch. The pile is the same size. Only one person trusts that it has a plan. The fastest improvement is not cleaning sooner every time. Give delayed chores a visible date so [A] can stop holding the deadline mentally and [B] can keep a batching style without creating uncertainty.
outcomes.actions_a: Choose the backlog that causes the most stress and name how long you can realistically wait.
outcomes.actions_b: Choose a completion time within that window and initiate the task without another reminder.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a ‘Later Has a Date’ rule with maximum wait times for dishes, laundry, clutter, cleaning, admin, and repairs.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Later is now a real time, not a mystery.

outcomes.verdict: You both dislike the backlog, so this is not a difference in values. You are getting stuck at task initiation. The chore looks too large, the first step is unclear, or each person waits for enough energy to finish it properly. That shared struggle can become a point of closeness instead of mutual disappointment. Make starting tiny and visible. Once one of you begins, the other should know exactly how to join without needing a planning meeting.
outcomes.actions_a: Choose one repeat pile and define a first step that takes less than two minutes.
outcomes.actions_b: Choose a different pile and define its two-minute starting step.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you create a saved ten-minute reset list with six tiny starting actions, then schedule one shared reset and record which actions created the most momentum.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Starting gets smaller, teamwork gets easier.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = starts chores earlier; [B] = lets them build longer.
outcomes.verdict: [A] is the starter. [A] keeps small tasks from becoming large ones and gives the home regular forward motion. [B] is the batcher. [B] can tolerate buildup and often works more efficiently once there is enough to justify the effort. Both styles have value because neither person feels used or controlled. The relationship stays strongest when [A] is not automatically assigned every urgent task and [B] has clear batch categories that reliably get completed.
outcomes.actions_a: Keep ownership of one early-action chore where quick intervention genuinely prevents extra work.
outcomes.actions_b: Own one batch-friendly chore with a fixed completion day and finish the whole category at once.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Starter and Batcher plan assigning each recurring chore by the timing style that suits it best, with one deadline beside every batch task.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Different timing can still make one reliable system.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = starts chores earlier and is dissatisfied; [B] = lets them build longer and is currently content.
outcomes.verdict: [A] experiences every unfinished chore like an open browser tab using a little attention in the background. [B] can leave those tabs open until there are enough to close together. [A] starts early to regain mental space, then feels stuck doing more because [B] has not reached the same activation point. [B] sees the tasks being handled and never receives a clear chance to own the later reset. Give [B] protected categories with deadlines, and [A] gets permission to stop rescuing them early.
outcomes.actions_a: Choose one chore category you will stop completing before the agreed deadline.
outcomes.actions_b: Own that category and close the full backlog by the deadline without waiting for [A] to start.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a ‘Do Not Rescue Before’ agreement for two batchable chores, add their deadlines to the calendar, and review the result after three cycles.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. The open tabs finally have assigned closers.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = starts chores earlier; [B] = lets them build longer.
outcomes.verdict: [A] keeps stepping in because the backlog becomes uncomfortable before [B] is ready to start. [B] dislikes the backlog too, but repeated rescue means [B] rarely reaches the moment of full ownership. That pattern trains [A] to expect abandonment and trains [B] to expect the task may disappear first. The correction is one protected responsibility that [B] carries through a real deadline while [A] stops absorbing it early. Reliability has to become visible to both of you.
outcomes.actions_a: Release one chore category until its agreed deadline, even if you would personally start sooner.
outcomes.actions_b: Own that category every cycle and complete it before the deadline without reminders or partial handback.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you choose one recurring backlog, save its owner and deadline, track four completed cycles, and schedule a review after the fourth result.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Ownership gets enough space to become believable.

cases.title: How Should Meal Planning Actually Work Between You Two?
cases.subtitle: How much of the meal-planning load do you currently handle?

options.label: Almost none
A smaller share
About half
Most of it
Nearly all of it

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: How do you feel about the current meal-planning setup?

options.label: It genuinely works for me
Mostly okay, but it could be easier
It regularly drains or frustrates me
I really need the setup to change

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: Which part takes the most mental energy?

options.label: Coming up with meal ideas
Balancing both people’s preferences
Checking schedules and choosing realistic meals
Knowing what ingredients are already available
Keeping meals healthy or within budget
Planning leftovers, takeout, and backup options

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: Which planning style sounds most realistic for you?

options.label: Plan the whole week at once
Choose three anchor meals and keep the rest flexible
Alternate who decides each day
Give each person fixed meal nights
Keep a shared list of approved defaults
Decide on the day based on time and energy

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: Anything the court should know about your schedules, food preferences, or daily ‘what should we eat?’ debate? (optional)
questions.interactionRule: Private context is used only to personalize the selected deterministic branch.

outcomes.verdict: You have shared food timing. Both of you understand how much planning the week needs and how much can stay flexible. That means dinner decisions are less likely to become a hidden test of who knows the other person better. You already know when to suggest a favorite, when to keep things easy, and when nobody has the energy to be creative. That everyday understanding is a quiet form of intimacy. Saving your reliable options will protect it during chaotic weeks.
outcomes.actions_a: Choose two meals you can confidently plan when both of you are tired.
outcomes.actions_b: Choose two different meals you can confidently plan when both of you are tired.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you create a saved ‘We Can Always Eat This’ list with eight approved meals, required ingredients, effort level, and one default decision-maker for each.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Dinner already understands the relationship.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = dissatisfied with the current setup; [B] = content with it.
outcomes.verdict: [A] and [B] may contribute similar amounts, but [A] is probably doing more decision closing. Both people suggest ideas, discuss preferences, and reject options, yet one person still has to say, ‘Okay, this is what we are eating.’ [B] experiences shared participation. [A] experiences a conversation that still ends with one final responsibility. The useful change is giving [B] full decision authority on specific days, including choosing when the first few ideas do not land.
outcomes.actions_a: Choose the meal-planning days when you most need to stop making the final call.
outcomes.actions_b: Own the final decision on those days, including handling preferences, timing, and backup choices.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a weekly meal calendar with named Decision Days, one final decision-maker per day, and a cutoff time after which that person chooses without more debate.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Suggestions are shared, and final calls now are too.

outcomes.verdict: Meal planning has become a group chat that restarts the same conversation every evening. Both of you participate, but nothing from yesterday makes tonight easier. That is why equal effort can still feel exhausting. You do not need more meal ideas. You need fewer decisions that begin from zero. A short list of repeatable defaults gives you energy for the nights when choosing something special is actually fun.
outcomes.actions_a: Choose three default meals you would happily repeat without another discussion.
outcomes.actions_b: Choose three different defaults and name any easy substitutions you would accept.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you build and save a twelve-meal default menu tagged Quick, Cheap, Healthy, Comfort, and Takeout, then choose three options for next week.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. The dinner conversation finally remembers yesterday.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = handles more meal planning; [B] = handles less.
outcomes.verdict: [A] plans more because [A] may enjoy structure, know the household food rhythm better, or feel more confident balancing schedules and preferences. [B] contributes less, but the arrangement works because [B] is responsive, appreciative, and not adding resistance to every decision. Your strength is trust around a daily need. Keep the split you both like while giving [B] enough planning practice to cover a busy week without turning [A] into remote support.
outcomes.actions_a: Choose one week or three-day block whose meal decisions you can comfortably release.
outcomes.actions_b: Plan that block completely, including realistic meals, one backup, and any needed ingredients.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a simple meal-planning guide with favorite defaults, dietary limits, budget range, busy-night backups, and one scheduled [B]-owned planning week.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Trust stays, and backup gets stronger.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = handles more meal planning and wants change; [B] = handles less and is currently content.
outcomes.verdict: [A] is carrying future meals before either of you feels hungry. [A] checks the calendar, anticipates low-energy nights, remembers ingredients, and keeps the same question from becoming a daily emergency. [B] joins when dinner is close enough to feel real, after most of the uncertainty has already been handled. The need is not more feedback from [B]. It is complete ownership of recurring meal windows so [A] can stop preparing for every day in advance.
outcomes.actions_a: Release two recurring meal windows and share only the real dietary, budget, or scheduling limits.
outcomes.actions_b: Own those windows from decision through ingredient check, including a backup when the original plan fails.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you place the next two weeks of meal windows on a shared calendar with one owner, one backup option, and a decision deadline for each.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Planning now includes actual time off.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = handles more meal planning; [B] = handles less.
outcomes.verdict: [A] is overloaded by having to anticipate meals and may be making faster decisions just to keep the week moving. [B] is doing less but may also feel that preferences arrive too late to matter or that plans are already settled. That leaves [A] feeling unsupported and [B] feeling consulted without real influence. Both of you want the same improvement: fewer daily negotiations and more meaningful input. A short weekly planning ritual gives [B] real decision space and keeps [A] from carrying the whole week alone.
outcomes.actions_a: Bring the schedule and practical limits to the planning session, then release half of the final meal decisions.
outcomes.actions_b: Arrive with specific meal choices and take ownership of the ingredients or ordering attached to them.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you schedule a recurring fifteen-minute menu date, save the selected meals and owners in one note, and record one flexible night with no advance decision.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Both voices now arrive before dinner is urgent.

cases.title: Who Handles Scheduling Home Maintenance and Appointments?
cases.subtitle: Between you two, who is better suited to schedule home maintenance and household appointments?

questions.prompt: Between you two, who is better suited to schedule home maintenance and household appointments?

options.label: Me, no contest
Probably me
Probably them
Definitely them
Honestly, either of us could handle it

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: What best proves it?

options.label: remember when recurring appointments are due
book things before they become urgent
compare providers, prices, and availability
stay patient through calls, forms, and rescheduling
keep confirmations and important details organized
follow up when the first appointment does not solve the issue

questions.interactionRule: Display as the answering player’s own voice.

questions.prompt: Which scheduling lane needs the clearest owner?

options.label: Appliance, HVAC, plumbing, or repair service
Medical and dental appointments
Pet appointments
Car maintenance
Inspections, renewals, or annual services
Deliveries, installations, or building access

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: Where does the current system usually fail?

options.label: Nobody remembers when something is due
Both assume the other person booked it
The appointment is booked but not added to the calendar
Rescheduling falls through
Provider details and records are hard to find
Nobody follows up after the appointment

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: Anything the court should know about the appointments, maintenance, or follow-ups you are currently juggling? (optional)
questions.interactionRule: Private context is used only to personalize the selected deterministic branch.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = the partner both identified as better suited.
outcomes.verdict: [A] is good at turning a future obligation into a real date, confirmation, and completed follow-up. [B] trusts that reliability, which means you already know whose strengths make shared life run more smoothly. The hidden cost is that [A] may be carrying a private calendar of everything that could become urgent later. Keep [A] as the lead where that skill matters, but move one full scheduling lane to [B] so care for the future is something both of you practice.
outcomes.actions_a: Choose one scheduling lane you can release with its due dates, records, and provider details.
outcomes.actions_b: Own that lane through booking, calendar entry, rescheduling, and final follow-up.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you create a saved maintenance and appointments tracker with each item, due date, lead, backup, provider, confirmation, and next follow-up.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. One strong coordinator, two people protecting the future.

outcomes.role_note: [B] = the partner both identified as better suited.
outcomes.verdict: [B] is good at turning a future obligation into a real date, confirmation, and completed follow-up. [A] trusts that reliability, which means you already know whose strengths make shared life run more smoothly. The hidden cost is that [B] may be carrying a private calendar of everything that could become urgent later. Keep [B] as the lead where that skill matters, but move one full scheduling lane to [A] so care for the future is something both of you practice.
outcomes.actions_a: Take ownership of one scheduling lane through booking, calendar entry, rescheduling, and final follow-up.
outcomes.actions_b: Choose that lane and transfer its due dates, records, and provider details.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you create a saved maintenance and appointments tracker with each item, due date, lead, backup, provider, confirmation, and next follow-up.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. One strong coordinator, two people protecting the future.

outcomes.verdict: You both know how to turn ‘we should book that’ into an appointment that actually happens. The important match is follow-through. Neither person treats scheduling as finished while the confirmation is missing, the calendar is blank, or the next step is unclear. That makes you excellent backups for each other. The remaining issue is ownership. When both people are capable, a task can be duplicated or silently assumed. Separate the lanes and keep shared visibility.
outcomes.actions_a: Claim the scheduling lanes where you already know the providers, history, or recurring dates.
outcomes.actions_b: Claim different lanes where your existing knowledge makes you the cleaner owner.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a scheduling ownership list covering Home, Health, Pets, Car, Renewals, and Deliveries, with one lead and one backup in every row.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Equal ability now has separate lanes.

outcomes.verdict: One of you may be the booker, while the other is the closer. The booker acts early, finds a time, and gets the event onto the calendar. The closer remembers the paperwork, asks the right questions, handles rescheduling, and makes sure the issue is actually resolved. Both people can reasonably feel better at appointments because the job contains several different skills. Your strongest system uses both roles on purpose instead of asking one person to prove they are better at the entire process.
outcomes.actions_a: Name the scheduling stage where you are most reliable and provide one recent example.
outcomes.actions_b: Name your strongest different stage and provide one recent example.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a four-stage scheduling map for Remember, Research, Book, and Follow Up, then assign each stage for your next three appointments.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. The booker and closer both get credit.

outcomes.verdict: You are both standing beside the calendar and pointing at the other person when the reminder goes off. Each of you has seen the other handle appointments competently, but neither wants to become the permanent keeper of every due date and service call. The respect is genuine. The missing piece is commitment to a lane. Once each person claims a category, scheduling stops being a surprise request and becomes a predictable way of showing up for shared life.
outcomes.actions_a: Claim one scheduling category you can own without checking whether [B] wants to do it first.
outcomes.actions_b: Claim a different category you can own without checking whether [A] wants to do it first.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you hold a ten-minute scheduling draft, save the claimed categories, and add the next known due date for each category to the shared calendar.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. The reminder now knows who it belongs to.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = named a specific partner; [B] = said either person could handle it.
outcomes.verdict: [A] sees a dependable lead whose memory or follow-through makes scheduling safer. [B] sees enough capability on both sides that availability could decide who handles each appointment. The real issue is continuity. A flexible system works only when records, confirmations, and next steps remain visible to both people. Choose a lead by lane and keep a backup who can take over without asking for a full history lesson.
outcomes.actions_a: Name the scheduling lane where the proposed lead has the strongest repeated evidence.
outcomes.actions_b: Choose one backup responsibility that proves your shared-capability view in practice.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save one scheduling handoff card with the lead, backup, provider, history, confirmation location, and the condition that activates the backup.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Flexibility gets a memory system.

cases.title: How Fair Does the Current Chore Split Actually Feel to Each of You?

options.label: A small share
Less than half
About half
More than half
Almost all of it

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: How do you feel about the current split?

options.label: It feels fair and sustainable
Mostly fair, with a few pressure points
It regularly feels unfair
I really need the split to change

options.label: Total time spent
Energy and difficulty
Who handles the most disliked tasks
Who carries planning and reminders
Each person’s work schedule and capacity
Whether the effort is noticed and appreciated

questions.prompt: Where does the current split lose fairness fastest?

options.label: Tasks have no clear owner
One person has to keep reminding

One person handles most urgent surprises

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: Anything the court should know about the part of the chore split that feels fair or quietly unfair? (optional)
questions.interactionRule: Private context is used only to personalize the selected deterministic branch.

outcomes.verdict: You both see the workload similarly and feel good about the result. That usually means you share more than a roughly balanced task count. You understand each other’s capacity, recognize invisible effort, and adjust before a difficult week becomes evidence that someone stopped caring. Your real strength is responsiveness. Fairness can move without either person assuming the relationship itself is becoming unfair. Capture what makes the system work so it survives schedule changes.
outcomes.actions_a: Name one adjustment [B] makes that helps the split stay fair during busy periods.
outcomes.actions_b: Name one different adjustment [A] makes that helps the split stay fair.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a short ‘Our Fairness Recipe’ with the three principles that guide your split and the signs that mean it needs rebalancing.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Fairness here is active, not accidental.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = dissatisfied with the current split; [B] = content with it.
outcomes.verdict: [A] and [B] estimate the task share similarly, so the disagreement is probably about cost rather than quantity. [A] may be carrying the chores that interrupt rest, feel especially unpleasant, require reminders, or land during the worst part of the day. [B] sees comparable volume and reasonably assumes comparable burden. The next conversation should not restart the task count. Identify which chores cost [A] more and move one of those costs directly.
outcomes.actions_a: Name the specific chore whose timing, difficulty, or emotional cost makes your share feel heavier.
outcomes.actions_b: Take that chore or trade it for something [A] experiences as genuinely lighter.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a one-week chore record with Time, Energy, Interruption, and Reminder Cost, then make one trade based on the completed record.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Equal quantity now has a real cost check.

outcomes.verdict: You both see a similar split and both dislike it. That means redistributing the same pile may only move exhaustion from one person to the other. Your household is asking too much from the total capacity available right now. The intimate move is deciding together what can be done less often, simplified, automated, or dropped without turning lower standards into a personal failure. outcomes.actions_a: Choose one chore you are willing to simplify, reduce, or stop policing.
outcomes.actions_b: Choose a different chore you are willing to simplify, automate, or remove.

outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. The court reduced the workload instead of redistributing burnout.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = feels they carry more; [B] = feels they carry less.

[A] carries more, and both of you accept it because the arrangement fits your current schedules, strengths, health, preferences, or contributions outside household chores. The positive sign is that equality is not being confused with identical output. You are allowing the relationship to respond to real life. Keep the arrangement healthy by making appreciation visible and giving the heavier share an expiration or review date instead of letting a temporary season become permanent by default.
outcomes.actions_a: Name the condition that currently makes the heavier share acceptable and what would make it stop feeling sustainable.
outcomes.actions_b: Show specific appreciation and identify the task you will absorb when that condition changes.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a capacity agreement with the reason for the current imbalance, what [B] contributes instead, and a calendar date to review the split.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Unequal can be fair when it stays intentional.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = feels they carry more and is dissatisfied; [B] = feels they carry less and is currently content.
outcomes.verdict: [A] and [B] are looking at the same chore receipt, but [A] sees extra fees that never appear in the task total. Those fees may be reminders, planning, interrupted downtime, finishing incomplete work, or always handling the urgent version. [B] sees the visible items and believes the current difference is manageable. The fastest path to fairness is transferring one complete source of hidden fees, not debating the total bill again.
outcomes.actions_a: Choose the one chore domain with the highest hidden cost and describe its full cycle once.
outcomes.actions_b: Take ownership of that full cycle, including noticing, planning, reminders, and finishing.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Full-Cycle Chore Card for the transferred domain, list every hidden step, and schedule a review after three completed cycles.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. The hidden fees now have a new owner.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = feels they carry more; [B] = feels they carry less.
outcomes.verdict: [A] is overloaded and may have become the planner, reminder, and quality checker for work that is technically shared. [B] is carrying less but is unhappy too, possibly because participation feels reactive, heavily corrected, or never fully trusted. That is a painful loop, but your shared dissatisfaction is useful evidence. Neither person wants this dynamic to continue. Give [B] complete domains with clear outcomes, and give [A] real permission to stop managing how those domains get done.
outcomes.actions_a: Transfer one complete chore domain with only the essential outcome and safety requirements.
outcomes.actions_b: Own that domain from noticing through completion and report only the final result or a genuine blocker.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you create a two-week Chore Reset agreement with full-domain owners, essential standards, a no-reminder rule, and a dated review of what changed.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Shared frustration becomes a shared reset.
