outcomes.actions_b: Claim a different category you can own without waiting for [A] to add it to the list.

Use category leads for noticing, then make purchasing visible enough to hand off cleanly.

outcomes.actions_b: Claim one category or purchase window that turns shared responsibility into visible follow-through.

The issue is not willingness. You lack one agreed closing moment when scattered dish tasks become a finished room. A short reset with a clear finish line can stop dish duty from hovering over the whole evening.

outcomes.actions_a: Name the contribution from [B] that makes your larger dish share feel genuinely fair, plus the signal that you need relief.

Give [B] fixed dish windows with full ownership so [A] has predictable off-duty time.
outcomes.actions_a: Choose the recurring dish shifts you most need to release and stop checking them once assigned.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = handles more dish duty; [B] = handles less.

Separate the required outcome from personal method. Give one person the entire shift, one agreed finish line, and room to reach it without live supervision.
outcomes.actions_a: Define the essential finish line once, then do not supervise [B]’s assigned shifts unless there is a real safety issue.

cases.title: Who’s More Particular About How Things Get Done Around the House?

I have a few preferences

Extremely particular

questions.prompt: How do you feel about the way your different methods currently work together?

options.label: It genuinely works for me
Mostly okay, but it could be easier
It regularly drains or frustrates me
I really need the setup to change

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: What usually makes a specific method matter to you?

options.label: Hygiene or food safety
Preventing damage
Saving time later
Making things easy to find
The visible result
It is simply the habit that feels natural

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: What happens when a task is done differently from your preferred method?

options.label: I let it go
I explain my preference for next time
I quietly redo it
I correct the method while it is happening
I avoid delegating that task
We end up arguing about it

questions.prompt: Anything the court should know about the household method debate that keeps coming back? (optional)
questions.interactionRule: Private context is used only to personalize the selected deterministic branch.

outcomes.verdict: You share a believable definition of done. Both of you can care about the result without treating one exact route as proof of love or competence. That creates real trust inside ordinary tasks. Each person can act without waiting for approval, and small differences do not become character judgments. Preserve that freedom by naming the few outcomes that truly matter, especially before life gets busier or a new task enters the household.
outcomes.actions_a: Name one method [B] uses differently that you trust because the result still works.
outcomes.actions_b: Name a different method [A] uses differently that you trust for the same reason.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Done Means note for three recurring tasks, listing the required outcome and the methods that can stay flexible.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Trust lives in the space between two valid methods.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = dissatisfied with how methods are handled; [B] = content with the setup.
outcomes.verdict: [A] and [B] are similarly particular, so the friction is probably not one person having impossible standards. The problem is when the preference arrives. [A] may hear a new requirement during the task or after it is complete, which makes the finish line feel movable. [B] experiences a normal clarification and assumes the shared level of care should make it easy to understand. Put the important outcome up front and cap the number of instructions.
outcomes.actions_a: Ask for the essential outcome before starting a task instead of trying to predict every preference.
outcomes.actions_b: State no more than two true requirements before the task begins and leave the remaining method open.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Before We Start card for one recurring task with two requirements, one flexible choice, and a clear finish line.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. The finish line stops moving after the work begins.

outcomes.verdict: You are two quality checkers sharing one clipboard. Both of you notice details and want the home to function well, but neither person is fully off duty when both keep inspecting the same tasks. Equal particularity becomes duplicated attention, corrections, and quiet rework. The useful shift is not lowering care. It is giving each recurring task one final owner whose acceptable method closes the case.
outcomes.actions_a: Claim one task where your method can become the household default and final check.
outcomes.actions_b: Claim a different task where your method can become the household default and final check.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Final Owner list for five recurring tasks and agree that only the named owner performs the routine quality check.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Care remains high while duplicate inspection retires.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = less particular; [B] = more particular.
outcomes.verdict: [A] keeps household work moving without needing every detail controlled. [B] protects the details that prevent damage, preserve order, or make the finished result feel genuinely complete. You are using the difference as a division of strengths instead of a reason to disrespect each other. Keep flexible-method tasks with [A], precision-sensitive tasks with [B], and make sure each person still has a few jobs where their own judgment is final.
outcomes.actions_a: Choose a flexible-method task you can own completely and finish without seeking approval.
outcomes.actions_b: Choose a precision-sensitive task you are willing to own without asking [A] to reproduce your method.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a task map labeled Flexible Method, Precision Matters, and Either Works, then place your recurring chores into it.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Speed and precision each get the right assignment.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = less particular and content; [B] = more particular and dissatisfied.
outcomes.verdict: [A] feels like completed work is being graded with criteria revealed after submission. [A] values momentum and believes a functional result should count. [B] sees details that can create future cleanup, lost items, damage, or a room that never quite feels settled. Those concerns are not all the same. Separate real consequences from personal preferences, then let [A] choose the method inside the true requirements.
outcomes.actions_a: Ask for the two consequences that genuinely need preventing, then own your method within those limits.
outcomes.actions_b: Label each concern as Safety, Future Work, or Preference, and release the preference when [A] owns the task.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Definition of Done card for one disputed task with two required outcomes, optional preferences, and one named owner.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. The rubric is visible before the work starts.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = less particular; [B] = more particular.
outcomes.verdict: [A] may feel monitored and start avoiding tasks that seem impossible to complete without correction. [B] may feel unable to trust delegation because the details that matter keep disappearing from the result. The more [B] supervises, the less true ownership [A] gets. The less ownership [A] develops, the more [B] feels supervision is necessary. Rebuild trust with one task, one essential outcome, and three full cycles where method belongs to the owner.
outcomes.actions_a: Choose one recurring task to own for three cycles and ask questions only before the first cycle begins.
outcomes.actions_b: State the essential outcome once, then do not redo or live-correct the task during the trial.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a three-cycle trust trial with the chosen task, essential outcome, owner, completion dates, and a review after cycle three.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Trust gets practice instead of another debate.

outcomes.actions_b: State your real budget, function, and comfort limits up front, then release the remaining design choices within them.

outcomes.actions_a: Choose the minimum useful budget view and stop chasing data past the agreed submission deadline.
outcomes.actions_b: Enter or send your shared expenses on time and take the lead on one decision created by the monthly results.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Budget Tracker Job Description with data duties, update day, review agenda, decision rights, and what the tracker is explicitly not responsible for.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. [A] keeps the numbers visible without becoming the money parent.

outcomes.role_note: [B] = the partner both identified as the stronger shared-budget tracker.

The job becomes unfair when [B] also has to investigate [A]’s spending, enforce limits, and deliver every uncomfortable update. [B] should own the dashboard, not financial discipline for two adults. outcomes.verdict: You both can track a budget, which means the real decision is ownership rather than ability. Without a lead, two competent people can create duplicate systems, assume the other person updated a charge, or avoid reviewing a budget that technically exists. Give one person the current month and the other person an audit-and-decision role, then rotate. Your shared financial fluency is strongest when each partner can maintain the system and neither partner can quietly opt out of understanding it.
outcomes.actions_a: Track the next month using the simplest system that still answers your shared money questions.
outcomes.actions_b: Audit the categories once, bring the two decisions that matter, and take the following month’s rotation.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a three-month Budget Rotation with tracker, auditor, update deadline, review date, and the exact decisions each monthly summary must support.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Two capable budget brains use one source of truth.

outcomes.verdict: [A] may be better at capture, making sure every transfer, receipt, and subscription enters the system. [B] may be better at interpretation, noticing why a category moved and what the couple should change next. Each person claims the role because each is strong at a different stage. A useful budget needs clean inputs and a decision-ready readout. Split those jobs for two months, then rotate if both of you want full ownership experience. The goal is a system that gets updated and gets used.
outcomes.actions_a: Claim either transaction capture or monthly interpretation and define the completion signal for that stage.
outcomes.actions_b: Own the opposite stage and state what data or summary must arrive for you to do it well.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Capture and Decide workflow with stage owner, deadline, required fields, monthly questions, and one handoff check.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. The budget stops choosing between accurate data and useful decisions.

outcomes.verdict: Each of you nominates the other because budget tracking looks easier from the summary than from the update process. You remember the clean number [B] produced or the expense [A] caught, while your own mistakes feel more visible. The mutual confidence is a bright spot, but unclaimed confidence still leaves receipts on read. Rotate the tracker for one full cycle at a time and limit the system to information both people will actually maintain. The best tracker is the person currently named, supported by a partner who submits clean inputs.
outcomes.actions_a: Take the first full cycle and list the information [B] must provide without being chased.
outcomes.actions_b: Meet that input standard and take the next cycle using the same categories before proposing changes.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Two-Cycle Budget Trial with tracker, submission rules, category set, review date, unresolved items, and handoff notes.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. The compliment becomes a rotation instead of an empty job opening.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = identified a specific budget tracker; [B] = said either partner could do it.
outcomes.verdict: [A] sees a proven lead whose consistency lowers errors and mental load. [B] sees a transferable adult skill and does not want the shared budget tied permanently to one person. Preserve the reliable lead for the main dashboard while giving the other partner ownership of a complete supporting lane, such as subscriptions, reimbursements, or travel spending. Add a quarterly role swap test. Continuity stays intact, and the relationship gains backup if work, health, or life makes the usual tracker unavailable.
outcomes.actions_a: Name the budget tasks where continuity genuinely prevents errors and the tasks that can be transferred safely.
outcomes.actions_b: Own one full supporting lane and prepare to run the complete monthly update during the scheduled swap.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Lead and Backup budget chart with primary duties, supporting lane, access details, swap month, and handoff checklist.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. The budget keeps a steady lead and gains a real backup.

cases.title: How Much Should Big Purchases Require a Conversation First?
cases.subtitle: How much advance conversation should a large personal or shared purchase require?

questions.prompt: How much advance conversation should a large personal or shared purchase require?

options.label: Very little if personal money covers it
Only when it affects a shared bill or goal
A quick heads-up above an agreed amount
A real discussion before most major purchases
Full agreement whenever the amount is significant

options.label: It genuinely works for me
Mostly okay, with a few surprises
I often feel monitored, excluded, or financially blindsided
I really need the purchase rule to change

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: Which purchase most clearly deserves a conversation?

options.label: Anything using shared money
Personal purchases above a set amount
Financing, credit, or installment plans
Items that take up shared space
Travel, gifts, or commitments with ongoing costs
A purchase that delays a shared goal

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: What makes these conversations go badly?

options.label: A heads-up is mistaken for asking permission
The total cost appears only after add-ons
The conversation happens after the purchase
One person’s category gets more scrutiny
Urgency or a sale replaces real discussion
A no comes without an alternative or review date

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: Anything the court should know about the purchase, price threshold, or surprise charge behind your answers? (optional)
questions.interactionRule: Private context is used only to personalize the selected deterministic branch.

outcomes.verdict: You share a purchase boundary that protects trust without making personal money feel supervised. The deeper match is in what a conversation means: it is coordination when shared goals, credit, space, or future costs are involved, not a request for one adult to approve the other adult’s taste. That distinction keeps transparency from becoming control. Preserve it by writing down the threshold and the non-price triggers, since a cheaper subscription or giant piece of furniture can affect shared life more than one expensive personal item.
outcomes.actions_a: Name one non-price impact that should always trigger a conversation even below the dollar threshold.
outcomes.actions_b: Name one personal-money purchase that should remain fully independent and explain why it has no shared impact.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Purchase Conversation Rule with dollar threshold, shared-impact triggers, response time, personal-money lane, and emergency exception.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. The rule protects shared consequences without putting personal taste on trial.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = dissatisfied with the current purchase process; [B] = content with it.
outcomes.verdict: [A] and [B] want about the same amount of discussion, but [A] may be receiving information too late to have a real voice. A message sent from the checkout screen technically counts as a heads-up, yet the emotional and practical decision has already happened. [B] sees disclosure and assumes the process works. [A] experiences a completed purchase dressed as a conversation. Move the check-in earlier and include full cost, funding source, ongoing expense, and the shared goal or space affected before momentum makes disagreement feel hostile.
outcomes.actions_a: Name the latest point when a purchase conversation still feels genuinely open rather than ceremonial.
outcomes.actions_b: Bring the next qualifying purchase at that stage with full cost and shared impact, not only the sticker price.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Before Checkout message template with item, total cost, payment method, recurring cost, shared impact, and decision deadline.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. A heads-up becomes early enough to matter.

outcomes.verdict: You agree that big purchases need discussion, but the rule probably depends on the mood of the moment. A sale feels urgent, a personal purchase feels exempt, and a series of smaller add-ons avoids a threshold that one large charge would trigger. Replace case-by-case debate with two gates: a dollar amount and a shared-impact test. Either one can require a conversation. Then decide how long the other person has to respond, so checking in does not become indefinite permission-seeking or a convenient excuse to buy first.
outcomes.actions_a: Propose the dollar threshold and include financing or combined add-ons in the total.
outcomes.actions_b: Define the shared-impact triggers and a response window that respects both urgency and real consideration.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Two-Gate Purchase Policy with amount, impact triggers, full-cost definition, response deadline, and what happens when either partner needs more time.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. The checkout rule works even when the purchase comes with a countdown timer.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = wants more purchase discussion; [B] = wants more personal discretion.
outcomes.verdict: [A] treats a major purchase like opening a door into the shared future because the cost, object, or commitment can stay in your life for years. [B] treats personal money as a room where adult autonomy should not require a visitor badge. The boundary works because it follows impact rather than curiosity. Keep shared money, debt, space, and delayed goals in the conversation lane, while truly personal purchases stay independent. [B] does not hide shared consequences, and [A] does not expand concern into general financial surveillance.
outcomes.actions_a: Limit required conversations to the impacts that genuinely enter shared life and release purchases outside those lines.
outcomes.actions_b: Disclose any debt, recurring cost, storage need, or goal delay even when personal money funds the purchase.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Shared Impact checklist with Money, Debt, Space, Time, Goal Delay, and Personal-Only examples from your real spending.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Autonomy keeps a room, and shared consequences still knock first.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = wants more purchase discussion and is dissatisfied; [B] = wants more personal discretion and is currently content.
outcomes.verdict: [A] is not necessarily asking to approve [B]’s preferences. [A] may be trying to protect a savings goal, credit health, household space, or the basic experience of not discovering a major decision afterward. [B] protects adult autonomy and may hear every requested check-in as financial parenting. Right now, [B] keeps discretion while [A] absorbs surprise. [B] owes advance notice for one clearly defined impact category. [A] owes a fast response and must avoid turning the conversation into a character review.
outcomes.actions_a: Choose the single shared impact that most needs advance discussion and commit to responding within the agreed window.
outcomes.actions_b: Bring every purchase touching that impact before checkout with full numbers and at least one lower-impact alternative.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a ninety-day Purchase Pilot with one protected impact, notice threshold, response deadline, alternative requirement, and review date.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. One concrete boundary replaces a vague fight about permission.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = wants more purchase discussion; [B] = wants more personal discretion.
outcomes.verdict: [A] asks more questions after being surprised, while [B] shares less after feeling interrogated. The result is predictable: [A] gets more suspicious and [B] gets more protective, even when neither person intends secrecy or control. Put the disagreement on a calendar instead of reopening it at checkout. For the next month, log purchases above a neutral threshold without requiring approval, then review which ones truly affected shared money, credit, space, or goals. Use that evidence to set the permanent rule together.
outcomes.actions_a: During the trial, ask only for the agreed facts and save broader concerns for the scheduled review.
outcomes.actions_b: Log qualifying purchases before completion and include every ongoing or shared consequence without minimizing it.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a one-month Big Purchase Log with item, full cost, funding, recurring cost, shared impact, notice time, and a dated rule-setting review.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Real purchases write the policy instead of fear writing it first.

cases.title: Who Checks the Bill Twice Before Paying?
cases.subtitle: Between you two, who is more likely to check the details before a bill gets paid?

questions.prompt: Between you two, who is more likely to check the details before a bill gets paid?

Probably me
Probably them
Definitely them
Honestly, we check about equally

compare the bill with what we actually ordered or used
check due dates, autopay, and account balance together
catch a changed rate or subscription price
keep proof when a charge needs to be disputed
verify the split before requesting reimbursement

Shared credit cards or payment requests

outcomes.role_note: [A] = the partner both identified as the stronger bill checker.
outcomes.verdict: [A] is the relationship’s financial proofreader. [A] catches the duplicate charge, changed rate, or reimbursement mistake before a small error becomes permanent. [B] trusts that eye for detail, but trust can quietly become total disengagement from accounts and due dates. Keep [A] as the final checker for high-risk bills, while [B] owns clean first-pass preparation: correct account, due date, split, receipt, and enough balance. [A] should verify a nearly finished payment, not reconstruct the entire story behind it.
outcomes.actions_a: Define which bills deserve your second check and stop auditing low-risk charges below the agreed threshold.
outcomes.actions_b: Prepare those bills with every required detail and resolve missing receipts or unclear splits before [A] reviews them.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Bill Check Ladder with low, medium, and high-risk bills, first-pass owner, checker, proof required, and dispute deadline.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. [A] catches the typo without writing the whole financial document.

outcomes.role_note: [B] = the partner both identified as the stronger bill checker.
outcomes.verdict: [B] is the relationship’s financial proofreader. [B] catches the duplicate charge, changed rate, or reimbursement mistake before a small error becomes permanent. [A] trusts that eye for detail, but trust can quietly become total disengagement from accounts and due dates. Keep [B] as the final checker for high-risk bills, while [A] owns clean first-pass preparation: correct account, due date, split, receipt, and enough balance. [B] should verify a nearly finished payment, not reconstruct the entire story behind it.
outcomes.actions_a: Prepare those bills with every required detail and resolve missing receipts or unclear splits before [B] reviews them.
outcomes.actions_b: Define which bills deserve your second check and stop auditing low-risk charges below the agreed threshold.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Bill Check Ladder with low, medium, and high-risk bills, first-pass owner, checker, proof required, and dispute deadline.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. [B] catches the typo without writing the whole financial document.

outcomes.verdict: You both pay attention before money leaves the account. That shared caution is useful because billing systems make real mistakes, and neither person has to convince the other that details matter. The risk is spending ten dollars of emotional energy to recover a two-dollar error or delaying payment while two reviewers repeat the same work. Assign risk levels. Routine bills get one checker, changed or unfamiliar bills get two, and disputes above a threshold get saved proof. Your care becomes efficient when precision matches the size and reversibility of the charge.
outcomes.actions_a: Choose the routine bill categories you can approve alone and the error amount worth pursuing.
outcomes.actions_b: Choose different categories and define which changes automatically trigger a second set of eyes.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a One Check or Two checklist with bill categories, change triggers, dispute minimum, proof location, and payment deadline.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Careful money gets a speed setting.

outcomes.verdict: [A] may catch mathematical errors and duplicate charges, while [B] catches context errors such as an incorrect split, forgotten credit, changed plan, or service nobody uses. Each person claims the sharper eye because each notices mistakes the other person does not naturally scan for. Combine those strengths in sequence. One partner checks the numbers, the other checks whether the bill matches real life. Rotate the first pass so both people keep account knowledge instead of becoming specialists who cannot cover each other.
outcomes.actions_a: Name whether your strongest check is numerical accuracy or real-life context and own that lane on the next high-risk bill.
outcomes.actions_b: Own the opposite lane and list the information you need to complete it without repeating [A]’s work.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Numbers and Context bill card with separate checks, rotating first pass, discrepancy owner, and final payment signal.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Two different sharp eyes stop reviewing the same line.

outcomes.verdict: Each of you trusts the other person’s checking because the catches are memorable while the routine bills you personally verified disappear into normal life. That mutual confidence is valuable, but it can produce a payment where both people assumed a second look was coming. Name one checker per bill category and keep the other person as backup only for changes, unusually high totals, or disputed charges. The shared win is not having two skeptical people hover over every payment. It is knowing exactly when another set of eyes will appear.
outcomes.actions_a: Claim the bill categories you will check without prompting and define the change that triggers [B]’s backup review.
outcomes.actions_b: Claim different categories and set alerts that let you cover [A] when a due date or total falls outside the normal range.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Bill Checker Matrix with category owner, normal range, backup trigger, due-date alert, and proof location.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Mutual trust gets named coverage instead of mutual assumption.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = identified a specific bill checker; [B] = said the habit is roughly equal.
outcomes.verdict: [A] sees one person making the catches that prevent fees, overpayment, or long dispute calls. [B] sees both partners checking and may be counting the many ordinary bills that pass without incident. You are measuring visible saves against total participation. Keep the proven checker on complex or changeable bills, then assign routine categories to the other partner and measure completion without rescue. This preserves the skill [A] trusts while testing whether the workload is more balanced than the dramatic error stories suggest.
outcomes.actions_a: Identify the bill types where the proposed checker’s track record creates real value, not only reassurance.
outcomes.actions_b: Own a routine category end to end for two cycles, including checking, payment, proof, and any follow-up.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a two-cycle Bill Coverage Test with category, owner, errors found, time spent, missed details, and final assignment.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Dramatic catches and everyday competence both enter the record.

cases.title: How Should Savings Goals Actually Get Prioritized?
cases.subtitle: Which savings goal should get the most attention from you right now?

questions.prompt: Which savings goal should get the most attention from you right now?

options.label: An emergency cushion
A home, move, or major life setup
Travel and meaningful experiences
Debt payoff and financial freedom
Retirement and long-term security
Career, education, or a major personal goal

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: How much emotional weight does this savings priority carry for you?

options.label: It would be nice, but it is not urgent
It matters and I want steady progress
It feels important to our next chapter
It feels urgent or deeply tied to my sense of safety

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: What do you most need the goal to protect or create?

options.label: Safety if income or health changes
A concrete shared next step
Memories while life is happening
Freedom from monthly pressure
Confidence about the distant future
Personal growth without burdening the relationship

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: What most often blocks progress?

options.label: The target is too vague
Every urgent expense raids the savings
One goal always gets treated as more mature
The monthly amount is unrealistic
We agree on the goal but not the timeline
Personal and shared goals compete for the same money

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: Anything the court should know about the future you are saving for or the fear behind the goal? (optional)
questions.interactionRule: Private context is used only to personalize the selected deterministic branch.

outcomes.verdict: You picked the same goal without loading it with crisis-level pressure. That gives you something surprisingly useful: a shared direction that can create momentum without making every coffee or night out feel like sabotage. The goal can become part of your couple identity before it becomes a financial emergency. Give it a real name, an attainable first milestone, and a small automatic contribution. Light emotional weight is not lack of commitment. It is room to build consistency while still enjoying the life you are saving inside.
outcomes.actions_a: Name the part of this goal that would make daily life feel more exciting or secure to you.
outcomes.actions_b: Choose the first milestone that would make the goal feel real without demanding a harsh lifestyle change.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a named Goal Card with target, first milestone, automatic monthly amount, one visual reminder, and a celebration for the first checkpoint.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. A low-pressure shared goal gets enough structure to become real.

outcomes.verdict: You are saving toward the same destination, but the goal may be carrying two different pieces of emotional luggage. One of you might see the emergency fund as freedom from panic, while the other sees it as permission to take a career risk. A home fund could mean stability to one person and belonging to the other. Shared urgency creates powerful teamwork, but it can also hide different finish lines. Define what success changes for each of you, then set the number and date that satisfy both meanings rather than only sharing a category label.
outcomes.actions_a: Describe the exact fear, freedom, or future moment this savings goal represents for you.
outcomes.actions_b: Describe your version and identify where your preferred target or timeline differs from [A]’s.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Two Meanings, One Goal brief with each person’s reason, shared target, milestone dates, access rules, and what counts as complete.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. The same goal now knows which two futures it is carrying.

outcomes.role_note: [A] and [B] selected different savings priorities with relatively light emotional weight.
outcomes.verdict: [A] is noticing one future worth funding, while [B] is noticing a different part of life that could become easier, richer, or more secure. Because neither goal currently carries emergency weight, the difference is information rather than a threat. You have room to run two small savings lanes and learn which one gains urgency through real progress. The bright spot is that neither dream has to disappear for the couple to be responsible. Small parallel contributions keep both people represented while shared essentials stay protected.
outcomes.actions_a: Choose a modest automatic amount for your goal and define the first checkpoint that would justify increasing it.
outcomes.actions_b: Do the same for your different goal without treating [A]’s lane as money taken from your future.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Parallel Goals board with separate targets, equal starting periods, monthly amounts, first checkpoints, and a three-month comparison date.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Two futures get funded before either one has to disappear.

outcomes.role_note: [A] and [B] selected different savings priorities with high emotional weight.
outcomes.verdict: [A]’s goal is protecting a specific version of safety, freedom, or forward movement. [B]’s different goal is carrying an equally real need, which is why a simple ranking can feel like choosing whose future matters. This is a two-alarm savings problem, not a lack of shared values. Fund a minimum floor for both goals, then send the remaining amount toward the goal with the nearest deadline or largest consequence for delay. Revisit at a fixed checkpoint so temporary priority does not quietly become permanent abandonment.
outcomes.actions_a: Define the minimum monthly contribution that keeps your goal alive and the consequence of delaying it.
outcomes.actions_b: Define the same for your goal and name the date or event that makes its urgency measurable.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Two-Alarm Savings Plan with minimum floors, urgency factors, temporary priority, checkpoint date, and the condition that shifts extra money to the other goal.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. One goal can lead for a season without erasing the other future.

options.label: It genuinely works for me
Mostly okay, with a few topics left untouched
I often feel exposed, shut out, judged, or forced to guess
I really need our money conversations to change

questions.prompt: Anything the court should know about the number, fear, or money story that is hardest to say out loud? (optional)

outcomes.verdict: You have financial emotional safety. Both of you can bring up a number, mistake, fear, or changing goal without expecting the conversation to become a character judgment. That openness does more than prevent surprises. It lets money become usable relationship information, showing where each person needs security, freedom, generosity, or control. Protect the quality of these talks as much as the frequency. Keep room for feelings before solutions and schedule occasional conversations when nothing is on fire, so honesty does not become associated only with financial problems.
outcomes.actions_a: Name one money topic [B] makes easier to discuss and the response that creates that safety.
outcomes.actions_b: Name a more vulnerable topic you want to keep normalizing before it becomes urgent.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Money Talk Menu with Easy, Planning, Vulnerable, and Urgent topics, plus the response each category needs before problem-solving begins.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Money can tell the truth here without putting either person’s worth on trial.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = dissatisfied with the current money conversations; [B] = content with them.
outcomes.verdict: [A] and [B] report similar comfort, but [A] may be doing more of the emotional exposing. [A] shares fears, mistakes, or exact numbers, while [B] participates through practical updates and solutions. [B] experiences a functional money conversation and assumes openness is mutual. [A] experiences one-way vulnerability. Balance the depth, not just the airtime. [B] should bring one uncertainty or personal money story before offering advice, while [A] asks for the kind of response needed instead of hoping [B] guesses.
outcomes.actions_a: Start the next talk by naming whether you need listening, reassurance, brainstorming, or a decision.
outcomes.actions_b: Share one real uncertainty, fear, or past influence of your own before moving into solutions.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Money Talk Depth Card with topic, numbers shared, feeling shared, response requested, decision needed, and one follow-up date.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. The conversation becomes mutual disclosure instead of one person presenting a case.

outcomes.verdict: You both have access to the money conversation, but it currently opens only like an emergency door. A late bill, big purchase, or scary account balance forces the topic, so both nervous systems learn that money talk means trouble. You agree on roughly how open you want to be. Change the timing before changing the depth. Hold a short regular check-in with one number, one feeling, and one upcoming decision. Normal conversations when nothing is broken will make the vulnerable topics less likely to arrive carrying sirens.
outcomes.actions_a: Choose one neutral number you can share regularly without turning it into a performance review.
outcomes.actions_b: Choose one feeling prompt and one upcoming-decision prompt that keep the check-in human and useful.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save four recurring Money Check-In dates with One Number, One Feeling, One Decision, and a ten-minute time limit for each.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. The money door opens on ordinary days too.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = is more comfortable talking openly about money; [B] = is less comfortable.
outcomes.verdict: [A] processes money by putting the facts and feelings into the room, which helps uncertainty become manageable. [B] needs more privacy or preparation and may speak best after checking numbers and sorting out shame, fear, or family history. Your current rhythm works because [A] does not force instant disclosure and [B] does not use processing time to disappear. Keep a preview-and-return system: [A] names the topic and purpose early, while [B] chooses a near-term time to come back prepared. Openness can have pacing without becoming avoidance.
outcomes.actions_a: Give the topic, reason, and minimum information needed without demanding an immediate full response.
outcomes.actions_b: Choose a return time, prepare the relevant numbers, and bring one personal reaction instead of only facts.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Money Talk Preview template with topic, purpose, requested numbers, emotional stakes, preparation time, and scheduled return.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Honesty keeps momentum without requiring the same speaking speed.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = is more comfortable talking openly and is dissatisfied; [B] = is less comfortable and currently content.
outcomes.verdict: [A] experiences missing information as risk. When income, debt, spending, or family obligations stay vague, [A] may ask more questions to rebuild a sense of shared reality. [B] experiences those questions as exposure and may feel the current level of disclosure is already generous. That leaves [A] guessing and [B] bracing. [B] owes one predictable disclosure habit around facts that affect shared life. [A] owes a contained format with no surprise follow-up interrogation once the agreed information has been shared.
outcomes.actions_a: Choose the smallest set of shared-impact facts you genuinely need and keep the conversation inside that scope.
outcomes.actions_b: Share those facts on the agreed schedule and flag changes before [A] has to discover or repeatedly ask about them.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Shared Money Facts agreement with required disclosures, privacy boundaries, update frequency, question limit, and change-alert rule.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Shared reality gets reliable facts, and privacy gets clear edges.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = is more comfortable talking openly about money; [B] = is less comfortable.
outcomes.verdict: You are stuck in a disclosure pressure cycle. [A] raises the topic with extra urgency after waiting too long, while [B] hears pressure and protects personal information more tightly. The resulting silence makes [A] even more urgent next time. Create a recurring ritual that separates disclosure, feelings, and decisions into three short rounds. [B] gets the questions in advance and can prepare. [A] gets a guaranteed conversation and does not need to chase. Repetition will make money talk less emotionally expensive than another giant breakthrough conversation.
outcomes.actions_a: Send the agreed questions before the meeting and hold new topics for the next check-in unless a real deadline exists.
outcomes.actions_b: Prepare direct answers, name one emotional reaction, and stay through the decision round instead of ending after disclosure.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a monthly Three-Round Money Ritual with advance questions, Facts, Feelings, Decisions, time limits, and the next meeting date.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Openness becomes a rhythm instead of a pressure event.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = dissatisfied with the current recurring-cost system; [B] = content with it.

outcomes.actions_b: Own the review, downgrade, or cancellation of those services without asking [A] to keep reminding you.

You agree on the desired level of management, so the missing piece is a recurring decision date. Review every charge quarterly and require one of three outcomes: keep with a named user, change the plan, or cancel with confirmation saved. The system stays simple because indecision is no longer a fourth option.
outcomes.actions_a: Gather the recurring charges from one payment source and flag anything you cannot immediately identify.
outcomes.actions_b: Gather the other sources and recover the login information needed to change or cancel each service.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a quarterly Keep, Change, Cancel board with total monthly cost, owner, usage, next renewal, decision, and cancellation confirmation.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = wants more active subscription management; [B] = prefers a lighter approach.

[B] protects convenience and does not want low-risk services to create constant admin. The arrangement works because [A] manages visibility without turning visibility into control, while [B] responds when a service needs a decision. Keep one dashboard and use exception-based reviews. Stable charges stay quiet, while price changes, duplicate services, low usage, and annual renewals trigger attention.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = wants more active management and is dissatisfied; [B] = prefers a lighter approach and is currently content.
outcomes.verdict: [A] sees recurring charges as a row of taps that can drip for years after nobody needs the water. [B] sees small payments buying convenience and feels the cost of constant reviewing more than the cost of a few unused services. Right now, [B] keeps the convenience while [A] absorbs the financial irritation and cleanup. [B] owes one concrete habit: every service [B] chooses gets a renewal alert and personal cancellation ownership. [A] owes a minimum dollar or usage threshold before raising a review.
outcomes.actions_a: Set the threshold where a recurring charge becomes worth discussing and leave lower-impact services alone until the scheduled review.
outcomes.actions_b: Add renewal alerts for your services and complete any cancellation or downgrade before the next charge.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Recurring Cost Threshold rule with review amount, low-use definition, personal-service ownership, renewal alerts, and one quarterly sweep.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Convenience pays for itself, and cleanup follows the person who subscribed.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = wants more active subscription management; [B] = prefers a lighter approach.

Then [A] gets less information and becomes even more intense at the next surprise. Separate visibility from judgment. Put all recurring charges on one list, assign each to an owner, and discuss only renewals due in the next thirty days. A rolling monthly checkpoint keeps the workload small and prevents one forgotten trial from triggering a relationship-wide financial search.
outcomes.actions_a: Build the shared list once and restrict each review to charges approaching renewal or crossing an agreed exception.
outcomes.actions_b: Keep your services current on the list and make the final Keep, Change, or Cancel decision before renewal.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a rolling Renewal Calendar with thirty-day alerts, service owner, cost, decision deadline, and cancellation receipt link.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. One small monthly checkpoint replaces the surprise audit.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = the partner both identified as the more reliable bill payer.
outcomes.verdict: [A] is good at closing the loop. [A] does not only remember a due date, but also checks the funding account, completes the payment, and notices when confirmation never arrives. [B] trusts that reliability, which protects both of you from fees and last-minute panic. The role becomes risky if [A] is the only person who knows where bills live or how they get paid. Keep [A] as payment lead, while [B] maintains access, funds the agreed share on time, and learns the backup route for every essential bill.
outcomes.actions_a: Create one payment sequence for essential bills and save confirmation where both partners can find it.
outcomes.actions_b: Fund the payment account by the agreed date and learn the backup steps for two essential bills this month.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Monthly Bill Runbook with due date, funding date, payment method, lead, backup, login location, and confirmation field.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. [A] closes the payment loop without becoming the only person who knows the route.

outcomes.role_note: [B] = the partner both identified as the more reliable bill payer.
outcomes.verdict: [B] is good at closing the loop. [B] does not only remember a due date, but also checks the funding account, completes the payment, and notices when confirmation never arrives. [A] trusts that reliability, which protects both of you from fees and last-minute panic. The role becomes risky if [B] is the only person who knows where bills live or how they get paid. Keep [B] as payment lead, while [A] maintains access, funds the agreed share on time, and learns the backup route for every essential bill.
outcomes.actions_a: Fund the payment account by the agreed date and learn the backup steps for two essential bills this month.
outcomes.actions_b: Create one payment sequence for essential bills and save confirmation where both partners can find it.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Monthly Bill Runbook with due date, funding date, payment method, lead, backup, login location, and confirmation field.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. [B] closes the payment loop without becoming the only person who knows the route.

outcomes.verdict: You both can execute a bill payment reliably. The issue is not competence. It is preventing duplicate payments, split assumptions, and a shared account that nobody checks because both people could. Give each bill one permanent lead and one backup, then use the same completion signal for everything. Your shared reliability becomes valuable when either partner can cover an emergency without two people hovering over every ordinary due date.
outcomes.actions_a: Claim the bill categories you can pay consistently and publish the completion signal immediately after payment.
outcomes.actions_b: Claim different categories and define when you step in as backup rather than paying a bill twice.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Bill Lead Matrix with permanent owner, backup, funding deadline, completion signal, and emergency takeover rule.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Two reliable payers use one clear handoff.

outcomes.verdict: [A] may be stronger at predictable monthly bills, building a rhythm and never missing the standard due dates. [B] may be stronger at irregular payments, catching annual fees, medical invoices, or a changed total that falls outside the routine. Each person claims the role because each is rescuing a different failure point. Split the payment system by predictability rather than choosing one universal bill payer. Then rotate one category quarterly so both of you retain enough knowledge to cover the other person.
outcomes.actions_a: Claim either predictable or irregular bills and define the trigger that tells you payment is complete.
outcomes.actions_b: Own the opposite category and prepare one quarterly handoff that teaches [A] the backup process.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Predictable and Irregular Bill Map with owners, due-date source, funding check, confirmation location, and rotation date.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Routine and surprise bills finally get the payer best suited to each.

outcomes.verdict: Each of you trusts the other because the payment saves are visible while your own routine reliability is easy to forget. That compliment leaves the actual bills sitting between two open hands. Bill payment needs named ownership more than a naturally gifted person. Divide the essential bills now, keep a shared completion record, and rotate only after a clean handoff. The relationship wins when either person can pay, but one person is unmistakably responsible today.
outcomes.actions_a: Take the first group of essential bills and complete payment plus confirmation without waiting for [B] to check.
outcomes.actions_b: Take a different group and verify that you have access, due dates, and funding information before the payment window.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a two-month Bill Ownership Board with current payer, backup, due date, funding status, confirmation, and handoff date.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. The bill gets one owner before it gets two assumptions.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = identified a specific bill payer; [B] = said either partner could handle it.
outcomes.verdict: [A] sees one person’s track record as the safest protection against late fees and failed payments. [B] sees bill paying as a transferable task and wants shared resilience rather than permanent dependence on one partner. Keep the proven payer on high-consequence bills, while the other partner takes full ownership of lower-risk payments for three cycles. Success means paying on time, checking funds, and saving confirmation without rescue. The test produces a real backup instead of an honorary one.
outcomes.actions_a: Identify the high-consequence bills where continuity matters and stop reclaiming the lower-risk test category.
outcomes.actions_b: Run the assigned category for three cycles and document every step well enough that either partner can repeat it.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Three-Cycle Payment Test with bill, owner, due date, funding check, confirmation, error, and final assignment.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Proven reliability stays where it matters, and backup becomes an actual skill.

cases.title: How Much of a Financial Cushion Actually Feels Safe to Each of You?

About one month of essential costs

Medical, car, pet, or home emergencies

outcomes.verdict: You have a shared definition of enough, which means safety has an address instead of moving every time the news gets scary. The match usually comes from a similar read on job stability, family backup, essential expenses, and how much uncertainty your bodies can tolerate. That clarity protects more than savings. It gives you permission to use money above the target for life now. Keep the number tied to named risks and review dates so the cushion stays a safety tool rather than becoming a scoreboard with no finish line.
outcomes.actions_a: Name the specific risk your preferred cushion covers and the expense number behind it.
outcomes.actions_b: Name a different risk or source of backup and the event that should trigger a target review.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save an Enough Number note with essential monthly cost, target months, covered risks, allowed uses, refill rule, and next review date.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Safety gets a number, and the rest of your money gets a life.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = dissatisfied with the current cushion plan; [B] = content with it.
outcomes.verdict: [A] and [B] want a similar cushion, but [A] may not experience the fund as equally accessible or protective. The account could sit under [B]’s control, exclude risks [A] worries about, or require an argument before money can be used. [B] sees the target amount and assumes safety has been achieved. [A] experiences savings that exist without fully belonging to the shared emergency plan. Define access, valid uses, and refill rules so the same balance provides the same protection to both partners.
outcomes.actions_a: Name the emergency you are unsure the fund would cover and the access or consent issue behind that doubt.
outcomes.actions_b: Change the rule or account access that keeps [A] from receiving equal protection from the existing cushion.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Cushion Access Agreement with account access, valid emergencies, approval limits, withdrawal notice, refill owner, and backup proof.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. The cushion counts only when both people can actually land on it.

outcomes.verdict: You agree on the desired cushion, but the goal may be getting whatever money survives the month instead of a protected contribution. That makes progress slow and keeps every surprise expense feeling like proof that safety is impossible. Reverse the order. Automate a realistic amount on payday, define a minimum floor that cannot fund ordinary overspending, and create a refill rule after legitimate use. A smaller plan that happens every month will calm more uncertainty than an ambitious target fed only by leftovers.
outcomes.actions_a: Choose the automatic contribution you can sustain even during an ordinary expensive month.
outcomes.actions_b: Define the minimum floor and the categories that must use another budget before touching it.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Cushion Build Plan with payday transfer, minimum floor, valid uses, refill percentage, milestone dates, and the first three transfers scheduled.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Safety gets paid before the month spends everything else.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = needs a larger financial cushion; [B] = feels safe with less.
outcomes.verdict: [A] uses a larger cushion to lower the background noise of uncertainty and preserve options if work, health, or housing changes. [B] sees extra cash sitting still and wants some of it supporting experiences, goals, or investments while life is happening. Your current balance works because the cautious target has a ceiling and the present-focused partner can trust that reaching it unlocks other money. Keep a base cushion that protects both people, then let [A] add personal safety savings beyond the shared target if more margin still matters.
outcomes.actions_a: Define the shared base target you can stop expanding and fund any additional comfort from your personal lane.
outcomes.actions_b: Respect the base target and wait until it is funded before redirecting the agreed surplus toward current goals.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Base and Extra Cushion chart with shared target, personal extra lane, milestone release points, surplus destination, and review date.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Shared safety gets a ceiling, and personal comfort can keep building separately.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = needs a larger cushion and is dissatisfied; [B] = feels safe with less and is currently content.
outcomes.verdict: [A] may be carrying risks [B] does not feel as strongly: unstable income, limited family backup, past scarcity, or the knowledge that a crisis would land harder on [A]. [B] sees money accumulating past the point of practical need while current plans keep getting postponed. Right now, [B] gets the preferred stopping point and [A] keeps the alarm. Set a temporary higher target tied to one named risk and one deadline. [A] gets measurable protection, while [B] gets a date when surplus money starts moving again.
outcomes.actions_a: Name the uncovered risk, calculate the additional amount it requires, and accept a fixed ceiling for this phase.
outcomes.actions_b: Support contributions until the deadline and choose the first current goal that receives money after the ceiling is reached.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Temporary Safety Sprint with named risk, target amount, monthly contribution, finish date, surplus destination, and no-extension rule without a new review.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. The extra cushion covers a real risk instead of an endless feeling.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = needs a larger financial cushion; [B] = feels safe with less.
outcomes.verdict: [A] keeps moving the safety line after every new threat, while [B] pushes back harder as trips, upgrades, or other goals stay permanently paused. The cushion becomes a locked waiting room where current life keeps missing its appointment. Use checkpoints rather than one final answer. Fund the first essential milestone, release a fixed portion of new savings to a current goal, then resume the next cushion stage. Alternating progress lets [A] see safety growing and lets [B] see life continuing before the entire target is complete.
outcomes.actions_a: Break the desired cushion into risk-based milestones and stop treating only the final number as meaningful progress.
outcomes.actions_b: Choose one current goal with a fixed allocation that does not raid completed safety milestones.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Cushion Checkpoint Calendar with three safety milestones, release percentages, current-goal transfers, protected floors, and review dates.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Safety and current life take turns moving forward.

outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. One person spots the signal without taking over the whole dashboard.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = avoids checking more often and is dissatisfied; [B] = checks more readily and is currently content.
outcomes.verdict: [A] may avoid the account because checking has become paired with shame, immediate questioning, or a problem [A] does not yet know how to solve. [B] sees direct information as basic responsibility and may believe more reminders are the obvious answer. The reminders can make [A] feel even less capable, while [B] quietly becomes the financial monitor. [B] owes a neutral, scheduled check-in with no live commentary. [A] owes one complete action after checking, so information leads to restored agency rather than another promise to look later.
outcomes.actions_a: Open the account at the scheduled time and complete one chosen action before closing it.
outcomes.actions_b: Stop surprise check-ins and save questions for the agreed review after [A] has completed the first action.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Check, Act, Then Talk routine with scheduled time, private review period, action menu, proof of completion, and question time.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Account checking returns to [A] as a skill instead of staying with [B] as supervision.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = avoids checking more often; [B] = checks more readily.
outcomes.verdict: [A] delays because the number feels emotionally expensive. [B] checks more often because uncertainty feels expensive. Then [B] reports changes with urgency, [A] feels ambushed and withdraws, and both people become more anxious. Replace constant monitoring with a fixed rhythm and an emergency threshold. [B] waits for the scheduled check unless the threshold is crossed. [A] attends the check and takes ownership of one action. Predictability lowers the cost for both nervous systems without hiding the information your shared life needs.
outcomes.actions_a: Attend the recurring check with account access ready and choose the first action tied to your own spending or obligations.
outcomes.actions_b: Limit unscheduled alerts to the agreed emergency threshold and bring ordinary observations to the recurring check.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a four-week Account Rhythm with check dates, emergency threshold, three required numbers, action owner, and a short anxiety rating after each session.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Money information gets a schedule instead of chasing either of you through the week.

outcomes.verdict: You share the same emotional meaning for paying on dates. Whether you split, alternate, or treat each other, neither person is secretly translating the check into love, debt, or status in a different language. That shared meaning lets money leave the moment without taking the romance with it. Keep one simple fairness check outside the date itself, especially when incomes or price levels change. The goal is to preserve generosity while making sure one partner is not consistently choosing the experience and sending the cost to the other.
outcomes.actions_a: Name the payment gesture from [B] that makes you feel cared for rather than financially measured.
outcomes.actions_b: Name the price or frequency change that should trigger a practical reset before resentment appears.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Date Money Style note with preferred default, treat meaning, price-choice rule, income adjustment, and one monthly fairness check.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. The check follows your shared meaning instead of writing one for you.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = dissatisfied with the current date-payment pattern; [B] = content with it.
outcomes.verdict: [A] and [B] prefer a similar level of balance, but [A] may be paying a hidden cover charge. [A] could be booking the dates, handling rides, buying the small extras, or accepting venues priced around [B]’s comfort. [B] sees the visible dinner checks and believes the exchange is balanced. [A] feels the full cost of participation. Count the complete date for a short period, then move either planning labor, small extras, or the price-setting role so the shared experience stops producing one-sided effort.
outcomes.actions_a: Identify the hidden date costs you carry and distinguish money from planning or travel effort.
outcomes.actions_b: Take ownership of one hidden-cost category and choose options that fit both partners’ real comfort levels.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a four-date Full Cost Note with meal, tickets, transport, extras, planning owner, and how the final balance felt.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Date fairness includes everything that got you to the table.

outcomes.verdict: You agree on how balanced date spending should feel, but the payment plan keeps arriving with the check. That timing forces a romance question, a budget question, and a fairness question into the same thirty seconds. Choose the payment mode while choosing the date. Mark it as split, alternate, inviter treats, or shared-date fund before the reservation is made. Then the person suggesting a pricier plan also has to name how the added cost will work. Clarity before the date lets generosity feel voluntary again.
outcomes.actions_a: Choose the default payment mode you can use without fresh negotiation on ordinary dates.
outcomes.actions_b: Define the rule for expensive suggestions and when the inviter covers the upgrade beyond the shared comfort level.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Date Booking Note with plan, expected cost, payment mode, inviter, upgrade coverage, and reimbursement deadline.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. The payment decision happens before the waiter becomes the mediator.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = prefers a more even date split; [B] = prefers more treating or loose balance.
outcomes.verdict: [A] feels relaxed when contribution is visible and neither person has to wonder whether the balance is drifting. [B] enjoys generosity, spontaneity, and the feeling that care can move back and forth without immediate accounting. Your system works because [A] receives enough evidence of reciprocity while [B] still has room to treat without creating debt. Keep a loose monthly total or alternating anchor in the background, then leave individual moments free. Structure protects the baseline, and generosity gets to remain a gift.
outcomes.actions_a: Choose the lightest tracking method that gives you confidence without reviewing every receipt.
outcomes.actions_b: Offer treats clearly as gifts and use the balancing anchor before the month drifts too far in one direction.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Date Balance Compass with monthly comfort range, alternating anchor, gift language, price cap, and reset date.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Fairness stays visible enough for generosity to stay romantic.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = prefers a more even split and is dissatisfied; [B] = prefers more treating or loose balance and is currently content.
outcomes.verdict: [A] may be carrying uncertainty about debt, dependence, or whether accepting a treat creates an expectation later. [B] experiences flexible paying as warmth and may see exact splitting as stripping personality from the date. The current ambiguity serves [B] because [B] can treat or be treated without needing a system, while [A] keeps the internal score to feel safe. [B] owes one visible balancing habit. [A] owes a clear thank-you or reimbursement choice instead of treating every gift as a future liability.
outcomes.actions_a: State whether you want to accept a treat, split now, or balance the next date instead of silently recording a debt.
outcomes.actions_b: Use one dependable balancing habit, such as alternating planned dates or funding the next comparable experience.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a No Silent Scorecard agreement with three payment phrases, balancing method, gift definition, comparable-date rule, and reset point.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Treating stays warm because nobody has to decode the bill later.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = prefers a more even split; [B] = prefers more treating or loose balance.
outcomes.verdict: [A] keeps a mental ledger because ambiguity feels risky. [B] resists the ledger because being measured makes affection feel transactional. Then [A] tracks more carefully and [B] becomes less willing to discuss the numbers. Stop trying to settle every date with one philosophy. Assign different payment modes to different date types: ordinary dates use a predictable split, inviter-led upgrades follow the inviter, and deliberate treats are named as gifts. A small monthly reset catches drift without putting each romantic gesture through accounting.
outcomes.actions_a: Define the ordinary-date baseline and stop carrying informal debts outside that rule.
outcomes.actions_b: Name treats explicitly and cover the difference when your preferred plan exceeds the shared price range.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Date Payment Menu for Ordinary, Inviter-Led, Special Occasion, and Gift dates, plus one monthly reset reminder.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Different dates get different money rules, and the relationship drops the hidden ledger.

cases.title: Who Should Take the Lead on Long Term Financial Planning?
cases.subtitle: Between you two, who should lead long-term financial planning?

Probably me

questions.prompt: What best proves it?

options.label: turn distant goals into actual numbers and dates
think about retirement, insurance, and risk before they become urgent
compare options without freezing in research forever
keep long-term plans connected to the life we actually want
update assumptions when income or priorities change
explain tradeoffs without making the future feel terrifying
