questions.prompt: Which long-term area most needs a lead?

options.label: Retirement and investing
Buying a home or relocating
Insurance and emergency protection
Debt payoff and credit strategy
Career changes or education
Caregiving, children, or family support

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: Where does long-term planning currently fail?

options.label: The conversation stays abstract
Research never becomes a decision
Only one partner knows the accounts
The plan reflects one person’s future
Short-term spending repeatedly overrides it
You agree once and never update the assumptions

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: Anything the court should know about the future decision that keeps staying too far away to plan? (optional)
questions.interactionRule: Private context is used only to personalize the selected deterministic branch.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = the partner both identified as the stronger long-term planning lead.
outcomes.verdict: [A] can turn a distant future into choices that exist this year. [A] links retirement, housing, insurance, or career plans to numbers and checkpoints without losing the life those numbers are meant to support. [B] trusts that ability, which gives the relationship direction. The risk is letting [A] design a technically strong future that [B] only approves at the end. Keep [A] as planning lead, while [B] supplies priorities, risk limits, and a real vote at every major assumption and decision point.
outcomes.actions_a: Build the next planning decision around two or three understandable options instead of presenting one finished answer.
outcomes.actions_b: Bring your desired future, risk tolerance, and nonnegotiables before [A] begins comparing the options.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Long-Term Planning Brief with shared goal, assumptions, three options, risks, decision date, and the next review checkpoint.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. [A] maps the route, and both of you still choose the destination.

outcomes.role_note: [B] = the partner both identified as the stronger long-term planning lead.
outcomes.verdict: [B] can turn a distant future into choices that exist this year. [B] links retirement, housing, insurance, or career plans to numbers and checkpoints without losing the life those numbers are meant to support. [A] trusts that ability, which gives the relationship direction. The risk is letting [B] design a technically strong future that [A] only approves at the end. Keep [B] as planning lead, while [A] supplies priorities, risk limits, and a real vote at every major assumption and decision point.
outcomes.actions_a: Bring your desired future, risk tolerance, and nonnegotiables before [B] begins comparing the options.
outcomes.actions_b: Build the next planning decision around two or three understandable options instead of presenting one finished answer.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Long-Term Planning Brief with shared goal, assumptions, three options, risks, decision date, and the next review checkpoint.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. [B] maps the route, and both of you still choose the destination.

outcomes.verdict: You both can think beyond the next bill without turning the future into either fantasy or panic. That shared skill means you can challenge assumptions, cover for each other, and notice when a plan no longer matches the life you want. The main risk is parallel planning: two investment ideas, two housing timelines, or a lot of smart research with no final owner. Assign one lead per long-term goal and one decision date. Shared expertise becomes progress only when someone closes the current question.
outcomes.actions_a: Claim the long-term goal where you can turn research into a clear decision path.
outcomes.actions_b: Claim a different goal and define which decisions still require both partners’ explicit agreement.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Long-Term Goal Ownership Map with lead, shared assumptions, next decision, deadline, documents, and quarterly review date.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Two future thinkers stop producing two unfinished futures.

outcomes.verdict: [A] may be the numbers planner, comfortable with projections, risk, taxes, and comparing financial products. [B] may be the life planner, better at noticing which future would actually feel worth funding and what sacrifices the couple can sustain. Each person claims the lead because each sees the other person’s blind spot. Long-term planning needs both architecture and livability. Give one partner the model and the other the reality check, then require both signatures before the plan becomes active.
outcomes.actions_a: Name whether your strongest contribution is financial architecture or testing whether the plan fits real life.
outcomes.actions_b: Own the opposite role and define the question that must be answered before either person calls the plan complete.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Numbers and Life planning sheet with separate role owners, assumptions, lifestyle test, decision rule, and final approval date.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. The future becomes financially sound and emotionally livable.

outcomes.verdict: Each of you sees the other as the long-term planner because the other person’s future thinking is easier to notice. One partner may start the retirement research while the other keeps the home or career goal alive in ordinary choices. The compliment is real, but planning with no named lead stays permanently almost started. Choose the next single long-term decision and rotate leadership by project. The non-lead partner still supplies values and approval, but does not wait for the lead to generate every opinion too.
outcomes.actions_a: Lead the next long-term project through one concrete decision and request [B]’s input by a specific date.
outcomes.actions_b: Bring complete priorities and constraints for that decision, then take leadership of the following project.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a three-project Financial Future Queue with rotating lead, first decision, input deadline, completion date, and handoff.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Mutual confidence turns into a future that actually moves.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = identified a specific long-term planning lead; [B] = said either partner could lead.
outcomes.verdict: [A] sees a dependable pilot whose financial knowledge or follow-through helps distant plans leave the runway. [B] sees two qualified adults and wants leadership to follow interest, time, or the specific goal. Use a captain-per-project model. Keep the proven planner on the highest-complexity goal, and give the other partner full leadership of a smaller long-term project with the same research and decision standard. The relationship preserves continuity while building a second person who can fly the plan when life changes.
outcomes.actions_a: Identify the goal where the proposed lead’s experience genuinely reduces risk or wasted time.
outcomes.actions_b: Choose a separate long-term project you will lead from first research through final decision and review.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Financial Captain board with project, lead, co-decisions, research limit, decision deadline, and backup documents.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Each future gets one captain, and the relationship keeps two trained pilots.

cases.title: How Should Debt One of You Brought Into the Relationship Get Handled?
cases.subtitle: Which approach feels fairest for debt one partner brought into the relationship?

questions.prompt: Which approach feels fairest for debt one partner brought into the relationship?

options.label: The original borrower handles it fully as a personal responsibility
The borrower pays it, but both partners plan around it openly
The borrower pays while the household adjusts shared costs to create room
Both partners contribute after shared basics and protections are secure
The approach depends on the debt’s cause, benefit, and current impact

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: How much emotional weight does this debt carry in the relationship?

options.label: Very little, it is manageable background information
Some, because it affects a few choices
A lot, because it shapes timelines or trust
A great deal, because it affects safety, freedom, or the future together

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: What does the debt represent most strongly?

options.label: Education or career investment
Medical or family necessity
Past survival during a difficult period
Consumer spending or lifestyle choices
A previous relationship or legal obligation
A shared benefit even though one name holds the balance

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: Which boundary matters most?

options.label: Full disclosure of balance, rate, and payment status
No automatic access to the other partner’s income
Shared goals should not wait forever
Contribution must not buy extra control
New debt requires a different agreement
Progress needs a visible timeline

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: Anything the court should know about where the debt came from, what it affects now, or what support would actually feel fair? (optional)
questions.interactionRule: Private context is used only to personalize the selected deterministic branch.

outcomes.verdict: You chose the same general debt boundary and neither person currently experiences the balance as a relationship emergency. That suggests the debt has context, a workable payment path, and enough transparency that it does not dominate how you see each other. The useful move is to make the quiet agreement explicit before a job change or shared goal raises the stakes. Record who pays, what information gets shared, and which future decisions trigger a review. Low pressure is the best time to build a plan that will still hold under pressure.
outcomes.actions_a: Name the part of the current approach that protects your independence or sense of fairness.
outcomes.actions_b: Name the future change that would make the debt a shared planning issue even if repayment ownership stays personal.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Debt Boundary Note with payer, disclosure rhythm, current payment, protected shared goals, and review triggers.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. A manageable debt gets clear boundaries before life makes the question harder.

outcomes.verdict: You agree on who should carry the debt, but the balance holds more emotional weight than the simple rule can explain. One of you may see repayment as accountability, while the other hears the debt as delayed housing, travel, children, or freedom. Shared policy does not guarantee shared emotional impact. Separate repayment ownership from timeline impact. Keep the chosen payer structure, then give both partners a voice in milestones, shared-goal protection, and what happens if income or interest changes.
outcomes.actions_a: Name what repayment responsibility means to you and the milestone that would restore the most freedom.
outcomes.actions_b: Name the shared timeline or security concern that needs protection even if you are not the debt payer.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Repayment and Relationship Timeline with debt owner, milestones, shared-goal minimums, risk triggers, and the date each delayed plan gets reconsidered.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. One person can own the debt while both people protect the future it affects.

outcomes.role_note: [A] and [B] selected different debt approaches with relatively light emotional weight.
outcomes.verdict: [A] is protecting one fairness principle, such as personal accountability or shared capacity. [B] is protecting another, such as independence, transparency, or keeping joint goals moving. Because the debt is currently manageable, you can test the practical difference without turning either view into a statement about love. Keep legal and repayment ownership unchanged for a trial period, then adjust one household contribution or planning rule and measure whether it improves both people’s breathing room.
outcomes.actions_a: Name the concrete outcome your preferred approach should improve and the boundary it must not cross.
outcomes.actions_b: Name a different outcome and propose one reversible household adjustment that respects the current debt ownership.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a ninety-day Debt Approach Trial with legal owner, payment owner, household adjustment, protected boundary, success measures, and review date.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Two fairness instincts get tested through one reversible change.

outcomes.role_note: [A] and [B] selected different debt approaches with high emotional weight.
outcomes.verdict: [A]’s approach is protecting a deep need, perhaps accountability, autonomy, or relief from carrying the past alone. [B]’s different approach is protecting trust, present-day security, or a shared future that keeps being delayed. The debt has become both a balance and a relationship timeline. Set a responsibility floor and a support ceiling. The borrower makes a protected minimum payment. The other partner or household may add defined support only after shared basics and personal safety are funded. Review at fixed milestones so help never becomes unlimited and personal responsibility never becomes relational isolation.
outcomes.actions_a: Define the minimum responsibility your preferred approach requires and the support that would still preserve dignity or accountability.
outcomes.actions_b: Define the maximum support you can give freely and the shared protection that must be funded first.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Responsibility Floor and Support Ceiling agreement with payment minimum, support cap, shared protections, decision rights, milestones, and exit terms.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. The debt gets a firm owner, bounded support, and a future neither person has to abandon.

outcomes.verdict: You have low-drama transparency. Both of you can enjoy personal splurges without treating disclosure as confession or permission. That usually means personal money has a clear lane and shared-impact purchases have an equally clear reason to be mentioned. The relationship benefit is freedom without missing context. Preserve it by defining what counts as shared impact, since a purchase can matter through debt, space, recurring cost, or delayed goals even when personal money covered the checkout total.
outcomes.actions_a: Name one kind of splurge you appreciate hearing about because sharing the excitement builds closeness.
outcomes.actions_b: Name one impact that always deserves practical disclosure even when the purchase remains a personal decision.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Splurge Transparency Guide with Personal Fun, Mention Soon, and Discuss First categories, plus real examples for each.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Personal fun stays personal without making shared reality incomplete.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = dissatisfied with the current transparency around splurges; [B] = content with it.
outcomes.verdict: [A] and [B] keep quiet about splurges at similar rates, but [A] may be receiving a different reaction when a purchase surfaces. [A] could face more questions, have a spending category treated as less legitimate, or disclose quickly while [B] mentions purchases only after they are visible. [B] sees equal freedom and assumes the pattern works. [A] experiences unequal scrutiny or timing. Use the same disclosure window and the same shared-impact questions for both partners, regardless of what each person likes to buy.
outcomes.actions_a: Name the reaction or timing difference that makes transparency feel less safe or less equal for you.
outcomes.actions_b: Apply the same questions and disclosure deadline to your own splurges before reviewing [A]’s choices.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Same Disclosure Standard with time window, shared-impact questions, no-comment personal lane, and examples from both spending styles.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Transparency stops changing rules when the shopping category changes.

outcomes.verdict: You both want more openness, but mentioning a splurge may have become socially expensive. A simple heads-up can trigger a budget audit, a defense of personal taste, or a debate about whether the purchase was necessary. Both people then learn to delay the mention even while disliking the secrecy it creates. Separate disclosure from discussion. Use a short FYI format for purchases that do not require agreement, and schedule a later conversation only when a named shared impact exists. Transparency becomes easier when every mention does not open a trial.
outcomes.actions_a: Draft the neutral facts you need in a splurge FYI without turning them into a request for justification.
outcomes.actions_b: Define the shared impacts that earn a later discussion and release purchases that do not cross those lines.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Splurge FYI template with item category, amount range, funding source, shared impact, and Discuss Later or FYI Only status.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Mentioning a purchase becomes information, not an automatic argument.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = is more likely to splurge without mentioning it; [B] = is more likely to mention it.
outcomes.verdict: [A] keeps personal purchases in a private drawer and does not experience privacy as dishonesty when shared obligations remain untouched. [B] naturally leaves the drawer open because sharing purchases feels like ordinary context, excitement, or financial teamwork. The difference stays comfortable because [A]’s privacy has a boundary and [B]’s openness is not a demand for matching disclosure. Keep debt, recurring costs, shared space, and delayed goals outside the private drawer. Everything else can follow each person’s natural style.
outcomes.actions_a: Mention any purchase that crosses the agreed shared-impact boundary without waiting for [B] to discover it.
outcomes.actions_b: Share your own splurges freely while avoiding the expectation that [A] narrate every personal-money choice.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Private Drawer Boundary with protected personal purchases, mandatory-disclosure impacts, mention window, and three examples from each partner.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Privacy keeps a drawer, and shared consequences stay out of it.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = is more likely to splurge without mentioning it and is dissatisfied; [B] = is more likely to mention purchases and is currently content.
outcomes.verdict: [A] may stay quiet because disclosure has started to feel like applying for approval, especially when [B] asks questions immediately or has a different idea of worthwhile spending. [B] shares purchases naturally and may read [A]’s silence as evidence that something is being hidden. The current system gives [B] information while [A] loses autonomy. [B] owes a no-interrogation response inside the personal-money lane. [A] owes timely disclosure whenever the purchase changes a shared number or creates a continuing obligation.
outcomes.actions_a: Use the agreed FYI format for shared-impact splurges and stop postponing disclosure until the purchase is discovered.
outcomes.actions_b: Respond to personal-lane FYIs without cross-examination and save shared-impact questions for the scheduled money talk.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Mention Without Permission agreement with personal lane, disclosure triggers, FYI wording, response rule, and question time.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. [A] gets autonomy, and [B] gets the facts that genuinely belong to both of you.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = is more likely to splurge without mentioning it; [B] = is more likely to mention purchases.
outcomes.verdict: [A] withholds purchases after expecting judgment. [B] asks harder questions after discovering them late. Each round makes silence and suspicion feel more necessary. This is a surprise-cost cycle, and the surprise now costs more trust than some of the purchases cost money. For thirty days, require a simple disclosure only when a splurge crosses one shared-impact trigger. [B] acknowledges receipt without debating it in the moment. Review the pattern on a fixed date and adjust the triggers using real examples.
outcomes.actions_a: Send the agreed disclosure before the purchase becomes discoverable through a statement, package, or changed shared balance.
outcomes.actions_b: Acknowledge the disclosure neutrally and record concerns for the review unless an immediate shared payment is at risk.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a thirty-day Surprise Cost Log with disclosed purchase, trigger crossed, timing, response, actual shared impact, and rule-review date.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Fewer surprises create room for less suspicion.

options.label: It genuinely works for me
Mostly fair, with a few sensitive categories
I often feel controlled, dismissed, or exposed to choices I cannot influence
I really need the boundary to change

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: When does personal spending stop feeling fully personal?

options.label: Shared bills or goals become harder to fund
Debt or credit risk increases
The purchase needs shared storage or upkeep
One partner subsidizes necessities afterward
A repeated pattern affects trust
It never stops being personal if personal money pays

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: What kind of input feels most respectful?

options.label: A factual heads-up
A question about shared impact
A suggestion without veto power
A mutually agreed category limit
A pause before a major decision
No input unless I ask for it

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: Anything the court should know about the spending category, comment, or shared consequence behind this boundary? (optional)
questions.interactionRule: Private context is used only to personalize the selected deterministic branch.

outcomes.verdict: You share a stable border between personal choice and shared consequence. That means independence is not being used to hide costs, and concern is not being used to supervise taste. The deeper win is mutual adulthood: each of you can spend personal money while trusting the other person to notice when a choice starts affecting bills, debt, space, or shared goals. Keep the border written in impacts rather than categories. Shoes, games, beauty, travel, and hobbies deserve the same rule even when one partner understands the appeal more than the other.
outcomes.actions_a: Name one shared-impact trigger that makes partner input legitimate regardless of the spending category.
outcomes.actions_b: Name one personal category that deserves freedom from commentary when no shared trigger is crossed.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Personal Spending Border with protected autonomy, shared-impact triggers, input style, response time, and category-neutral examples.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Personal choice keeps freedom, and shared consequences still get a voice.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = dissatisfied with the current personal-spending boundary; [B] = content with it.
outcomes.verdict: [A] and [B] want similar levels of influence, but [A] may be receiving more commentary or less protection from consequences. [A] could have ordinary purchases questioned while [B]’s categories seem automatically reasonable. Or [A] may repeatedly cover necessities after [B] uses personal money freely. [B] sees the stated boundary and assumes it applies evenly. [A] experiences a double standard. Compare the shared-impact test and the amount of commentary across both partners before changing the overall level of influence.
outcomes.actions_a: Bring two matched examples that show unequal scrutiny or unequal cleanup rather than arguing from a general feeling.
outcomes.actions_b: Apply the same impact questions to your own spending and own any necessity gap created afterward.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a two-week Boundary Fairness Check with purchase category, amount, comment received, shared impact, cleanup required, and rule applied.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. The same border now runs around both people’s money.

outcomes.verdict: Your personal-spending boundary is written in pencil. Both of you think there is a rule, but it gets erased and redrawn whenever the category, amount, or mood changes. That uncertainty turns casual comments into control and silence into disregard. Rewrite the border with three zones: Independent, Inform, and Joint Decision. Place purchases by shared impact, not by whether either partner personally approves of them. Then choose the exact response allowed in each zone so input cannot quietly expand into veto power.
outcomes.actions_a: Draft the Independent and Inform zones with examples that protect personal autonomy.
outcomes.actions_b: Draft the Joint Decision triggers using debt, bills, goals, space, and continuing obligations.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Three-Zone Personal Spending Map with examples, amount guides, allowed input, decision rights, and review date.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. The boundary becomes visible before either person accidentally crosses it.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = wants more influence over personal spending; [B] = wants more autonomy.
outcomes.verdict: [A] sees personal spending as part of a connected financial system, where one person’s choices can change the couple’s options later. [B] needs a protected area of adult freedom and does not want partnership to turn every preference into a committee decision. Your current setup works because influence follows consequence. [A] can raise shared impacts, while [B] keeps final control when personal money, credit, space, and obligations remain truly personal. Keep a fixed personal allowance or account lane so the boundary does not need to be re-earned with every purchase.
outcomes.actions_a: Limit your input to the shared consequence and avoid arguing that your preference should decide a personal purchase.
outcomes.actions_b: Keep the personal lane funded only after shared commitments and disclose any consequence that leaves that lane.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save an Influence Follows Impact rule with personal lane, shared triggers, comment limits, final decision owner, and monthly reset.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Partnership gets a voice where consequences connect, and autonomy keeps the final word elsewhere.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = wants more influence and is dissatisfied; [B] = wants more autonomy and is currently content.
outcomes.verdict: [A] may be watching personal spending create indirect costs: delayed savings, recurring debt, crowded space, or the need to cover shared basics later. [B] experiences the money as personal and may hear [A]’s concern as an attempt to control identity or pleasure. Right now, [B] keeps decision freedom while [A] absorbs part of the aftermath. [B] owes a consequence firewall, such as a funded personal account and no rescue from shared money. [A] owes freedom from commentary when that firewall holds.
outcomes.actions_a: Define the consequence you need contained and stop reviewing purchases once [B] keeps that impact inside the personal lane.
outcomes.actions_b: Create the firewall with funded shared obligations, no new shared debt, and personal responsibility for later shortfalls.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Personal Spending Firewall with shared funding order, personal balance, debt rule, no-rescue boundary, and a thirty-day test.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. [B] keeps autonomy by keeping the consequences personal too.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = wants more influence over personal spending; [B] = wants more autonomy.
outcomes.verdict: [A] comments more after seeing personal choices affect shared plans. [B] shares less or defends harder after feeling controlled. The lack of information makes [A] push further, and the extra pressure makes [B] guard autonomy more intensely. Stop debating individual purchases for one month. Fund shared obligations and personal lanes in a fixed order, then allow each partner complete freedom inside the remaining amount. Review only whether any consequence crossed the border. The system, rather than repeated persuasion, decides when input becomes legitimate.
outcomes.actions_a: Avoid item-by-item commentary during the trial and record only consequences that cross into shared money or commitments.
outcomes.actions_b: Keep purchases within the funded personal lane and disclose any debt, recurring cost, or shortfall before it reaches [A].
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a one-month Fund First Trial with shared funding order, personal amounts, prohibited spillovers, consequence log, and review appointment.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. A funding order replaces the fight over who gets to approve personal taste.

Preparing a simple account-status update

A low balance creates blame instead of action
Management quietly becomes ownership or extra decision power

questions.prompt: Anything the court should know about the joint balance, transfer, access issue, or alert that keeps causing uncertainty? (optional)

outcomes.role_note: [A] = the partner both identified as the stronger joint-account manager.
outcomes.verdict: [A] is good at keeping the joint account operational. [A] notices low balances, mismatched transfers, unusual activity, and access issues before they interrupt the bills the account exists to serve. [B] trusts that awareness, which protects the shared system. Management must not become financial ownership. Keep [A] as operating lead, while [B] retains equal access, follows the contribution and withdrawal rules, and receives a short status update that supports equal decision power.
outcomes.actions_a: Set the monitoring rhythm and alert rules, then report exceptions without making unilateral policy changes.
outcomes.actions_b: Maintain working access, transfer contributions on time, and review the account status before making an unusual withdrawal.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Joint Account Operating Agreement with access, contribution timing, withdrawal rule, alerts, operating lead, and equal decision rights.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. [A] runs the controls without owning the account more than [B].

outcomes.role_note: [B] = the partner both identified as the stronger joint-account manager.
outcomes.verdict: [B] is good at keeping the joint account operational. [B] notices low balances, mismatched transfers, unusual activity, and access issues before they interrupt the bills the account exists to serve. [A] trusts that awareness, which protects the shared system. Management must not become financial ownership. Keep [B] as operating lead, while [A] retains equal access, follows the contribution and withdrawal rules, and receives a short status update that supports equal decision power.
outcomes.actions_a: Maintain working access, transfer contributions on time, and review the account status before making an unusual withdrawal.
outcomes.actions_b: Set the monitoring rhythm and alert rules, then report exceptions without making unilateral policy changes.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Joint Account Operating Agreement with access, contribution timing, withdrawal rule, alerts, operating lead, and equal decision rights.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. [B] runs the controls without owning the account more than [A].

outcomes.verdict: You both can manage the joint account, which gives the relationship two keys instead of one emergency contact. That resilience matters, but two active managers can also move money twice, change alerts, or assume the other person investigated a mystery charge. Give one partner operating duty for a fixed month while both retain visibility and equal authority. Rotate after a clean handoff. Competence stays shared, and the account gets one current operator.
outcomes.actions_a: Take the first operating month and record transfers, exceptions, and unresolved activity in the shared status note.
outcomes.actions_b: Stay informed without duplicating actions, then take the next month using the same rules and alert settings.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a three-month Joint Account Operator rotation with current lead, contributions, alert owner, exceptions, access check, and handoff date.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Two people keep the keys, and one person drives the routine this month.

outcomes.verdict: [A] may be the balance watcher, noticing cash flow, pending charges, and when the account needs funding. [B] may be the systems manager, stronger at security, access, disputes, and keeping bank settings clean. Each person claims management because each protects a different kind of failure. Split operations into Money Flow and Account Control, then give each lane one owner with shared visibility. A quarterly role swap keeps both partners capable without making daily management a competition.
outcomes.actions_a: Claim either Money Flow or Account Control and define the alerts and tasks that belong in that lane.
outcomes.actions_b: Own the opposite lane and document the backup steps [A] would need during an emergency.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Money Flow and Account Control chart with lane owners, alerts, permissions, dispute steps, and quarterly swap date.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Cash flow and account safety each get the sharper operator.

outcomes.verdict: Each of you nominates the other because joint-account management carries a strange mix of visibility, responsibility, and fear of appearing controlling. The person who watches closely can feel anxious, while the person who steps back can look disengaged. Remove the personality question and assign a short operating shift. One partner manages for thirty days, the other follows the contribution rules and audits access once. Then switch. The record will show which duties fit naturally and which should stay rotated.
outcomes.actions_a: Take the first operating shift and report only balance risks, unusual activity, and decisions that need both partners.
outcomes.actions_b: Complete contributions on schedule, verify access, and take the next shift without redesigning the system first.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Two-Shift Joint Account Trial with operator, contribution status, alerts handled, exceptions, time spent, and final role decision.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Thirty days of ownership answers what mutual politeness could not.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = identified a specific joint-account manager; [B] = said either partner could manage it.
outcomes.verdict: [A] sees one partner’s attention as the safest protection against overdrafts, missed transfers, or suspicious activity. [B] sees the account as deliberately joint and wants management to remain transferable. Keep the proven lead for routine monitoring, then give the other partner ownership of one complete control, such as contributions, security, or monthly reconciliation. Require equal access and a quarterly backup drill. The account gains continuity without becoming dependent on one phone, one password memory, or one person’s availability.
outcomes.actions_a: Identify the monitoring duties where continuity prevents real risk and release one complete control lane.
outcomes.actions_b: Own that lane, maintain access, and run the full account process once during the scheduled backup drill.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Joint Account Lead and Backup card with routine lead, control-lane owner, access test, emergency steps, and drill date.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. The account keeps a steady operator and a backup who can truly step in.

cases.title: How Should You Actually Handle Financial Emergencies When They Come Up?
cases.subtitle: How quickly should shared money become available when a real financial emergency hits?

questions.prompt: How quickly should shared money become available when a real financial emergency hits?

options.label: Only after every other option is exhausted
After a quick check that it truly qualifies
Fairly quickly, with a short conversation
Immediately for most urgent needs

questions.prompt: How do you feel about your current emergency-money plan?

options.label: It would genuinely carry us through
Mostly solid, with one or two unclear parts
I am not sure it would work under pressure
I do not feel protected by it

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: Which situation should clearly unlock emergency funds?

options.label: Urgent medical or dental care
Sudden job or income loss
Essential home or car repair
Emergency travel for close family
A legal or safety issue
Only events you both approve in advance

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: What is the biggest risk during an emergency?

options.label: Debating the definition while time runs out
One person spending first and explaining later
Using credit because cash is hard to access
Draining the fund with no rebuild plan
One partner carrying the whole response
Treating a stressful want like an urgent need

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: Anything the court should know about the emergency, access issue, or past scare shaping your answer? (optional)
questions.interactionRule: Private context is used only to personalize the selected deterministic branch.

outcomes.verdict: You already share the same crisis reflex: protect the urgent need first, then restore order. The hidden strength is not simply having savings. It is knowing that neither person will turn a scary moment into a morality trial while the clock is running. Preserve that trust by defining access, proof, and the rebuild step now. A calm plan lets compassion move fast without leaving either partner confused about what happened to the money.
outcomes.actions_a: Choose one emergency category and write the exact first payment or call you would handle.
outcomes.actions_b: Choose a different category and define the information you would record once the immediate danger passes.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save an Emergency Money Card with qualifying events, account access, first steps, notification rule, spending cap, and rebuild date.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Your calm coordination becomes part of the emergency fund.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = less secure about the current emergency plan; [B] = more content with it.
outcomes.verdict: [A] and [B] agree on how readily emergency money should move, so the disagreement is not generosity. [A] doubts the plan will still work when a bank is closed, a password fails, or one person is unreachable. [B] trusts the intention and may assume access will sort itself out. Turn the promise into a usable route. The relationship already has shared instincts; it now needs proof that both people can execute them alone on a bad day.
outcomes.actions_a: Name the exact failure point making you feel unprotected and the access test that would settle it.
outcomes.actions_b: Run that access test and document the steps without asking [A] to keep being the plan's memory.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a screenshot-free Emergency Access Guide with account name, contact route, approval threshold, backup payer, and next test date.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. The shared instinct now has working access behind it.

outcomes.verdict: You are not fighting over what deserves help. You are both reacting to a plan that disappears the second adrenaline arrives. If every emergency requires a fresh debate about accounts, limits, and who calls whom, stress becomes the decision maker. Give the first hour and the next seven days different rules. The first hour protects health, safety, housing, or income. The following week documents the cost, adjusts the budget, and schedules the refill.
outcomes.actions_a: Draft the first-hour rule with the payments that can happen before a full discussion.
outcomes.actions_b: Draft the seven-day recovery checklist with records, insurance claims, budget changes, and refill steps.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a First Hour and First Week emergency page with triggers, spending authority, contacts, receipts folder, and recovery meeting date.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Urgency gets a lane, and recovery gets one too.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = prefers more verification before using shared emergency money; [B] = prefers faster access.
outcomes.verdict: [A] protects the fund from panic spending and wants a quick reality check before shared reserves move. [B] protects the couple from dangerous delay and wants help available while the problem is still containable. Your current setup works because caution guards the definition while speed guards the response. Assign those jobs openly: [B] can authorize a limited first move for named emergencies, while [A] confirms the larger follow-up spending within a set window.
outcomes.actions_a: Create the verification checklist and promise an answer within the agreed emergency window.
outcomes.actions_b: Use fast-access money only for listed first-response costs and record what was paid immediately.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Two-Stage Emergency Release with instant-access amount, qualifying events, verifier, decision deadline, and follow-up limit.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Speed handles the first hit, and caution protects the rest.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = prefers more verification and is dissatisfied; [B] = prefers faster access and is content.
outcomes.verdict: [A] sees an emergency fund with a door but no lock, especially if [B] can define urgency and spend before a real check. [B] sees a safety exit and feels relieved that it opens quickly. That comfort is currently being financed by [A]'s uncertainty. [B] owes the plan a clear first-response ceiling and immediate record. [A] owes quick approval once the situation meets the written test, so safety rules do not become a second emergency.
outcomes.actions_a: Write three objective qualifiers and a response deadline you can honor even when anxious.
outcomes.actions_b: Accept a first-response ceiling and log the amount, payee, and reason as soon as money moves.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save an Emergency Exit Rule with qualifying facts, first-spend ceiling, notification message, approval clock, and review appointment.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. The exit stays fast, but it no longer opens on guesswork.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = prefers more verification before using shared emergency money; [B] = prefers faster access.
outcomes.verdict: [A] slows the decision because losing the reserve would create another threat. [B] pushes for speed because delay can make medical, housing, travel, or repair costs worse. Each person is trying to prevent a different second disaster. Stop asking one rule to cover the entire event. Put a modest amount in a rapid-response tier, then require a short checkpoint before the larger reserve opens. The sequence protects urgency first and long-term stability next.
outcomes.actions_a: Set the checkpoint questions and commit to answering them within a fixed number of hours.
outcomes.actions_b: Define the rapid-response costs and stop at that tier until the checkpoint happens.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Two-Tier Crisis Fund plan with rapid amount, reserve amount, triggers, checkpoint time, and refill schedule.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Two different fears now protect the same recovery path.

cases.title: Who's More Likely to Overthink a Financial Decision?
cases.subtitle: How much analysis do you need before you feel ready to make a meaningful money decision?

questions.prompt: How much analysis do you need before you feel ready to make a meaningful money decision?

options.label: A quick check is usually enough
A few facts and one conversation
Several comparisons before I commit
A detailed review with time to sit on it
I can keep researching long after the useful answer is clear

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: How do you feel about the pace of your money decisions as a couple?

options.label: It protects us without slowing us down
Mostly good, with a few frustrating cases
We regularly move too fast or get stuck
The pace creates real stress or missed opportunities

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: What usually keeps the decision open?

options.label: Fear of finding a better option later
Unclear downside or hidden fees
Different risk tolerance
Too many comparisons
Wanting complete agreement
No deadline that forces a choice

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: What would help the most?

options.label: A clear decision deadline
A maximum number of options
One person researching and one checking
A reversible trial
A written risk ceiling
Permission to choose good enough

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: Anything the court should know about the purchase, investment, or decision that keeps reopening? (optional)
questions.interactionRule: Private context is used only to personalize the selected deterministic branch.

outcomes.verdict: You two have built a shared stopping point. You gather enough information to catch expensive surprises, then let the decision close before research eats the benefit. That balance usually means you trust each other's judgment, not just the spreadsheet. Keep the pace healthy by naming which choices deserve depth and which only need a basic check. Your real asset is knowing that careful does not have to mean frozen, and confident does not have to mean careless.
outcomes.actions_a: Name one money decision that deserves your full research mode and the reason it earns that time.
outcomes.actions_b: Name one recurring decision that should use a quick default so attention stays available for bigger calls.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Decision Depth Guide with quick, compare, and deep-review tiers plus deadlines and spending examples.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. You know when to investigate and when to let a solid choice be enough.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = frustrated with the current decision pace; [B] = content with it.
outcomes.verdict: [A] and [B] need a similar amount of analysis, but [A] is likely carrying more of the waiting cost. [A] may chase the information, watch prices change, or keep plans on hold while the decision stays open. [B] experiences the same process as appropriately careful because the delay lands more lightly. Put an owner and an expiration date on the open question. Agreement on depth becomes useful only when someone is responsible for bringing the choice home.
outcomes.actions_a: Name the concrete cost of delay and the latest date when an answer is still useful.
outcomes.actions_b: Own the remaining research and present a recommendation by that date, including what is still unknown.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save an Open Decision Sheet with owner, three required facts, delay cost, final date, and default choice if time expires.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Carefulness gets a finish line.

outcomes.verdict: Neither of you lacks decision skill. Your process lacks a rule for when more information stops changing the answer. That is why a purchase, rate, or plan can survive five conversations without becoming safer. Before researching, choose the three facts that could actually reverse the decision. Once those are known, decide. Everything else goes into a future-learning note instead of reopening the case. You keep the wisdom of caution while ending the loop that drains time and confidence.
outcomes.actions_a: Write the three facts that would genuinely change your preferred choice and ignore cosmetic comparisons.
outcomes.actions_b: Set the deadline and identify the default option that activates if no new deal-breaker appears.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Money Decision Stop Rule with reversal facts, option limit, deadline, default, and one post-decision review date.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Research now has a job instead of an unlimited lease.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = needs more analysis; [B] = prefers quicker decisions.
outcomes.verdict: [A] is the stress tester, looking for fees, fragile assumptions, and consequences that only appear later. [B] is the closer, noticing when delay costs more than the remaining uncertainty. You are satisfied because those instincts can work as a relay instead of a tug of war. Give [A] a bounded research window, then let [B] call time and choose among the options that passed. The handoff keeps rigor without asking either person to imitate the other's brain.
outcomes.actions_a: Research only the agreed risks and deliver a short pass, fail, or unknown summary by the deadline.
outcomes.actions_b: Wait through the research window, then choose from the passed options without dismissing documented risks.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Research to Decision Relay with risk questions, researcher, closing time, qualified options, and final chooser.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. One partner tests the road, and the other gets you moving.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = needs more analysis and is dissatisfied; [B] = prefers quicker decisions and is content.
outcomes.verdict: [A] keeps searching because moving with unanswered risk feels exposed. [B] feels fine because the current pace usually ends near [B]'s preferred speed. The missing compromise is not halfway between fast and slow. It is deciding which unknowns [B] agrees not to rush and which low-impact choices [A] agrees not to reopen. Create a dollar and consequence threshold. Above it, [A] gets protected review time. Below it, [B] gets a quick decision lane.
outcomes.actions_a: Choose the risks that deserve protected review and release smaller choices after the basic check.
outcomes.actions_b: Honor the review window above the threshold and stop treating unanswered material risks as mere hesitation.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Fast Lane and Review Lane chart with thresholds, risk triggers, time limits, and decision owner for each lane.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Speed and scrutiny each get the decisions they are built for.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = needs more analysis; [B] = prefers quicker decisions.
outcomes.verdict: [A] experiences pressure to decide before the downside feels understood. [B] experiences every extra comparison as another postponement of life. The fight looks like caution versus impulse, but the real problem is that neither person knows when control changes hands. Split the job. [A] owns risk discovery until a fixed checkpoint. [B] then owns selection among options that meet the written guardrails. Revisit the outcome later without using hindsight to punish the person who closed the call.
outcomes.actions_a: List the nonnegotiable guardrails and finish risk discovery by the checkpoint instead of adding new criteria later.
outcomes.actions_b: Select within those guardrails and record why the chosen option was reasonable with the information available.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Financial Decision Handoff with guardrails, research cutoff, approved options, selector, rationale, and learning review date.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. The decision has two owners, but only one job at a time.
