outcomes.verdict: [A] and [B] want about the same amount of structure, so [A]'s stress probably comes from an unwritten obligation inside the current system. [A] may feel required to match price, react perfectly, or treat every occasion as a test. [B] experiences generosity, not pressure, because that hidden assignment is not landing on [B]. Remove the emotional invoice. Agree that a gift cannot create a repayment duty, and that honest budget limits are part of care rather than evidence of weak effort.
outcomes.actions_a: Name the obligation you feel after receiving or planning a gift and ask for it to be explicitly released.
outcomes.actions_b: State what you never expect in return, then respect [A]'s stated range without upgrading it through hints.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a No Emotional Invoice agreement with spending range, response expectations, reciprocity rule, opt-out phrase, and next occasion plan.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. A gift gets to be received, not repaid.

outcomes.verdict: You agree on roughly how structured gift spending should be, yet both of you still leave occasions feeling tense. The number is not the missing piece. You may be solving different gift jobs: one person wants surprise, the other wants accuracy; one wants a keepsake, the other wants relief or shared time. Before the next occasion, choose what the gift is meant to communicate and only then choose a price range. Shared intent will do more than a tighter cap to stop thoughtful effort from missing its target.
outcomes.actions_a: Choose one message you want your next gift to carry and one format that would feel natural to give.
outcomes.actions_b: Describe how you most enjoy receiving care and identify one format that reliably creates pressure.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Next Gift Brief with intended message, preferred formats, avoid list, budget range, and occasion date.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. The gift starts with the message instead of the receipt.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = prefers clearer gift-spending structure; [B] = prefers more spontaneity.
outcomes.verdict: [A] enjoys giving more when the shared budget and reciprocity expectations are predictable. [B] experiences a surprise as part of the affection and does not want every sweet idea approved in advance. You are content because the relationship has room for both security and delight. Keep a private surprise lane inside a public limit. Agree on the maximum shared financial impact, then let the giver choose the object, timing, and meaning without previewing the fun.
outcomes.actions_a: Set a limit based on shared affordability, then avoid managing how [B] uses the surprise lane.
outcomes.actions_b: Keep the total impact inside that lane and make the surprise about insight, not financial shock value.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Surprise Lane rule with occasion cap, shared-money boundary, excluded categories, reveal window, and rollover choice.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. The budget knows the ceiling, but the recipient does not know what is coming.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = prefers clearer structure and is dissatisfied; [B] = prefers spontaneity and is content.
outcomes.verdict: [A] may be smiling through gifts while calculating the shared cost, the pressure to match, or the goal that just moved farther away. [B] sees a generous tradition that feels loving and assumes the good intention settles the money question. Right now, [B]'s surprise is partly funded by [A]'s private stress. [B] owes a protected ceiling. [A] owes genuine freedom inside it, including no criticism when the chosen gift is not how [A] would have spent the same amount.
outcomes.actions_a: Name the maximum financial impact you can welcome without resentment and release control below it.
outcomes.actions_b: Accept that ceiling before shopping and do not use romance as a reason to cross it.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Welcomeable Gift Limit with amount, funding source, reciprocity release, freedom inside the cap, and review after the next occasion.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. The surprise stops asking one partner to hide the cost of receiving it.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = prefers clearer gift-spending structure; [B] = prefers more spontaneity.
outcomes.verdict: [A] hears an unplanned gift as two messages at once: love, plus a bill or standard that was never discussed. [B] hears a preset limit as advance censorship of a feeling that should be freely expressed. Neither of you needs to surrender the meaning you care about. Alternate the design authority. For one occasion, use a shared range with full creative freedom inside it. For the next, choose a no-price gift built from time, skill, or a saved memory. The sequence tests what actually creates warmth.
outcomes.actions_a: Set the range for the first occasion and promise not to direct the idea once the limit is respected.
outcomes.actions_b: Design the no-price occasion and show that spontaneity can come from attention rather than escalation.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Two-Occasion Gift Experiment with dates, first-event range, creative freedom rule, no-price format, and warmth ratings.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Structure and spontaneity each get a real turn to prove their value.

cases.title: Who Should Be the One to Bring Up Money When Something Feels Off?
cases.subtitle: Between you two, who should be the first to raise a money concern when something feels off?

questions.prompt: Between you two, who should be the first to raise a money concern when something feels off?

options.label: Me, no contest
Probably me
Probably them
Definitely them
Honestly, either of us should be able to

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: What best proves it?

options.label: notice a pattern before it becomes a problem
bring up numbers without making the conversation personal
choose a moment when both people can actually engage
say the concern clearly instead of hinting
stay open after the first defensive reaction
turn the concern into a next step

questions.interactionRule: Display as the answering player’s own voice.

questions.prompt: What usually makes the first sentence hard?

options.label: Fear of sounding controlling
Embarrassment about my own part
Bad timing after a stressful day
Not having the exact numbers yet
Past talks becoming bigger fights
Hoping the issue fixes itself

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: What should happen within a day of the concern being raised?

options.label: Check the actual transactions or balance
Agree whether the issue is urgent
Pause a risky purchase or transfer
Set a longer conversation time
Assign one fact-finding task each
Confirm the concern was heard without solving it yet

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: Anything the court should know about the money concern that keeps getting hinted at or delayed? (optional)
questions.interactionRule: Private context is used only to personalize the selected deterministic branch.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = the partner both identified as the stronger money-conversation starter.
outcomes.verdict: [A] notices the early signal and can put words around it before a strange charge, missed goal, or uneasy feeling turns into a crisis. [B] trusts [A] to open the door, which is useful as long as noticing does not become permanent emotional labor. Keep [A] as the first-alert lead, but require [B] to take the next concrete step, such as pulling statements or scheduling the follow-up. One person starts the conversation; both people carry it.
outcomes.actions_a: Use one factual observation, one impact, and one request instead of presenting the entire case at once.
outcomes.actions_b: Respond by owning the first follow-up task and naming when you will bring the information back.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Money Yellow Flag script with opener, listening reply, first task, follow-up time, and urgent exception.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. [A] rings the alert, and [B] helps answer it.

outcomes.role_note: [B] = the partner both identified as the stronger money-conversation starter.
outcomes.verdict: [B] can name a financial wobble while it is still small enough to solve, whether the clue is a balance, a pattern, or a shift in the household mood. [A] values that directness, but the role should not make [B] responsible for detecting every issue and regulating every reaction. Let [B] make the first call when [B] sees the signal. Then [A] owns the evidence check or next scheduled conversation so concern turns into shared work.
outcomes.actions_a: Receive the opener without demanding perfect proof, then own the first fact-finding or scheduling step.
outcomes.actions_b: Raise the observation early and stop after a clear request instead of carrying the whole solution alone.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Money Yellow Flag script with opener, listening reply, first task, follow-up time, and urgent exception.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. [B] opens the topic, and [A] moves it forward.

outcomes.verdict: Either of you can bring up money, which means financial honesty is not trapped behind one person's courage. A concern can enter the relationship from either side before resentment writes a story around it. Your risk is two simultaneous alarms that feel like cross-examination. Use a shared opener and let the person who noticed the issue lead the first five minutes. The other partner's first job is understanding, not presenting a counter-case.
outcomes.actions_a: Use the shared opener for the next concern and keep the first five minutes to facts, impact, and one question.
outcomes.actions_b: Reflect what you heard before adding your own concern, then agree on whether the issue needs action or a scheduled talk.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Five-Minute Money Check format with opener, listener response, urgency rating, one next step, and revisit date.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Two honest voices get one orderly doorway.

outcomes.verdict: Both of you claim the starter role because you are probably detecting different warning lights. [A] may notice spending drift, missing details, or a budget mismatch. [B] may notice anxiety, avoidance, or a future plan becoming unrealistic. Both of you claim the early read because your dashboards show different data. Keep both signals, but label them. The person who sees a numbers flag brings the numbers; the person who sees a stress flag names the felt impact and requests a factual check.
outcomes.actions_a: Choose whether your strongest signal is numerical or emotional and use the matching opener without claiming the whole issue.
outcomes.actions_b: Own the other signal lane and bring one piece of usable evidence when you raise it.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Two-Signal Money Dashboard with numbers flags, stress flags, lane owner, opener for each, and response deadline.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Different warning lights can protect the same financial system.

outcomes.verdict: Each of you wants the other person to start because the first sentence can feel like volunteering to be the controlling one, the anxious one, or the person admitting a mistake. That mutual politeness is expensive when a small issue keeps compounding. Replace courage with a recurring appointment. At the same short weekly check, either person can add a yellow flag to the note before you meet. The calendar becomes the initiator, so neither partner has to manufacture a dramatic opening.
outcomes.actions_a: Add one factual yellow flag to the shared note before the next check, even if the numbers are incomplete.
outcomes.actions_b: Open the scheduled check by reading the flag neutrally and asking what outcome would feel useful.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a recurring fifteen-minute Money Pulse with a shared yellow-flag note, fixed day, opener, task owner, and next check.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. The calendar says the first sentence for you.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = identified a specific conversation starter; [B] = said either partner should be able to raise the concern.
outcomes.verdict: [A] sees a practical first responder, the person more likely to notice the signal or speak without freezing. [B] wants money honesty to remain a shared right and responsibility. Those views fit if the reliable starter becomes a lead, not a gatekeeper. Let that person raise recurring or technical concerns, while both partners keep a simple anytime phrase for personal worry. Then require the listener to own one next step so initiating never turns into chasing.
outcomes.actions_a: Define the recurring concerns where a lead starter genuinely reduces delay and use the short opener elsewhere.
outcomes.actions_b: Practice the anytime phrase and take one follow-up task whenever the other partner initiates.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Lead Plus Anytime plan with lead topics, universal opener, listener task, response window, and monthly role check.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. A dependable lead does not silence the second voice.

cases.title: How Should You Actually Divide Costs When One of You Uses Something More?
cases.subtitle: How strongly should unequal use affect the way a shared cost gets divided?

questions.prompt: How strongly should unequal use affect the way a shared cost gets divided?

options.label: Hardly at all, shared means shared
Only when the difference is obvious and ongoing
Somewhat, using a simple adjustment
A lot, each person should cover most of what they use
Almost completely, the split should track actual use

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: How do you feel about the way you currently handle unequal-use costs?

options.label: It feels fair without being fussy
Mostly fair, with a few annoying exceptions
One of us regularly pays for more than they use
The current split creates real resentment

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: Which cost makes this question most real?

options.label: Groceries or household supplies
A car, parking, or fuel
Streaming or memberships
Utilities or home-office use
A larger room or extra storage
A service one partner wanted more

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: What would make an adjusted split feel reasonable?

options.label: A simple fixed percentage
One person covers a related cost instead
Only large differences count
The adjustment is reviewed occasionally
Convenience and access count too
No tracking of tiny everyday use

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: Anything the court should know about the item, usage gap, or recurring cost behind this answer? (optional)
questions.interactionRule: Private context is used only to personalize the selected deterministic branch.

outcomes.verdict: You share the same definition of practical fairness: usage matters enough to notice, but not so much that the home needs a meter on every shelf. That judgment works because both of you appear willing to absorb small unevenness without treating it as evidence of being taken for granted. Protect that generosity by naming the point where a difference becomes recurring and material. The goal is not perfect accounting. It is making sure convenience never quietly assigns one partner the permanent subsidy.
outcomes.actions_a: Name one small uneven cost you are genuinely happy to leave untracked.
outcomes.actions_b: Name one recurring usage gap that should trigger a simple adjustment before annoyance builds.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save an Unequal Use Threshold with ignored small costs, adjustment triggers, default percentage, swap option, and review month.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. You keep generosity for the small stuff and clarity for the patterns.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = dissatisfied with the current unequal-use split; [B] = content with it.
outcomes.verdict: [A] and [B] agree on the principle, but only [A] is feeling the drip of the current exception. A few extra groceries, fuel stops, or subscription upgrades can look tiny one at a time while adding up to a standing role: [A] funds the convenience, [B] gets used to the baseline. [B] sees the simple rule and assumes it is working. Audit one disputed category for a month, then replace exact tracking with one fixed correction if the pattern is real.
outcomes.actions_a: Track only the disputed category and record cost plus use without adding unrelated grievances.
outcomes.actions_b: Review the record openly and propose a fixed correction if your use is creating the repeated difference.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a thirty-day Usage Check with category, total cost, rough use, current split, proposed correction, and end date for tracking.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. One measured month replaces a permanent low-grade annoyance.

outcomes.verdict: You agree about how much usage should matter, yet the current method still feels unfair. That usually means the couple is measuring too narrow a unit. Minutes watched, miles driven, or servings eaten may ignore access, convenience, ownership, maintenance, or who asked for the upgrade. Pick one fuller fairness rule for each major category. Use can matter, but it does not have to be the only fact. A good split is explainable in one sentence and simple enough to repeat next month.
outcomes.actions_a: Choose one disputed cost and list the non-usage benefit you receive from having it available.
outcomes.actions_b: Choose the same cost and list the extra usage or maintenance burden your behavior creates.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a One-Sentence Split Rule for three costs, including use, access, upkeep, current percentages, and review date.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Fairness gets measured by the whole benefit, not one convenient number.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = wants usage to affect the split more; [B] = prefers a more equal shared split.
outcomes.verdict: [A] feels cared for when payment reflects the actual share each person consumes. [B] feels cared for when shared life includes some generous pooling instead of constant personal invoices. Your system works because you already know which costs symbolize togetherness and which are basically individual upgrades. Keep a shared base for ordinary access, then charge the extra tier to the person creating it. That preserves the feeling of a common home without asking one partner to subsidize unlimited preference.
outcomes.actions_a: Identify the extra-use threshold and accept an equal base for the ordinary shared benefit.
outcomes.actions_b: Name the shared base you value and pay the incremental cost when your preference pushes beyond it.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Shared Base Plus Extras list with base amount, extra triggers, payer, three example costs, and quarterly check.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Togetherness covers the base, and personal upgrades carry their own price.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = wants usage to affect the split more and is dissatisfied; [B] = prefers equal splitting and is content.
outcomes.verdict: [A] sees the equal split turning repeated personal use into a shared bill. [B] sees the same split as part of not nickel-and-diming a life together. The current simplicity benefits [B] more because [B] is using more while [A] is swallowing the difference. [B] owes one concrete correction for the high-use category. [A] owes restraint everywhere else, so the repair does not turn the relationship into itemized billing.
outcomes.actions_a: Choose the single recurring category that matters most and propose one simple correction rather than tracking everything.
outcomes.actions_b: Take the correction through a higher percentage or a related bill, and keep it in place for the trial period.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a One-Category Fairness Fix with chosen cost, baseline, correction method, start date, and sixty-day review.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. One real adjustment protects generosity from becoming a subsidy.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = wants usage to affect the split more; [B] = prefers a more equal shared split.
outcomes.verdict: [A] is fighting against invisible overpayment. [B] is fighting against a household where every snack, mile, and screen becomes evidence. Both concerns are valid, and neither requires a universal formula. Sort costs into three lanes: shared access, measurable high use, and personal upgrade. Split the first evenly, adjust the second with a rough fixed ratio, and assign the third to the chooser. Review the lanes, not individual daily behavior. That keeps fairness visible without making surveillance part of intimacy.
outcomes.actions_a: Place the disputed costs into the three lanes and suggest rough ratios only for meaningful high-use patterns.
outcomes.actions_b: Protect equal splitting in the shared-access lane and accept full ownership of clear personal upgrades.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Three-Lane Cost Map with shared access, high use, personal upgrades, split rule, examples, and review date.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. The system tracks categories, not each other's every move.

cases.title: Who's More Financially Cautious, Generally?
cases.subtitle: How cautious are you with money when the outcome is uncertain?

questions.prompt: How cautious are you with money when the outcome is uncertain?

options.label: I am comfortable taking a real chance
I can move with a basic safety check
I balance upside and downside pretty evenly
I prefer strong protection before committing
I avoid the move unless the downside is tightly contained

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: How do you feel about the level of financial caution in your relationship?

options.label: It gives us a healthy balance
Mostly good, with a few recurring debates
It either limits us or leaves us exposed
The difference regularly undermines trust

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: Where does your caution level show up most?

options.label: Investing or retirement choices
Changing jobs or starting a business
Large purchases
Borrowing or using credit
Travel and lifestyle spending
Helping family or friends financially

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: What makes risk feel worth taking?

options.label: A protected emergency reserve
A reversible first step
Clear upside with a time limit
Independent expert information
A worst-case plan
Enough room for both partners to sleep at night

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: Anything the court should know about the risk, missed chance, or close call behind this answer? (optional)
questions.interactionRule: Private context is used only to personalize the selected deterministic branch.

outcomes.verdict: You share a financial risk temperature, so neither person has to translate every opportunity into a completely different language. That shared setting creates predictable trust because each of you roughly knows what evidence, protection, and upside the other needs before saying yes. Keep that alignment from becoming an echo chamber. On meaningful decisions, assign one partner to argue the strongest downside and the other to argue the strongest upside, even if both already agree. Shared caution becomes sharper when it still invites a real challenge.
outcomes.actions_a: Take the downside role on the next meaningful decision and define the loss the couple cannot comfortably absorb.
outcomes.actions_b: Take the upside role and define what gain would justify the time, money, and uncertainty involved.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Risk Temperature Card with protected floor, acceptable loss, worthwhile upside, challenge roles, and decision date.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Matching instincts become stronger when agreement still gets tested.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = dissatisfied with the current level of financial caution; [B] = content with it.
outcomes.verdict: [A] and [B] have similar risk tolerance, but [A] may be living with a different consequence. [A] could feel opportunities keep getting delayed, or feel exposed because safeguards are discussed but never funded. [B] sees a generally sensible approach and does not feel the same urgency. Identify whether the pain is too little movement or too little protection, then repair that exact gap. Changing the couple's whole financial personality would miss the real issue.
outcomes.actions_a: Name one concrete opportunity or protection that the current caution level has failed to deliver.
outcomes.actions_b: Fund or schedule one response to that gap instead of defending the overall system.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Caution Reality Check with the missed need, current safeguard, one correction, owner, deadline, and success sign.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. The relationship fixes the consequence, not a personality label.

outcomes.verdict: You are similarly cautious, yet neither of you likes what that caution is producing. If both of you lean protective, opportunities may die without a clear rejection. If both lean bold, recovery plans may stay vague because each assumes the other is equally comfortable. Add the missing counterweight as a rule, not a personality change. Protective couples need a small experiment budget. Bold couples need a nonnegotiable safety floor. The system supplies the instinct neither partner naturally brings to the room.
outcomes.actions_a: Define the protected floor that cannot be used for uncertain bets or the experiment amount that must be available for growth.
outcomes.actions_b: Choose one upcoming decision where the new counterweight will be tested and set its stopping rule.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Risk Counterweight plan with natural tendency, missing safeguard, experiment amount, protected floor, and test decision.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Your shared instinct keeps its strength and gains the brake or gas it was missing.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = more financially cautious; [B] = more comfortable with risk.
outcomes.verdict: [A] protects continuity, making sure one bad outcome does not threaten housing, bills, or future choices. [B] protects possibility, noticing that excessive safety can have its own cost in missed growth and delayed experiences. You are content because each instinct is being heard before money moves. Preserve that balance with two separate numbers: a protected floor that [B] cannot gamble with, and an opportunity pool that [A] cannot repeatedly freeze once the written criteria are met.
outcomes.actions_a: Set the protected floor from actual obligations, then release the agreed opportunity pool without moving the goalposts.
outcomes.actions_b: Keep uncertain moves inside the opportunity pool and state the stopping point before committing.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Floor and Opportunity Pool agreement with amounts, eligible uses, stop-loss rule, replenishment order, and review date.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Safety guards the foundation, and possibility gets a funded room of its own.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = more cautious and dissatisfied; [B] = more comfortable with risk and content.
outcomes.verdict: [A] feels like the relationship is driving with the fuel gauge hidden, because [B]'s comfort depends on risks [A] would be left helping repair. [B] feels energized by the current freedom and may read [A]'s alarm as chronic pessimism. The pleasure of risk is landing on [B], while part of the downside sits with [A]. Before another bold move, [B] owes a funded worst-case plan. Once that protection exists, [A] owes a fair evaluation instead of an automatic no.
outcomes.actions_a: Define the specific protection that would make one proposed risk tolerable and agree to reconsider when it is funded.
outcomes.actions_b: Fund the downside plan first and cap the amount, duration, and shared exposure of the move.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Fund the Downside First sheet with proposed risk, protected costs, exposure cap, exit trigger, and reconsideration date.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. The upside can stay exciting without outsourcing the landing.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = more financially cautious; [B] = more comfortable with risk.
outcomes.verdict: [A] may slow every uncertain choice because protection never feels complete. [B] may push harder because each delay feels like proof the opportunity will never get a fair hearing. The harder one brakes, the harder the other accelerates. Use scheduled gates instead of persuasion. Gate one protects core obligations. Gate two tests the idea with a small reversible amount. Gate three expands only after real evidence appears. Neither instinct wins upfront; the decision earns its way forward.
outcomes.actions_a: Define the core obligations at gate one and the evidence required before expanding beyond the test.
outcomes.actions_b: Design the smallest meaningful trial and accept the exit trigger if the evidence does not arrive.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Three-Gate Risk Plan with protected obligations, pilot amount, evidence target, expansion date, and exit trigger.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. The choice moves forward only as fast as the evidence can carry both of you.

cases.title: How Often Should You Actually Be Spending Quality Time Together?
cases.subtitle: How often do you need intentional quality time to feel connected?

questions.prompt: How often do you need intentional quality time to feel connected?

options.label: Once every few weeks is enough
About once a week
Two or three times a week
Most days
Every day

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: How do you feel about your current quality-time rhythm?

options.label: It genuinely works for me
Mostly okay, but it could be better
I regularly feel disconnected or pressured by it
I really need the rhythm to change

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: What most reliably feels like quality time to you?

options.label: An uninterrupted conversation
Doing a shared activity at home
Going somewhere together
Relaxing side by side without other demands
Learning or trying something new together
A small daily ritual with full attention

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: What most often makes together time miss the mark?

options.label: It only happens with leftover time
Phones or other people keep interrupting
One person always has to initiate it
You have different energy levels when time opens up
One person counts proximity while the other needs engagement
Planning it makes the time feel pressured

questions.prompt: Anything the court should know about the time you spend together that looks connected but does not always feel connected? (optional)

outcomes.verdict: You have a shared connection rhythm. Both of you know how often you need to turn toward each other on purpose, and you can feel the difference between being nearby and actually being together. That makes closeness easier because neither partner has to manufacture urgency before getting attention. Your rhythm also leaves enough room for work, friends, rest, and separate interests. Protect the specific moments that keep it working, especially when a busy week tries to replace focused time with accidental proximity.
outcomes.actions_a: Name one quality-time signal from [B] that reliably makes you feel chosen and present.
outcomes.actions_b: Name a different signal from [A] that turns ordinary time into real connection for you.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Quality Time Recipe with your ideal frequency, three activities that genuinely count, and the warning signs that your rhythm is slipping.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Your calendar already knows the difference between available and connected.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = dissatisfied with the current quality-time rhythm; [B] = content with it.
outcomes.verdict: [A] and [B] want roughly the same amount of time, so frequency is unlikely to be the part hurting [A]. [A] may be counting moments with protected attention, while [B] includes errands, shared screens, meals, or simply being in the same room. [B] experiences plenty of togetherness. [A] experiences access without enough engagement. Keep the amount close to what you already have, but upgrade one recurring block so both people would confidently call it quality time.
outcomes.actions_a: Describe the attention, activity, or emotional tone that would make one existing block feel genuinely connecting.
outcomes.actions_b: Choose that block, remove its usual interruption, and take responsibility for starting it this week.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Does This Count list with three shared yeses, three shared nos, and one recurring time slot you will intentionally upgrade.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. The same hours can finally land the same way.

outcomes.verdict: You agree on how much connection you need, but quality time keeps receiving whatever crumbs remain after the week has eaten. Equal needs do not help when neither person protects a place for them. That is why both of you can feel underfed while also believing you tried. Choose one dependable anchor that survives ordinary busyness, then keep a lighter backup for rough weeks. Reliability will create more closeness than repeatedly waiting for the perfect open evening.
outcomes.actions_a: Choose the recurring day or moment you can protect most reliably and define what would make it feel worthwhile.
outcomes.actions_b: Choose a low-effort backup ritual for weeks when the main plan genuinely cannot happen.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a four-week connection plan with one primary anchor, one backup ritual, named initiators, and the dates you will use each.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Quality time gets a seat before the week fills the table.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = wants quality time more frequently; [B] = wants it less frequently.
outcomes.verdict: You have a flexible closeness rhythm. [A] feels connected through more frequent moments of shared attention and helps keep the relationship active in daily life. [B] needs more space between intentional plans and brings fuller energy when the time arrives. Both of you are comfortable because frequency is not being used as a loyalty test. Mostly okay, but it could be better
I regularly feel rushed, blamed, or emotionally stranded
I really need the recovery process to change

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: What helps you recover when a plan falls through?

options.label: A clear reason for what happened
A moment to be disappointed without fixing it
A ready backup plan
An apology or acknowledgment
Time alone to reset
Humor and a quick change of scene

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: What creates the most friction after a cancellation?

options.label: One person moves on before the other has processed it
Problem-solving starts too quickly
The disappointed person is treated like they are overreacting
The flexible person becomes responsible for rescuing the whole day
Nobody knows whether to stay together or split up
The replacement plan feels like a consolation prize

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: Anything the court should know about the canceled plan that somehow created a second problem afterward? (optional)
questions.interactionRule: Private context is used only to personalize the selected deterministic branch.

outcomes.verdict: You recover at a similar pace and know how to let disappointment exist without letting it take over the entire day. That shared timing is valuable. Neither person has to perform instant positivity or wait hours for the other to become reachable again. You can acknowledge what was lost, decide whether a backup would help, and move together. Save the recovery moves that work, because a bigger cancellation involving travel, money, or anticipation may need more care than your usual change of plans.
outcomes.actions_a: Name one response from [B] that helps disappointment feel understood without making it bigger.
outcomes.actions_b: Name a different response from [A] that helps you become open to a backup plan.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Plan Fell Through note with acknowledgment language, processing time, backup categories, refund tasks, and the cue for deciding what comes next.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Disappointment gets heard without owning the rest of the day.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = dissatisfied with the recovery process; [B] = content with it.
outcomes.verdict: [A] and [B] recover at a similar speed, but [A] may be carrying the emotional reset for both people. [A] names the disappointment, proposes the backup, lightens the mood, and checks whether [B] is ready. [B] experiences a smooth pivot and assumes the process works naturally. [A] experiences another moment where connection depends on their initiative. Let [B] lead the next recovery sequence, including acknowledgment and the first realistic option, so flexibility becomes a shared skill.
outcomes.actions_a: State the part of the emotional reset you usually perform and leave it open next time instead of immediately rescuing the mood.
outcomes.actions_b: Acknowledge the loss first, then offer one backup and ask whether [A] wants company, space, or a different plan.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a three-step Recovery Lead card with Acknowledge, Ask, and Offer, then alternate the lead for the next three disruptions.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. The pivot stops depending on one person’s emotional labor.

outcomes.verdict: You are both capable of pivoting, but the backup conversation becomes a menu with too many pages. Nobody wants to choose the wrong consolation plan, so you trade suggestions until the open time feels more disappointing than the cancellation. Your recovery needs fewer options and a faster finish. Build a short list for different energy levels, then let one person choose from it when the original plan falls through. A simple replacement can still feel good if neither partner has to audition ten ideas first.
outcomes.actions_a: Choose three low-energy backups you would accept without another long discussion.
outcomes.actions_b: Choose three higher-energy backups and the situations where staying separate would actually be better.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Backup Menu labeled Stay In, Go Out, Do Separately, and Reschedule, with three pre-approved options in each.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. The backup plan no longer needs its own planning crisis.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = recovers more quickly; [B] = needs more time with disappointment.
outcomes.verdict: [A] can release the original plan quickly and keeps a canceled event from ruining everything around it. [B] honors anticipation. When something mattered, [B] needs a moment before replacing it with a new activity and accidentally acting like it meant nothing. Both of you value these differences because [A] brings motion and [B] protects meaning. Use them in sequence. Let [B] name the disappointment first, then let [A] offer movement when [B] signals that the next part of the day can begin.
outcomes.actions_a: Wait for [B]’s ready signal before launching into solutions, then offer one clear next step.
outcomes.actions_b: Name what you are disappointed about and give [A] a realistic estimate of when you can consider a pivot.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Recovery Sequence with acknowledgment, processing window, ready signal, backup owner, and reschedule decision.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Meaning gets a moment, then flexibility gets the wheel.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = recovers more quickly and is dissatisfied; [B] = needs more time and is currently content.
outcomes.verdict: [A] may be the person who repeatedly absorbs the change, manages refunds or logistics, and invents a way to save the day. [B] gets time to feel disappointed because [A] keeps everything else moving. The difference in emotional pace is real, but it does not require [A] to become the permanent recovery manager. [B] can take one concrete responsibility while processing, such as rescheduling, canceling the booking, or choosing when to revisit the plan.
outcomes.actions_a: Stop volunteering for every cleanup task and name the one responsibility you need [B] to carry after a cancellation.
outcomes.actions_b: Own that task within an agreed time even if you are not ready to feel positive or choose a backup yet.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Cancellation Split with emotional space, refund tasks, communication, backup choice, reschedule owner, and completion deadlines.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Processing time stays valid without outsourcing the whole aftermath.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = recovers more quickly; [B] = needs more time with disappointment.
outcomes.verdict: [A] moves toward solutions because sitting inside disappointment feels pointless or uncomfortable. [B] stays with the loss because moving on too fast feels like erasing how much the plan mattered. [A] then feels trapped in a mood, while [B] feels emotionally abandoned. Both reactions are attempts to protect the day or the meaning behind it. Use a two-stage response: acknowledgment first, pivot decision second. A short, agreed pause can stop either person from forcing their timing onto the other.
outcomes.actions_a: Offer acknowledgment without immediately adding a solution, and return at the agreed time with one practical option.
outcomes.actions_b: Use the pause to identify what you need, then choose connection, space, backup, or reschedule when the pause ends.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a two-stage cancellation ritual with acknowledgment words, pause length, decision time, four next-step options, and a reschedule rule.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Nobody has to skip the feeling or live there all day.

cases.title: How Far in Advance Do You Each Like to Plan Things?

A few days ahead
About one or two weeks ahead
Several weeks ahead
As early as possible, especially for important plans

Mostly okay, but it could be better
I regularly feel boxed in or left uncertain
I really need the planning rhythm to change

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

Appointments and household tasks

Busy work periods and personal deadlines

options.label: Tentative ideas get treated like firm commitments
Waiting too long removes the good options
Early planning feels like losing freedom

Changes make earlier effort feel wasted
Nobody revisits decisions that were made months ago

questions.prompt: Anything the court should know about the plan one person wants booked now and the other person is not ready to think about yet? (optional)
questions.interactionRule: Private context is used only to personalize the selected deterministic branch.

outcomes.verdict: You share a planning horizon. Both of you know when an idea is early enough to stay light, when it needs a real decision, and how much future certainty helps rather than traps you. That alignment protects anticipation. You can look forward to things without one partner secretly wondering whether the plan is real. It also protects freedom because neither person has to overbook the future just to feel secure. Keep your language for tentative and confirmed plans clear as life becomes busier.
outcomes.actions_a: Name one kind of plan you appreciate deciding early and the lead time that makes it feel easy.
outcomes.actions_b: Name a different plan that benefits from staying open longer and the point when you want it confirmed.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Planning Horizon Guide for same-day, weekly, monthly, and travel plans, including when Tentative becomes Confirmed.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Your future has the right amount of focus.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = dissatisfied with the current planning process; [B] = content with it.
outcomes.verdict: [A] and [B] prefer a similar amount of lead time, but [A] may be missing status clarity. A dinner mentioned two weeks ahead can feel confirmed to [A] and merely possible to [B]. [B] sees plans being discussed at the right time and assumes the system works. [A] keeps holding space without knowing whether to decline something else. Add a visible status and a decision deadline. Then shared lead time becomes useful information instead of a collection of soft promises.
outcomes.actions_a: Name the plans you are currently holding space for and the date when you need a real yes or no.
outcomes.actions_b: Label future ideas as Tentative, Awaiting Decision, or Confirmed and close them by the agreed deadline.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Plan Status key and apply it to the next month of shared plans with one decision date beside every tentative item.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Early planning stops leaving one calendar on hold.

outcomes.verdict: You both like planning ahead, yet the future may be collecting too many placeholders. Each tentative dinner, possible trip, family event, and maybe-weekend occupies attention even when no decision has been made. Your planning instinct is useful. The calendar simply needs maintenance after ideas enter it. Hold a short review where every soft plan gets confirmed, released, or given one final decision date. Clearing false commitments will make the plans you truly want feel lighter and more trustworthy.
outcomes.actions_a: Review the next six weeks and release the tentative plans you no longer feel motivated to protect.
outcomes.actions_b: Choose the open plans worth confirming and take responsibility for the missing decision or booking.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you schedule and save a monthly Future Cleanup with Confirm, Release, and Decide By columns for every open plan.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. The future gets cleaned before it becomes cluttered.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = prefers planning farther ahead; [B] = prefers deciding closer to the moment.
outcomes.verdict: [A] builds the runway. Early dates, reservations, and calendar holds make important plans easier to reach. [B] keeps the cabin from filling with commitments before either of you knows your energy, work, or actual interest. Both of you benefit because structure and freshness have separate jobs. Let [A] secure the limited or expensive pieces early, then leave lower-stakes details open for [B] to shape closer to the date. Your shared skill is knowing which decisions become costly when delayed.
outcomes.actions_a: Identify the decisions with real deadlines or price consequences and handle only those early.
outcomes.actions_b: Choose the details that should stay flexible and commit to deciding them by a specific later checkpoint.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Book Early, Decide Later trip and events list with deadlines, owners, flexible details, and decision checkpoints.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. The runway is built without deciding every snack on the flight.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = prefers planning farther ahead and is dissatisfied; [B] = prefers deciding closer to the moment and is currently content.
outcomes.verdict: [A] is using early planning to protect options, budget, and emotional bandwidth. [B] waits because future energy feels hard to predict and an early yes can feel like handing away freedom. The current delay works better for [B] because [A] absorbs the uncertainty, watches prices, and keeps calendar space open. [B] owes one concrete habit: respond by the real cost deadline, even if the answer is no. [A] can stop asking for certainty before any consequence exists.
outcomes.actions_a: Separate true deadlines from preference and ask only when waiting would cost money, access, or calendar space.
outcomes.actions_b: Give a firm yes, no, or alternative by that deadline instead of leaving [A] to carry the open decision.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Decision Deadline list with consequence, latest safe date, required answer, owner, and what happens automatically if no answer arrives.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Freedom stays, and uncertainty gets an expiration date.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = prefers planning farther ahead; [B] = prefers deciding closer to the moment.
outcomes.verdict: You are stuck in a certainty loop. [A] plans earlier and in more detail because [B] delays decisions. [B] delays more because [A]’s detailed future can feel already decided. Then [A] sees the hesitation as proof that even more planning is necessary. Split the future into two layers. Firm plans hold true commitments and deadlines. Tentative plans hold ideas that remain movable. A weekly review lets [A] see progress and lets [B] influence the plan before it hardens.
outcomes.actions_a: Move ideas without real deadlines into Tentative and stop building details before the checkpoint.
outcomes.actions_b: Attend the weekly review with a real decision on the items whose checkpoint has arrived.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a two-layer calendar with Firm and Tentative labels, decision checkpoints, edit rights, and a recurring ten-minute review.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. The future can be visible without being fully locked.

cases.title: Who Tends to Run Late More Often?
cases.subtitle: Between you two, who tends to run late more often?

questions.prompt: Between you two, who tends to run late more often?

options.label: Me, no contest
Probably me
Probably them
Definitely them
Honestly, we run late about equally

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: What best explains the pattern?

options.label: underestimate how long getting ready will take
start one more task before leaving
treat departure time like the time to start wrapping up
lose track of keys, clothes, tickets, or other essentials
forget travel, parking, or transition time
wait too long to say the original arrival time is no longer realistic

questions.interactionRule: Display as the answering player’s own voice.

questions.prompt: Where does lateness create the biggest cost?

options.label: Dinner reservations or ticketed events
Meeting friends or family
Flights, trains, or road trips
Appointments and errands
Work-related commitments
Ordinary plans where one partner ends up waiting

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: What has the lateness pattern started doing to the relationship?

options.label: The waiting partner becomes the reminder system
Departure begins with tension or rushing
Someone gives a fake earlier time
Apologies repeat without a process change
The on-time partner loses their own preparation time
Both people arrive stressed before the plan begins

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: Anything the court should know about the phrase ‘I’m basically ready’ in your relationship? (optional)
questions.interactionRule: Private context is used only to personalize the selected deterministic branch.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = the partner both identified as more likely to run late.
outcomes.verdict: [A] is probably optimistic about transitions. [A] sees the individual steps, getting dressed, finishing one task, finding the route, and assumes each will go smoothly. The missed cost lands on [B], who waits, sends reminders, or gives up part of their own preparation time to protect the arrival. Your shared agreement is useful because nobody needs a trial about whether the pattern exists. Build the fix around departure, not character. [A] needs a repeatable launch sequence that does not require [B] to manage it.
outcomes.actions_a: Work backward from arrival, set a real stop-doing-things alarm, and own your keys, clothes, route, and buffer.
outcomes.actions_b: State the true departure time once and stop providing a chain of reminders that makes you responsible for [A]’s launch.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Leaving Checklist with arrival time, travel buffer, ready deadline, stop-task alarm, essential items, and the consequence if one person misses departure.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. [A] gets a departure system, and [B] gets their waiting time back.

outcomes.role_note: [B] = the partner both identified as more likely to run late.
outcomes.verdict: [B] is probably optimistic about transitions. [B] sees the individual steps, getting dressed, finishing one task, finding the route, and assumes each will go smoothly. The missed cost lands on [A], who waits, sends reminders, or gives up part of their own preparation time to protect the arrival. Your shared agreement is useful because nobody needs a trial about whether the pattern exists. Build the fix around departure, not character. [B] needs a repeatable launch sequence that does not require [A] to manage it.
outcomes.actions_a: State the true departure time once and stop providing a chain of reminders that makes you responsible for [B]’s launch.
outcomes.actions_b: Work backward from arrival, set a real stop-doing-things alarm, and own your keys, clothes, route, and buffer.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Leaving Checklist with arrival time, travel buffer, ready deadline, stop-task alarm, essential items, and the consequence if one person misses departure.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. [B] gets a departure system, and [A] gets their waiting time back.

outcomes.verdict: You share time optimism. Both of you believe the shower will be quick, traffic will cooperate, and the extra task will take two minutes. That makes the final rush feel weirdly surprising every time. At least neither partner is carrying a moral scorecard about punctuality. You can redesign the departure as a team. Use one external buffer and a firm stop-task moment, then decide in advance which events require strict arrival and which plans can honestly stay loose.
outcomes.actions_a: Choose the events where being late creates a real cost and calculate the buffer from actual recent travel times.
outcomes.actions_b: Choose the flexible plans where you can stop pretending an exact arrival matters and communicate a realistic window.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Strict Time and Flexible Window list, then track planned departure, actual departure, and arrival for five outings.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Optimism stays, and the important events get real math.

outcomes.verdict: You may both claim the lateness because you are late at different stages. [A] might finish getting ready slowly, while [B] keeps adding tasks before anyone heads out. Or one person delays departure and the other underestimates travel. Each remembers the stage they personally disrupted and is taking more responsibility than expected. That honesty is a relationship strength. Map one actual departure from invitation to arrival and assign ownership at every stage, so mutual accountability becomes a working sequence instead of two apologies.
outcomes.actions_a: Identify the exact stage where your timing usually slips and choose one cue that will move it earlier.
outcomes.actions_b: Identify your different delay point and remove the task or assumption that keeps repeating there.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Departure Timeline for five outings with Ready, Stop Tasks, Leave, Travel, and Arrive stages, plus the owner of each delay.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Two honest admissions become one punctual route.

outcomes.verdict: Each of you remembers being the one waiting. That can happen when [A] is late for social plans, [B] is late leaving home, or each partner cares about punctuality in different contexts. Your memories are organized around personal inconvenience, so the other person’s delay stands out more sharply. You do not need to crown one permanent late partner. Find the situations that need a new departure rule and identify who controls the delay in each of them.
outcomes.actions_a: Track the plans where you waited and note whether [B] controlled the actual delay.
outcomes.actions_b: Track different plan types and note when [A] was waiting on you versus on traffic, work, or a third party.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a five-outing Time Log with plan type, ready time, departure owner, outside delay, arrival, and who actually waited.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. The timestamps can settle what memory keeps editing.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = named a specific partner as more frequently late; [B] = said both are about equal.
outcomes.verdict: [A] sees one repeat offender because the same partner may create the visible final delay. [B] sees a two-person traffic jam where one person runs behind and the other keeps changing the route, adding tasks, or starting preparation late too. Both readings can be true. Separate the first delay from the delay that determines arrival. Give each person a personal ready deadline, then record who held the actual departure after both deadlines were clear.
outcomes.actions_a: Name the repeated late behavior you believe has the strongest effect on arrival and test it against the next three outings.
outcomes.actions_b: Identify your own contribution before the final departure and remove one behavior that makes equal responsibility plausible.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a three-outing departure test with separate ready deadlines, actual ready times, leave time, travel buffer, and final delay owner.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. The traffic jam gets separate lanes before anyone gets labeled.

cases.title: How Should Weeknights Versus Weekends Actually Get Used?

Couple time and everyday connection

options.label: I am flexible most weeks
It matters, but I can trade nights when needed
I need it protected regularly for the week to feel good

options.label: The bigger social plans and adventures
The chores and errands that do not fit during the week
Longer dates and focused couple time
Family visits and existing commitments
Mostly recovery with only one or two priorities
A flexible mix based on the week you just had

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: What currently makes the weekly rhythm feel off?

options.label: Weeknights disappear into chores
Weekends become payback for everything unfinished
One person assumes every open evening is shared

Personal goals never receive a reliable slot
You disagree about what counts as a productive night

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: Anything the court should know about the Tuesday night expectation or overloaded weekend behind this case? (optional)
questions.interactionRule: Private context is used only to personalize the selected deterministic branch.

outcomes.verdict: You chose the same general weeknight mode, but neither person needs every evening to follow it perfectly. That gives you a useful shared default without turning Tuesday into policy. You already agree on what ordinary nights should restore or make possible, whether that is quiet, connection, hobbies, fun, or practical progress. Keep the default visible, then leave room for invitations and rough weeks. Your match is strongest when flexibility feels like a choice, not when the shared priority quietly disappears for a month.
outcomes.actions_a: Choose one night where the shared priority would make the biggest difference and name what it looks like in practice.
outcomes.actions_b: Choose a different night that should stay flexible for changing energy, invitations, or unfinished life admin.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Weekly Default with two priority nights, two flexible nights, one catch-up night, and the rule for changing the plan.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Your week has a default without becoming a script.

outcomes.verdict: You both chose the same weeknight priority and both need it protected. That is deeper than liking similar activities. You agree on what weekday life must provide for the relationship and the two people inside it to stay healthy. The danger is assuming strong agreement will protect the time automatically. Work, chores, and invitations will still take whatever is left undefended. Put the shared priority on specific nights and decide which weekend block absorbs the tasks that would otherwise keep stealing it.
outcomes.actions_a: Name the weekday demand you will stop allowing to consume the protected priority night.
outcomes.actions_b: Choose the weekend or alternate slot where that demand will go instead of simply leaving it undone.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a four-week Weekly Rhythm with protected priority nights, overflow blocks, exception rules, and one review after the first two weeks.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Strong agreement gets real space on the calendar.

outcomes.role_note: [A] and [B] chose different weeknight priorities, but both are relatively flexible about protecting them.
outcomes.verdict: [A] wants weeknights to meet one need, while [B] naturally reaches for a different one. Because neither preference is rigid, this difference can make the week more complete rather than split it. One person may bring connection or fun, while the other protects recovery, personal progress, or practical stability. Do not blend every evening into a compromise that satisfies nobody. Give each preference one clear night, then let the remaining evenings respond to energy and actual obligations.
outcomes.actions_a: Claim one weeknight for your priority and design it so [B] can join or opt out without derailing it.
outcomes.actions_b: Claim a different night for your priority and state what support or space you need from [A].
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Weeknight Trade with one [A]-led night, one [B]-led night, two flexible nights, and a weekend overflow block.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Two preferences make a fuller week when they get separate rooms.

outcomes.role_note: [A] and [B] chose different weeknight priorities, and both need their preference protected.
outcomes.verdict: [A] and [B] are protecting different resources. One preference may preserve energy or personal identity, while the other protects connection, momentum, or the practical order of shared life. Asking either person to treat their need as optional will make the week feel unfair long before the weekend arrives. Assign different nights instead of negotiating every evening from scratch. Then use the weekend to repay whichever need the week could not fully serve, with the payback written down rather than vaguely promised.
outcomes.actions_a: Choose the minimum number of nights your priority needs and release the remaining nights from that expectation.
outcomes.actions_b: Choose your own minimum, then name the weekend block that can cover overflow without taking over the whole weekend.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a six-week Rhythm Agreement with protected nights for each priority, flexible nights, weekend payback blocks, and a dated rebalance check.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Both needs get a home before the week gets crowded.

Pretty often when a better option appears
Very often, I prefer keeping plans flexible

options.label: A rare invitation from friends
A family request or obligation
A work opportunity or networking event
A ticket, trip, or event with limited availability
Someone who needs emotional support
A spontaneous plan that simply sounds more fun

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

options.label: The replacement option was clearly more exciting
The decision was made before asking me
Our plan had already required effort or money
This happens more often in one direction
There is no replacement time offered
My disappointment gets treated like pressure or control

questions.prompt: Anything the court should know about the plan that got bumped for something else? (optional)

outcomes.verdict: You both use a similar priority rule and trust how the other person applies it. A rare family moment, important work opportunity, or friend in need can replace a plan without making the relationship feel replaceable. That trust usually comes from transparency and repair. The person changing the plan explains early, acknowledges the cost, and protects another time. Your strength is knowing that commitment can survive flexibility. Write down the exceptions that feel fair so a stressful decision does not rely on guessing.
outcomes.actions_a: Name one kind of competing plan you would willingly release couple time for and why.
outcomes.actions_b: Name a different exception and the repair you would expect if it displaced a shared plan.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Keep, Ask, or Move list for common competing plans, including notice expectations and the rule for replacing couple time.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Flexibility works because the relationship still gets a return date.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = dissatisfied with the current priority pattern; [B] = content with it.
outcomes.verdict: [A] and [B] cancel couple plans at similar rates, but the cancellations may not cost you equally. [A] might move plans after a casual evening at home, while [B] changes dates that required anticipation, emotional preparation, or turning down another invitation. [B] sees equal frequency and assumes equal fairness. [A] experiences different stakes. Start naming the investment already attached to a plan before either person decides it is movable. The same cancellation rule cannot treat every shared plan as interchangeable.
outcomes.actions_a: Name the kinds of plans that carry enough effort or meaning that you need them treated as protected.
outcomes.actions_b: Before changing a protected plan, ask about its hidden cost and offer a replacement that matches the original level of effort.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Plan Protection Scale with Casual, Meaningful, and High-Investment levels, plus the cancellation rule for each.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Equal frequency gets an equal-stakes check.

outcomes.verdict: You have a mutual backup-plan problem. Both of you change shared plans often enough that couple time can start feeling provisional, even when neither person intends to send that message. The issue is not one dramatic cancellation. It is the repeated sense that your plan remains open until every other option has arrived. Choose which couple plans become firm once confirmed, and require a real conversation before moving them. Reliability will make the flexible plans feel lighter because some time is finally safe from comparison.

You are each seeing the charge on the statement that the other person made. Track commitments for two weeks without scoring individual choices. The goal is to reveal which yeses spend shared time, money, space, or recovery before either partner labels those commitments personal plans.
outcomes.actions_a: Log every plan you confirm before checking and note which shared resource it uses.
outcomes.actions_b: Do the same without using [A]’s entries to minimize or justify your own.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a two-week Early Yes Ledger with inviter, plan type, shared resource used, notice, and whether a check happened first.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Memory steps aside, and the calendar supplies the receipts.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = identified a specific partner as more likely to say yes early; [B] = said the habit is roughly equal.
outcomes.verdict: [A] notices a clear repeat pattern, probably because one person’s early commitments create more cleanup or land in higher-impact categories. [B] notices that both people occasionally answer before checking and does not want one partner turned into the permanent problem. Both views can be true. Frequency and impact are different measurements. Run the same check for a short period, then give extra responsibility to the person whose yeses most often consume shared resources or force a reversal.
outcomes.actions_a: Define the exact behavior and impact you are counting so the concern does not expand into every spontaneous plan.
outcomes.actions_b: Track your own early commitments with the same standard and acknowledge differences in impact even if frequency is similar.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a fourteen-day Yes Audit with time, cost, space, recovery, reversal, and partner consultation fields, then set one rule from the results.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Equal mistakes and unequal fallout finally get separate columns.

outcomes.verdict: You share a clear idea of how much family belongs inside your couple life. That usually reflects more than matching social appetite. You have learned how to show up without surrendering every weekend, how to value traditions without treating attendance as automatic, and how to leave as partners rather than reverting to old family roles. Your balance works because family connection and couple boundaries support each other. Keep the agreement visible before holidays, caregiving periods, or major life changes quietly increase access.
outcomes.actions_a: Name one boundary [B] protects around family that helps you participate more warmly.
outcomes.actions_b: Name one family connection [A] supports that makes you feel more fully known as a partner.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Family Time Compass with valued traditions, ordinary visit rhythm, couple-only time, exit rules, and boundaries that apply to both families.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Family gets a meaningful place without taking over the whole floor plan.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = dissatisfied with the family-time balance; [B] = content with it.
outcomes.verdict: [A] and [B] want about the same total amount of family time, but [A] may be missing reciprocity inside those hours. One family might get the easy drop-ins while the other gets only major holidays. Or [A] may spend visits coordinating, translating tension, or managing the exit while [B] simply attends. [B] sees similar calendar space and reads it as balance. [A] experiences different effort and presence. Measure who gets engaged participation, not only how many dates appear on the calendar.
outcomes.actions_a: Name whether the gap is frequency, visit quality, coordination work, or how present [B] feels while there.
outcomes.actions_b: Take responsibility for one concrete part of [A]’s family time, such as planning, active participation, or ending the visit on time.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Family Balance Scorecard for the next month with hours, travel, coordination, presence, and recovery time for each side.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Fairness counts the quality and labor inside the visit.

outcomes.verdict: Family time is currently arriving like an open group chat. Invitations, traditions, and requests appear one by one, and each seems too small to justify a bigger boundary conversation. Together they can occupy far more of your month than either person chose. You agree on the desired level, so take control of the pattern before individual relatives fill it for you. Reserve family weekends, protect couple weekends, and decide visit length in advance. A shared calendar answer is kinder than repeated last-minute resentment.
outcomes.actions_a: List the recurring commitments from your family that deserve a stable place rather than fresh negotiation every time.
outcomes.actions_b: Do the same for your family and flag the requests that should remain optional.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a three-month Family Rhythm calendar with recurring traditions, visit caps, couple-only weekends, travel burden, and one open recovery block.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Family time becomes a choice you two make before the group chat makes it for you.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = wants more family involvement; [B] = wants less.
outcomes.verdict: [A] experiences family involvement as belonging, continuity, and a way for the relationship to join a larger story. [B] needs more separation to stay socially present instead of showing up depleted or guarded. Both of you are comfortable because participation is meaningful rather than constant. [A] builds the bridge and keeps [B] informed. [B] shows up for the moments that carry real value and protects personal limits without dismissing what family means to [A]. Keep choosing priority moments instead of using attendance volume as the proof of care.
outcomes.actions_a: Identify the family moments where [B]’s presence has the highest emotional value and release lower-priority invitations.
outcomes.actions_b: Commit fully to those priority moments and communicate personal limits before frustration appears during the visit.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Family Priority List with Must-Share, Nice-to-Join, and Solo-Okay events for each family, plus expected visit length.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Belonging is measured by meaningful presence, not perfect attendance.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = wants more family involvement and is dissatisfied; [B] = wants less and is currently content.
outcomes.verdict: [A] may experience participation with family as part of participating in the relationship itself. When [B] frequently stays home or leaves early, [A] can feel required to keep two important parts of life separate. [B] may experience those same visits as optional social demand and see the current amount as generous enough. Right now, [B]’s lower preference sets the default. Agree on a minimum level of genuinely present involvement, while [A] stops treating every additional invitation as a fresh test of devotion.
outcomes.actions_a: Choose the smallest set of family moments that would make you feel accompanied rather than alone in that part of life.
outcomes.actions_b: Commit to those moments with a clear arrival, active participation, and agreed exit instead of reluctant attendance.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Minimum Meaningful Presence agreement with priority events, visit length, travel limits, solo invitations, and review date.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Family participation gets a dependable baseline without becoming unlimited access.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = wants more family involvement; [B] = wants less.
outcomes.verdict: [A] may push for more visits after feeling unsupported, while [B] withdraws further when family time feels compulsory or boundaryless. The families then become the stage for a couple problem they did not create. Separate connection from management. [A] should coordinate [A]’s family, [B] should coordinate [B]’s family, and both of you should communicate the couple’s limits without making the partner absorb the discomfort of saying no. Then set family time together at regular intervals instead of reopening the entire value debate for every invitation.
outcomes.actions_a: Own communication with your family and stop using [B] as the reason a request is declined.
outcomes.actions_b: Offer specific dates and visit limits rather than only resisting the options [A] brings forward.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a monthly Family Council note with invitations, priority level, coordinator, visit cap, couple boundary, and final response owner.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Family decisions return to the couple before they reach the relatives.

A loose rhythm for the important parts

Mostly good, with a few rough spots
I often feel boxed in, scattered, or left to manage the week
I really need the weekly rhythm to change

options.label: Meals and groceries
Chores and home upkeep
Work and focus time
Exercise, sleep, and health
Social plans and couple time
Rest and time alone

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: When does structure stop helping?

options.label: The routine has no room for low-energy days
One person creates it and has to enforce it
Every open hour starts getting assigned
A missed task makes the whole week feel failed
The system takes more work than the tasks
The routine serves one person’s schedule better
