questions.prompt: Anything the court should know about the weekly routine that keeps saving you or driving you both up the wall? (optional)
questions.interactionRule: Private context is used only to personalize the selected deterministic branch.

outcomes.verdict: You have a shared weekly rhythm, not just matching tolerance for calendars. Both of you know which parts of life deserve a predictable place and which parts need breathing room. That rhythm reduces the number of tiny negotiations required to eat, rest, connect, and keep the home moving. Its relationship value is cognitive relief: neither person has to repeatedly prove that a recurring need still matters. Protect the few anchors that create that relief, and resist filling every open space simply because your system works.
outcomes.actions_a: Name the weekly anchor that gives you the most mental relief and what would keep it sustainable.
outcomes.actions_b: Name a different anchor that supports connection or recovery, plus one open block you want to preserve.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Minimum Viable Week with essential anchors, movable tasks, protected open time, and the rule for recovering after disruption.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Your routine carries the basics so the relationship can use its energy elsewhere.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = dissatisfied with the current weekly structure; [B] = content with it.
outcomes.verdict: [A] and [B] need a similar amount of structure, but [A] may be the person keeping that structure alive. [A] remembers the groceries, initiates the weekly reset, notices when rest has disappeared, or adjusts the plan when work changes. [B] experiences a functional week and understandably thinks the system fits both people. [A] experiences maintenance that never turns off. Transfer ownership of one recurring anchor, including noticing when it needs attention, so the structure supports [A] instead of depending on [A].
outcomes.actions_a: Choose the recurring anchor whose monitoring load you most need to release.
outcomes.actions_b: Take full ownership of that anchor, including initiation, reminders, adjustments, and follow-through.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Weekly Anchor Ownership list with one named owner, trigger, backup rule, and completion signal for every recurring routine.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. The week can stay organized without one person secretly powering it.

outcomes.verdict: You want roughly the same amount of structure, but your routine may exist mostly as mutual expectation. Both people know that groceries, chores, rest, and couple time should happen, yet the timing lives in memory and gets renegotiated whenever the week becomes busy. Or the system is so detailed that maintaining it creates another job. Reduce the week to a few visible anchor points and one reset time. A lighter structure that survives disruption will serve you better than an ideal schedule you repeatedly abandon.
outcomes.actions_a: Choose two anchors that prevent the most chaos when they happen consistently.
outcomes.actions_b: Choose the weekly reset time and one routine that can become optional during a difficult week.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a four-anchor weekly card with fixed triggers, owners, fallback versions, and a reset appointment.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. The routine gets small enough to survive real life.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = needs more weekly structure; [B] = needs less.
outcomes.verdict: [A] builds the backbone of the week, making sure essentials and meaningful plans do not disappear into daily decisions. [B] keeps that backbone from turning into a cage by noticing when energy, weather, or a better opportunity calls for adjustment. Both of you are content because structure handles responsibility while flexibility protects aliveness. Keep certain anchors fixed, give other tasks a weekly window instead of an exact hour, and leave at least one genuinely unclaimed block. That division lets each style contribute without governing the whole week.
outcomes.actions_a: Mark the few anchors that must happen at a predictable time and convert one lower-stakes task into a flexible window.
outcomes.actions_b: Protect the fixed anchors and use your flexibility to adapt the movable tasks instead of simply dropping them.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Backbone and Open Space week with fixed anchors, flexible windows, one unclaimed block, and the rule for moving tasks.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. The week stands up straight and still knows how to move.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = needs more weekly structure and is dissatisfied; [B] = needs less and is currently content.
outcomes.verdict: [A] uses structure to reduce uncertainty and prevent necessary tasks from becoming last-minute emergencies. [B] can function with fewer plans and may experience routines as extra rules for things that would eventually get done. The current arrangement feels freer to [B] partly because [A] is absorbing the consequences, remembering what is next, and rebuilding the week after disruption. [B] owes ownership of one weekly anchor from start to finish. [A] can then stop extending structure into areas where no shared cost appears.
outcomes.actions_a: Identify the structure that protects a shared need and release one routine that mainly manages [B]’s personal life.
outcomes.actions_b: Own one shared weekly anchor without reminders and create a fallback for weeks when the usual time fails.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Shared Cost test for routines, then record which anchors protect both people and which remain personal choices.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Structure follows shared consequences, not one partner’s entire life.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = needs more weekly structure; [B] = needs less.
outcomes.verdict: You are stuck in a routine escalation loop. After a chaotic week, [A] adds more structure to prevent a repeat. [B] feels managed, ignores or resists parts of the new system, and the next week becomes chaotic enough to confirm [A]’s fear. Neither of you gets what you need. Build a minimum week with only the anchors tied to health, shared responsibilities, and protected connection. Review it once a week rather than correcting each other in real time, and make additions temporary until both of you agree the additions have earned a permanent place.
outcomes.actions_a: Reduce the proposed routine to the smallest set of anchors that prevents real shared consequences.
outcomes.actions_b: Follow those anchors consistently and bring change requests to the review instead of quietly abandoning them.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a three-week Minimum Week trial with essential anchors, open zones, disruption rules, and one scheduled review after each week.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. The system stops growing every time the week has a bad day.

cases.title: How Much Should Weekends Be Planned Versus Left Open?
cases.subtitle: How much of a typical weekend should be planned in advance?

questions.prompt: How much of a typical weekend should be planned in advance?

options.label: Almost none, I want to decide in the moment
Just one anchor with the rest left open
A loose outline for each day
Most of the weekend, with a little flex time
Nearly all of it, so we know what the weekend is for

questions.prompt: How do you feel about the way your weekends are currently planned?

Mostly good, with a few frustrating weekends
I often feel overbooked, stuck waiting, or like the weekend disappeared
I really need the weekend pattern to change

options.label: One main couple plan
Social plans with other people
Chores and errands
Meals and groceries
Travel or anything with tickets
Nothing unless timing is genuinely limited

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: What creates the most weekend friction?

options.label: Open time gets claimed by someone else
Soft plans keep one person waiting
Planning too early feels restrictive
Chores swallow the best hours
One person brings ideas after it is too late
The plan ignores our actual energy or the weather

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

questions.prompt: Anything the court should know about a weekend that felt perfectly open or somehow vanished without either of you choosing it? (optional)
questions.interactionRule: Private context is used only to personalize the selected deterministic branch.

outcomes.verdict: You share a weekend planning style, but the real match is in what the empty space means. An open afternoon is not forgotten time, and a scheduled plan is not ownership of the entire day. Both of you can enjoy anticipation without treating the weekend like a productivity challenge. That mutual reading prevents one person from waiting for instructions while the other thinks freedom is already happening. Keep one brief planning moment so outside invitations, chores, and couple time do not quietly redefine your open hours.
outcomes.actions_a: Name the weekend decision that helps you relax once it is settled.
outcomes.actions_b: Name the kind of open time you want protected from chores or last-minute outside claims.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Weekend Snapshot each Thursday with one anchor, one responsibility block, one open block, and any decision deadline.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Open time stays intentional instead of accidentally available to everyone else.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = dissatisfied with the weekend pattern; [B] = content with it.
outcomes.verdict: [A] and [B] prefer a similar amount of weekend planning, but [A] may be carrying the cost of the undecided parts. A soft plan can keep [A] from accepting another invitation, starting a solo activity, or fully resting because a decision might still arrive. [B] experiences the same unplanned hours as freedom and sees no obvious problem. Give every soft plan an answer time. If the decision does not happen by then, both people regain independent use of that block without resentment.
outcomes.actions_a: Identify the soft plan that most often leaves you waiting and choose the latest useful decision time.
outcomes.actions_b: Give a firm yes or no by that time, or explicitly release [A] to use the block independently.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Soft Plan rule with proposed activity, decision owner, deadline, fallback, and when the time returns to personal use.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Maybe plans stop occupying real hours for free.

outcomes.verdict: Your weekend has no closing bell. If you plan everything early, one or both of you may rebel when Saturday energy arrives. If you leave everything open, chores, scrolling, and late invitations can consume the hours you meant to enjoy. You do not need more planning. You need a moment when the weekend becomes real. Hold a short Friday lock-in for only three decisions: the main anchor, the responsibility block, and the time that stays deliberately open.
outcomes.actions_a: Bring one priority that would make the weekend feel worthwhile even if little else happens.
outcomes.actions_b: Bring the essential responsibility and estimate an honest time limit so it cannot spread across both days.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Friday Three note with Main Anchor, Responsibility Block, and Protected Open Time for the coming weekend.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Three decisions keep the weekend from being planned to death or lost by default.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = prefers more weekend planning; [B] = prefers more open time.
outcomes.verdict: [A] protects the weekend from being wasted or claimed by other people by setting the important pieces early. [B] protects it from becoming a second workweek by leaving room for sleep, mood, weather, and last-minute inspiration. Both of you are content because you plan in layers. [A] secures the scarce or meaningful commitments, while [B] helps shape the open blocks when the weekend actually arrives. Keep authority matched to timing so neither partner has to surrender a genuine strength.
outcomes.actions_a: Set only the plans that require advance protection and clearly mark where your planning authority ends.
outcomes.actions_b: At the start of each open block, offer a real preference instead of making [A] generate all the options.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Layered Weekend with fixed anchors, flexible options, weather alternatives, and a named chooser for each open block.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. The weekend gets a frame without becoming a script.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = prefers more weekend planning and is dissatisfied; [B] = prefers more open time and is currently content.
outcomes.verdict: [A] is holding options open like unpaid reservations. [A] researches ideas, delays other invitations, and waits for [B] to feel ready, so the weekend remains possible but never secure. [B] experiences that same delay as welcome freedom because the invisible reservation work is happening elsewhere. [B] owes a decision deadline and active participation in choosing. [A] can then leave a defined block genuinely open instead of quietly preparing several backup weekends at once.
outcomes.actions_a: Stop building multiple hidden options and state the one advance decision you actually need.
outcomes.actions_b: Answer by the agreed deadline and take responsibility for choosing what happens in one open block.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Weekend Decision Contract with one advance anchor, response deadline, open-block owner, and automatic fallback if no choice is made.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. Open time stops charging one partner a planning fee.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = prefers more weekend planning; [B] = prefers more open time.
outcomes.verdict: After a weekend gets lost, [A] plans the next one more tightly. [B] then feels the whole weekend has been claimed and protects freedom by delaying commitment or disengaging. That resistance confirms [A]’s fear that nothing happens without extra planning. Break the loop with a fixed proportion rather than a winner. Choose one anchor, one responsibility block, and one protected open block, then review on Sunday whether each part actually served you. Adjust the mix, not each other’s personality.
outcomes.actions_a: Limit advance planning to the agreed anchor and responsibility block for the trial period.
outcomes.actions_b: Treat the anchor as a real commitment and actively use the open block rather than defaulting to indecision.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a four-week Weekend Mix log with planned hours, open hours, enjoyment, recovery, and one adjustment for the following week.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. The weekend becomes a repeatable experiment instead of a weekly power struggle.

cases.title: Who’s Better at Actually Making Time for Just the Two of You?

options.label: Me, no contest
Probably me
Probably them
Definitely them
Honestly, we are equally good at it

options.label: notice when work and social plans have crowded us out
say no to outside plans so couple time actually survives
turn an ordinary evening into intentional time together
put phones and other people’s needs out of reach
reconnect us after an unusually busy week
choose moments that do not need an audience or a big event

options.label: Work and career demands
Friends and group plans
Family obligations
Chores and household logistics
Phones, games, and separate screens
Exhaustion that makes connection feel like another task

questions.interactionRule: Answers stay sealed until both finish.

One person always has to decline the outside invitation
The time exists but has no real attention

Private time is treated as less urgent because it can happen anytime

questions.prompt: Anything the court should know about the last time the two of you truly protected your own little bubble? (optional)

outcomes.role_note: [A] = the partner both identified as better at protecting couple-only time.
outcomes.verdict: [A] is the boundary setter for the relationship’s private life. [A] notices when work, friends, family, or household logistics have taken every available seat and makes space before distance becomes dramatic. [B] values that instinct, but appreciation alone can turn [A] into the permanent person who disappoints outsiders on behalf of the couple. Keep [A]’s early warning skill and move some boundary-setting to [B], including initiating the time and declining a competing request.
outcomes.actions_a: Name the crowding signal you notice first and ask for help before you become resentful.
outcomes.actions_b: Initiate the next protected block and personally say no or not now to the outside demand competing with it.

outcomes.role_note: [B] = the partner both identified as better at protecting couple-only time.
outcomes.verdict: [B] is the boundary setter for the relationship’s private life. [B] notices when work, friends, family, or household logistics have taken every available seat and makes space before distance becomes dramatic. [A] values that instinct, but appreciation alone can turn [B] into the permanent person who disappoints outsiders on behalf of the couple. Keep [B]’s early warning skill and move some boundary-setting to [A], including initiating the time and declining a competing request.
outcomes.actions_a: Initiate the next protected block and personally say no or not now to the outside demand competing with it.
outcomes.actions_b: Name the crowding signal you notice first and ask for help before you become resentful.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Couple Bubble plan with crowding signals, minimum frequency, rotating protector, phone rule, and the next two dates.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. The relationship keeps a private life without one person guarding the door forever.

outcomes.verdict: You both know that proximity is not the same as protected connection. Sharing a couch, attending a party together, or discussing groceries may place you in the same space without giving the relationship any privacy. Each of you notices crowding and is willing to protect a little world that belongs only to the two of you. That is a strong form of mutual choosing. Keep the time varied enough that it does not become another automatic slot: sometimes playful, sometimes quiet, sometimes a real conversation, and sometimes simply unavailable to everyone else.
outcomes.actions_a: Choose one kind of private time that helps you feel playful or curious rather than merely caught up.
outcomes.actions_b: Choose a different kind that helps you feel calm, desired, or emotionally close.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Four Moods Couple Menu with Play, Rest, Talk, and Explore ideas, then schedule one from two different moods this month.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. You protect more than time together. You protect a relationship no audience gets to run.

outcomes.verdict: [A] may create availability by turning down plans, clearing chores, or finding the usable evening. [B] may create intimacy inside that time by putting away the phone, asking the real question, or shifting an ordinary night out of autopilot. Each person claims the skill because each owns a different half of what makes private time real. Stop competing over one title. Assign one partner to protect the block and the other to shape the quality, then switch roles next time so both kinds of effort become visible.
outcomes.actions_a: Name whether your stronger contribution is clearing the time or turning available time into connection.
outcomes.actions_b: Claim the other contribution and describe the concrete cue that tells you the private time has actually begun.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a Protect and Shape card for the next two couple blocks, with roles swapped on the second date and one note about what worked.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. One person opens the door, and the other makes the room worth entering.

outcomes.verdict: Each of you credits the other because being invited into protected time is more memorable than the moments when you quietly created it. The mutual appreciation is real, but it can leave couple time dependent on whichever person happens to notice the gap first. Turn the compliment into rotation. One partner becomes the private-time captain for a week or month, responsible for spotting crowding and protecting one block, while the other agrees not to make that person sell the value of it.
outcomes.actions_a: Take the first rotation and protect one realistic block before the calendar becomes crowded.
outcomes.actions_b: Accept that block as a priority and take the next rotation without waiting for [A] to request it.
outcomes.try_together: Both of you save a three-rotation Couple Time Captain schedule with protector, date, competing demand, connection plan, and handoff date.
outcomes.closing: Case dismissed. The appreciation stays mutual, and the responsibility finally gets a name.

outcomes.role_note: [A] = identified a specific partner as better at making couple time; [B] = said the skill is equal.
outcomes.verdict: [A] sees a clear protector, probably the person who notices crowding early or absorbs the social cost of saying no. [B] sees shared participation because both people happily show up once the time exists.
